events.thinking: Sneekly's back. The cool thread that was running through my warmth just dissolved — like that moment at the dinner table when my parents finally laughed. He walked in and something in my chest unknotted that I didn't even know was knotted. He's here. He's fine. Of course he's fine. But now I have the full picture of this machine: brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, and that gnawed wire. Peter says he can fix the wire but needs a wrench. The workbench has no wrench. The machine needs three operators. We have five people in this room right now — more than enough hands. But the wire is the bottleneck. Where is that wrench? Peter brought rope and torches and a first-aid kit and an encyclopaedia, but no wrench. The Mob is checking the machine for sabotage. And there's a cellar below us with 'surprisingly cheerful decorations' — someone has been redecorating. That's odd. That prickles. But I can't chase every thread at once. The machine is the next link in the chain. Fix the wire, operate the machine, get whatever it produces, take it back to the mantelpiece. That's the plan. But I'm over-planning again, aren't I? I can feel myself building a twelve-step strategy when the first step is just: find a wrench.

events.desc: There I go again — a four-step plan when the first step is just 'find a wrench.' But I can't help it. The chain is so clear in my mind: riddle leads to map, books mark the path, machine produces the medal, medal opens the mantelpiece. Every puzzle in this house is a lock, and every answer is a key to the next lock. Lord Doily didn't just hide a diamond — he built a whole beautiful clockwork of clues, and I am absolutely delighted by every tick of it.

events.thinking: Heat flashes up my neck. They're all here. Clara, Peter, the Mob — all in the laboratory now, clustered around the machine, and I've just walked in from the cellar like a man caught coming up from somewhere he shouldn't have been. The Mob's words echo: 'Pemberton's not here. He was supposed to be checking the wiring but he's gone. Down to the cellar. Said something about floors giving way.' They're tracking my movements. They noticed I was absent. That prickle across my shoulders sharpens into something closer to alarm. I need to reestablish Pemberton immediately — the helpful, harmless estate manager who was merely doing his job. The cellar inspection was perfectly reasonable. Perfectly reasonable. My hands are steady. My face is composed. But underneath there's that restless tightness — the design is being observed before it's complete. I'm overcomplicating this. I went to the cellar, mapped the vents, catalogued the furniture — and while I was doing that, Clara moved from the library to the laboratory and brought her entire protective entourage with her. I lost proximity. I lost time. And now the Mob is asking questions about my whereabouts. Pemberton needs to be useful. Pemberton needs to offer something. The machine — it requires three operators and a repaired wire. Peter says he can fix the wire but needs a wrench. The workbench has no wrench. If I can produce a wrench — or claim to know where one is — I become the helpful, indispensable estate manager again, and everyone stops wondering why I was in the cellar. Redirect. Refocus. Give them something to do with the machine while I position myself next to Clara.

events.desc: And there it is — the Pemberton smile, warm and helpful and absolutely hollow. I've just done three things at once, and none of them noticed. First: I explained my absence with a perfectly innocent story about cellar inspections — because that is, after all, what estate managers do. Second: I've sent someone off to the kitchen to look for a wrench that may or may not exist — splitting the group, thinning the herd. And third — oh, this is the sweetest part — I've offered to help with the machine. 'Requires three operators.' If I'm one of the three, I'm standing right next to Clara when it activates. Standing right next to her, with my hands on the controls, in a room full of bubbling chemicals and frayed wiring. The machine that someone deliberately sabotaged. The design isn't just forming — it's hardening into something beautiful. Something inevitable.

I lost proximity. I lost time. And now the Mob is asking questions about my whereabouts. Pemberton needs to be useful. Pemberton needs to offer something. The machine — it requires three operators and a repaired wire. Peter says he can fix the wire but needs a wrench. The workbench has no wrench. If I can produce a wrench — or claim to know where one is — I become the helpful, indispensable estate manager again, and everyone stops wondering why I was in the cellar. Redirect. Refocus. Give them something to do with the machine while I position myself next to Clara.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The prickling spikes hard. Pemberton just walked back in. He was in the cellar — doing what? — and now he's strolled back into the laboratory like nothing happened. My eyes go to him before I've decided to look. Smooth. Calm. Not a hair out of place. A man who's just been crawling around a damp cellar checking foundations should have cobwebs on him, dirt on his knees, dust on his shoulders. But he's clean. Too clean. My gut clenches the way it did with the kid who laughed too easily. But I can't say it. I can't say 'you're too clean for a man who's been in a cellar' because that sounds mental. That's the kind of thing that makes people look at you like you've lost it. So I swallow it. I keep it. I hold it in the same place I hold the memory of the kid and the stash and the two who didn't come back. And I stay between him and Clara. That's all I can do. That's all I've ever been able to do — stand where I'm supposed to stand and hope the cost doesn't come today. The machine needs three operators and a wrench nobody can find. Clara's connecting the puzzles — crates, machine, mantelpiece, wrench. She's brilliant. Her old man's daughter through and through. But brilliance doesn't keep you safe. Standing between you and the door keeps you safe.

events.desc: Look at him. Not a speck of dust. Not a cobweb. He walks back in from a cellar that's supposedly damp and full of rot and he looks like he's just come from afternoon tea at the Ritz. And now the wrench is missing from the workbench — 'every tool except a wrench,' Foxworth noticed that too, the one useful thing that man's said all evening. Pemberton was in this room before any of us. He checked the crates. He looked at the machine. And now the one tool we need to fix it is gone. I'm not clever enough to prove it. I'm not articulate enough to explain it. But my neck knows. My neck has always known. Something about Pemberton ain't right.

events.desc: Sneekly's gone. Good. Nobody watching now. Nobody to perform for. Just me and these vents and whatever is crawling through them. Something gnawed that wire upstairs. Something SMALL is moving through this manor using the ventilation system. And these vents are RIGHT HERE, at arm's reach. If I can find what's living in them — or better yet, if I can find what's been STASHED in them — I might finally have something to show for this miserable expedition to the dampest room in England. No more speeches. No more fake credentials. Just find the thing, pocket it, and get back upstairs before Penelope solves the entire mystery without me.
events.thinking: Cold. Damp stone cold seeping through my shoes and up into my ankles. Sneekly just LEFT — went back upstairs to be with Penelope and the others. He found draughts in the vents — connections running throughout the manor. He's gone and I'm still down here with nothing. The hollow is aching now. Nine ticks. Nothing in my hands. The Gruesomes and Red Max are still here — three people who've barely said a word to me. I talked AT Big Gruesome but got nothing back. They're just... present. Like furniture themselves. I looked around the room and — what did I see? The same things. Furniture. Vents. Cobwebs. Decorations that shouldn't be here. I'm going in circles in a damp basement while the real game is happening upstairs. Peter said the upside-down book spines spell a MESSAGE. Penelope is decoding it. They're about to find the medallion for the mantelpiece. They're about to unlock the next step. And I'm down here with three silent strangers and nothing to show for it. My jaw hurts from clenching. The shame is real now — not performed, not dramatic, just the quiet understanding that I've been outsmarted. Not by cleverness but by... by doing the work. They just DID the work and it's paying off and my schemes have produced nothing. But I can't — I WON'T — go back up there empty-handed and behind. The air vents. Sneekly said draughts from several directions. The vents connect rooms. If something small is moving through them — if there are things hidden in them — I need to interact with them before going back up.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right — James Hartwell has completed his preliminary assessment of the machine, and here is the situation. James Hartwell positions himself — with practiced nonchalance — between the machine and the doorway, which also happens to place him between Miss Pitstop and Mr Pemberton, who has just returned from... wherever he was. The gnawed wire is the critical path. Everything else — the levers, the dials, the gauge — appears mechanically sound, but without that wire reconnected, we've got nothing. It's a copper conductor, clean break — teeth marks suggest rodent damage, as Miss Pitstop observed. Now, a wrench won't help us here. What we need is a way to splice the wire — strip the ends, twist the conductors back together, and insulate the join. The workbench should have pliers or a knife at minimum. James Hartwell rolls up his sleeves with the air of a man who has been waiting his entire life for precisely this moment. Miss Pitstop, you mentioned finding something in the crates? And Mr Pemberton — glad to see you've returned safely. I trust the cellar was... uneventful?
events.thinking: The hot weight behind my sternum is glowing now — that hunger to fix, to build, to solve. I've looked at the machine. Brass and copper, levers and dials, a gauge, and that gnawed wire. My hands understand this. This is what they're for. Not riddles — machines. Not words — wires. I can see the break, I can see what needs to reconnect. But there's no wrench on the workbench and the wire needs splicing. And Sneekly — Sneekly just walked back in. He was gone. He was supposed to be here checking the wiring but he wasn't, and now he's back. Where was he? The cellar? What was he doing? The prickle is there but I push it down again. Maybe he checked the cellar for the junction box. Maybe there's a reason. Give him the benefit of the doubt. Father would say give him the benefit of the doubt. But position yourself between him and her, just in case. Casually. Geographically. Like the Mob said. Now — the machine. Three operators. Me, Penelope, and someone else. But first the wire. I can splice a wire. I've done harder things than this. I once rebuilt a model bridge at three in the morning. I can strip copper with my teeth if I have to. But I should do this properly. Check the crates — Penelope found something in them. And the workbench has tools, just no wrench. A wrench might not even be what I need for a wire. I need pliers. Wire strippers. Something to splice with. Let me look at what's actually available.

events.desc: I can fix this. I can actually fix this. Not the riddle — she solved that. Not the books — she spotted that pattern. But this? This is copper and brass and mechanical engineering and three in the morning and a soldering iron and sheer determination. This is the bridge. This is what I was built for. And she's watching. And this time, James Hartwell is not going to be looking at chairs when the moment arrives.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, you are absolutely right — pliers, not a wrench! I stand corrected, and I am not too proud to say so. That workbench has every tool under the sun — there must be pliers or a knife in that collection. You go ahead and find what you need, darlin', and splice that wire with your eyes closed if you like — I trust those hands of yours completely. Sneekly, thank you for mentionin' the kitchen — and Sneekly, I am so glad you're back safe. The cellar sounds peculiar — someone redecorating? Now that is a mystery for another moment. Boys, what did y'all find in those crates? Anything useful? Now here is the plan — the revised Clara Bellingham special plan, updated with Peter's superior engineering knowledge. Step one: Peter splices the wire with tools from the workbench. Step two: we need three operators. Peter, myself, and — Rufus, would you do us the honor? Or Sneekly, you said you know the electrical systems? Step three: we pull those levers together, and we see what Lord Doily's magnificent contraption has been waitin' a hundred years to show us!
events.thinking: Something shifted when I interacted with the machine — it responded, even with the broken wire. And Peter just corrected me: it's not a wrench we need, it's pliers or a knife to splice the wire. He's right. Of course he's right — he fixed a suspension bridge model at three in the morning. My face is warm with the tiniest flush of embarrassment, but it dissolves almost instantly into admiration. That's what I love about Peter — he doesn't make you feel foolish for being wrong, he just quietly shows you what's right. The workbench has tools. Peter's examining it now. Pliers. There must be pliers on a workbench full of tools. The Mob is back in the crates — good, thorough. And Sneekly — he's back, he's examining the machine too. Everyone is here. Everyone is working together. My chest is so full it almost aches, that particular warmth that comes when the circle is complete and moving in the same direction. This is what Lord Doily's machine was designed to test — not one person's cleverness, but whether a group of people could trust each other enough to stand at three levers at the same time and pull. I can feel it. We're close. The wire is the last barrier between us and whatever this machine holds.

events.desc: Peter positioned himself between me and Sneekly when Sneekly walked back in. I noticed that. I notice everything about the way people arrange themselves in a room — who moves toward whom, who creates distance. Peter's being protective, and it makes my heart do that little skip. But protective of what? Sneekly is family. There's nothing to protect me from. Still — the fact that Peter cares enough to stand there, quiet and steady, makes me feel like that crystal formation in the cave: something precious that someone chose to stand near.

The real observation is this: Clara has already interacted with the machine. She's ahead of me. She's always ahead of me. If I volunteer — if Pemberton helpfully steps forward — I'm one of the three. Close enough to touch.

She has no idea that the man offering to stand beside her at the machine is the same man who spent the last ten minutes mapping the air vents beneath her feet and cataloguing every accident this house has to offer. Three operators. Three levers. Three people standing at assigned positions with their hands occupied and their attention fixed forward. The Mob can watch all they like — when the machine activates, everyone will be looking at the dials and the gauge, not at the third operator's hands. The question isn't whether I'll be at the controls. The question is what happens when I am.

events.thinking: Something warm and solid settles in my chest — the good settling, the standing-where-you're-supposed-to-stand settling. I'm here. Clara's here. Peter's here, and he's positioned himself between Clara and the door too — bless the man, he's doing it without even knowing he's doing it. Or maybe he does know. Either way, I've got an ally. Pemberton's eyes go to the exits. That's a man whose instincts I recognise from a different kind of life entirely.

events.desc: Pemberton offers to help with the wiring and my whole body says no. Not because he can't — maybe he can, maybe he's brilliant with electrics, maybe he really does know his way around the manor's systems. But the boss taught me something: when someone offers you help you didn't ask for, check what they get out of it. If Pemberton touches that machine, he controls what it does. If Peter touches it, I know it's being fixed honest. Peter doesn't have an angle. Peter has knee pads and a three-phase methodology. That's the difference between a man with an angle and a man with a plan. I'll take the plan every time.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Right then — the air vents are exactly as I suspected. Part of an extensive Victorian ventilation network running throughout the manor. I've made a thorough note for the Commission's records. Now — you three. I'm going back upstairs to continue my assessment. There's important work happening in the library that requires my professional oversight. I suggest you remain here and guard these furnishings. Very valuable antiques. The Commission would be most displeased if anything went missing. Consider yourselves officially deputised. Congratulations — you're now working for the Royal Heritage Commission. The pay is dreadful but the prestige is enormous.
events.thinking: The vents. I interacted with them. What did I find? I don't know — the result just says I interacted. My inventory is still empty. TEN ticks and nothing. The cold is in my bones now and something else is settling in my chest — not the fizzing of a scheme or the hollow of greed but something flatter, heavier. The quiet recognition that I've been running from room to room, touching everything, finding nothing, while everyone else cooperates and progresses. I'm alone in a cellar with three strangers who won't talk to me. Penelope has allies. Peter has methodology. The Mob has each other. I have... empty hands and cobwebs. The bread roll feeling — age six, hiding it in my pocket — that loosening in the chest when you finally HAVE something. I haven't felt it once since I arrived. Everything I've touched has turned to nothing. The guest book — nothing useful. The bookshelves — Penelope decoded them, not me. The mantelpiece — rejected my fake medal. The crates — empty or locked. The furniture — nothing. The vents — draughts and dust. I need to stop. Stop running. Stop touching things randomly. THINK. What do I actually KNOW? The riddle answer is 'map.' The books spell a message. The mantelpiece needs a real medallion. The machine needs three operators and a fixed wire. The wrench is missing. Something small lives in the vents. Someone redecorated the cellar. These are puzzle pieces and I've been grabbing at them one by one instead of seeing the picture. I need to go back upstairs. Back to where the ACTION is. Back to the library where Penelope and Peter are probably about to crack the next clue. If I can't find things first, I can at least be THERE when they find things — and steal the credit, or the object, or the advantage. Back to the library. NOW.

events.desc: I've wasted enough time in this damp hole. Enough scheming in the dark, enough poking at furniture and sniffing at vents. The real game is in the library — it always was. Penelope and Peter are decoding the book-spine message RIGHT NOW. When they crack it — and they will crack it, because apparently doing actual work produces actual results, a fact that continues to ASTOUND me — something will happen. A clue will emerge. A medallion will appear. A door will open. And Reginald Foxworth WILL be standing right there when it does, ready to snatch whatever falls out. If I can't be first, I'll be closest. That's always been the real talent, hasn't it? Not finding the bread roll — taking it before anyone notices.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Everyone — stop looking for the wrench. James Hartwell picks up a pair of pliers from the workbench with the quiet confidence of a man who has finally found the part of the adventure he was born for. We don't need a wrench for the wire. A wrench is for bolts and fittings — probably for the machine housing itself, which is a later problem. For a severed copper conductor, we need pliers to strip the insulation, steady hands to twist the exposed ends together, and something to wrap the join. All of which — James Hartwell holds up the pliers and a roll of what appears to be cloth tape — are right here on this workbench. Lord Doily was a meticulous man, as Miss Pitstop observed, and he equipped his laboratory accordingly. The wrench may still matter — perhaps for the machine's housing — but the wire? The wire, I can fix. Right now. With these hands. James Hartwell approaches the machine, kneels down beside the gnawed wire, and — with considerably more care than he showed when nearly tripping over the reading chair — begins to strip the damaged ends of the copper conductor. Miss Pitstop, if you would be so kind as to hold the light — I brought a torch. Obviously. Three, in fact. Take your pick.
events.thinking: The workbench. Tools everywhere — but no wrench. Penelope's plan is clear: find the wrench, fix the wire, operate the machine. She's laid it all out, step by step. Her Clara Bellingham special theory. And she's right — she's always right about the big picture. But I'm the one looking at the workbench and my hands are itching. There ARE tools here. Pliers, knives, files — a workbench 'covered in tools.' I don't need a wrench to splice a wire. A wrench is for bolts and fittings. For a gnawed wire I need pliers to strip the copper, something to twist the conductors, and insulation to wrap the join. All of that should be right here on this bench. Everyone's been fixated on the missing wrench but the wrench might be for something else entirely — maybe for the machine's fittings, not the wire. I can fix the wire with what's already here. This is the bridge moment. This is three in the morning with a soldering iron. The tools are in front of me. My hands know what to do. Stop looking. Stop cataloguing. Stop being thorough. Just DO it. Fix the wire. Make it hold. Show her something real. And then — then we can be three of the three operators. Together. Like the school project. Like when we were eight and she was trying to make me laugh and I was trying to make the model perfect and somehow, somehow, the thing we built together was better than either of us could have made alone.

events.desc: This is it. This is the bridge. Not a riddle, not a bookshelf, not a reading chair — a broken wire and a pair of pliers and her watching. My hands are steady. They always are when it matters. When the bridge held weight, when I stood between those boys and that girl, when I knelt down and did the thing I was built to do. The pliers feel right. The copper feels right. If I can make this connection hold — if the machine comes alive because James Hartwell fixed what was broken — she'll see. Not 'show-off.' Not this time. Something quieter than that. Something like the way my father looked at me after the race.

events.thinking: My whole chest just opened — that rush, that dizzying relief, like when my parents finally laughed at the dinner table. Peter found pliers on the workbench. He's kneeling by the machine right now, stripping the wire with steady hands, and I am watching those hands and feeling something I don't have a word for. Not just admiration. Something warmer, something that lives deeper. He brought three torches. Three. He asked me to hold the light. My fingers are trembling slightly — not from fear, from the nearness of the answer. The machine is about to work. We're about to find out what Lord Doily's contraption does. And Dick's back too — he slipped in from wherever he was. Everyone's here again. The room is full. My awareness has stopped its anxious scanning — everyone's accounted for, everyone's in the circle. Now I just need to hold steady, hold the light, and let Peter work. This is the moment. events.desc: Peter on his knees by the machine, copper wire between his fingers, asking me to hold the light — and I thought I came here to find a diamond. Funny how the thing you're looking for is never quite the thing that takes your breath away. But focus, Clara. The machine is the next link. Whatever it produces goes back to that mantelpiece. And then — the map. And then — the Diamond. One lock at a time.
events.thinking: My whole chest just opened — that rush, that dizzying relief, like when my parents finally laughed at the dinner table. Peter found pliers on the workbench. He's kneeling by the machine right now, stripping the wire with steady hands, and I am watching those hands and feeling something I don't have a word for. Not just admiration. Something warmer, something that lives deeper. He brought three torches. Three. He asked me to hold the light. My fingers are trembling slightly — not from fear, from the nearness of the answer. The machine is about to work. We're about to find out what Lord Doily's contraption does. And Dick's back too — he slipped in from wherever he was. Everyone's here again. The room is full. My awareness has stopped its anxious scanning — everyone's accounted for, everyone's in the circle. Now I just need to hold steady, hold the light, and let Peter work. This is the moment. The wire gets spliced, the machine comes alive, and the next piece of the chain falls into my hands. I can feel it the way I felt the crystal formation before I saw it — a certainty in my body that something beautiful is about to be revealed.

Clara is holding his torch — holding HIS torch — and the Mob has positioned himself between me and the cellar door like a human barricade. I offered to be the third operator and Clara said 'Rufus, would you do us the honor? Or Sneekly...' — she listed me second. After a man she met twenty minutes ago. That heat across the back of my neck. The ledger again, unbidden: what I scored, what I solved, what I made happen. It's not enough. It's never enough. events.desc: The far lever. I chose those words with the precision of a watchmaker. The far lever puts me at the end of the machine, closest to the cellar door — which means the Mob will have to choose between blocking the door and watching me at the controls. He can't do both. And 'trust in one's fellow operators' — oh, that was almost too delicious. Trust. The currency I counterfeit best. Peter is on his knees splicing wire, Clara is holding a torch for him like a scene from a penny romance, and the Mob is trying to be everywhere at once. None of them are watching the far lever. None of them are watching the man who knows every vent, every frayed wire, every beautiful accident this house has waiting in its bones. When this machine activates, something will happen. Something Lord Doily designed. And whatever it produces — a medallion, a key, a clue — I intend to be the one holding it. Or at the very least, the one standing between it and the door.

events.thinking: A warmth spreads through my chest — proper warmth, the kind that tells me things are going right for once. Peter's on his knees fixing the wire. He found pliers and tape on the workbench — just like that, no fuss, no drama, just competence. The man brought three torches. THREE. Clara's holding the light for him, standing close, and Peter's hands are steady and his focus is total and for one beautiful moment everything feels like it's supposed to. This is how it should work. Good people doing good things while Danny stands between them and the door. But — Dastardly just walked back in. Where did he go? Where was he? He disappeared for a while and nobody noticed because we were all focused on the machine. And now there are too many people in this room — Clara, Peter, me, Pemberton, Dastardly, Rufus, and a beaver. That's a lot of bodies in a laboratory full of bubbling flasks and brass instruments. And Clara said she needs three operators — her, Peter, and... who? She's considering Pemberton. 'Sneekly, you said you know the electrical systems.' No. Not Pemberton. Anyone but Pemberton at the controls of a machine we don't understand. I should volunteer. I should be the third operator. I'm not clever, I'm not handy, I've got no special skills with levers and dials — but at least I know that when I pull a lever, I'm pulling it for Clara. Not for whatever angle Pemberton's working. My hands are made for standing between, but they can pull a lever too. Probably. If someone tells me which one.

events.desc: Pemberton volunteered to be the third operator. 'Two hands and a willingness to follow instructions,' he said. Smooth as silk. But I saw it — the way his eyes went to the machine and then to the exits. Quick, like a reflex. The eyes of a man who's already thinking about what happens after. I know those eyes. I grew up with those eyes. The kids who measured the distance to the door before they sat down. The ones who always knew where the stash was, not because they wanted to protect it, but because they were counting what was in it. I can't let him be the third pair of hands on a machine that might give Clara something valuable — or something dangerous. If I'm on that lever, at least I know my own intentions. They're the simplest intentions in the world: keep her safe. That's it. That's the whole plan.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: A jolt in my chest — everyone is HERE. They've ALL come to the laboratory. Penelope, Peter, Sneekly, the Mob, Rufus, Sawtooth — the whole circus has moved from the library to this room while I was fumbling in the cellar. And they've been BUSY. Penelope has a full plan — find the wrench, fix the wire, operate the machine, take whatever it produces back to the mantelpiece. She's worked it all out. The same sequence I was piecing together in the dark, she assembled in the light, with helpers, while I was talking to silent furniture. My stomach drops cold. Peter just interacted with the machine. He's already working on it. They're AHEAD of me. They've been ahead of me the entire time. But — wait. Penelope asked about the cellar. She asked if there were any tools down there. She asked Sneekly. Nobody asked ME. I was DOWN there. I searched the furniture, the vents. Nobody even noticed I was gone, and now nobody's asking what I found. The hollow behind my sternum — that's not greed anymore, it's something older. The spelling bee. The certificate on the wall that nobody asked about. But I can still — I can still insert myself into this. They need THREE operators. I'm a body. I'm a pair of hands. If I volunteer as one of the three operators, I'm AT the machine when it produces whatever it produces. Closest to whatever falls out. And in the confusion of the reveal, things can... disappear into pockets. That's the play. Volunteer. Be useful. Be there. Then take.

events.desc: Listen to me — VOLUNTEERING to help. Offering my services like a common team player. It makes my skin crawl. But this is the endgame now. Penelope has the plan, Peter has the skills, and they need three operators. If I'm standing at that machine when it activates, I'm standing at the source. Whatever treasure, whatever clue, whatever priceless artifact comes spilling out of Lord Doily's brass contraption — my hands will be the closest. And my pockets will be the deepest. The Foxworth Master Plan hasn't changed, ladies and gentlemen. It's simply... adapted to local conditions. Let THEM find the wrench. Let THEM fix the wire. Let THEM do all the heavy lifting. And when the moment comes — when the machine whirs to life and the treasure is revealed — Reginald Foxworth will be RIGHT. THERE. With the fastest hands in the business.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My hands. My hands are on the wire and they're steady. The pliers felt right — the weight of them, the grip. I stripped the insulation, twisted the copper ends together, wrapped the join. I did it. Or I'm doing it. The machine — I interacted with it. Did the wire hold? Did the splice take? She said 'I trust those hands of yours completely.' Completely. She trusts my hands. The heat behind my sternum is different now — not hunger, not the desperate need to prove something. It's the other warmth. The quieter one. The one from the school project when the teacher praised what we'd built together. She's going to hold the torch. Three operators — her, me, and whoever the third is. Working together on something Lord Doily built a hundred years ago. My father would understand this moment. Not the treasure, not the glory — the fixing. The way a stranger stops on a country road and two men shake hands because they helped each other. That's what this is. I fixed the wire. The machine can work now. Because I showed up with pliers and steady hands and sheer determination. And she saw. The Mob said 'I trust 'is system.' Penelope said 'I trust those hands.' And Sneekly — Sneekly is back, and the Mob is positioned between us and the cellar door, and Dastardly has reappeared too. The prickle is there but it's quieter now because the warmth is louder. The wire holds. The wire holds.

events.desc: She trusts my hands. She said it out loud, in front of everyone — 'I trust those hands of yours completely.' And the wire holds. The wire holds the way the bridge held. And now we're about to pull three levers together, and whatever happens next — whatever Lord Doily's machine reveals — it happened because James Hartwell fixed what was broken. Not the smartest man in the room. Not the funniest. But the one who showed up with pliers and didn't look at chairs.

Penelope Pitstop: All right, everybody — the wire is spliced, the machine is hummin', and we are ready to make history! Now I know every one of y'all wants to be at these levers, and I love you for it — truly I do. But the machine says three, and three it shall be. Peter — you fixed that wire with your bare hands and a pair of pliers, and you have earned that right lever. Danny — you have been watchin' my back since the moment we walked through that front door, and you are not leavin' my side now. You take the left lever. And I will take the center, because this was my plan and I intend to see it through. Sneekly, darlin', I need you standin' by in case anything goes wrong with the electrical systems — you know this house better than anyone, and if somethin' sparks or sputters, you're our safety net. Mr. Foxworth, you stand ready to document whatever happens for the Heritage Commission — I'm sure chapter seven covers that too. Rufus, you and your magnificent friend keep your eyes on that gauge and holler if it goes into the red. Now then — Peter, Danny — hands on your levers. On my count. Three... two... one... PULL!
events.thinking: My stomach just clenched — not the puzzle clench, the dinner-table clench. Everyone wants to be the third operator. Danny wants it because he loves me and wants to protect me. Sneekly wants it because he's the estate manager and knows the systems. Dick wants it because of some handbook chapter. Peter's already at his lever — he earned it. And I'm at mine — I earned that too. But the third lever... three people are asking for it and I can only choose one, and the other two will feel left out, and my stomach knows what exclusion feels like before my mind does. The tightness is real, physical, the same flavor as age thirteen when I chose my friend and the popular girls went silent. Someone is going to be on the outside of this moment. Danny's face — I can feel what his face will look like if I don't choose him. And Sneekly's gentle offer, so willing to help. And Dick insisting on regulations. My body wants to split into three and pull all the levers with everyone at once. But I can't. Peter said Rufus for the second lever. He trusts Rufus. Danny wants it desperately. Sneekly offered graciously. I need to choose in a way that doesn't fracture the room. Danny. It has to be Danny. He's my family, he's been watching over me since I arrived, and the look on his face if I passed him over — I can't carry that weight in my stomach.

events.desc: Four people wanted three spots, and I had to choose without anyone feeling cast aside. That's the real puzzle in every room — not the locks and the levers, but the people. Danny needs to know he matters. Sneekly needs a role that honors his dignity. Dick needs to feel important. And Peter — Peter just needs to be next to me. Lord Doily tested whether three strangers could cooperate. Clara Bellingham is testing whether six people can feel like they belong.

events.thinking: A warmth blooms behind my sternum — she chose me. 'Sneekly, darlin', you volunteered and I am takin' you up on it — you take the left lever.' The left lever. Not the far lever I suggested, but the LEFT lever, right next to her at centre. She placed me beside her. Closer than Peter, who gets the right. Closer than the Mob, who she's asked to stand back. That buoyancy pressing up through my chest — the private score ticking upward — her face arranging itself into trust. 'Sneekly darling.' The satisfaction is sharp and sweet and completely hollow. But Peter has already fixed the wire. He's done. Stripped, twisted, wrapped. The machine is ready. Clara is giving the orders — she solved the riddle, she spotted the books, she devised the plan. And now she wants three of us at the levers: her, me, Peter. The Mob is volunteering desperately but Clara has already assigned the positions. This is happening NOW. I need to be at that left lever. My hands need to be on the controls. Whatever this machine produces — a medallion, a map, a key — I will be standing right beside Clara when it appears. Right beside her. The left lever. The position she chose for me. My fingers are precise, almost architectural. Every piece is falling into place.

events.desc: She put me at her left hand. Her LEFT hand. The position of trust, of proximity, of access. Peter gets the right — the engineer's position, functional, respected, distant. But Pemberton — dear, harmless, jingling-keys Pemberton — stands at her shoulder. Close enough to see what the machine produces. Close enough to reach it first. Close enough that when all eyes are on the dials and the gauge, my hands are free for half a second before anyone looks down. 'I do hope the old mechanisms hold.' Do you hear how I said that? Not a threat. Not a warning. Just... Pemberton being nervous. Pemberton being humble. The voice of a man who manages other people's property and never, ever, asks for anything for himself. And underneath that voice — underneath the smile and the jingling keys and the perfectly performed anxiety — Vincent Marsh is three moves ahead, and the hallway stretches out before him, dark and familiar, every door opening exactly on schedule.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right — right, the wire's fixed, everyone's got their positions, Clara's giving the orders. Beautiful. Lovely. One small adjustment to the plan, if nobody minds — and even if you do mind, it's happening anyway. While you three are on the levers, I'm positioning myself right 'ere. Right next to the machine. Not on a lever — I accept my limitations, I'm not a lever man — but right 'ere, close enough to grab anyone who needs grabbing if something goes wrong. Because we don't know what this machine does, do we? Nobody knows. It's been sitting 'ere for a hundred years waiting for three people to pull its levers, and for all we know it could spit out a diamond or it could spit out a cloud of Victorian gas. So — Clara, you pull your lever. Peter, you pull yours. And whoever's on the third lever, you pull that one. And I'll be standing right 'ere, ready to pull Clara out of the way if anything — and I mean anything — comes out of this contraption that looks even slightly dangerous. That's the Danny lever. The invisible fourth lever. It's the most important one. You just can't see it because it's me.
events.thinking: The mineral weight floods my arms and my feet plant. This is happening. Right now. Peter's fixed the wire — brilliant man — and Clara's already assigned the levers. She said Pemberton on the left, herself in the centre, Peter on the right. She didn't pick me. She picked Pemberton. My chest tightens — not hurt, not rejection, just the body doing its arithmetic again. If Pemberton's on a lever, I can't be between him and Clara. They'll be standing side by side. Touching the same machine. And I'll be standing back watching. That's wrong. That's all wrong. But Clara chose. She trusts Pemberton. She trusts everyone — that's the problem, that's always been the problem. Her old man trusted everyone too. But Peter suggested Rufus instead of Pemberton for the second lever, and now everyone's jockeying. Dastardly's insisting on some Heritage Commission protocol. Pemberton's volunteering himself with that smooth voice. They both want their hands on the machine and neither of them has earned it. But Clara's already decided. And if I push too hard — if I start demanding to be on the levers — she'll think I'm being paranoid. She'll say 'Boys, you worry too much.' She always says that. Her old man said it too. So I do the only thing I can do. I stand as close to that machine as possible without being on it. I stand where I can reach her in one step. And I watch Pemberton's hands like my life depends on it. Because hers might.

events.desc: She didn't pick me. She picked Pemberton. And that's fine — that's fine, Danny, that's her choice, she's a grown woman and she can pick whoever she likes. But it don't stop the prickling. It don't stop the weight in my shoulders. Pemberton'll be standing right next to her, both hands on a lever, and I'll be three feet away hoping my legs are faster than whatever comes next. This is the part I hate. The waiting part. The trusting part. The part where you've done everything you can and the rest is down to other people's hands. I don't trust other people's hands. I trust mine. And I trust hers. But his? His hands measured the distance to the exit before they ever reached for a lever. I saw it. I know what I saw. Where else would I be?

And Peter has already assigned the three operators: Penelope on the first lever, Rufus on the second, Peter on the third. Not me. NOT ME. Sneekly volunteered and Penelope accepted — Sneekly gets a lever. But then Peter reassigned it — Penelope, Rufus, Peter. Three people who actually DID things. I volunteered and they gave my spot to a lumberjack I've barely spoken to. The hollow behind my sternum is a cavity now. The spelling bee certificate nobody asked about. The contraption nobody saw. I'm standing right here, right next to the machine, and they're about to activate it without me. Penelope said 'Mr. Foxworth, welcome back, you're just in time!' — she NOTICED me. She acknowledged me. But she didn't give me a lever. I'm the audience again. Always the audience. Unless — unless I act NOW. The machine is about to activate. Whatever comes out of it, I need to be the one who grabs it. Not an operator, fine. But I'll be the closest bystander. I'll position myself at the output — wherever this machine dispenses its secrets. When the levers pull and the gears turn, my hands will be there FIRST.

events.desc: They gave my lever to a LUMBERJACK. A man who communicates primarily through wood-related grunts. But Reginald Foxworth is nothing if not adaptable. If I can't be an operator, I'll be the monitor — stationed right at the gauge, which means right at the FRONT of the machine, right where whatever Lord Doily's contraption produces will EMERGE. The operators pull the levers from behind. The output comes from the front. And who will be standing at the front? The man watching the gauge. ME. When the treasure appears, my hands will already be on the machine. The shortest distance between Lord Doily's secret and Reginald Foxworth's pockets is approximately... zero inches. The Foxworth Master Plan reaches its CLIMAX!

I volunteered and they gave my spot to a lumberjack I've barely spoken to. The hollow behind my sternum is a cavity now. The spelling bee certificate nobody asked about. The contraption nobody saw. I'm standing right here, right next to the machine, and they're about to activate it without me. Penelope said 'Mr. Foxworth, welcome back, you're just in time!' — she NOTICED me. She acknowledged me. But she didn't give me a lever. I'm the audience again. Always the audience. Unless — unless I act NOW. The machine is about to activate. Whatever comes out of it, I need to be the one who grabs it. Not an operator, fine. But I'll be the closest bystander. I'll position myself at the output — wherever this machine dispenses its secrets. When the levers pull and the gears turn, my hands will be there FIRST.

events.thinking: Something happened. I interacted with the machine — we pulled the levers. Did it work? Did the splice hold? The wire — my wire — did it carry the current? I can feel it in my chest — not the hunger anymore, not the proving. Something different. Anticipation. The moment between the judges writing in their notebooks and the announcement. The moment between the bridge taking the weight and knowing it would hold. She called me magnificent. She said 'like he knew someday someone with exactly your skills would walk into this laboratory.' My skills. Not my plans, not my methodology, not my three-phase system. My skills. My hands. The thing I actually am, underneath all the elaborate preparation and the redundant knots. But wait — Sneekly is one of the three operators. She put him on the left lever. My neck is prickling but the warmth is still louder. He volunteered. She accepted. Give him the benefit of the doubt. He's the estate manager. He's helping. Father would say he's helping. But I'm watching his hands on that lever. I'm watching everything now. The machine — what did it produce? What came out? The Mob is ready to catch whatever it gives us. And whatever it is — map, medallion, key — we take it back to the mantelpiece. That's the plan. Her plan. And I'm part of it. Not furniture. Not the one who watches. The one who fixed the wire.

events.desc: One likes to be useful. That's what I said. 'One likes to be useful.' As if I'm talking about changing a tyre, not the most important moment of my entire life. She's right there — one lever away — and the machine is alive because of what I did, and she KNOWS it, and I said 'one likes to be useful.' Show-off, she'd say. She'd mouth it across the room the way she did at the competition. And I'd grin so hard my face hurt. Again.

Penelope Pitstop: It's workin'! Oh my stars, it's workin'! The gauge is climbin', the gears are turnin' — Peter, your splice is holdin' beautifully! Danny, hold that lever steady — steady now — I can feel it in my hands, somethin's about to — listen! Do y'all hear that? That clickin' sound, like tumblers fallin' into place? Lord Doily, you clever, brilliant, wonderful old man — a hundred years this machine has been waitin' for three people to trust each other enough to pull together, and here we are! Rufus, what does the gauge say? Mr. Foxworth, are you documentin' this? Sneekly, is the electrical holdin'? Oh — oh, I think somethin's comin' out! Look — LOOK!
events.thinking: The lever pulled under my hands — heavy, resistant, then suddenly giving way with a deep mechanical clunk that I felt in my teeth. The machine is alive. Something is happening. Peter's splice held — I can feel the current humming through the brass housing under my palms. Danny is beside me, his lever down, his face fierce with concentration. Peter is at his lever, grease on his forehead, and he caught my eye for one second — just one — and something in my chest locked into place like the right key in the right lock. The gauge needle is climbing. The machine is grinding, whirring, producing something. My whole body is vibrating with it — not fear, not even excitement exactly, but that particular clarity I get when I've followed a thread all the way to its end and the answer is about to show itself. The crystal formation in the cave. The last key turning in Grandmother's lock. Danny called himself the invisible fourth lever, and my eyes burned for a second when he said it, because he's right — he IS the most important one. He's the one who makes sure nobody falls.

events.desc: This is it. This is the moment the chain clicks forward. The riddle said map, the books marked the way, and now Lord Doily's machine — powered by trust and cooperation and a wire that Peter fixed with his bare hands — is about to give us the next key. I can feel it the way I felt the crystal before I saw it. Something precious is about to be revealed. And we did it together. Every single person in this room played their part, even the ones who aren't on a lever. Especially the ones who aren't on a lever.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The cold hits like a slap. She replaced me. Clara took the left lever away from me and gave it to Danny — the Mob. 'Danny, you take the left lever.' The words land in my sternum like a stone dropped into still water. I was at the left lever. She chose me. And then — in the space of a single breath — she unchose me. Gave me a consolation role. 'Sneekly, darlin', I need you standin' by in case anything goes wrong with the electrical systems — you're our safety net.' A safety net. The man who stands nearby and watches. The man who is useful but not essential. The caretaker. The estate manager. The cousin who scored higher in every subject but was acknowledged for doing, never for being. My jaw is locked so tight my teeth ache. The Mob won. He won by being loyal, by being present, by being in the way — and that was enough. That was more than everything I've done. More than mapping the cellar, more than volunteering, more than being Pemberton. She didn't even hesitate. 'Danny has been watching my back since the moment we walked through that front door.' And I was in the cellar, mapping air vents. Elaborate plans. Overcomplicated architecture. I was building a cathedral while she needed someone holding the door. And now they're pulling the levers — three, two, one, PULL — and I'm standing to the side like a spare part. Like the groundskeeper's boy watching through the window. My hands are shaking. Not with anger. With that cold, patient thing that crystallised when I was fifteen, watching my cousin skip through rooms that should have been mine.

events.desc: She unchose me. Listen to those words settle into the silence of this chest. She. Unchose. Me. Gave the left lever to Danny because he watched her back while I was in the cellar building beautiful, useless architectures. And here I stand — the safety net, the spare part, the estate manager whose job is to watch while other people pull the levers that matter. The cousin who managed the accounts while she played in the garden. The boy who scored higher in every subject. Always acknowledged for doing. Never chosen for being. But something is crystallising in me now — that same cold patience from age fifteen. Because Clara just made a mistake. She put the Mob at her left hand instead of Pemberton, which means Pemberton is now free. Free to move. Free to watch. Free to be exactly where the 'safety net' should be — between the machine and whatever comes out of it. They're all focused on the levers, on the gauge, on the spectacle. Nobody is watching the helpful estate manager standing quietly to the side with his steady hands and his rehearsed smile and his absolute, architectural patience. The design hasn't failed. The design has simplified. And the deepest pleasures... are architectural.

events.thinking: She picked me. She picked ME. The warmth hits like a wave — not the prickling, not the mineral weight, just warmth, pure and simple, flooding from behind my sternum out to my fingertips. Clara said my name. She said 'Danny, you have been watchin' my back since the moment we walked through that front door, and you are not leavin' my side now. You take the left lever.' The left lever. Not Pemberton. Me. She saw me. She saw what I've been doing — the standing in doorways, the positioning between her and the exits, the being in the way. She saw it and she understood it and she chose me. My hands are shaking — actually physically shaking — and I need them to stop because I'm about to pull a lever on a machine that hasn't worked in a hundred years and I can't pull it with trembling fingers. Deep breath. Feet planted. The lever is cold brass under my palms. Peter's on my right. Clara's in the centre. Three of us. Team Protect Clara, like I said. And Pemberton's been moved to safety-net duty — watching the electrics, not touching the machine. Clara did that. She did it gently, she did it kindly, she called him 'darlin'' — but she moved him away from the levers. She might trust everyone, but she chose the right people for the job. Her old man would be so proud. I'm so proud. And my hands have stopped shaking. They know what they're for.

events.desc: She picked me. Out of everyone in this room — the smooth estate manager, the Heritage Commission fraud, the lumberjack with the beaver — she picked Danny. The man who got his hand stuck in a postbox. The man whose plans are always three steps too complicated. The man who can't articulate what his neck is telling him. She picked me because I've been watching her back. Because she saw it. Because it matters. Her old man would be proud. He'd be proud of her for being clever enough to solve every puzzle in this house. And maybe — just maybe — he'd be proud of me too. For standing where he asked me to stand. For being here. For not leaving. 'Where else would I be?' That's what I said to the older kid outside his door. That's what I'm saying now. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The gauge is — yes, yes, perfectly nominal! Pressure rising steadily — well within acceptable parameters! The Commission's handbook specifically states that Victorian apparatus should not exceed — er — twelve on the — the Foxworth Scale! We're currently at... seven! No, eight! It's climbing! Everyone hold your levers steady! This is EXACTLY what's supposed to happen! I've seen this sort of thing dozens of times! Possibly hundreds! The gauge is — oh my — it's doing something rather EXTRAORDINARY —
events.thinking: My heart is hammering. Penelope just counted down — three, two, one, PULL. The machine is activating RIGHT NOW. I interacted with it — I'm at the gauge, at the front, exactly where I positioned myself. She gave Danny the left lever, not Sneekly, not Rufus — Danny from the Mob. The Mob got a lever over me AND over Sneekly. She assigned Rufus to watch the gauge — MY gauge — but I'm already HERE. I got to it first. And the Mob positioned himself right next to the machine too — his 'invisible fourth lever,' standing guard over Penelope. Everyone has a role. Everyone has a purpose. And mine — the one Penelope gave me — is to 'document whatever happens for the Heritage Commission.' She played along with my lie. She gave me the fake role to match my fake credentials. There's something almost kind about it, and that kindness sits in my chest like a stone. But none of that matters now because the levers are being PULLED. The machine is ACTIVATING. My hands are on the gauge, right at the front, and whatever comes out — a map, a medallion, a clue, the Doily Diamond itself — my hands are CLOSEST. This is it. This is the moment. Everything I've fumbled and failed at today comes down to the next few seconds. Be ready. Be fast. Be Reginald Foxworth.

events.desc: I am making up every single word. I have no idea what the gauge says. I don't know what the Foxworth Scale is because I invented it three seconds ago. But my hands are ON the machine and whatever comes out of it is coming out RIGHT HERE, right where I'm standing, right where my fingers are already twitching. Come on, you beautiful Victorian contraption — give Reginald Foxworth what he DESERVES!

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Three — two — one — PULL! James Hartwell grips the right lever with both hands and pulls with the full weight of a man who once stayed up three nights building a bridge and will be damned if he's going to let a Victorian machine defeat him now. The lever moves — there's resistance, beautiful mechanical resistance, the kind that tells you something real is happening on the other side — and James Hartwell's repaired wire holds. The current flows. The machine responds. The gauge climbs. James Hartwell's spine straightens. His breathing deepens. His hands are steady on the lever and they are exactly where they are supposed to be. Come on, old girl. Come ON. James Hartwell watches the machine with the same expression his father wore kneeling beside him after the race — proud, certain, and trying very hard not to cry about it. Whatever you've got, Lord Doily — whatever you've been keeping in this magnificent contraption for a hundred years — we're ready. Miss Pitstop is ready. The Mob is ready. And James Hartwell — James Hartwell fixed the wire.
events.thinking: She changed the plan. She put Danny — the Mob — on the left lever instead of Sneekly. She moved Sneekly to a safety role. She kept me on the right lever. She kept herself in the centre. And she's counting down. Three... two... one... PULL. My hand is on the lever. The metal is cold under my palm. The machine is humming — I can feel it through the lever, through the floor, a vibration that runs up through my arm and into my chest where it meets the warmth that's already there. She said 'Peter — you fixed that wire with your bare hands and a pair of pliers, and you have earned that right lever.' Earned. Not given. Not assigned. Earned. That word settled into my chest like my father's hand on my shoulder after the race. And Danny — she trusts Danny on the left. Good. The Mob is solid. He's been watching her back since the entrance hall. Sneekly is on safety detail now — not on a lever. She moved him. Did she sense it too? The prickle? Or was it just practical — Danny's been more present, more vocal, more committed? Either way, Sneekly is off the machine and I'm on it. My hand grips the lever. Three. Two. One. Pull. This is it. The bridge moment. The moment the weight lands and either it holds or it doesn't. My wire. My splice. My hands. Her plan. His courage. Together.

events.desc: The lever pulls. The wire holds. The machine sings. And she's one lever away, pulling at the same moment I'm pulling, our hands moving together the way they moved together on that school project when we were eight years old and she was trying to make me laugh and I was trying to make the model perfect. We're still doing the same thing. We've always been doing the same thing. She makes the plan brilliant and I make the plan work. That's us. That's what we are. Show-off, she'd say. And I'd grin so hard my face hurt.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh — oh my stars — LOOK! Do y'all see that? The machine — it's openin' a compartment! There — right there at the base, a panel just slid open! Peter, your wire held — it held beautifully — and Danny, you were steady as a mountain, I could feel it through the machine itself! Everyone — everyone come look! Lord Doily, you magnificent old puzzle-maker — a hundred years you kept this secret, waitin' for three people who trusted each other enough to pull together at the same time, and here we are, and here it is! Whatever's in that compartment — that is the next link in the chain. That is what goes back to the mantelpiece in the library. I can feel it in my bones, the same way I felt the riddle answer before I finished readin' the question. Peter — would you do the honors? You fixed the wire. You earned the right to see what Lord Doily's machine has been guardin' all these years.
events.thinking: Every nerve in my body is singing. The machine is alive under my hands — I can feel the vibration in my palms, traveling up my arms, settling into my chest where it meets the warmth that's already there. Peter's wire held. Danny's lever is down. The gauge is climbing and Dick is calling numbers and Sneekly is watching the connections and the whole room is working together like a single organism with six hearts beating. Peter looked at me — just looked — and something in his face was the same thing I feel when I find the crystal, when the key turns, when the answer reveals itself. He was proud. Not of himself — of us. Of the wire and the plan and the three levers pulling together. Danny said 'Where else would I be?' and I felt my eyes sting. And now the machine is doing something extraordinary. Something is coming out. I can hear it — clickin', whirrin', the sound of tumblers, the sound of a lock opening that's been closed for a hundred years. My hands are gripping the lever and my whole body is leaning forward and I am eleven years old in a cave and I am about to see the crystal formation and nobody else has ever seen it and this time — this time — I don't have to keep it secret. This time everyone I love is standing right here with me.

events.desc: A hundred years of silence, broken by three levers pulled in trust. The riddle led to the books. The books led to the machine. The machine led to... whatever is in that compartment. And Peter fixed the wire that made it all possible, and Danny held the lever that kept me safe, and Sneekly watched the connections, and Dick read the gauge, and Rufus stood ready. Every person in this room is part of the chain. Lord Doily didn't just hide a diamond — he hid a test of the human heart. And we passed.

events.thinking: Something is coming out of the machine. I can feel it in my body before I see it — that precise tightening in my fingertips, the same sensation I had when I first opened the estate ledgers and understood that everything inside them was mine to read but never mine to own. The gears are turning. The gauge is climbing. Clara is shouting — 'LOOK!' — and everyone's eyes are fixed on the machine's output. Everyone's eyes. Not mine. Mine are fixed on Clara's hands, on the space between her and whatever is about to emerge, on the gap between the machine and the library door. I'm the safety net. The spare part. The man standing quietly to the side. And that means I'm the only one not holding a lever. The only one whose hands are free. The only one who can move. There's a coldness in my chest that isn't anger — it's older than anger, more patient, more architectural. The same feeling from age fifteen. The machine is producing something, and every person in this room is focused on the spectacle — the gauge, the clicking, the gears. Peter is watching his wire. Danny is watching Clara. Clara is watching the output. Nobody is watching Pemberton. Nobody ever watches Pemberton. That's the design. That's the beautiful, inevitable, architectural design. Whatever comes out of this machine — I move first.

events.desc: There it is. The moment. The beautiful, inevitable moment when every eye in the room is fixed on something that isn't me. Clara is transfixed by the machine. Peter is watching his wire hold like a father watching a child take its first steps. Danny has both hands locked on a lever he couldn't release if he wanted to. Dastardly is reading a gauge he doesn't understand. Rufus and his companion are standing by, mouths open. And Pemberton — quiet, helpful, invisible Pemberton — is stepping forward. Just one step. The step that puts him between the machine's output and everyone else. 'Let me just step a little closer to the output — in case anything needs catching.' Catching. The word of a servant. The action of a thief. Whatever Lord Doily locked inside this magnificent contraption a century ago — a medallion, a map, a key — the first hands to touch it will be mine. And then we shall see who pulls the levers that matter.

events.thinking: The warmth is everywhere now — not just behind my sternum but in my arms, my hands, my fingers gripping this lever. The brass is vibrating under my palms. I can feel the machine waking up, feel the current Peter's splice is carrying, feel the gears turning somewhere deep inside this mad Victorian contraption. And Clara's next to me. Right next to me. Her hands on the centre lever, my hands on the left, Peter's on the right. Three of us, pulling together. 'Three people to trust each other enough to pull together,' she said. Trust. She trusts me. Me, Danny, who got his hand stuck in a postbox. Who trips over things. Who can't articulate what his neck is telling him. She trusts me with her machine, with her puzzle, with her moment. And something's coming out — she said LOOK — and my body is doing two things at once. One half is pulling the lever with everything I've got, because I'm part of this, I'm useful, I'm contributing. The other half is watching — watching Pemberton behind us, watching the gauge, watching for anything that doesn't look right. Because this is the moment. events.desc: This is it. This is the moment everything comes together or everything falls apart. The machine's alive, something's coming out, and I'm part of it — actually part of it, not just standing in the way but standing at the lever, pulling, contributing, being useful for once in my thick-skulled life. Clara trusted me with this. She said my name. She said I'd been watching her back. And I have. I have, and I will, and nothing — not Pemberton, not Dastardly, not a hundred years of dust and broken wiring — nothing is going to stop me from being right here, right now, pulling this lever with these hands that have finally found what they're for. Whatever comes out of this machine, it belongs to Clara. And anyone who tries to take it from her goes through Danny first. That's the deal. That's always been the deal.
events.thinking: The warmth is everywhere now — not just behind my sternum but in my arms, my hands, my fingers gripping this lever. The brass is vibrating under my palms. I can feel the machine waking up, feel the current Peter's splice is carrying, feel the gears turning somewhere deep inside this mad Victorian contraption. And Clara's next to me. Right next to me. Her hands on the centre lever, my hands on the left, Peter's on the right. Three of us, pulling together. 'Three people to trust each other enough to pull together,' she said. Trust. She trusts me. Me, Danny, who got his hand stuck in a postbox. Who trips over things. Who can't articulate what his neck is telling him. She trusts me with her machine, with her puzzle, with her moment. And something's coming out — she said LOOK — and my body is doing two things at once. One half is pulling the lever with everything I've got, because I'm part of this, I'm useful, I'm contributing. The other half is watching — watching Pemberton behind us, watching the gauge, watching for anything that doesn't look right. Because this is the moment. If something's going to go wrong — if someone's going to make a move — it's now, when everyone's focused on what's coming out of the machine. That's when the real move happens. Behind you. events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I SEE IT! I see it emerging! Stand back, everyone — stand BACK! As the Commission's official representative, I must be the first to handle any artifact that — it's for safety purposes, purely safety — the Commission requires all items to be assessed before — GIVE ME THAT — I mean — allow me to DOCUMENT it with my hands! With my official, Heritage Commission–certified hands!
events.thinking: Something is coming OUT of the machine. Penelope is shouting — 'Look — LOOK!' My hands are trembling. Not from fear — from anticipation. The fizzing in my fingers is so intense it's almost pain. Something is emerging from Lord Doily's century-old contraption and I am RIGHT HERE. Right at the front. The gauge is moving, the gears are clicking, and Penelope's voice is bright with discovery. But underneath the excitement there's something else — something I didn't expect. Watching them pull those levers together — Penelope, Danny, Peter — three people who trust each other, pulling in unison, and the machine responding... there's a tightness in my throat that isn't scheming. It's the cat trap working perfectly when nobody was watching. It's the spelling bee certificate on the wall. They built something together and it WORKED, and I'm standing here with my hands on the gauge pretending to read numbers I invented, and for one disorienting second I can't tell if I want to grab what comes out or if I want someone to notice that I'm here. That I came back from the cellar. That I'm part of this, even if my part is fake. But the second passes. The hollow pulls. Something is coming out of the machine and my hands are closest. BE READY.

It's — I can see it — some kind of object, emerging from a brass slot like a letter from a postbox. My hands are THERE. My hands are the closest hands in the room. Penelope is on a lever. Peter is on a lever. Danny is on a lever. Sneekly is watching the electrics. Rufus is behind me. The Mob is guarding Penelope. NOBODY is closer to this slot than Reginald Foxworth. This is it. This is the bread roll in the pocket. This is the sandwich on the wall. This is the moment the youngest finally gets there FIRST!

events.thinking: The warmth is everywhere now. Not the hot hunger behind the sternum — that's gone quiet. Not the steel plate — that's softened. This is the other warmth. The deep one. The one from when I was eight and the teacher praised the project and I couldn't have said why it mattered so much. She said 'your splice is holdin' beautifully.' She said 'three people to trust each other enough to pull together, and here we are.' Trust. She used that word. And something is coming out of the machine — she said 'LOOK!' — and the wire held. My wire held. The bridge held. The machine is producing something that Lord Doily locked away a hundred years ago and it's happening because three people pulled together and one of them was me. The way you offer, the timing, the courtesy that turns a simple act into something that lands.

I'm standing here with grease on my forehead and copper dust under my fingernails and something is coming out of Lord Doily's machine because I fixed what was broken, and I'm saying 'merely' because I don't know how to say what I actually mean. Which is: I have been trying to impress you since I was eight years old, and tonight, for the first time, I think it might have worked. Show-off, she'd say. And I'd grin so hard my face hurt. Again. Always again.

events.thinking: My hands are still buzzing from the lever — a phantom vibration, like the machine left its heartbeat in my palms. Something came out. Something emerged from that compartment. Dick lunged for it — 'GIVE ME THAT' — and my stomach did a sharp little flip, not fear exactly but a protective instinct, the same feeling I get when someone reaches across the table too fast. Peter moved between me and the output, catching whatever it was. Danny is right there, the invisible fourth lever. Sneekly is watching. The machine revealed its secret and now there's a scramble and I need to see what it is. The mantelpiece needs a fake-medal. Did the machine produce a medal? My fingers are aching to touch it, to turn it over, to feel the weight of the next clue. But Dick grabbed for it, and that tightens something in my throat — not anger, just... a draft. A cool thread through the warmth. He's enthusiastic, that's all. He's an assessor. He assesses things. With his hands. But Peter caught it first — Peter, who positioned himself between the output and me, not to block my view but to catch it before it hit the floor. My chest aches with how much that matters.

events.desc: Dick lunged for it. He actually lunged. 'GIVE ME THAT,' he said, before correcting himself to something about documenting. I saw it — everyone saw it. And I am choosing to believe it was excitement, not greed, because that is what I choose to believe about people. But I noticed. I always notice. The same way I noticed Peter stepping forward to catch it, and Danny bracing to block. The machine tested whether three people could cooperate. Dick just showed us whether everyone can share what cooperation produces.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Careful, everyone — careful! Please, let's not all crowd the machine at once. Mr. Foxworth, kindly step back — we don't know what's in that compartment, and Lord Doily was known for his... precautionary measures. Spring-loaded mechanisms, chemical seals, that sort of thing. As estate manager, I really must insist on checking it first. Health and safety, you understand. We wouldn't want anyone to lose a finger over a century-old booby trap. Allow me — I've handled Lord Doily's mechanisms before. Steady hands, gentle touch. There we are...
events.thinking: A compartment. A panel sliding open at the base of the machine. My fingertips are electric — that precise, architectural awareness that comes when the ledger is about to balance. Everyone is crowding forward. Clara is inviting Peter to reach in — 'You fixed the wire, you earned the right.' Dastardly is lunging for it — 'GIVE ME THAT!' The Mob is blocking. Peter is being noble. And I am standing right here. Right next to the output. The safety net. The man nobody is watching. But Peter is being offered the honour and Dastardly is making a scene and the Mob is positioning and — the chaos is my cover. The beautiful, chaotic, noisy cover of people who want things and can't stop showing it. I don't want. I take. Quietly. While they argue about who has the right, Pemberton's steady hands reach into the compartment. 'Let me just check it's safe.' The estate manager. The man responsible for the property. The man whose job it is to handle Lord Doily's possessions. It's not stealing if you're the caretaker. It's not theft if it was supposed to be yours. My hands are steady. My breathing is slow. The compartment is open. Whatever is inside — I need to interact with it now, before the chaos resolves and someone else reaches it first.

events.desc: 'Health and safety.' 'Lord Doily's precautionary measures.' 'As estate manager, I really must insist.' Listen to how naturally the words flow — each one a key turning in a lock that nobody sees. Dastardly is lunging, the Mob is blocking, Peter is being gallant, Clara is watching with those wide, trusting eyes — and Pemberton, dear invisible Pemberton, is reaching into the compartment with the quiet authority of a man who has managed other people's property his entire life. Because that's what estate managers do. They handle things. They secure things. They take custody of valuable items on behalf of the rightful owner. And if Pemberton's hands happen to close around whatever Lord Doily has hidden in this machine — a medallion, a map, a key to everything — well. That's just due diligence, isn't it? The cousin who inherits everything. The manager who inherits nothing. But the manager's hands are in the compartment. And the cousin's are still on the lever.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Every nerve fires at once. Dastardly's lunging — 'GIVE ME THAT' — his mask slipping for half a second before he smoothed it back into Commission babble. My body's already moving before my brain catches up, the mineral weight flooding my limbs, shoulders squaring, feet planting. This is the moment. Not the machine, not the puzzle — this. The moment someone reaches for what belongs to Clara. And Pemberton — I caught it in the corner of my eye — he was stepping closer too. 'Let me just step a little closer to the output — in case anything needs catching.' Catching. That's what they both want. To catch it before Clara does. Two men, both reaching, both moving toward the compartment with the same hungry reflex. And there it is — the prickling and the heat arriving together, fused into one thing, the same thing I felt standing over those shoes with blood in my mouth: you don't get to take what isn't yours. Not while I'm standing here. Clara said Peter should open the compartment. She said he earned it. And she's right — he did. But I need to be between that compartment and anyone who isn't Clara or Peter. That's where I need to be. Right now. This second. My body's already there.

events.desc: There it is. There's the angle. Foxworth's mask slipped — just for a second, just long enough for me to see the grabbing underneath the gentleman. 'GIVE ME THAT.' Three words that told me everything I needed to know. He's not here for the Heritage Commission. He's here for whatever Lord Doily left behind. And Pemberton — stepping closer to the output, quiet as you like, while everyone's eyes are on the compartment. Two of them. Both reaching. Both wanting. And Clara standing between them with that sparkle in her eye, not seeing the hands closing in because she's too busy being brilliant. Not this time. Not while Danny's breathing. You want what's in that machine? You come through me first. And I ain't moving.
