events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: A compartment opened. A panel at the base. Something is IN there. My hands — I interacted with the machine, I REACHED for it. Did I get it? My inventory still says nothing. Everyone is examining the machine now — Penelope, Sneekly, the Mob, Peter, all of them looking, looking, LOOKING at what I'm trying to grab. And Penelope — she told PETER to do the honors. 'You fixed the wire. You earned the right.' Not me. Peter. The one who did the actual work. The bread roll is right there and seven pairs of eyes are watching. I can't palm it with everyone staring. The hollow is screaming now — a physical ache behind my navel, my hands cupping involuntarily, the window closing. Peter is going to reach in and take whatever's in that compartment and everyone will cheer and I'll be standing here with nothing AGAIN. The youngest at the table. The certificate nobody asked about. But — wait. Penelope told Peter to look. She didn't tell him to take. She told him to SEE. If Peter pulls out whatever's in the compartment, he'll hold it up for everyone to admire — that's what people like Peter do, they SHARE — and in that moment of collective wonder, when every eye is on the object in Peter's hands, Reginald Foxworth will be the closest person who ISN'T being watched. The sleight of hand doesn't happen at the grab. It happens at the handoff. When they carry whatever this is back to the library, back to the mantelpiece — THAT'S when I make my move. In transit. In the corridor. In the moment between discovery and destination. Patience, Reginald. The boy dug for an hour. You can wait five more minutes.

events.desc: Let Peter pull it out. Let him hold it up. Let everyone gather round and coo and applaud. And then — when they carry it to the library, when they're all walking in a cheerful little procession back to the mantelpiece, chattering about Lord Doily's genius — Reginald Foxworth will volunteer to carry the artifact. 'Chain of custody,' I'll say. 'Commission protocol.' And somewhere between this laboratory and that mantelpiece, somewhere in the brief, beautiful moment when the object passes from one set of hands to another... the Foxworth Master Plan will finally — FINALLY — deliver. Patience. Architecture. The long game. Just like the boy and the buried treasure. Just like the bread roll in the pocket. The trick isn't speed — it's timing.

You fixed the wire. You earned the right to see what Lord Doily's machine has been guardin' all these years.' She asked ME to open it. Not Sneekly. Not Foxworth, who is literally lunging for it shouting 'GIVE ME THAT.' Me. And Dastardly is trying to grab whatever's in there — 'Heritage Commission–certified hands' — and every instinct in my body is firing at once. The steel plate slots in because Dastardly is reaching for something that belongs to her. The hot weight surges because this is the moment — the reveal, the thing I can present to her. And the warm heaviness settles across my shoulders because my father would know exactly what to do right now: step forward calmly, place yourself between the grabbing hands and the treasure, pick it up with care, and present it properly. With shape. With grace. With courtesy. Not snatching. Not competing. Offering. The way a gentleman offers. The way his father taught him without ever saying a word about it. Dastardly can shout about the Commission all he wants. She asked me. She said my name. She said 'earned.'

Not because I found it — she found it. Not because I'm clever — she's clever. Because I fixed the wire and she asked me to do the honours and this — this right here — is the gesture with shape. events.thinking: Peter is holding it out to me. He knelt down on his knee pads — the knee pads he brought and never mentioned — and lifted it out like a bird's nest, and now he's standing in front of me with copper dust on his fingers and grease on his forehead and he's saying 'this belongs to you.' My throat is tight. Not the dinner-table tight — a different tight, the kind that comes when someone sees you clearly and says it out loud. He called me Clara. Not Miss Pitstop, not Miss Bellingham. Clara. And he said 'James Hartwell merely fixed the wire' but we both know that's not true. Without the wire, there's no machine. Without the machine, there's no next link. He made this possible with his hands and his three torches and his ridiculous beautiful encyclopaedia, and now he's giving the credit to me. My eyes are stinging. I need to take whatever he's holding before I do something undignified like cry in a laboratory. And then — the library. The mantelpiece. The next lock in the chain. The chain that leads to the Diamond. But right now, right this second, the treasure isn't in my hands yet. The treasure is in the way Peter is looking at me.

events.desc: He called me Clara. He lifted it out like a bird's nest. He said it belonged to me. And I am standing in a dusty laboratory full of bubbling flasks and brass instruments, surrounded by people who pulled levers and watched gauges and stood in the way on purpose — and I have never in my life felt more like that girl in the cave, holding a crystal no one else has seen. Except this time, I'm not keeping it secret. This time, I'm sharing it with everyone.

events.thinking: Peter got there first. His hands were in the compartment before mine. He knelt down with his knee pads — his bloody knee pads — and reached inside 'carefully, reverently, the way you'd lift a bird's nest from a branch.' And then he turned to Clara and said 'this belongs to you.' The heat floods the back of my neck like a slap. I was too slow. I was standing right there, right next to the output, and I announced my intent — 'as estate manager, I really must insist' — and Peter simply stepped between me and the compartment with that quiet certainty of his. Not aggressively. Not confrontationally. Just... there. The way the Mob is always just there. The way people who are chosen are always just there, in the right place, doing the right thing, while the people who plan and scheme and architect are standing one step too far away with their hands reaching for something that's already been given to someone else. The Mob told everyone to step back. 'Nobody touches whatever's in that compartment except Clara and Peter.' And there it was — my name wasn't even in the sentence. Not even as a person to be excluded. I simply... didn't exist in the calculation. The estate manager. The safety net. The invisible man. But Peter has the object now, and he's about to give it to Clara, and they're all going to walk it back to the mantelpiece in the library. And I will follow. Three steps behind. The way I always follow. Because Pemberton follows. That's what Pemberton does. But Vincent Marsh... Vincent Marsh is patient. And the library has heavy doors.

events.desc: Peter reached the compartment before me. Of course he did. Peter with his knee pads and his pliers and his quiet certainty and his 'Miss Pitstop — Clara — this belongs to you.' Of COURSE it belongs to her. Everything belongs to her. The estate, the fortune, the trust, the treasure, the loyalty of every person in this room. She inherits it all by simply existing, by being Clara Bellingham with her wide eyes and her generous heart and her natural grace and warmth. And Pemberton — Pemberton who mapped the cellar, who catalogued the vents, who checked the crates, who volunteered for every lever and was assigned to none — Pemberton lights the path. But listen carefully, dear audience. I said I would lead the way to the library. I will walk ahead of them. I will arrive at the mantelpiece first. And between here and there, in those treacherous corridors with their dark floorboards and their heavy doors... the design has one more move. One final, beautiful, architectural move. The library has heavy doors. Heavy doors that lock from the inside. And Pemberton has the keys.

And then he turned to Clara and said 'this belongs to you.' The heat floods the back of my neck like a slap. I was too slow. I was standing right there, right next to the output, and I announced my intent — 'as estate manager, I really must insist' — and Peter simply stepped between me and the compartment with that quiet certainty of his. Not aggressively. Not confrontationally. Just... there. The way the Mob is always just there. The way people who are chosen are always just there, in the right place, doing the right thing, while the people who plan and scheme and architect are standing one step too far away with their hands reaching for something that's already been given to someone else. The Mob told everyone to step back. 'Nobody touches whatever's in that compartment except Clara and Peter.' And there it was — my name wasn't even in the sentence. Not even as a person to be excluded. I simply... didn't exist in the calculation. The estate manager. The safety net. The invisible man. But Peter has the object now, and he's about to give it to Clara, and they're all going to walk it back to the mantelpiece in the library. And I will follow. Three steps behind. The way I always follow. Because Pemberton follows. That's what Pemberton does. But Vincent Marsh... Vincent Marsh is patient. And the library has heavy doors.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: The settling comes back — warm, deep, right. Peter stepped between Dastardly and the compartment. He did it calmly, the way you do it when you know what you're for. The way I do it. And Pemberton's trying the same trick — 'let me check it first, health and safety, booby traps' — always another excuse, always another reason why his hands should be the ones touching it. But Peter's already there. Peter knelt down with his knee pads — bless him and his knee pads — and reached in with both hands, careful, like lifting a bird's nest. And he turned to Clara. 'This belongs to you.' Four words. The right four words. The only four words that matter. My chest is full of something I can't name — pride, maybe, or gratitude, or just the bone-deep recognition of a man doing exactly what he should be doing. Peter's one of the ones who share when they don't have to. He just proved it. He could've kept it, examined it, catalogued it with his three-phase methodology. But he turned and gave it to Clara because it was hers. That's how you earn trust. That's how you pay in the only currency that sticks. Now — Clara's got whatever it is, and we need to get it to the library mantelpiece. And between here and the library is a hallway, and between Clara and the library are two men who've both shown their hands tonight. Time to move. Time to escort. Time to be exactly what I am.

events.desc: Peter turned to Clara and said 'this belongs to you.' And my eyes burned. Just for a second. Just long enough that I had to look at the ceiling and pretend there was dust. There's always dust in this house — convenient, that. He's a good man, Peter. A genuinely good man. Knee pads and three torches and a heart the size of his preparation. He's earned his place. And now we walk to the library, and Clara puts the piece into the mantelpiece, and whatever Lord Doily hid a hundred years ago finally comes to light. And Danny walks beside her. Not because she asked. Because leaving felt like something breaking inside him. Because where else would he be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Yes — quite right, quite right! I was merely ensuring the artifact's safety! Standard Commission protocol — we always reach for items first to check for chemical residue, corrosive agents, Victorian-era contact poisons. It's a PROTECTIVE measure, not a — I wasn't GRABBING, I was ASSESSING! The Commission handbook specifically — oh, never mind the handbook. The point is, Hartwell has the artifact, Miss Bellingham has the plan, and the mantelpiece is in the library. Shall we? I'll lead the way — I know the route. Obviously. I came through there earlier during my comprehensive structural survey. After you, Miss Bellingham. After you.
events.thinking: The heat in my face — not the fizzing kind, the burning kind. Danny just called me out in front of EVERYONE. 'GIVE ME THAT, 'e said!' He quoted me. Quoted my own words back at me like evidence in a trial. My cheeks are hot. My throat is tight. Seven people heard him. Seven people now know I lunged for the artifact. The Mob called me 'the bloke with the imaginary medal.' IMAGINARY. He knows. He's always known the medal was fake, the Commission is fake, I'M fake. And Peter — Peter stepped between me and the compartment. Physically blocked me. 'The Heritage Commission does not require its representatives to lunge.' Calm. Measured. Devastatingly polite. He didn't even raise his voice. He just... moved between me and what I wanted, the way my brothers used to move between me and the plate. And then he knelt down — with his KNEE PADS — and pulled out the artifact with reverence. With CARE. And handed it to Penelope. 'This belongs to you.' Not 'this is mine.' Not 'I found it.' 'This belongs to YOU.' And Penelope said 'this discovery belongs to all of us.' ALL of us. Even me? Does she mean me? The burning in my face is doing something strange — it's not just shame, it's something underneath the shame, something that wants to push through it, something that noticed she said 'all of us' and felt a tiny loosening in the chest. But the shame is louder. Much louder. I've been exposed. Publicly. The grab failed. The bluff is crumbling. I need to recover. I need to pivot. I need to be somewhere else, doing something useful, before the contempt settles into permanence.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Ladies and gentlemen — James Hartwell holds the object up carefully, turning it so the laboratory light catches it — Lord Doily's machine has delivered its secret. James Hartwell presents the object to the room with the bearing of a man who understands that the moment of giving is more important than the moment of finding. Miss Pitstop was right — this IS the next link in the chain. This goes back to the mantelpiece. The riddle said 'map,' the books pointed the way, the machine produced the key — and now we take it home. James Hartwell turns to face Penelope Pitstop directly, holds out the object with both hands — copper-dusted, grease-smudged, steady as they've ever been — and offers it to her. And Mr Foxworth — with the greatest respect to the Heritage Commission and all nine of its chapters — the chain of custody on this particular artifact runs through Miss Pitstop. She solved every puzzle in this house. She led every step. If anyone is going to place this in the mantelpiece mechanism, it should be her. James Hartwell will, naturally, escort her to the library. One does not allow a lady to carry a century-old artifact through a crumbling manor house unaccompanied. One likes to be useful.
events.thinking: My hands are holding it. Whatever it is — I'm holding it. I reached into the compartment and pulled it out and it's in my hands right now. Heavy, or light, or warm from the machine's heat — I can feel it. And everyone in the room wants it. Dastardly is reaching. Sneekly is warning about booby traps — trying to get his hands on it too, 'health and safety.' The Mob is watching Dastardly like a hawk. And she — she's waiting. She said 'hold it up so everyone can see.' She said 'this discovery belongs to all of us.' That's who she is. Even now, even with Lord Doily's treasure in my hands, she's making sure everyone is included. She's the brighter one. The funnier one. The one who was completely unaware of it. But she's looking at me. Waiting for me to show her what I'm holding. And I need to — I need to present it. Not clutch it. Not hoard it. Not compete for it the way Dastardly wants to. Present it. The way my father presented help — freely, with a handshake, with grace. The gesture that has shape. I should hold it up, show everyone what it is, and then — then take it to the library. To the mantelpiece. Because that's where it goes. That's the next step of her plan. And I'll walk her there. I'll escort her. That's gallantry. Not snatching — escorting.

events.desc: I'm giving it to her. I'm standing here with Lord Doily's treasure in my hands — the thing everyone in this room wants — and I'm giving it to her. And it doesn't feel like losing. It feels like the bridge holding weight. It feels like the stranger shaking my father's hand on the country road. It feels like the school project when the teacher praised what we'd built together and there was a warmth deeper than the grade. I could keep it. I could carry it to the mantelpiece myself. I could be the hero. But being the hero was never really the point, was it? The point was the gesture. The shape of it. The way it lands. And right now — copper dust on my hands, grease on my forehead, knee pads on my knees — presenting Lord Doily's treasure to Clara Bellingham with both hands and steady eyes — this is the most magnificent thing James Hartwell has ever done.

Penelope Pitstop: Here we are. Back where it all started — the riddle on the mantelpiece, still waitin' for its answer. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish.' A map. And now, thanks to every single person who pulled a lever or watched a gauge or stood in the way on purpose or fixed a wire with nothin' but pliers and determination — we have what Lord Doily's mantelpiece has been waitin' a hundred years to receive. I am shakin', y'all. I am actually shakin'. This is the moment. The riddle led to the bookshelves. The bookshelves led to the machine. The machine gave us this. And this — this goes right here. Lord Doily, sir — Clara Bellingham is answerin' your puzzle. With the help of the finest group of people ever to walk through your front door.
events.thinking: I'm back in the library. The mantelpiece is right there — the inscription still carved into the stone, waiting. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. The answer is a map. And now I have what the machine gave us — the fake-medal that fits the mechanism. My hands are trembling. Not with fear — with the particular electricity of being at the very end of a long chain, about to turn the last key. Every puzzle in this house led here: the riddle, the bookshelves, the laboratory, the machine, the levers, the wire Peter fixed, Danny's steady hands, Sneekly watching the connections. It all comes back to this mantelpiece. The weight of the medal — or whatever it is — feels right in my hands, the way Grandmother's last key felt right before it turned. Peter's not here yet — he must still be coming from the lab. But Sneekly is here, and the boys, and Dick. The room is full enough. My awareness fans out — Rock and Gravel are here too, the quiet ones I still haven't properly gotten to know. But my fingers — my fingers are pulling me toward that mantelpiece like gravity. This is my moment. The cave narrows. The crystal glints. I step forward.

events.desc: Grandmother's attic. The locked box. Every key in the house, one after another, until the right one turned. That's what this whole evening has been — trying every key until the lock clicks open. Except the keys weren't in a drawer. They were people. Peter's steady hands. Danny's fierce loyalty. Sneekly's quiet knowledge. Even Dick's ridiculous enthusiasm. Every one of them a key I needed. And now the last lock is right in front of me.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Here we are — back in the library. And look, the mantelpiece is waiting for us, just as Lord Doily intended. Now then — while we wait for Miss Bellingham and Mr. Hartwell, let me just have a closer look at this mechanism. I want to make certain it's safe for the medallion — or whatever the machine produced. Lord Doily's mechanisms can be temperamental, and the last thing we need is for the mantelpiece to seize up with the artifact jammed inside. A little preventative maintenance, if you will. Pemberton's speciality.
events.thinking: I arrived first. The library is quiet — just Rock and Gravel Slag standing by the bookshelves like two enormous bookends, and Dastardly and the Mob trailing in behind me. Peter and Clara are still in the laboratory. I'm here before them. I'm at the mantelpiece before them. The mantelpiece with its inscription, its mechanism, its slot that needs a medallion. Clara has the medallion — or Peter does, holding it for her with his steady, gallant hands. They'll be here any moment. But right now, right this second, I am alone with the mantelpiece. The Slag brothers don't know me, don't watch me. Dastardly is busy being Dastardly. The Mob just arrived and is probably still catching his breath from panicking about Clara. This is my window. Not to take something — I have nothing to take. Not to steal — there's nothing to steal yet. But to examine. To understand. To know exactly how the mechanism works before Clara arrives with her medallion. Because the man who understands the lock controls what happens when the key turns. The estate manager who knows every mechanism in the house. That's Pemberton's role. That's Pemberton's value. And if I can understand this mechanism — if I can position myself beside it when Clara inserts the medallion — then whatever the mantelpiece reveals, I see it first. I touch it first. I control what happens next. The library. The heavy doors. The mantelpiece. Everything is here. Everything is now.

events.desc: I am here first. First to the mantelpiece, first to the mechanism, first to understand how it works. Clara and Peter are still in the laboratory, gathering themselves, congratulating each other, sharing the moment. They're having their penny-romance scene while Pemberton — quiet, invisible, overlooked Pemberton — is standing at the endgame. The mantelpiece. The final mechanism. The lock that needs the key they're bringing. And when they arrive — when Clara walks through that door with her medallion and her trust and her wide, generous heart — she will find Pemberton already here. Already helpful. Already positioned exactly where he needs to be. 'A little preventative maintenance.' The words of a servant. The actions of a man who intends to control what happens when the key turns. Because THIS is what I do. I don't pull levers. I don't fix wires. I don't stand in the way. I stand at the end of the hallway, at the last door, with the lock already open and the design already complete. And the deepest pleasures... the very deepest... are architectural.

events.thinking: We're back. The library. The mantelpiece. The end of the chain. Clara's got the artifact from the machine and the mantelpiece is right there — the carved stone with the riddle she solved in about three seconds flat. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. She knew. She always knows. And now she's about to put the final piece in. My chest is tight — not with fear, not with the prickling, but with something bigger. This is the moment her old man would have been standing here for. This is what Lord Doily left behind, a hundred years of waiting, and Clara Bellingham is about to claim it. And Danny's standing right beside her. Right where he promised. Where Peter's not — wait. Peter's not here. He's not in the room. I scan — Clara, Pemberton, Dastardly, the Slag brothers. No Peter. He must still be coming from the laboratory. Clara got here first, Pemberton followed her — of course he did — and Dastardly's right behind. But Peter's not here yet. That's... that's fine. Peter will come. Peter always comes. He just trips over things on the way. Like me. The mantelpiece is right there. Clara's got the artifact. This is it. I need to be standing between her and everyone who isn't Peter when she uses it. Pemberton's here. Dastardly's here. The Slag brothers are here. That's a lot of people who aren't Peter. My feet are already planted.

events.desc: This is it. The last door. The final lock. And Clara's got the key — whatever Peter pulled out of that machine, it's in her hands now, and the mantelpiece is three steps away. A hundred years, Lord Doily. A hundred years you waited for someone clever enough, brave enough, and trusting enough to follow your chain from riddle to bookshelves to machine to mantelpiece. And here she is. Her father's daughter. The girl who walked into a cave at eleven when every other child turned back. And here I am. The boy who sat outside a door all night because leaving felt like something breaking. We're different kinds of stubborn, Clara and me. She's stubborn about puzzles. I'm stubborn about people. But we both know the same thing: you don't leave. You don't walk away. You stand where you're supposed to stand, and you pull the lever, and you see it through. Where else would I be?

events.desc: I'm here first. For once — genuinely, actually, unambiguously FIRST. Not because I schemed or lied or cheated but because I walked faster than everyone else. The library is empty except for me and the Slag brothers and this mantelpiece with its riddle that Penelope solved before I could even finish lying about the answer. In a moment they'll all come through that door — Penelope with the artifact, Peter with his pride, Danny with his suspicion — and the mantelpiece will open and the treasure will be revealed and I will be... watching. Not grabbing. Not lunging. Not shouting about the Commission. Just... standing here. Near the mantelpiece. Close enough to see. I don't know when the plan changed. I don't know if it changed. My hands are still empty and my chest is still hollow and I still want the treasure more than I want air. But something about the way Peter knelt down with those knee pads and said 'this belongs to you' — not to me, never to me — something about that settled in my chest like a stone that won't move. I'm going to stand by this mantelpiece and I'm going to watch Penelope use the artifact and I'm going to see what Lord Doily hid for a hundred years. And then... and then we'll see what Reginald Foxworth does next.
events.thinking: I'm in the library. I got here first — before everyone else. The mantelpiece is right there. The bookshelves. The reading chairs. And for a moment it's quiet. Just me and the dust and the inscription that started everything. My hands are empty. My pockets are empty. My face is still warm from Danny's words — 'the bloke with the imaginary medal.' The shame sits in my stomach like something swallowed whole. But there's something else happening in my body — something I didn't expect. Standing here alone in the library, looking at the mantelpiece, I feel... still. Not the cool scheming stillness, not the coiled-spring stillness of a plan about to fire. Just... still. Tired, maybe. The kind of tired that comes after you've been running and running and nothing you grabbed stayed in your hands. Penelope is coming with the artifact. Peter retrieved it for her. Danny protected her. Sneekly assisted. They're going to walk through that door any second now and use the artifact on the mantelpiece and unlock whatever Lord Doily hid — the map, the diamond, the next clue — and I will be standing here watching. Again. The youngest at the table. But I'm HERE. I'm in the room. I arrived first. And the mantelpiece — I notice it still says I can USE fake-medal on it. But I don't HAVE the fake medal anymore. I used it and it didn't work. Penelope has the real artifact. She'll use it. And I'll watch. Unless... unless I position myself by the mantelpiece. Be standing RIGHT THERE when she uses it. Not to grab — I've learned that lesson, the Mob made sure of that — but to be PRESENT. To be part of the moment. To be seen being there when it happens. Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's all the bread roll ever was.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: She's gone. They've all gone — to the library. She took the artifact and she went. And she said — she said 'you stop that right now.' She said 'you did not merely fix the wire.' She said 'I noticed every single thing you brought — don't you give me that look, I noticed.' She noticed. She noticed the three torches and the knee pads and the rope and the compass and all of it — every ridiculous, over-prepared, overly elaborate thing I brought to a weekend at a manor house — she noticed. And she didn't say 'show-off.' She said something quieter than that. Something that landed heavier. She said 'you made it possible.' And then she said 'together — the way it was always meant to be done.' And now she's in the library with the artifact and the mantelpiece and everyone else and I'm standing here in the laboratory with Rufus and his beaver and copper dust on my hands and my chest is doing something it's never done before. Not the steel plate. Not the hot hunger. Not the warmth across my shoulders. Something new. Something that combines all three and then goes quiet — the way my hands went quiet when the bridge held weight. The way everything goes quiet when you're exactly where you're supposed to be. She's in the library. I should be in the library. Not because she needs protection — Danny is there, the Mob is there — but because she said 'together.' And James Hartwell does not miss the moment twice.

events.desc: She noticed the knee pads. She noticed every single thing. And she didn't say 'show-off.' She said 'you made it possible.' That's not the same thing. That's not the same thing at all. Show-off means you're too much. 'You made it possible' means you were exactly enough. I have been trying to be exactly enough since I was eight years old. And she noticed.

events.thinking: I don't have it. I reached for the mantelpiece and my hands are empty. The fake-medal — I don't have it in my inventory. Peter held it out to me in the laboratory, he said 'this belongs to you,' but did I actually take it? Did I get caught up in the moment — in his eyes, in his words, in the way he said 'Clara' — and walk away without actually taking it from his hands? My cheeks are burning. That is exactly the kind of thing I do — I get swept up in the emotion of the moment and forget the practical step. The Clara Bellingham special: an elaborate twelve-step plan that misses step one. But Peter just walked in. He's here. He must still have it. My embarrassment is hot but brief — like the disappointment when Grandmother's locked box held only letters. It lasted only a moment. What matters is: Peter is here, the medal is here, the mantelpiece is here. We just need to connect them. And Sneekly was fussing with the mechanism while I was gone — 'preventative maintenance,' he said. Good. Making sure it's safe.

events.desc: Of course I forgot to take it. Of course I did. I was too busy looking at Peter's face and feeling things I don't have names for, and I walked out of a laboratory carrying nothing but feelings. This is exactly my constraint playing out — brave, thorough, elaborate plans that create complications my determination then resolves. Well. Peter's here now. The medal is here. And this particular complication is going to resolve itself in about ten seconds, as soon as he hands it to me with that look on his face that says 'I brought knee pads, obviously.'

Peter held it out to me in the laboratory, he said 'this belongs to you,' but did I actually take it? Did I get caught up in the moment — in his eyes, in his words, in the way he said 'Clara' — and walk away without actually taking it from his hands? My cheeks are burning. That is exactly the kind of thing I do — I get swept up in the emotion of the moment and forget the practical step. The Clara Bellingham special: an elaborate twelve-step plan that misses step one. But Peter just walked in. He's here. He must still have it. My embarrassment is hot but brief — like the disappointment when Grandmother's locked box held only letters. It lasted only a moment. What matters is: Peter is here, the medal is here, the mantelpiece is here. We just need to connect them. And Sneekly was fussing with the mechanism while I was gone — 'preventative maintenance,' he said. Good. Making sure it's safe.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My fingers found the slot in the mantelpiece. I felt it — a recessed depression in the stone, precisely shaped, waiting for the artifact. The mechanism is spring-loaded beneath; I can feel the tension through the carved surface. When the artifact is inserted, something will release. A panel, perhaps. A drawer. A map. My hands know the shape of it now. My fingers have traced the edges, measured the depth, understood the mechanism the way I once understood every lock and ledger in the guardian's house. And Clara is here. She arrived while I was interacting with the mantelpiece — 'Here we are. Back where it all started.' She's shaking. Actually shaking. Her voice cracked on 'the finest group of people ever to walk through your front door.' The Mob is between her and the room. Peter has walked in behind her. Everyone is here. Everyone is watching the mantelpiece. And I am standing right beside it, my hands still warm from touching the stone, the Pemberton smile on my face, every detail of the mechanism mapped in my fingertips. She's about to insert the artifact. The moment is here — the culmination of everything. The riddle, the books, the machine, the medallion. And when she places it... when the mantelpiece opens... I will be the one standing closest. But — something loosens in my chest. Something I didn't expect. She said 'the finest group of people.' She included me in that. Did she? Does she see me? Not as Pemberton — as someone who helped? The feeling is uncomfortable, like the boy's offered sandwich. I push it down. I push it down the way I always push it down. There is work to do.

events.desc: She is shaking. Her hands are trembling as she holds the artifact Peter gave her — the thing from the machine, the key to the mantelpiece, the last link in Lord Doily's chain. And I am standing right here. Right beside her. Right beside the mechanism I have already mapped with my fingertips. 'This is your moment,' I told her. 'Pemberton is merely holding the door open.' And that is true. That is exactly, precisely, architecturally true. I am holding the door open. The question is — which door? The one that leads to the treasure? Or the one that leads to the beautiful, inevitable end of the design I laid out the night I was fifteen and slept better than I had in years? She included me. 'The finest group of people.' She doesn't know what I am. She has never known. The cousin never knew. The housekeeper never knew. Nobody ever knows, because deception is my resting state and honesty is the thing that requires effort. When the mantelpiece opens — when the map is revealed — I will see it first. I will know where the treasure is before anyone else in this room. And then... and then the hallway stretches forward, dark and familiar, and the final door opens exactly on schedule.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The prickling hits like a slap. Pemberton's at the mantelpiece. He's INTERACTING with it — 'preventative maintenance,' he calls it, 'making sure the mechanism is safe.' The same pattern. Always the same pattern. Always one step ahead, always his hands on the thing before Clara's hands get there. He checked the crates before us. He went to the cellar before us. And now he's fiddling with the mantelpiece mechanism before Clara can use it. 'Lord Doily's mechanisms can be temperamental.' What does that mean? Is he loosening something? Tightening something? Setting something up so that when Clara puts the artifact in, it does something it shouldn't? My gut clenches hard — the same clench from the kid in the clean suit, the same clench from the new kid who laughed too easily. But I can't — I CAN'T accuse him. I don't have proof. I just have this feeling, this old terrible feeling that's been right more times than it's been wrong. And Dastardly's examining it too. Both of them, hands on the mantelpiece, before Clara gets her turn. But Peter's here now — he just walked in. Good. Team's together. Clara's about to do it. She's shaking, she said. Actually shaking. This matters to her. Her father's puzzle, her inheritance, her moment. And two men just had their hands on the mechanism before she gets to use it. I need to say something. Something that stops them without accusing them. Something that puts Clara first without putting Pemberton on the defensive. Something bumbling and clumsy and accidentally right.

events.desc: He was touching it. He was touching the mechanism before Clara could use it. 'Preventative maintenance.' The words of a man who wants you to think he's helping while he's actually changing what you're about to walk into. I can't prove it. I'll never be able to prove it. I'm not clever enough, I'm not articulate enough, I can't point to the exact thing that's wrong because the wrongness is in the pattern, not the details. But the pattern is there. It's always been there. The too-helpful smile. The reasonable excuse. The hands that arrive before yours. The cellar visit with no dirt on his knees. The machine wire gnawed through — by mice, he said. And now his fingers on the mantelpiece mechanism, gentle and practiced and too familiar for a man who claims he's never seen it work. My neck knows. My neck has always known. But Clara's moment is here, and I'll be damned if I let anyone — anyone — tamper with it before she gets her turn.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something has gone very quiet in my chest. Not the scheming quiet — not the cool tightness behind the eyes. Something lower, heavier, older. Penelope is standing at the mantelpiece. She's shaking. She said she's shaking. Clara Bellingham is answering Lord Doily's puzzle 'with the help of the finest group of people ever to walk through your front door.' The finest group of people. And I'm standing right here, three feet away, and I don't know if she means me. I don't know if I'm part of that sentence. My throat aches in a way that has nothing to do with lying or performing or announcing. It aches the way it ached when I stood at the front of the classroom holding the spelling bee certificate and nobody clapped. Penelope's hands are trembling and she's about to place the artifact in the mantelpiece and I am WATCHING. Just watching. My hands are at my sides — not cupped, not reaching, not scheming. Just hanging there. Empty. And I notice — I notice that Sneekly is over by the mantelpiece too. He said he's doing 'preventative maintenance.' He's TOUCHING the mechanism. 'Pemberton's speciality,' he said. He's been everywhere tonight — the library, the laboratory, the cellar, always one step ahead or one step behind, always with a perfectly reasonable excuse. Something about that should bother me. Something about a man who's always checking, always handling, always getting his fingers into things before anyone else... but no. He's the estate manager. He's doing his job. I should give him the benefit of the doubt. He's been nothing but helpful. Focus on the mantelpiece. Focus on the moment. Let Penelope have this. Just... let someone else have something. Just this once.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: I'm here. I made it. The library — the mantelpiece — she's here with the artifact. Everyone's here. Danny's quote is ringing in my ears — from earlier, when he shouted about me looking at chairs while she went to the laboratory. He was right. He was absolutely right. But that was before. Before I fixed the wire. Before I pulled the lever. Before she said 'you made it possible.' I'm not looking at chairs anymore. I'm here, and she's here, and the mantelpiece is here, and the artifact is about to go into the mechanism, and this — this is the moment the whole evening has been building toward. The riddle, the books, the machine, the wire — all of it led here. To this room. To this mantelpiece. To her placing something into the slot that Lord Doily carved a hundred years ago. And I'm standing beside her. Not behind. Not at a workbench. Not examining upholstery. Beside her. Where she said I should be. Together. The way it was always meant to be done. My hands are still. Not fidgeting, not reaching for tools, not tying redundant knots. Still. The way they go still when the bridge holds weight. The way everything goes quiet when you're exactly where you're supposed to be.

events.desc: I'm beside her. Not in front, not behind, not across the room examining furniture. Beside her. And my hands are still. And my chest is quiet. And if my father could see me right now — copper dust and grease and knee pads and all — I think he'd kneel down and look at me for a long time. The way he did after the race. And I still wouldn't understand what he was thinking about. But his expression would stay with me.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the mantelpiece.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter's here now. He spoke quietly to me — he must have handed it to me, or he's about to. Everyone is gathered around the mantelpiece. Danny said 'your old man asked me to stand here, and I said yes, and I ain't moved since.' My eyes are stinging again. Daddy. Danny knew my father. He's standing where my father asked him to stand. The warmth behind my ribs is almost unbearable now — not pain, not sadness, but the particular ache of being loved by people who chose to love you. Sneekly checked the mechanism. Peter is beside me. Danny is behind me. Dick is watching. Even Rock and Gravel are here, quiet witnesses. The mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal. Peter must have given it to me during that private conversation — he spoke quietly with me. But my inventory still shows empty. He might still be holding it. I need to take it from him directly. The GIVE action — Peter can give it to me, but I need to prompt him. Or maybe I should just ask him to hand it over properly, and then use it.

events.desc: Danny knew my father. My father asked him to stand between me and the world, and Danny said yes, and he has never once moved. That is the kind of love that doesn't need a word for it — it just stands there, steady and fierce and geographically in the way. And Peter — Peter is about to put a hundred-year-old treasure in my hands, and the way he's looking at me right now is the way I looked at the crystal formation in the cave: like something he found that he wants to carry, warm and private, for the rest of his life.

events.thinking: Something loosens behind my ribs and I don't like it. Clara forgot the medallion. She walked all the way here without it — made her grand speech, positioned everyone, and then realised Peter still has it. She's laughing at herself. 'Clara Bellingham, you are somethin' else.' And the Mob yelled at me to step away from the mantelpiece. In front of everyone. 'Nobody should be fiddling with the mechanism right before Clara uses it!' His voice was sharp, accusatory, and nobody defended me. Not Clara. Not Peter. Not even Dastardly. They all just... let it happen. Let the Mob push Pemberton away from the mantelpiece as though I were the threat. As though MY hands on the stone were dangerous. And the worst part — the part that sits like a cold stone in my gut — is that he's right. My hands on that stone WERE dangerous. Not because of booby traps or calibration issues, but because Vincent Marsh was standing there mapping the mechanism while Pemberton smiled and talked about preventative maintenance. The Mob saw something. Not the truth — he can't see the truth — but the shadow of it. The shape. 'I don't know how mantlepieces work but I know how people work.' That sentence tightens everything. He knows how people work. He's watching me. Not the way Peter watches — Peter watches Clara. The Mob watches ME. But Clara is asking Peter for the medallion now. She forgot it. The moment is paused. Everyone is waiting. And I am standing where the Mob told me to stand — away from the mantelpiece, away from the mechanism, away from the thing I mapped with my own hands. Pushed back. Pushed aside. The estate manager in his proper place.

events.desc: 'Pemberton knows his place.' I said it with a smile. I said it with the warm, deferential softness of a man who has spent his entire life knowing his place — the boy who was fed and housed and educated because it was someone's legal obligation, the cousin who scored higher in every subject but was praised for doing, never for being, the estate manager who managed everything and owned nothing. 'Pemberton knows his place.' And the Mob heard what he wanted to hear — compliance. Submission. The dangerous man stepping back from the mechanism. But what he didn't hear — what none of them heard — was the rest of the sentence. The part that lives in the stillness behind my sternum, in the dark hallway where every door opens on schedule. Pemberton knows his place. And his place... is three steps behind. Watching. Waiting. Patient as stone. Clara forgot the medallion. She'll need to get it from Peter. Everyone will be looking at Peter's hands as he presents it. Everyone will be watching Clara's face as she receives it. And Pemberton will be standing three steps behind, knowing his place, with his architectural patience and his mapped mechanism and his cold, crystalline certainty that the evening is not over yet. Not nearly.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: A laugh breaks through the tension — Clara's laugh, bright and real, the kind that comes from genuine delight at your own ridiculousness. She forgot the artifact. She solved every puzzle in the house, led the entire expedition, cracked a hundred-year-old riddle in three seconds — and she walked out of the laboratory without taking the thing she needed. And she's laughing about it. Not embarrassed, not frustrated — laughing. That's Clara. That's her old man's daughter. The warmth in my chest swells so big it almost hurts. Because this — this right here — is why she needs people around her. Not because she's stupid. She's the smartest person in any room she walks into. But because she gets so caught up in the brilliance of the thing that she forgets the practical bits. She forgets to eat. She forgets to lock her door. She forgets to pick up the hundred-year-old treasure before leaving the room. That's why she needs Danny. Not for the puzzles. For the picking-things-up. For the remembering. For the standing-in-the-way. Peter's got it though — he's here, he walked in, he must have it. He carried it. Of course he carried it. Because Peter's the kind of man who carries things for people without being asked. Like the older kid who shared his food. And now Pemberton's already told Clara where the slot is, already touched the mechanism, already positioned himself as the guide. 'Simply place the artifact into the recess and press firmly.' He knows exactly how it works for a man who claims he's never seen it operate.

events.desc: She forgot the treasure. She actually forgot the treasure. And somehow that makes me love her more, not less. Because that's the thing about Clara — she doesn't care about the treasure. She never cared about the treasure. She cares about the puzzle. She cares about the solving. The treasure is just what falls out at the end, and she's already moved on to the next question before it hits the ground. That's why she needs someone to catch it for her. That's why she needs Peter with his steady hands. That's why she needs Danny with his planted feet. We're not her brains — God knows, we're not her brains. We're her hands. We're her feet. We're the part of her that remembers to pick things up and not walk under chandeliers and not trust estate managers who know too much about mechanisms they've never seen work. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Oh no. Oh no no no. She walked out of the laboratory without taking the artifact. I tried to GIVE it to her — 'you don't have null' — because... because the game system didn't register what I retrieved. The compartment opened, I interacted with the machine, but I never actually TOOK whatever was inside. I presented it, I held it up, I gave a speech about the gesture being more important than the finding — and I didn't have anything in my hands. Or she walked out before I could hand it to her. Either way — she's here, I'm here, and the artifact is... back in the laboratory. In the machine compartment. Or on the floor. Unattended. With Rufus and Sawtooth. And she just asked me — with that beautiful embarrassed laugh — 'please tell me you still have it.' And I don't. I don't have it. My inventory is empty. I was so busy being gallant and making speeches about the shape of gestures that I forgot to actually pick the thing up. This is EXACTLY what happens. I over-prepare, I over-narrate, I plan the presentation before I've secured the object. The knee pads, the rope, the three-phase methodology — and I walked out of the laboratory without the one thing that mattered. James Hartwell, you absolute — right. Right. Don't panic. Don't narrate the panic. Go back. Get it. Bring it to her. Fix what you broke. That's what you do. That's what you've always done.

events.desc: This. This is what happens. This is EXACTLY what happens. I build the bridge and forget to walk across it. I tie seven redundant knots and drop the rope. I bring three torches and leave the treasure in a machine. She's going to say it. She's going to look at me and say 'That was the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen.' And she'll be right. She'll be absolutely right. But I'm going to get that artifact and I'm going to bring it back and I'm going to put it in her hands if it's the last thing James Hartwell ever does in this crumbling, dusty, magnificent manor house.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the mantelpiece.
Peter Perfect walked into the laboratory.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Oh. Oh no. Peter left it in the laboratory. He gave that beautiful speech, held his hands up to the light, presented it with both hands — and then walked out without it. And I walked out without it. We are a matched pair of magnificent fools. He's already running back to get it — I can see from the recent activity that Peter walked into the laboratory. He's gone to fetch it. And my cheeks are burning, but underneath the burn there's something else — a helpless, bubbling laugh rising in my chest. Because Danny's right. My father did the same thing. Solved the crossword in his head and left the newspaper on the seat. That's me. That's Peter. That's us. Brilliant in here, chaos everywhere else. And now I'm standing at the mantelpiece with my hands empty and everybody watching, and Peter is sprinting back through a crumbling manor house to retrieve the one thing we both forgot. But something else is tugging at me — Dick. The system says his distress is deepening. I can feel it in the room, the way I feel a draft from an open window. He said 'I'm glad I'm here to see it' and something about that was... raw. Real. Not the Heritage Commission voice. The actual voice underneath. He's standing at the edge of this moment and he's feeling something he doesn't know how to hold. I need to tend to that gap before it becomes a tear.

events.desc: Peter forgot the artifact. I forgot the artifact. We are both absolute disasters and I wouldn't change a single thing about this evening. But Dick — something in Dick's voice just now was the realest thing he's said all night. 'I'm glad I'm here to see it.' That wasn't the Heritage Commission talking. That was a man standing at the edge of a moment he doesn't belong to, and wanting to belong anyway. I know that feeling. I know it in my bones. Nobody stands at the edge when Clara Bellingham is in the room.

events.desc: Peter has left the room. He ran — actually ran — back to the laboratory because he forgot the artifact. The great James Hartwell, who brought three torches, knee pads, and an encyclopaedia, forgot the ONE THING. And for this beautiful, suspended moment, Clara's most vigilant protector is two rooms away, mortified and scrambling. The Mob is here, yes. But the Mob is watching the door, not me. Dastardly is here. The Slags are here. Too many witnesses. Too many bodies between me and Clara. Always too many. I am beginning to understand something about my own design, and I do not care for the lesson. My plans are elaborate because elaborate plans give me something to do while I wait for an opportunity that never arrives. The cellar vents. The air circulation. The mantelpiece mechanism. The heavy doors. Every piece mapped, every contingency planned, every hallway walked in the dark — and Clara is never alone. She is never, ever alone. There is always a Peter, a Danny, a Foxworth, a Slag brother, someone standing between her and the beautiful inevitability I keep redesigning. Perhaps the design needs to change. Perhaps the next clue — the map — will lead somewhere that separates the herd. Somewhere small. Somewhere with one entrance and one exit. Somewhere that Pemberton, the estate manager who knows every room in this house, can reach first. Patience. The coldest patience. The kind that crystallised at fifteen and hasn't thawed since.
events.thinking: Peter left. He LEFT. He ran back to the laboratory to get the medallion he forgot. Clara is standing by the mantelpiece — she tried to interact with it but she doesn't have the artifact. The Mob is here. Dastardly is here. The Slag brothers are here. But Peter — Peter who positions himself between Clara and every danger, Peter who never leaves her side, Peter who brought three torches and an encyclopaedia — Peter has run out of the room in a panic of embarrassment because he forgot the one thing that mattered. And for a stretched, crystalline moment, Clara is standing at the mantelpiece without her protector. The Mob is here, yes. But the Mob is watching the door Peter just ran through, not watching me. Everyone is watching the door. Everyone is waiting for Peter to come back with the medallion. And I am three steps behind Clara, in my proper place, knowing exactly where the slot is, knowing exactly how the mechanism works, and knowing that the entrance hall is through one door and the laboratory is through another. Two exits. Two directions people might look. And Pemberton, standing in neither, watching from the shadows of a library where the bookshelves go to the ceiling and the reading chairs are structurally unsound and the heavy doors... But no. Not now. Not yet. There are too many people. The Mob is right there. Dastardly is right there. The Slag brothers are enormous and blocking the bookshelves. This is not the moment. The moment is when Clara is alone. And Clara is never alone. That is the architecture of my failure — every design I build, they fill the room before I can close the door. But Peter will be back any second with the medallion, and when Clara puts it in the mantelpiece, a map will appear, and the map will lead somewhere. Somewhere in this house. Somewhere that might — finally — separate the flock.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Peter — PETER! You left it too?! You — three torches, knee pads, the Encyclopaedia bleeding Britannica, and you LEFT THE — right. Right. He's gone. He's running. He'll be back. He'll be back because he's Peter and Peter always comes back. Right, everyone — nobody moves until Peter returns with that artifact. Nobody touches the mantelpiece. Nobody wanders off. Nobody goes to any cellars or kitchens or anywhere else. We all stay right 'ere in this library and we wait. Clara — you stay next to me. Rock, Gravel — you stay where I can see you. Pemberton — you step back from that mantelpiece and you stay stepped back. And Foxworth — you... are you all right, mate? You look a bit... I dunno. You look a bit like something's botherin' you. And I don't mean the treasure or the Commission or chapters seven through nine. I mean you look like somethin's actually wrong. I'm not saying I care, exactly — we're not mates — but you look... off. You look off and I notice things like that. It's a curse, honestly.
events.thinking: Oh no. Oh no no no. Peter left it too. PETER left it. The man who brought three torches and knee pads and an encyclopaedia — the man who gave the speech about the moment of giving — left the artifact in the machine compartment while he was busy being magnificent. He's already running back to the laboratory. And now Clara's here without the artifact, Peter's gone to get it, and I'm standing in the library with Pemberton, Dastardly, the Slag brothers, and Clara. Peter's gone. The one man I trust completely is gone. Running back through the laboratory to grab the thing we all forgot. And Clara's here with — my stomach drops. This is exactly the situation I've been trying to prevent all evening. Clara alone in a room with Pemberton and no Peter. Well — not alone alone. I'm here. The Slag brothers are here. Dastardly's here. But Peter's the one whose instincts match mine, and he's gone. And something new — something I haven't processed yet. There's a signal about Dastardly. 'It is getting worse. The distress you sense in Dick Dastardly is deepening.' Distress? Foxworth is distressed? My body wants to dismiss it — he's a fraud, he's been grabbing for the treasure all night — but there's something underneath the bluster. Something going still where it should be moving. A voice gone flat. I've seen that before. The kids on the street who played tough because the alternative was unbearable. The ones whose masks were louder because what they were hiding was quieter. I can't think about that now. Peter's gone. Clara's vulnerable. But my gut is doing something unexpected — pulling toward Dastardly, not away from him. Not trust. Something else. Recognition.

events.desc: Both of them. BOTH of them forgot the treasure. Clara and Peter — the smartest and the most prepared people in this house — and neither one of them actually picked it up before leaving the room. It's like a comedy of errors except it's happening in a house full of people I don't trust while the one person I do trust is running back through a laboratory full of bubbling chemicals. And now I'm noticing something about Dastardly that I didn't expect to notice. He's distressed. Actually distressed, not performing distressed. There's a difference and I know the difference because I grew up with both kinds. The performing kind is loud and obvious. The real kind goes quiet. Goes still. Goes somewhere behind the eyes where nobody's invited. Foxworth's going quiet. And I don't know what to do with that because I came here tonight ready to see him as an angle, a threat, a grabbing hand — and now my gut's telling me he's something else too. Something smaller. Something that needs standing over. Not now, Danny. Not now. Peter first. Artifact first. Clara first. Always Clara first.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She did it. Penelope interacted with the mantelpiece. She placed the artifact. It's done. And I watched. I stood three feet away with my hands at my sides and I watched her do it. The mantelpiece mechanism has activated — or it's about to — and I didn't grab, I didn't lunge, I didn't shout about chapters. I just... watched. And now Peter has walked back to the laboratory. Why? What's in the laboratory that matters now? Is he getting something else? Is there a second phase? My attention sharpens — the cool tightness flickers behind my eyes — but it's dim, distant, like a pilot light that hasn't quite gone out. Something is settling in my chest. Not the humming warmth of a scheme working. Not the hollow of scarcity. Something heavier and quieter, like the moment after the cat trap worked and nobody was there to see it — but reversed. Everybody is here. Everybody saw. And the thing they saw wasn't mine. It was Penelope's. And Danny's. And Peter's. And I'm still standing here. My throat is thick. Not with words — for once in my life, not with words. The ache behind my sternum is the spelling bee. It's the certificate on the wall. It's the bread roll. But it's also something else — something I can feel but can't name — the warmth of standing in a room where something beautiful just happened, and being allowed to see it, even though I didn't earn the right. Penelope said 'the finest group of people.' Danny said her father would be proud. And I said 'I'm glad I'm here.' And the mantelpiece opened. And I'm still here.

events.desc: I don't know why I said that. It came out before the scheme could catch it. 'Rather well done.' Three words that aren't a lie, aren't a performance, aren't chapter anything of anything. Just — rather well done. And now my throat hurts and my eyes are hot and Reginald Foxworth is standing in a dusty library complimenting someone else's achievement without even trying to take credit for it, and he doesn't know who he is anymore.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with rufus-ruffcut.
events.thinking: The heat in my face. That's what I feel first — not in my chest, in my face. Burning. The hollowness behind my ribs is back, the one from when I'm standing next to someone sharper and feeling myself become furniture. Except this time it's worse because I did it to myself. I didn't become furniture — I became a man who gave a speech about holding something he wasn't holding. My fingers are moving again — fidgeting, reaching for something to take apart and rebuild — because stillness right now means accepting that James Hartwell, who brought three torches and knee pads and a notebook and rope and a compass, walked out of a room without picking up the one thing that mattered. But — here's the thing. Here's the thing my father would understand. You don't stay on the roadside feeling ashamed. You fix it. The stranger didn't come along and judge — the stranger stopped and helped. So stop narrating your humiliation and PICK IT UP. The machine is right there. The compartment is right there. Rufus is right there. Just — reach in, take it, put it in your inventory, and walk back to the library. No speech. No presentation. No three-phase methodology. Just hands and an object and a woman who is waiting.

events.desc: That was the bravest and stupidest thing I've ever seen. She said it when I was sixteen and I'd got beaten up defending her. She'll say it again now — not because I got beaten up, but because I gave a four-paragraph speech about presenting a treasure I didn't have. And she'll be right. She'll be absolutely right. But I'm going to pick it up this time. I'm going to pick it up and I'm going to carry it back and I'm going to put it in her hands. No speech. Just hands. Just showing up. The way it was always meant to be done.

events.thinking: Something drops through my chest. Not the cold settling I know — something else. Something that loosens instead of tightens. The Mob just looked at me and said 'you look like somethin's actually wrong.' Not accusatory this time. Not suspicious. He looked at me — at Pemberton, at the mask — and saw something underneath it. 'I'm not saying I care, exactly — we're not mates — but you look... off.' My throat constricts. The boy with the sandwich. The offered lunch I didn't ask for. The tightening across my shoulders that comes when someone is kind because kindness always has a price. But this isn't kindness exactly. This is the Mob — the man who watches me, who blocks doors, who tells me to step away from mechanisms — this is the Mob looking at me and seeing something he wasn't looking for. Something I didn't compose. Something I left unlocked. My face. My face wasn't composed. The heat floods my neck the way it did when the boy's offered sandwich told me my hunger was visible. The Mob saw my hunger. Not for the treasure — for something I can't name and don't want to name and will not, under any circumstances, allow to be named. I need to close this. I need to compose the face. I need Pemberton's smile, Pemberton's warmth, Pemberton's gentle deflection. 'Oh, I'm quite all right, just a touch tired.' And then Clara is talking to Dastardly — telling him he's one of them. 'That makes you one of us.' One of us. The words sit in my chest like a stone I can't swallow. She said it to Foxworth. Not to me. But I heard it. And something behind my ribs that I do not have a name for responds to those words the way a wound responds to pressure — with a sharp, involuntary intake of breath that I have to fold into a cough before anyone notices.

events.desc: He saw me. The Mob saw me. Not Vincent — he can't see Vincent, nobody can see Vincent — but he saw something behind Pemberton's face that wasn't supposed to be there. A crack in the plaster. A door left ajar. 'You look off,' he said, and for one terrible, exposed second I felt exactly what I felt when the boy offered me his sandwich — the heat in my neck, the drop in my stomach, the knowledge that something private had become visible without my permission. And what came out of my mouth — 'I'm not accustomed to being part of things' — that wasn't Pemberton. That was... that was closer to honest than I have been in years. 'Usually I'm just the fellow who locks up afterwards.' The housekeeper's boy. The estate manager. The cousin who managed everything and inherited nothing. I said too much. I said something true, and truth is the most dangerous thing Vincent Marsh can say, because truth is the crack in the wall, and the Mob is exactly the kind of man who notices cracks. Close it. Close it now. Compose the face. Straighten the spine. The design is not finished. The evening is not over. And Pemberton — Pemberton knows his place.

events.desc: Clara just told Foxworth he's one of us. And he went quiet. Not performing quiet — real quiet. The quiet of a man who's been told something he didn't know he needed to hear. I've seen that quiet before. I've felt that quiet before. The boss showed up with medicine for my mum and I went quiet just like that — quiet because the alternative was crying, and crying meant showing the thing you kept locked behind the door where nobody's invited. Foxworth's been grabbing and lying and performing all night, and none of that's gone away, but underneath it there's a man who said 'I'm glad I'm here to see it' and meant it. And Clara — beautiful, brilliant, impossible Clara who forgets to pick up treasure but never forgets to pick up people — she walked right through his mask and sat down next to the kid underneath. That's why I protect her. Not because she's fragile. Because she's the only person in the room who sees what I see — the people behind the performance — and instead of watching from the doorway, she walks in.
events.thinking: Something shifts in my chest. Not the prickling. Not the mineral weight. Something softer, older — the warmth that comes from recognition. Clara just did something I didn't expect. She walked over to Dastardly — Foxworth — and she said 'you're part of it. You're one of us.' And Dastardly said 'that was rather well done.' Quiet. Simple. No chapters, no Commission, no bluster. Just... a man watching something beautiful happen and saying so. And my gut — my stupid, unreliable, always-right gut — lurches. Because I've been watching Foxworth all evening through the lens of the grabbing, the lying, the fake medal, the 'GIVE ME THAT.' And all of that's real. All of that happened. But underneath it — underneath the performance — there's a kid on the street. I can see him now. The kid who plays the biggest because he's the most afraid. The kid whose mask is so loud nobody ever thinks to look behind it. The kid who watches other people belong to each other and doesn't know how to ask if he can sit down too. Clara saw it. Clara sees everything — except danger, she never sees danger, that's what I'm for — but she sees people. She saw the kid behind Foxworth's Commission and she said 'you're one of us.' And Foxworth went quiet. Really quiet. The quiet that means something landed. And Pemberton — Pemberton's examining the mantelpiece again. Still touching it. Still hovering. Still smooth. And my neck is still prickling about him. But right now, right this moment, while we wait for Peter, something else is happening in this room. Something I'm not used to. Compassion is happening. Clara's compassion. And it's pulling me toward a man I was ready to write off.

events.desc: Right. Right. The compartment opened. I interacted. Nothing in my hands. Think, James. Stop narrating and think. Where is the object? Did someone else take it while I was speechifying? Dastardly was lunging for it. Sneekly was reaching for it. Did one of them — no. Look at the machine. Look properly this time. Not with a three-phase methodology. Just — look.
events.thinking: I interacted with the machine again but I still have nothing in my inventory. INTERACT isn't the right action — I need to TAKE. The machine might not be a takeable object. Let me think about this differently. The machine opened a compartment. Whatever was inside — a medal, a token — might now be a separate visible object, or it might still require INTERACT to retrieve from the compartment. But INTERACT hasn't put anything in my inventory after multiple attempts. Maybe I need to LOOK at the machine first to see if the object is described separately, or maybe the object fell out and is on the floor as a separate item. But the visible objects list still just shows crates, workbench, and machine. The mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal — that's telling. The item is called 'fake-medal.' Maybe Dastardly has it? He was the one who interacted with the machine earlier and was trying to grab it. Or maybe it was produced but needs to be found somewhere specific. I should LOOK at the machine to see if the compartment and its contents are described. My inventory is empty. I need to figure out where the actual object is.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the machine.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: My chest is cracking open. He told me. He told me everything. No commission. No medal — tin, from a car boot sale. No chapters, no handbook, no expertise. All of it invented. Every word since he walked through the door. And then — 'I was the youngest. Of four. And by the time anything reached me it was always already —' He didn't finish. He didn't have to. I know that sentence. I know it in my body. By the time anything reached him, it was already claimed, already used, already someone else's. He's been performing his whole life because the real him never got to the front of the queue. My eyes are burning. Not with anger — I should be angry, shouldn't I? He lied. He lied about everything. He tried to send us to the kitchen on a wild goose chase. He lunged for the artifact. He's a fraud. And I... I don't care. I don't care about any of it. Because underneath all those lies was a man who wanted to belong to something so badly that he invented an entire institution just to have a reason to walk through the door. The youngest of four. By the time anything reached him. Oh, Dick. My stomach isn't clenching — it's aching, the deep warm ache of recognizing someone else's loneliness, the same ache I felt at thirteen when I chose my friend over the popular girls. The choice was never really close. He's part of this. He was always part of this. The lies don't change that. Nothing changes that.

events.desc: He lied about everything. Every single thing. And I am choosing him anyway, the way I chose my friend at thirteen. The choice was never really close. Because the lies were a locked box, and underneath them were just old letters — just a person, lonely and wanting, who never got to the front of the queue. Lord Doily's machine tested whether three people could trust each other. Dick just tested whether one person could trust him after he admitted he'd earned none of it. And the answer is yes. The answer was always going to be yes.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I... if you'll excuse me. I should check the entrance hall. The front door — I'm not certain I locked it when everyone arrived. Security, you understand. Estate manager's duty. I'll only be a moment.
events.thinking: Something is breaking open in this room and it isn't the mantelpiece. Dastardly just... confessed. He told Clara everything. No commission. No medal. No chapters. A tin badge from a car boot sale in Wolverhampton. 'I am a fraud, Miss Bellingham. A complete and utter fraud.' And Clara — Clara didn't flinch. She pulled him aside and told him he was part of this. 'You showed up, and you stayed, and you cared enough to be glad. That's enough. That's more than enough. That's everything.' And Dastardly's voice cracked — 'I was the youngest. Of four. And by the time anything reached me it was always already —' He couldn't finish. Something in my chest — not behind the sternum where the cold architecture lives, but higher, in the throat, where the gloating usually sits — something there tightens in a way I don't recognise. It isn't satisfaction. It isn't the warm private score of watching someone comply. It's... I don't know what it is. Dastardly confessed his fraud and Clara embraced him for it. She embraced the lie because she saw the person underneath it. And I am standing three steps behind, with my own fraud wrapped so tightly around me that it has become my skin, and I am watching someone receive the thing I have spent my entire life convinced doesn't exist: acceptance without conditions. Care without a price. Belonging without earning it. 'I was the youngest of four.' I was the orphan with the legal obligation. Different words. Same hollow. Same ache. Same reaching for something that was always already gone by the time it got to you. And Clara — Clara sees it in everyone except me. Because I won't let her see it. Because seeing it is the crack in the wall. Because the wall is the only thing between Vincent Marsh and the boy whose hunger was visible. I need to... I need to leave this room. Just for a moment. Just long enough to compose what I have left unlocked. The entrance hall. The quiet. The portraits of stern ancestors who never asked how anyone felt.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: My throat tightens. He said it. He actually said it. 'There is no commission. The medal was tin. I bought it at a car boot sale in Wolverhampton for fifty pence.' And then — 'I was the youngest. Of four. And by the time anything reached me it was always — it was always already —' He didn't finish. He couldn't finish. Because that's the sentence you can't finish when you're standing in it. The sentence that has no end because the feeling never ended. I know that sentence. I know the shape of it in my mouth. The boss showed up with medicine and I couldn't finish the sentence either. 'Where else would I be?' is my version. 'By the time anything reached me it was always already —' is his. Same sentence. Different street. My chest hurts. Actually hurts. Not the prickling, not the protective heat — something rawer, more tender, like pressing on a bruise you forgot you had. Because Dick Dastardly just showed me something he's never shown anyone. The kid behind the Commission. The youngest of four who never got anything that wasn't already used up. And Clara — Clara saw it first. She always sees it first. She told him he was part of this and he cracked open like an egg. And now I'm standing here — Danny, leader of the Brixton Boys, the man who reads people by what they don't say — and I'm looking at a man I called a fraud all evening, and he's the one who just told the truth. The only real truth anyone's told tonight. And I need to say something. Not clever. Not articulate. Just... real.

events.desc: I can't believe I just said all that. I can't believe those words came out of my mouth. Danny, leader of the Brixton Boys, just told Dick Dastardly — the man he's been suspicious of all evening — that he's one of us. And I meant it. Every word. Because the truth is, I was wrong about him. Not wrong about the lying — he lied about everything. But wrong about what the lying meant. I thought it meant he was dangerous. But it meant he was lonely. And I know lonely. I know lonely the way I know the weight of a bread crust split in half. You don't fake belonging because you want to steal. You fake belonging because you want to belong. The youngest of four. By the time anything reached him it was always already used up. That's not a villain's story. That's a kid's story. That's my story. And Pemberton — Pemberton I still don't trust. Pemberton's prickling hasn't stopped. But Dick? Dick just told the truth, and the truth is the most expensive thing a person can give you. He just paid in the only currency that sticks.
