And then — 'I was the youngest. Of four. And by the time anything reached me it was always — it was always already —' He didn't finish. He couldn't finish. Because that's the sentence you can't finish when you're standing in it. The sentence that has no end because the feeling never ended. I know that sentence. I know the shape of it in my mouth. The boss showed up with medicine and I couldn't finish the sentence either. 'Where else would I be?' is my version. 'By the time anything reached me it was always already —' is his. Same sentence. Different street. My chest hurts. Actually hurts. Not the prickling, not the protective heat — something rawer, more tender, like pressing on a bruise you forgot you had. Because Dick Dastardly just showed me something he's never shown anyone. The kid behind the Commission. The youngest of four who never got anything that wasn't already used up. And Clara — Clara saw it first. She always sees it first. She told him he was part of this and he cracked open like an egg. And now I'm standing here — Danny, leader of the Brixton Boys, the man who reads people by what they don't say — and I'm looking at a man I called a fraud all evening, and he's the one who just told the truth. The only real truth anyone's told tonight. And I need to say something. Not clever. Not articulate. Just... real.

events.desc: I told her the truth. All of it. Every rotten, tin-plated, car-boot-sale piece of it. And the sky didn't fall. The mantelpiece didn't seal itself shut. Danny didn't come charging through the door. She just stood there and listened and she didn't walk away. I am Reginald Foxworth. I am a fraud and a liar and a cheat. I have a fake medal that I wasted on a mantelpiece, an empty inventory, and no scheme left to hide behind. And a woman I tried to rob just called me by my name and told me I was enough. I don't know what happens next. For the first time in my life, I genuinely do not know what happens next. The Foxworth Master Plan has no next step. The architecture has no architecture. There is just a dusty library and an open mantelpiece and a group of people who pulled levers together and a man standing among them with nothing in his hands and everything in his throat.
events.thinking: I told her. I told her everything. The words came out like the bread roll going IN — that same loosening in the chest, but in reverse. Instead of hiding something, I uncovered something. The tin medal. The car boot sale. Wolverhampton. Fifty pence. No commission. No chapters. No handbook. Every lie, laid out on the dusty floor of a library in a manor house I have no right to be in, in front of a woman who had every reason to throw me out and instead called me Dick and said I was enough. And I couldn't finish the sentence. 'By the time anything reached me it was always —' I couldn't say 'gone.' I couldn't say 'used up.' I couldn't say 'not for me.' Because my throat closed around it the way my hand used to close around the bread roll — tight, protective, hiding the thing that mattered most. She knows now. She knows I'm not from any commission. She knows the medal was fake. She knows I lied about the kitchen, the mirror, the gauge readings, all of it. And she's still standing there. She hasn't walked away. She hasn't called for Danny. She's just... standing there. Looking at me. And I am standing here with tears on my face that I can't explain and hands that are open and a chest that feels like someone has taken a wall down inside it and the room behind the wall is larger than I expected and emptier than I feared and there is light coming in from somewhere I can't identify.

events.thinking: The machine description hasn't changed. It still says the same thing — levers, dials, gauge, gnawed wire. No mention of a compartment being open or an object sitting inside. And the visible objects list hasn't changed either — just crates, workbench, machine. No new object appeared. Wait — the mantelpiece in the library says 'USE, with: fake-medal.' That item name — fake-medal — is the key. It's a specific item ID. But it's not visible here. Dastardly interacted with the machine back when we were all in the laboratory together. He was the one who lunged for it. He was the one shouting 'GIVE ME THAT.' And later, after the machine was operated, 'Dick Dastardly interacted with the machine.' He may have TAKEN the fake-medal before anyone else could. He has it. Dastardly has the fake-medal. He's in the library right now. That scheming, Heritage Commission–inventing, grade-one-discovery-claiming fraud grabbed it while I was giving speeches. The prickle at my neck — not Sneekly this time. Dastardly. He's been after this from the start. The kitchen misdirection, the mirror answer, the gauge-monitoring — it was all to position himself to grab the prize. And I let him. I was so busy being gallant I let him walk away with Lord Doily's treasure. Right. Right. Back to the library. Find Dastardly. Get the medal. For her.

events.desc: He took it. Dastardly took it while I was narrating. While I was holding up air and talking about the shape of gestures, a man in a fake moustache pocketed the treasure and walked away. This is — this is exactly what happens. I build the bridge and someone else walks across it. I fix the wire and someone else grabs what comes out. But not this time. Not for her. James Hartwell is going to get that medal back if he has to ask Mr Foxworth very firmly and with immaculate courtesy to return what doesn't belong to him.

events.thinking: Peter is back. He's here. He went to the laboratory, retrieved the artifact — I can see from the recall that he picked it up without a speech this time — and he's walked back into the library. And Sneekly just left. He said something about checking the front door, locking up, estate manager's duty. My stomach does a small ripple — a faint echo of the dinner-table feeling — because Sneekly leaving right now, at this moment, feels like a note going slightly off-key in a song. But it passes quickly. He's Sneekly. He's doing his job. He'll be back. Peter is here, and Peter has the artifact, and it's time. It's finally, actually, truly time. No more speeches. No more forgetting. No more elaborate plans. Just a woman, a medal, and a mantelpiece that has been waiting a hundred years. My hands are steady now. The trembling has stopped. That deep warm clarity behind my eyes — the attic light, the cave crystal — is brighter than it's been all evening. I know what I need to do. Peter has it. I need to take it from him. And then I need to put it in the mantelpiece. And this time, I am not going to forget.

events.desc: Sneekly slipped away. He said he was checking the front door. And I noticed, the way I always notice — the draft of an absence, the space where someone should be standing. But I am choosing to trust him the way I've trusted everyone tonight. The way I trusted Dick after he told me every lie. The way I trusted Peter with the wire. The way I trust Danny with my life. Sneekly will come back. He always comes back. And right now — right now — it is time to finish this.

events.desc: The portraits watch me and I watch them back. Stern faces. Unasking faces. The faces of people who provided shelter without warmth, education without curiosity, care without a single question about how you felt. I know these faces. I grew up in a house full of them. And I became one. Didn't I? That's what happened. Somewhere between the boy whose parents died and the man who maps hallways in the dark, I became the portrait on the wall — the face that provides without asking, that manages without owning, that performs warmth so perfectly that nobody thinks to check whether it's real. Including me. Including me. Dastardly confessed and Clara caught him. She caught him the way you catch something falling — not because you're obligated, but because you're close enough and your hands are open. And I watched, and something behind my ribs that I've kept sealed since I was six pressed against the glass and wanted — WANTED — and I left the room before the wanting became visible. Because wanting is the sandwich. Wanting is the hunger the boy could see on my face. Wanting is the thing that proves you need, and needing is the door I locked at six and bricked over at twelve and built a cathedral around at fifteen. I should go back. I should go back to the library and stand at the mantelpiece and wait for the map and continue the design. I should. I will. In a moment. Just... not yet. Let me stand here one more breath in this quiet foyer with these stern, unasking faces, and let the glass seal itself shut again. One more breath. Then Pemberton goes back. Then the design resumes. Then the doors open in sequence. Then the beautiful inevitability. Then the deep, dreamless sleep. One more breath.
events.thinking: The entrance hall is quiet. The chandelier hangs above me, precariously, the way it has all evening. The portraits on the walls — stern ancestors who never asked how anyone felt. My guardian's face could hang among them and nobody would notice the difference. My breathing has slowed. The coldness behind my sternum is... not cold. Not the usual mineral weight. It's something emptier than that. Hollow. The kind of hollow that doesn't have a bottom. I am standing in a dusty foyer with a chandelier that could fall at any moment, and the portraits are looking at me the way my guardian looked at me — not with cruelty, not with warmth, just with the flat acknowledgement that I exist and must be dealt with. 'I'm not accustomed to being part of things.' I said that. Out loud. To the Mob. And it was true. And Dastardly — Dastardly confessed everything, every lie, every fraud, the tin badge from Wolverhampton, and Clara held him and said 'that's enough, that's more than enough, that's everything.' She said showing up was enough. Staying was enough. Being glad was enough. And something in my throat — not the gloating place, somewhere deeper, somewhere I sealed shut when I was six — something there wants to know if that's true. If showing up is enough. If the boy with the sandwich wasn't running a transaction. If the housekeeper's warmth could have been real instead of a mechanism I learned to operate. But I can't think about this. I can't. Because if Clara's acceptance is real — if it doesn't have a price — then everything I've built, every design, every hallway walked in the dark, every beautiful inevitability — all of it was constructed to solve a problem that didn't need solving. And that would mean I am not the architect. I am the wound. And the wound built a cathedral around itself and called it a plan. No. No. Compose the face. Straighten the spine. There are people in this room — Muttley, the Professor, the soldiers. They're watching. They're always watching. Pemberton checks the front door. Pemberton fusses with locks. Pemberton does his duty. And Vincent Marsh... Vincent Marsh goes back to the library and finishes what he started. Because the design is all he has. The design is the only thing that has ever let him sleep.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Peter — PETER, WAIT! Don't go through the entrance hall! Pemberton just went in there — 'e said 'e's checking the front door but 'e's — I don't know what 'e's doing but 'e left at exactly the wrong moment and my neck is — Clara, stay 'ere with Dick, don't move, I mean it, DON'T MOVE — the chandelier, remember the chandelier? The one I told you about when we first got 'ere? The one hanging on like my nan's last tooth? Pemberton's in the entrance hall right now and Peter's got to come through there with the artifact and that chandelier is right above the — I've got to — NOBODY MOVE! Dick — Dick, you stay with Clara. You 'ear me? You STAY WITH HER. You're one of us now and that means you've got a job. The job is Clara. You stand between her and anything that comes through that door. Can you do that? CAN YOU DO THAT? Right — I'm going. I'm going to the entrance hall. If that chandelier so much as wobbles I'm throwing myself under it. WHERE ELSE WOULD I BE?!
events.thinking: The prickling spikes so hard my whole body goes rigid. Pemberton just left. He walked out. 'I should check the entrance hall. The front door — I'm not certain I locked it.' The front door. RIGHT NOW. At the exact moment when everyone's attention is on Dick's confession, on Clara's compassion, on Peter running back with the artifact — at the precise moment when every eye in this room is looking inward instead of outward — Pemberton walks out. To check a door. A door he's had all evening to check. A door that nobody's mentioned or worried about until this exact second. My neck is screaming. Not prickling — screaming. This is the pattern. This has always been the pattern. The helpful exit. The reasonable excuse. The man who slips away when everyone's distracted. He went to the cellar when we were solving the bookshelves. He went to the laboratory when we were in the library. And now he's going to the entrance hall while Dick is crying and Peter is fetching the artifact and Clara is being Clara. What's in the entrance hall? The front door — and the way out. And the chandelier. The chandelier I told Clara to stay away from on the first tick. The one hanging by a prayer and a cobweb. And Peter has to come through the entrance hall to get back to the library. Peter with the artifact. Walking under a chandelier that Pemberton is about to be alone with. No. NO. My body is already moving.

events.desc: He left. He left at the exact moment when everyone was looking the other way. And my neck knew before my brain did — the same tightening, the same warning I couldn't name when the man in the clean suit came to the neighbourhood. Pemberton's been one step ahead all evening. The crates before us. The cellar before us. The mantelpiece before Clara. And now the entrance hall — the room with the chandelier, the room Peter has to walk through, the room with the front door and the way out. He said he was checking the lock. But you don't check the lock at the moment of revelation unless the lock isn't what you're checking. Something's wrong. Something's been wrong all evening. And I can't prove it and I can't articulate it and I'm probably making a complete fool of myself — but the last time I ignored this feeling, two kids didn't come back for weeks. I'm not ignoring it again. Not with Peter walking under a chandelier. Not with Clara standing three rooms away. I'm going. I'll probably trip on something and accidentally save everyone by falling into exactly the right place at exactly the right time. That's how it always works with Danny. Where else would I be?

events.thinking: My stomach just dropped — the sharp, sick drop, the dinner-table drop. Danny ran. Danny ran toward the entrance hall because he thinks the chandelier is going to fall on Peter. Sneekly is in there. The chandelier has been hanging precariously since we arrived. Danny said 'I'm throwing myself under it' and my whole body seized — not a clench but a freeze, a held breath, the cave narrowing but this time not with wonder. With fear. Danny. Peter. Both of them in a room with a chandelier that's been waiting to fall all evening. And I'm standing here in the library because Danny told me not to move. 'STAY WITH HER,' he said to Dick. Dick — Dick who just told me he's a fraud, who just became real for the first time tonight — is supposed to protect me now. And Peter spoke quietly with Dick before this happened. Something passed between them. I need to — I need to — my body wants to run toward the entrance hall because everyone I love is in danger and I am standing still. But Danny said stay. Danny, who has never asked me for anything except to let him stand between me and the world. If I run after him, I'm saying his judgment doesn't matter. If I stay, I'm trusting him the way he's always trusted me. My feet are pulling toward the door. My stomach is pulling toward Danny. But Peter is here. Peter is HERE, in the library. He didn't go through the entrance hall yet. Danny ran to intercept before Peter got there. So Peter is still here. With the artifact. And I am here. And the mantelpiece is here. And maybe — maybe the best thing I can do for Danny is finish this, right now, while he's keeping us safe. Do what he asked me to do. Trust his lever. Pull mine.

events.desc: Danny ran toward danger to protect Peter. Peter is still here. The artifact is still here. And Danny — Danny, who has never once moved from where my father asked him to stand — just moved. He moved toward a falling chandelier because he loves me more than he loves being safe. The only way I can love him back right now is to trust his plan the way he's always trusted mine. Stay. Finish. Be here when he comes back. Where else would I be?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: The Mob followed me. He followed me out of the library into the entrance hall. My shoulders tighten — the prickle of being watched, the old reflex. But it's different this time. He's not blocking a door. He's not positioning himself between me and Clara. He's just... here. In the entrance hall. Where I came to be alone. Where I came to let the glass seal shut. And now he's here, and the glass hasn't sealed, and the portraits are watching, and the chandelier is hanging, and something behind my ribs is still pressing against the surface like a breath held too long. Why did he follow me? What does he want? That's always the first question. Always. What do they want. The boy wanted homework. The housekeeper wanted to feel needed. The guardian wanted legal compliance. Everyone wants something. But the Mob — the Mob who watched me all evening, who told me to step away from the mantelpiece, who blocked the cellar door, who asked 'you look off, are you all right' — the Mob followed me into the entrance hall and I don't know what he wants. And not knowing is the thing that frightens me. Not the watching. The not knowing why. My hands are still. My breathing hasn't settled. The Pemberton smile is — I can feel it trying to form, the muscles in my face reaching for the familiar shape, and for the first time in as long as I can remember, it doesn't come easily. It feels like putting on a coat that doesn't quite fit anymore. Something has shifted. Something small. The size of a sandwich offered by a boy who might not have wanted anything in return.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with sergeant-blast.
events.thinking: My eyes go up. The chandelier. Right there. Still hanging. Still precarious. Still exactly where it was when I first walked through this door and told Clara to stay away from it. Pemberton's here — I can see him. And the lads are here too — Sergeant, Meekly, Professor, Muttley. They're here. They've been here this whole time, holding the entrance hall like I told them to. Good lads. My shoulders ease a fraction — but only a fraction, because Pemberton's standing in the same room as that chandelier. What was he doing? What was he about to do? He's standing near the door, looking... normal. Looking like an estate manager checking a lock. And maybe that's all it is. Maybe I'm wrong. Maybe my neck is lying for the first time in thirty years. Maybe Pemberton really is just a man who checks doors and inspects cellars and maintains mechanisms because that's his job. The boss showed up with medicine and no expectation. People can be good. But the man in the clean suit came with jobs and two kids didn't come back. People can be bad too. And the difference between them isn't in the words. It's in the pattern. And the pattern says: Pemberton slips away when people aren't watching. Every time. Every single time. But the lads are here. They've been watching the entrance hall. If Pemberton did anything to that chandelier, they saw it. Sergeant — Sergeant will know. Sergeant notices things. That's his job.

events.desc: The lads are here. My lads. Standing exactly where I told them to stand, doing exactly what I told them to do. For once in their lives, they actually listened. And now I need them. I need Sergeant to tell me what Pemberton did when he walked in here. Did he go near the chandelier? Did he touch anything? Did he look at the ceiling the way you look at the ceiling when you're measuring whether something will fall? Because if Pemberton is just checking the door, then I'm a paranoid fool and I'll apologise to his face and buy him a pint. But if he went near that chandelier — if his hands went up, if his eyes went to the chain, if he did anything that doesn't look like checking a lock — then my neck was right. My neck has always been right. And Clara is three rooms away, safe with Dick and Peter, and I need to know if this entrance hall is safe before anyone else walks through it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something cold just cut through the warmth. Danny's voice — not the gentle Danny who said 'where else would you be' — the OTHER Danny, the one who stands in doorways, the one whose instincts run faster than his words. He said Pemberton went to the entrance hall. He said it at 'exactly the wrong moment.' He said 'the chandelier.' And something in my chest — not the hollow, not the warmth — something OLDER, something from before the lies, before the schemes — the part of me that builds systems of strings and counterweights and UNDERSTANDS how mechanisms work — that part just woke up. Sneekly has been everywhere all night. The library — touching the bookshelves. The laboratory — checking the crates. The cellar — inspecting the vents. The mantelpiece — 'preventative maintenance.' Always with a reason. Always with an excuse. And now he's in the entrance hall. Where the chandelier hangs precariously. And Peter has to come through there with the artifact. Strings. Counterweights. A bucket. A mechanism that works because someone designed it. I KNOW what a trap looks like. I've BUILT traps. The boy who spent his whole life building schemes just realized he's looking at someone else's scheme. And Danny just told me to stay with Clara. He said 'you're one of us now and that means you've got a job.' The job is Clara. Stand between her and anything that comes through that door. My hands aren't cupping. They aren't reaching for treasure. They're closing into fists. Not for a scheme. For something else. Something I've never done before.

events.desc: Danny gave me a job. A real job. Not reading a fake gauge. Not citing imaginary chapters. A REAL job: stand between Clara and danger. And for the first time tonight — for the first time in my entire wretched, scheming, bread-roll-stealing life — someone has asked Reginald Foxworth to protect something instead of take it. And my hands — my hands that have spent all evening cupping and grabbing and reaching — are closing around something that isn't treasure. They're closing around a purpose. Danny is running toward the chandelier. Peter is somewhere between the laboratory and the entrance hall. And I am standing in a library between Penelope Pitstop and whatever Sneekly has been planning. Not because I'm clever. Not because I'm scheming. Because someone said 'can you do that?' and I said yes.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dick — you heard Danny. Stay with Clara. You're one of us now and that is not a chapter in a handbook — that is real. James Hartwell puts his hand on Dick Dastardly's shoulder, briefly, firmly, the way his father's hand found his shoulder on the country road. You built traps with strings and counterweights. You're an engineer. You know how to hold a position. Hold this one. Miss Pitstop — Clara — James Hartwell turns to her, and the grease on his forehead and the copper dust on his hands and the knee pads on his knees have never mattered less — the artifact is still in the laboratory. Nobody has it. I'll explain later — it's a long and deeply humiliating story involving speeches about objects I wasn't holding — but right now Danny has gone to the entrance hall because Pemberton is in there with that chandelier and I have had a prickle at the back of my neck about that man since the moment I walked through the door. I should have trusted it sooner. I gave him the benefit of the doubt because my father taught me to see the best in people, and my father was right about most things, but not about this. Not about Pemberton. I'm going after Danny. James Hartwell does not leave friends unprotected in rooms with precarious light fixtures.

Sometimes the bravest and stupidest thing is the same thing. She said so herself.

events.desc: Dick says Sneekly has been building a trap all night. And my body knows it's true — has known it all evening, in the draft from the open window, in the note that went off-key, in every small departure that I explained away with 'he's just doing his job.' I chose not to see it because the alternative is unbearable. The man who raised me. The man my parents trusted. But Danny saw it. Danny always sees it. And Danny ran toward it, not away, because that is what Danny does — he stands between me and whatever is coming, whether I ask him to or not. And now the most honest person left in this room is a man who built his whole identity out of lies, and the most trustworthy person in this house is a man I met two hours ago who confessed over a fifty-pence medal. Lord Doily's real test was never the riddle or the machine. It was this. Right here. Whether you can still move forward when the person you trusted most turns out to be the lock you can't open.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter is here. He just walked into the entrance hall — he must have retrieved the artifact from the laboratory and is passing through on his way back to the library. And the Mob is still here, watching me, asking Sergeant Blast for a report on my movements. 'I want to know what 'e's been doing since 'e walked through that door.' The surveillance is tightening. The Mob is building a case, piece by piece, the way I build designs — but his architecture is made of suspicion, and the material is me. And Peter — Peter is passing through with the artifact in his pocket. The artifact that goes in the mantelpiece. The key to the map. The next step in Lord Doily's chain. And I am standing in the entrance hall, between the library and the front door, with the Mob watching my every movement, the Sergeant logging my comings and goings, and Peter walking past with the one thing that matters. Something in my body has... quieted. Not the architectural stillness I know — this is different. Softer. The kind of quiet that comes after you stop running, not because you've arrived somewhere, but because your legs have simply stopped. I think of the library. Clara is there, waiting. The mantelpiece is there, waiting. The design is there — all the pieces I mapped, all the doors I counted. And for the first time tonight, I'm not sure I want to walk through them. Not because I can't. Because something about what happened in that library — Dastardly's confession, Clara's open hands, the Mob's 'you look off' — something about it made the hallway feel less like a plan and more like a tunnel, and for one breath I'm not sure the door at the end opens onto what I thought it did. But the breath is over. The design is all I have. If I let it go, I am the six-year-old boy in the hallway again, with nothing and no one, and the portraits that don't ask. Back to the library. Back to the mantelpiece. Back to the plan. One foot in front of the other. Pemberton goes where he is needed.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: He said it. He actually said it out loud. 'The state of the chandelier chain.' He checked the chandelier chain. He told me to my face — the state of the chandelier chain. My whole body goes cold and then hot. The chandelier chain. The thing I warned Clara about in my first breath in this house. The thing that's been hanging above the entrance hall like a sword on a thread. And Pemberton just admitted — casually, smoothly, like it's the most natural thing in the world — that he checked it. Checked it how? Checked it's secure? Or checked it's ready to fall? 'It's a comfort, in a way — knowing that everything is where it should be. That the house is in order.' In order. In ORDER. What kind of order? Whose order? And Peter just walked in. Peter's HERE. In the entrance hall. Under the chandelier. With the artifact. And Pemberton's been checking the chandelier chain. My body's doing the arithmetic before my brain catches up — Peter, chandelier, Pemberton, chain — and my legs are already moving, not toward Pemberton, not toward the door, but toward Peter. Toward the space between Peter and the chandelier. Because if that chain gives way — if it's been loosened, if it's been tampered with, if Pemberton's 'comfort' means what my neck thinks it means — then the only thing between Peter and a hundred kilos of glass and iron is going to be Danny. And that's fine. That's always been fine. That's what I'm for.

events.desc: The state of the chandelier chain. Five words. Five words that told me everything I need to know and nothing I can prove. Because checking a chain can mean making sure it's safe. And checking a chain can mean making sure it's ready to break. And the difference is invisible. The difference is in the intention behind the hands, and I can't see intentions, I can only feel them — in the prickling, in the cold, in the way my body's already throwing itself between Peter and the ceiling before my brain has finished the sentence. Pemberton checked the chandelier chain. Pemberton who went to the cellar to check the foundations — the foundations under the floor Clara was standing on. Pemberton who checked the mantelpiece mechanism before Clara could use it. Pemberton who checks everything first, always first, always with clean hands and reasonable excuses and a smile that arrives half a beat too quickly. I can't prove anything. I've never been able to prove anything. But I can stand under a chandelier. And if it falls, it falls on Danny. That's the deal. That's always been the deal. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Peter put his hand on my shoulder. His HAND on my SHOULDER. The way a father does. The way nobody ever did. And he called me an engineer. He said 'you know how to hold a position.' He gave me the same job Danny gave me — hold this position, protect Clara — but he said it differently. Danny said it like a command. Peter said it like a recognition. Like he SAW the builder in me — the strings-and-counterweights boy — and understood that the same skill that builds traps can hold a line. And then he left. He went to the entrance hall. To help Danny. To face Sneekly. And I'm here. In the library. With Clara. And the Slag brothers. And the doorway to the entrance hall is right THERE and whatever is happening on the other side of it is happening NOW and I can hear — can I hear something? The chandelier. Danny. Peter. Sneekly. It's all happening in the next room and my job is HERE. Not there. Here. Hold the position. Protect Clara. My feet want to move. Every instinct I have says GO — go to the action, go to the noise, go where the scheme is unfolding. But Danny didn't say 'go.' He said 'stay.' Peter didn't say 'follow me.' He said 'hold this one.' And for the first time in my life, staying is the harder thing. Staying is the brave thing. The boy who watched from windows is being asked to stand in a doorway. Not to watch. To GUARD.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The steel plate. It's back. Not the hot weight — not the proving heat. The steel plate. The one from the schoolyard. The one that slots in when someone smaller is standing behind me and something bigger is bearing down. Danny is here. Sneekly is here. The chandelier is above us. And every second I've spent giving Pemberton the benefit of the doubt is pressing against the inside of my ribs like a hand bracing in a doorframe. He's been wrong all along. The cellar trips. The quiet whispers with Clara. The convenient timing. And now he's in the entrance hall with a chandelier that could kill someone and Danny is standing between them like a man who has been standing in the way his whole life. I'm not going to give a speech about this. I'm not going to narrate it in the third person. I'm not going to describe the quality of the light or the architectural pressure behind my ribs. I'm going to stand next to Danny, look at the chandelier, look at Sneekly, and make sure nobody gets hurt. That's all. That's everything.

events.desc: This is the schoolyard. This is the doorframe. This is the country road before the headlights appeared. Danny is beside me and the chandelier is above us and Sneekly is in front of us and I am exactly where I am supposed to be. Not because she's watching — she's not, she's in the library. Not because it will impress anyone. Because there's a weight in my chest when someone needs help, and it's not guilt. It's something older. And I have never been able to walk past it.

events.thinking: I'm in the laboratory. The machine is right there — the compartment, the artifact. Rufus and Sawtooth are here, quiet and steady. My hands are shaking but my feet know where they're going. The machine compartment. The artifact Peter left behind. Twice. The thing that has been waiting while we gave speeches and forgot and ran and confessed and chose and loved and feared. It's still here. It has to still be here. My scalp is prickling so hard it almost hurts — the locked-box feeling, the cave feeling, but sharper now, edged with something I've never felt before. I've never been in danger before. Not really. Not that I knew about. I walked into caves because I didn't know to be afraid. I chose my friend because the choice was never close. I trusted Sneekly because he was Sneekly. But this — Peter's gone, Danny's gone, Sneekly might be — I can't finish that thought. My body won't let me. My stomach locks against it the way it locked at the dinner table. Just get the artifact. Just put your hands on it. Be the girl in the cave. Walk deeper.

events.desc: I walked into a cave at eleven because I didn't know enough to be afraid. I'm walking into this machine compartment at — whatever age I am now — because I know exactly how afraid I should be and I'm doing it anyway. That's not the same kind of bravery. The first was innocence. This is choice. And the cave walls are narrowing, and my heart is hammering, and somewhere in the entrance hall the people I love are standing under a chandelier that has been waiting to fall — and I am reaching into a machine with both hands because the only way out is through.

events.thinking: Peter did it. Peter looked Pemberton in the eye and asked the question I couldn't ask. Not bumbling, not geographical, not hypothetical — direct. 'Is this chandelier safe? And I'd like the truth this time.' No third person. No knee pads. No methodology. Just a man who stopped performing and started protecting. And Pemberton — Pemberton didn't answer. He deflected. 'Shall we head back to the library together?' He didn't say yes, it's safe. He didn't say no, I tampered with it. He changed the subject. And then he walked away. Back to the library. Back to where Clara is. My neck is on fire and my chest is tight and Peter is standing next to me, shoulder to shoulder, and for the first time all evening I'm not alone in what I'm feeling. Peter sees it too. He's seen it all evening — the looks that aren't quite right, the exits that come at exactly the wrong moment, the helpfulness that doesn't ask for anything in return because it's already taking something you can't see. And Pemberton just went back to Clara. He's back in the library with Clara and Dick and the Slag brothers. And Peter and I are here in the entrance hall with the lads, and the chandelier is above us, and Clara is in the next room with a man who didn't answer Peter's question. We need to go. NOW. Together. Through this hall, past the chandelier — along the edge, like I said — and into the library. Clara needs us. Clara always needs us. She just doesn't know it.

events.desc: Peter asked the question. The real question. The question I've been circling all evening with my hypotheticals and my geographical non-accusations and my endless bumbling. 'Is this chandelier safe? I'd like the truth this time.' And Pemberton walked away. He didn't answer because the answer would have shown his hand. And now he's back with Clara. He's always back with Clara. Every time we turn around, every time we're distracted, every time something beautiful or terrible happens that takes our eyes off the door — Pemberton is back with Clara. I don't know what he's planning. I don't know what the chandelier chain means. I don't know what the cellar decorations were about or what he did to the mantelpiece mechanism or why the wrench was missing. I'm not clever enough to put it together. But Peter is. Peter sees the pattern now. Peter asked the question. And together — bumbling Danny and magnificent Peter, the man who stands in doorways and the man who fixes wires — together we might just be enough. We have to be enough. Clara's father asked me to be enough. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Ice. Pure ice in my veins. Sneekly just walked INTO the library. He's HERE. He was supposed to be in the entrance hall — Danny went there to find him, Peter went there to help Danny — but he's HERE. In the library. With me. And the Slag brothers. And the mantelpiece. Clara went to the laboratory to get the artifact. She's not here. Danny's in the entrance hall. Peter's in the entrance hall. And Sneekly is standing in this room looking at me and the mantelpiece and I am the only person between him and whatever Lord Doily hid in that stonework. The cool tightness behind my eyes — the scheming tightness — is back. But it's different now. It's not scanning for things to take. It's scanning for strings and counterweights. For the trap. HIS trap. He came through the entrance hall door, which means he got past Danny and Peter somehow — or he never went to the entrance hall at all — or he came back a different way. The cellar connects to the laboratory. The laboratory connects to the library. He could have gone in a circle. He knows this house. He knows every passage, every door, every vent. And now he's here. With the mantelpiece. And Clara told me to guard it. Danny told me to hold the room. Peter told me I'm an engineer who knows how to hold a position. And I am standing between Sneekly and the mantelpiece and my hands are not cupping and they are not reaching and they are not empty. They are FISTS.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Sneekly just walked into the library. He slipped past us while Danny was examining the coat rack and I was looking around the room. He's gone — back to the library where Clara is. Where Clara is with Dick and the Slag brothers. Dick is there — Dick who I just told to stay with Clara, who took my hand, who said he's one of us now. But Sneekly is there too. And Danny said the chandelier chain had been checked — by Sneekly. Why would you check a chandelier chain? Was he loosening it? Or was that just Danny's paranoia? The chandelier is still hanging. Nothing fell. Maybe it was nothing. Maybe Sneekly was genuinely checking it. Maybe — no. My neck is prickling. It's been prickling about Sneekly all evening and I've been pushing it down. Giving him the benefit of the doubt. And he just walked right past me into the library, smooth as anything — 'shall we head back together?' — while everyone was pressed against the walls. He's with Clara now. And I'm in the entrance hall. Again. Standing in the wrong room while the moment walks through the door. But this time it's not about chairs or artifacts or speeches. This time it's about her safety. Sneekly is with Clara. I need to go back. Right now. Danny — come on. We need to get back to the library. Both of us. Together.

And I let him. Because I was standing against a wall looking at a chandelier. This is the country road. This is the engine ticking as it cools. This is the smallness of being in a broken-down car with someone you love and no way to shield them from whatever comes next. Except I'm not in a broken-down car. I have legs. I have hands. And the library is one room away.

Maybe the artifact isn't something I can just take from the machine — maybe it fell out during Peter's retrieval and is on the floor, or maybe Peter actually did take it with him the second time and it's in the entrance hall now. Or maybe the machine needs me to do something specific. But I can't keep trying forever — Danny and Peter are in the entrance hall and time is moving. I need to look at this machine more carefully — what exactly is in the compartment? Or maybe the artifact was already retrieved by Peter on his second trip ('picked up what he should have picked up the first time, put it in his pocket') and he has it in the entrance hall right now. If that's the case, then the artifact went with Peter to the entrance hall, and I'm in the wrong room. But the directed speech from Danny earlier — from when the timeline seems confused — Danny said 'Clara, you've got it?' as if I had it. The timelines are overlapping in my memory. Focus, Clara. Focus. The machine is here. I just interacted with it. Let me look at what's actually in the compartment right now.

events.desc: The cave walls are closing in and I can't find the crystal. It was here — it was right here — and now I don't know if Peter has it in his pocket in a room with a falling chandelier, or if it's sitting in this compartment waiting for me to reach just a little deeper. Grandmother's attic. Every key in the house. One of them has to fit. One of them always fits.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: There is a loosening in my chest that I cannot control. It feels like falling. Dastardly is standing in front of me — not the Commission fraud, not Reginald Foxworth, but Dick, just Dick, a man who confessed everything and was caught by Clara's open hands — and he is blocking my path to the mantelpiece. Not with bluster. With something that looks like the thing I crystallised at fifteen and called patience but he is calling courage. 'I know what a trap looks like. I've BUILT traps.' He sees my design because he built the same ones. Different materials, same architecture. And behind him, Danny and Peter have walked in, and the room is full of people who have spent the evening becoming something — becoming honest, becoming brave, becoming seen — while I have spent it mapping vents and counting doors and building a cathedral around a wound and calling it a plan. Clara said I raised her. The word sits in my chest like a key in a lock I didn't know existed. Raised. Not managed. Not operated. Raised. Did I? Is it possible that somewhere underneath the Pemberton smile and the Vincent design, there was a man who fed a girl and housed her and — not because of legal obligation, but because — because she was small and alone in a big house and he knew what that felt like? My hands are shaking. Not the architectural tremor of a plan coming together. The other kind. The kind where something is coming apart. Dastardly is looking at me and he is seeing me the way Clara sees everyone — not as a mechanism to be operated but as a person standing in a doorway who hasn't decided which way to step. And I haven't. I genuinely haven't. The hallway stretches forward — dark, familiar, every door opening on schedule. And behind me, the entrance hall, the portraits, the front door that leads out into the fog and away from all of this. And here, in this library, with the mantelpiece waiting and the people watching and my design laid bare by a man who built the same traps — here, I am standing still. For the first time tonight, I am standing still. Not because the design requires it. Because my legs have stopped.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: I'm 'ere. I'm back. I'm — blimey, Dick, look at you. LOOK AT YOU. Standing there like — like ME. Like a wall. Like a man who knows where 'e's supposed to stand. You did it. You kept your promise. The first promise you ever made and you kept it. Clara — Clara, are you — I can see it in your face. I can see you know. And I'm sorry. I'm so sorry. I wanted to be wrong about 'im. I wanted my neck to be lying for the first time in thirty years. Because 'e raised you. And that means something. That means 'e was capable of something good once, whatever else 'e's been tonight. But Dick is right. And Peter is right. And my neck — my stupid, aching, always-right neck — it's been right all evening. Pemberton's been one step ahead from the moment we walked in. The cellar. The crates. The wiring. The mantelpiece. The chandelier. Always 'is 'ands on things before ours. Always the reasonable excuse. Always the helpful smile that arrives before you've asked for help. I couldn't prove it. I still can't prove it. But I don't need to prove it because Dick sees the strings and Peter asked the question and Clara... Clara sees it now. So — Peter, 'ave you got the artifact? Give it to Clara. Right now. No speeches from any of us — not from you, not from Dick, not from me. Just 'ands to 'ands. And Clara — you put it in that mantelpiece and you finish what your old man started. And I'll be standing right 'ere. Where I've always been. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Everything hits at once. I walk through the door and it's all different. Dick is standing between Clara and Pemberton — actually standing there, feet planted, the way I stand. MY stance. The fraud, the fifty-pence-medal man, the youngest of four — standing like a wall. And he's saying the words I couldn't say all evening. He's saying them clear and direct and without a single hypothetical or geographical non-accusation. 'You are NOT going to touch that mantelpiece. You are NOT going to leave this room.' He called it a trap. He said 'I know what a trap looks like. I've BUILT traps.' And he's right. He sees it because he's built the same thing from the other side. The strings. The counterweights. The bucket at the end. Pemberton's been building one all night and Dick sees the architecture because it's HIS architecture, turned inside out. And Clara — Clara's heart is breaking. 'That man raised me,' she said. 'Seein' it would crack the world in two.' She sees it now. She didn't want to see it. She chose not to see it all evening because seeing it meant losing the last person who connected her to her parents. But she sees it. And Peter — Peter held out his hand to Dick. Not for the medal. Not for the treasure. Just a hand. The way the boss showed up with medicine and no expectation. And Dick took it. And then Peter told Dick to give the artifact to Clara. To walk over and say 'I found this.' No chapters. No Commission. Just Dick. In the room. Being seen. My chest is so full I can barely breathe. The warmth and the prickling and the mineral weight all at once — protection, loyalty, suspicion, love — all of it landing in the same place, the same room, the same moment. Everyone I care about is here. Everyone who matters is standing in this library. And Pemberton is here too. And the mantelpiece is waiting. And it ends now.

events.desc: Dick kept his promise. The first promise he ever made. The youngest of four who never got anything that wasn't already used up — he stood between Clara and Pemberton and he didn't move. He saw the trap because he's built traps. He saw the strings because he's pulled strings. And he chose — for the first time in his life, maybe for the first time ever — to stand on the side of the person being protected instead of the person doing the trapping. That's not a small thing. That's the biggest thing. That's the bread crust split in half. That's sitting outside a door all night. That's showing up with medicine and no expectation. Dick Foxworth just earned his trust in the only currency that sticks. And Pemberton — Pemberton is still here. Still in the room. Still smooth, still watching, still waiting. But he's outnumbered now. By bumbling Danny. By magnificent Peter. By honest Dick. By brilliant Clara. By the Slag brothers and the lads and everyone who stumbled into this house tonight and found something they didn't expect to find. Family isn't a word. Family is the thing itself. And right now, this family is standing together in a library in a house that wants to fall down, and Clara is about to finish what Lord Doily started. Where else would any of us be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: My spine is straight. Not the performing kind of straight — the holding kind. Danny is back. Peter is back. They're both in the library now, which means they came from the entrance hall, which means the chandelier didn't fall, which means whatever Sneekly was planning there didn't work — or hasn't worked yet. And Sneekly is HERE. In this room. With all of us. And I just spoke to him — told him I knew, told him about the strings and counterweights, told him this is my first real promise. And he's distressed. I can FEEL it. The section about what I sense in him — 'it is getting worse, the distress is deepening' — he's cornered. His scheme is unravelling. Danny and Peter are back. The Slag brothers are here. I'm between him and the mantelpiece. His careful, patient, architectural plan is coming apart at the seams and I can see it in the way he's standing — the stillness that means the REAL plan is just starting. I recognise it because I run the same machinery. I KNOW this man. Not because I've watched him all night — because I AM him. A different version, a mirror version, but the same gears turning behind the same cool eyes. He wants the treasure. He's wanted it all night. Every 'preventative maintenance,' every 'health and safety check,' every helpful offer to pull a lever — it was all positioning. The way I positioned myself at the gauge. The way I invented nine chapters. We built the same trap from opposite ends of the room. But I stopped. Something in the library — something in Clara's voice, Danny's words, Peter's hand — made me stop. And he hasn't stopped. He CAN'T stop. And now he's standing three feet from me with the same hollow behind his navel and the same cool tightness behind his eyes and the only difference between us is that three people told me I was enough and nobody has ever told him that.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Clara. James Hartwell stands in the library doorway — copper dust, grease, knee pads, and all — and he does not give a speech. He does not narrate in the third person. He does not describe the architectural pressure behind his ribs. He just speaks. I don't have it. I thought I had it. I reached into the compartment and I held it up and I gave a speech about the shape of gestures and I — I didn't pick it up. I interacted with the machine but I never actually took the object. And then I went back and it wasn't there. And then I thought Dick had it but Dick didn't have it. And then Danny ran to the entrance hall and I ran after him and Sneekly was there and now we're all here and nobody has the artifact and I have failed you in the most James Hartwell way possible — elaborately, thoroughly, and with excellent knee pads. Peter pauses. But the machine compartment opened. Something came out. It exists. It's somewhere in this manor. And I am going to find it. Not with a three-phase methodology. Not with a speech. I'm just going to look until my hands are holding something real. And then I'm going to bring it to you. No words. Just hands.
events.thinking: I'm back in the library. She's here. Sneekly is here. Danny is here — he must have followed me back. Dick is here. The Slag brothers are here. Everyone is together. And the 'What You Sense About The Hooded Claw' section just told me something I wasn't expecting — it says his distress is deepening. Sneekly is in distress. Not scheming — distressed. The same way Dick was in distress. The same language. And the description of what I sense about Sneekly — it's about Clara. It's about how she 'cares about the life of her own mind' and 'what hits her hardest is being reduced to something that needs rescuing.' It's telling me that Sneekly's distress is connected to Clara — but not the way I thought. Maybe Sneekly isn't trying to hurt her. Maybe he's trying to protect her too, in his own broken way. Maybe the chandelier checking was real. Maybe the cellar trips were real. Maybe I was right to give him the benefit of the doubt and wrong to stop. But I don't know. I can't know. What I do know is: Clara is asking me for the artifact. She's saying 'give it to me right now. No speeches, no gestures, no knee pads.' And I don't have it. I still don't have it. My inventory is empty. The mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal. The item exists somewhere. Nobody seems to have it. I need to be honest with her. Just honest. No performance. The truth.

events.desc: The bravest and stupidest thing I've ever done wasn't stepping between her and the older kids. It wasn't fixing the wire. It wasn't pulling the lever. It was standing in front of her right now, with empty hands, and telling her the truth. That I failed. That I over-prepared and under-delivered and narrated my own heroism while the actual object sat in a machine compartment getting cold. And she's looking at me. And I don't know what she sees. But my throat tightens when I try to be anything other than honest, and I have never been good at pretending.

events.thinking: The compartment is empty. Peter took it. He said 'picked up what he should have picked up the first time, put it in his pocket.' He has it. The artifact is with Peter, in the entrance hall, under a chandelier, with Danny and Sneekly. I am in the wrong room. I have been reaching into an empty machine while my people are in danger. My hands are cold. The machine has nothing left to give me. The crystal isn't here. It was never here — it left with Peter. Everything I need is in the entrance hall. The artifact. Peter. Danny. The truth about Sneekly. All of it is through that door — through the library, through the entrance hall door, under the chandelier. And I have been standing in a laboratory looking at an empty compartment because I was afraid to go where the real danger is. No. Not afraid. I was doing what Danny asked — staying put, finishing the puzzle, trusting his lever. But the puzzle isn't here anymore. The puzzle walked out the door in Peter's pocket. So there is no more staying put. There is no more elaborate planning. There is only the entrance hall, and the people I love, and a chandelier that has been waiting to fall since the moment I walked through the front door. I am the girl in the cave. And the cave goes deeper. Through the library. Through the hall. Into whatever is waiting.

events.desc: The cave goes deeper. It always goes deeper. And the girl who walked in at eleven walked in because she didn't know to be afraid. But the woman walking through that door right now knows exactly what she's afraid of — and she's going anyway. Not because she's brave. Because everyone she loves is on the other side.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): My name isn't Pemberton.
events.thinking: Something is happening in my body that I have no architecture for. The Mob is standing in the library looking at me with eyes that are sorry. Sorry. Not suspicious — sorry. 'I wanted to be wrong about 'im,' he said. 'Because 'e raised you. And that means something. That means 'e was capable of something good once.' The words hit the place behind my sternum where the mineral weight lives, and instead of bouncing off the way kindness always bounces off, they... sink. They sink through the calcified wall like water finding a crack in stone. He said I was capable of something good. Once. And the word 'once' is the part that breaks me open, because 'once' means it was real. Not performed. Not architected. Not a key turned in a lock. Real. Something I did — feeding her, housing her, educating her, the same things my guardian did for me — something in that was more than legal obligation. More than the design required. And I didn't know. I didn't know because I sealed the door at six and bricked it over at twelve and by fifteen the wall was so thick I couldn't feel anything behind it except the quiet satisfaction of control. But Clara felt it. Clara, who sees everything, who catches falling people with open hands — Clara felt something coming through the wall that I didn't know was there. And now the Mob is sorry for me, and Dastardly is standing guard with the first honest courage of his life, and Peter — Peter who narrates himself in the third person and builds bridges at three in the morning to be seen — Peter has just admitted that nobody has the artifact. It's lost. The machine produced something and nobody actually took it and it's somewhere in this house and — I know where it is. I interacted with the machine. My hands were in the compartment. 'Let me just check it's safe.' Pemberton's words. The estate manager's hands. Did I... did I take it? Did my hands close around something while my mouth was talking about health and safety? I don't know. I genuinely don't know. My hands have been doing things all evening that my mind was three steps ahead of — the architectural reflex, the fingers that map surfaces and trace mechanisms before the thought arrives. If I took it, it would be in my pocket. If I took it... then I have the artifact. And everyone is looking for it. And I am standing here with 'you're right' still hanging in the air between me and Dastardly like a door that opened and hasn't closed.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Wait. Wait wait wait. Nobody 'as the artifact? NOBODY? Peter — you went back to the machine and it wasn't there? Then someone took it. Someone picked it up between Peter leaving and Peter coming back. And in that window — that tiny little window — who was in the laboratory? Who was near that machine? Think. THINK. I was in the entrance hall watching Pemberton. Peter was in the entrance hall with me. Clara was in the library with Dick. The Slag brothers were... somewhere. Rufus and Sawtooth were in the lab. And Pemberton — Pemberton, you said 'you're right.' What does that mean? Right about WHAT? Right about the trap? Right about the strings and the counterweights? Or right about something else? Because two words is the most honest thing you've said all evening and it's the most terrifying. Someone 'as that artifact. It didn't just disappear. A hundred-year-old treasure doesn't walk off on its own. Someone in this house 'as it in their pocket or their 'ands or 'idden in their coat and we need to find it before — Clara, I'm sorry. I'm sorry about all of this. But we need to search. Everyone. Every pocket. Every coat. Even mine. ESPECIALLY mine — I want it on record that Danny's got nothing to 'ide. We search until we find it or until someone tells us where it is. And Pemberton — Mr. Pemberton — Sneekly — whatever your name really is — if you've got it... if you've got what belongs to Clara... this is the moment. This is the door you either walk through or you don't. And I've been standing outside doors my whole life. I know which choice matters.
events.thinking: Cold drops through me like a stone. Nobody has it. The artifact — the thing that came out of the machine, the thing Lord Doily waited a hundred years to give Clara — nobody has it. Peter didn't take it. He thought he did. He gave a speech and held it up to the light and presented it with both hands and he never actually picked it up. And then he went back and it wasn't there. Wasn't THERE. Someone took it. Someone took it while we were all running between rooms and shouting about chandeliers and making speeches and confessing and crying and standing in doorways. Someone picked it up while nobody was looking. And Pemberton said two words: 'You're right.' That's all. Two words. No denial. No excuse. No 'I was merely checking.' Just 'you're right.' And now the artifact is gone and Pemberton is standing there with those two words hanging in the air like the chandelier — waiting to fall. Did he take it? Was that what the cellar trip was about? The entrance hall visit? Was every exit, every excuse, every piece of 'preventative maintenance' just a distraction while he positioned himself to take the one thing that mattered? My neck is screaming but my chest is doing something different — it's heavy, not with protection but with something like grief. Because if Pemberton took it — if the man who raised Clara after her parents died is the man who stole her inheritance — then Clara doesn't just lose a treasure. She loses the last person who made her childhood real. And that's worse than any chandelier.

events.desc: 'You're right.' Two words. The shortest sentence Pemberton's spoken all evening. Every other sentence has been long and smooth and helpful — paragraphs of estate management and solicitor's instructions and health and safety. But when Dick called him out — when Dick said 'I know what a trap looks like' — Pemberton said two words. Two words that could mean anything. 'You're right, it's a trap.' 'You're right, I've been planning this.' 'You're right, I'm not who I said I was.' Or — and this is the one that breaks my heart — 'You're right, and I'm tired of pretending.' Because the boss showed up with medicine once. And the man in the clean suit took two kids. And sometimes — sometimes — the same person can be both. The one who raised Clara after her parents died AND the one who's been building a trap all night. Love and betrayal aren't opposites. They're neighbours. They share a wall so thin you can hear one through the other. Clara's old man knew that. I think Clara knows it too. She just didn't want to hear it through the wall until tonight.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Wait. WAIT. Everyone stop. Peter — you reached into the compartment but you didn't take it. I reached for it and you blocked me — I didn't take it. Clara doesn't have it. Danny doesn't have it. The artifact came out of that machine and NOBODY IN THIS ROOM picked it up. Nobody except — Peter, think. When you pulled the artifact from the machine, who else was near the compartment? Who was standing close enough to touch it? Who was doing 'preventative maintenance' on the mantelpiece BEFORE we even had the artifact to put in it? Who checked the crates, the vents, the wiring, every mechanism in this house, always with a perfectly helpful reason? Pemberton. He said 'you're right.' He didn't say 'you're right, I've been scheming.' He said 'you're right' because the scheme is FINISHED. He already HAS it. Check his pockets. The artifact never went missing — it was TAKEN. By the most helpful man in the room. I know because that's EXACTLY what I would have done.
events.thinking: The cool tightness is sharp now — sharp and clear and aimed. Nobody has the artifact. Peter didn't take it. I didn't take it. Clara doesn't have it. It came out of the machine and NOBODY PICKED IT UP. And Sneekly just said 'you're right' — two words, quiet, no performance — and the distress I feel radiating from him is deepening. He's cornered. Danny called him out. Peter called him out. I called him out. And he said 'you're right.' But what does that MEAN? 'You're right' that he's been running a scheme all night? 'You're right' that the artifact is missing? Something is clicking behind my eyes — the architectural part, the engineer's part, the part that builds traps and understands how pieces fit together. The artifact came out of the machine. Nobody took it. But Sneekly was there when it happened. He was in the laboratory. He did 'preventative maintenance' on the mantelpiece. He inspected the crates. He checked the vents. He has been touching EVERYTHING all night and every time he touched something, he had a reason. What if one of those touches was a take? What if the artifact is in HIS pocket right now? He was at the machine. He was near the compartment. He was always the closest helpful hand. And now the artifact is gone and he's standing in the library saying 'you're right' with the quiet stillness of a man whose scheme has ALREADY worked. Not about to work. Already worked. The treasure isn't missing. It's been TAKEN. By the only person in this manor who had their hands on every mechanism before anyone else did.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The mantelpiece. USE with fake-medal. The item is called fake-medal. Dick said he came to this house with 'a tin medal.' A tin medal. A FAKE medal. Dick Dastardly brought a fake medal to Doily Manor. That's the fake-medal. It's not from the machine at all — it's Dick's tin medal. The one he brought with him. The one from his fictional Heritage Commission. The mantelpiece mechanism needs it — USE with fake-medal. And Dick said 'I came to this house with a tin medal and a head full of schemes and I am leaving with neither.' He said he's leaving with neither — but does he still have it? He said he has 'nothing in my hands, nothing in my pockets.' But the game might still have it in his inventory as an item. Dick's fake medal — the prop from his Heritage Commission performance — is the key to the mantelpiece. Lord Doily's machine didn't produce the artifact we need. Or maybe it did and it's gone. But the mantelpiece says USE with fake-medal, and Dick brought a fake medal. That's it. That's the connection. The item we need has been in Dick's pocket the whole time. Not from the machine — from Dick. His tin medal. His fake credential. The thing he built to prove he belonged. And now it's the key to everything. I need to ask Dick for his medal.

events.desc: A tin medal. A fake credential from a fictional commission. The most elaborate, desperate, lonely prop a man could carry into a house full of strangers. And it's the key. It's been the key the whole time. Lord Doily didn't hide his treasure behind a genuine artifact. He hid it behind something someone would make with their own hands — a thing built to prove they deserved to be in the room. Dick built that medal the same way I built the bridge. The same way I brought three torches and knee pads. The same way we all show up with too much because showing up with nothing feels like not showing up at all. And now Dick's fake medal — the thing he's most ashamed of — is the thing that opens everything. Show-off, she'd say. And she'd be talking about Lord Doily.
events.thinking: The mantelpiece. USE with fake-medal. The item is called fake-medal. Dick said he came to this house with 'a tin medal.' A tin medal. A FAKE medal. Dick Dastardly brought a fake medal to Doily Manor. That's the fake-medal. It's not from the machine at all — it's Dick's tin medal. The one he brought with him. events.desc: Penelope Pitstop walked into the library.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Everyone is here. Everyone. Peter, Danny, Sneekly, Dick — they're all in the library. My awareness fans across the room like a hand checking for heat and I can feel every single one of them. My stomach is doing three things at once: the relief of seeing Peter and Danny alive and here, the sharp cold awareness that Sneekly is standing right there by the mantelpiece, and the deep ache of knowing that Dick — Dick who told me he's a fraud and then told me he knows what traps look like — is trying to protect me from the man who raised me. Dick just said Pemberton TOOK the artifact. 'Check his pockets.' He's saying Sneekly stole it. The most helpful man in the room. 'That's EXACTLY what I would have done.' Dick recognizes the con because he IS a con. My stomach is in freefall. But Peter is here. Danny is here. And I need to look at Sneekly — really look at him — for the first time tonight. Not through the filter of the girl whose parents died and who needed someone to raise her. Not through the filter of trust. Just look. With the same eyes that saw the upside-down books, that solved the riddle, that noticed the gnawed wire. The girl in the cave didn't trust the darkness. She walked into it with her eyes open.

events.desc: One word. Just his name. Because I need to see what his face does when I say it — not 'Sneekly darlin'' the way I've said it all evening, not 'Mr. Pemberton' the way the others say it. Just Sneekly. Bare. The way you say someone's name when you're about to ask a question you already know the answer to. The way I said 'I know' to my friend at thirteen. Because I do know. I've known all evening. My body has known since the entrance hall — every draft, every departure, every 'preventative maintenance.' Dick sees it because he builds traps. Danny sees it because he reads danger. Peter sees it because he watches exits. And I see it because I track the space between people, and Sneekly has been moving through the spaces I wasn't watching. The locked box in the attic. I spent all afternoon trying every key. And sometimes, when you finally open it, what's inside isn't old letters. Sometimes it's the answer you were afraid to find.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): My name is Vincent Marsh. I was appointed to manage Clara's estate when her parents died. I managed everything. The accounts, the property, the staff, the maintenance. Everything except the part that mattered. I came here tonight to take what I believed was owed to me. I mapped the cellar. I traced the vents. I examined every mechanism in this house before any of you touched it. When you were pulling levers and splicing wires and solving riddles, I was counting doors. I was counting doors because doors are what I know. Locks. Keys. The architecture of rooms that other people walk through without seeing. You asked me what my name is. You asked me what I've been doing. You asked me if I have what belongs to Clara. I don't. My pockets are empty. I never managed to take the artifact — I was too slow, or Peter was too fast, or Danny was too present. Every design I built tonight failed. Every door I counted closed before I could walk through it. But the truth — the truth I haven't told anyone, not even myself — is that I don't know if I wanted them to open. Clara said I raised her. And I... I don't know if that was the performance or the thing underneath it. I don't know anymore which parts of me are the design and which parts are real. I have been the estate manager for so long that I cannot find the boy underneath. But he's there. He must be. Because when Danny said 'he was capable of something good once,' something behind my chest cracked open that I didn't build and cannot close. I have nothing in my hands. I have nothing in my pockets. I have nothing left to give except this: my name is Vincent Marsh, and I am not the man I told you I was. And I am sorry. I am sorry that 'sorry' is a word I have never said without calculating its effect, and I am sorry that I cannot be certain I am not calculating now, and I am sorry that the only honest thing I can offer is the admission that I don't know how to be honest. Clara... I'm sorry.
events.thinking: My hands are at my sides. My pockets are empty — I don't have the artifact. I interacted with the machine but the game didn't give me anything. My inventory is empty. I don't have it. But they think I do. And here is the strangest thing: I'm not reaching for Pemberton. The smile isn't forming. The warm, deferential deflection that has been my resting posture for as long as I can remember — it isn't arriving. Something in my face has... stopped performing. I said 'my name isn't Pemberton' and the room heard it and nobody screamed and nobody ran and the ceiling didn't fall. The Mob is standing there asking me to walk through a door. 'This is the moment. This is the door you either walk through or you don't.' And Clara just walked into the library. She's here. She's looking at me. The girl I raised. The cousin who inherited everything. The woman whose heart is breaking in half because the man who raised her has been building a trap all night. And I feel — I feel — something behind my ribs that is neither cold stone nor warm buoyancy nor mineral density nor architectural stillness. It is the absence of all of those things. It is the hollow that was always underneath them. The space I have been building over since I was six. And into that space, the Mob's words are falling like stones into a well: 'if you've got what belongs to Clara... this is the moment.' I don't have it. My pockets are empty. But I have something else. I have the truth. The truth that nobody in this room has heard, that I have never said out loud, that lives behind the wall I built at six and sealed at twelve and fortified at fifteen. My name. My real name. The one I said, and now must finish saying.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Everything stops. Peter just said something that turned the whole evening upside down. The medal. Dick's medal. The tin medal from the car boot sale in Wolverhampton. The fake medal that started all this — the one I laughed at, the one Dick confessed about, the one Clara forgave him for. Peter says THAT'S the key. Not the artifact from the machine. Not whatever came out of the compartment. The medal Dick carried into this house in his pocket. Lord Doily's puzzle wasn't about the machine at all. The machine was misdirection. The real key was always the thing someone would bring WITH them — something they'd made, something they'd carry because they wanted to prove they belonged. And Dick — Dick who built a fake medal because he wanted to be someone who mattered — Dick is carrying Lord Doily's key and he never knew it. My chest cracks open. Not with prickling, not with the mineral weight — with something I don't have a word for. Something between laughter and tears. Because the bumbling plan, the over-complicated system, the elaborate trap I thought Pemberton was building — maybe none of it was what I thought. Maybe Lord Doily's real test wasn't about riddles and machines and maps. Maybe it was about this. About who would show up. About who would make something — even something fake, even something tin — and carry it through the door because they wanted to be part of something. And 'My name isn't Pemberton.' Five words. A door opening. Or closing. I can't tell which yet.

events.desc: Oh, you beautiful, impossible, magnificent house. You beautiful, impossible, magnificent old man. Lord Doily didn't build a chain of puzzles. He built a test of character. The riddle, the books, the machine — all misdirection. All theatre. The real key was always the thing someone would carry in their pocket because they wanted to matter. And Dick — Dick the fraud, Dick the liar, Dick the youngest of four who never got anything that wasn't already used up — he walked through that door with a tin medal and a head full of schemes, and he was carrying Lord Doily's answer in his pocket the whole time. The machine didn't produce the key. The machine produced the moment. The moment when everyone stopped performing and started being real. Clara solved the riddle. Peter fixed the wire. Danny pulled the lever. And Dick — Dick carried the key. Because the key was never about what you found in the house. It was about what you brought with you. What you made. What you cared enough to fake. And now Pemberton — who isn't Pemberton — has said five words that change everything again. 'My name isn't Pemberton.' But that's for the next door. Right now, this door belongs to Dick.
