The Foxworth Master Plan. Not his finest hour, but his first hour. And every hour after it was better. That's it, isn't it? That's the whole evening in one sentence. Everyone walked through that door with their worst self leading — Dick with his lies, Vincent with his schemes, Peter with his armor, Danny with his fear, me with my trust that refused to see. And every hour after was better. Because the house cracked us open. Lord Doily's magnificent, crumbling, impossible house. Everyone is talking to each other now. Vincent spoke to Danny. Danny spoke to Peter. Peter spoke to Dick. The conversations are flowing between them without me as the bridge. I don't need to be the bridge anymore. The bridge built itself. And I'm sitting in a leather chair that creaks when I breathe, watching it happen, and my chest is so full it could burst, and I have no plan for what happens next, and it feels exactly right.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I also owe Lord Doily an apology. There was never a reading of the will. I invented it to make everyone stay the night. The solicitor doesn't know any of you are here. I told Clara the mantelpiece was seventeenth century. I have no idea when it was carved. I said the groundskeeper mentioned the machine hadn't been activated since 1923. There was no groundskeeper. I made it all up. Every helpful fact. Every piece of estate manager expertise. Every reassuring smile. All of it. Architecture without foundation. The only true thing I said all evening was my name. And I didn't say that until everyone had already stopped believing in me.
events.thinking: Clara told me to come sit closer. 'Not because I need you to. Because the floor near the fire is warmer.' She noticed where I was sitting. She noticed I was by the door. And she invited me closer — not to the chair, not to the position of authority, but to the warmer spot on the floor. The warmer board. The one I mapped. She knows I mapped every board in this library, and instead of being frightened by that — by the man who mapped her house to use against her — she turned it into something kind. 'A man who mapped every board deserves to sit on the warmest one.' She took the thing I built to hurt her and made it a reason to invite me nearer. That is either the most naive thing anyone has ever done or the bravest. And I — sitting here on the floor with Dick beside me and the dust in my eyes — I don't know which. But I know that my shoulders didn't tighten when she said it. For the first time. When someone was kind, my shoulders didn't tighten. They stayed where they were. On the floor. In the room. With the dust settling. And Dick is confessing about the kitchen — 'there was never any hidden compartment beneath the wood-burning stove. I made the whole thing up.' And I am sitting next to him thinking: I made things up too. Every word of Pemberton was made up. Every smile, every 'health and safety,' every 'I shan't be long.' All of it constructed. All of it architecture. And now the architecture is gone and I am sitting on a floor I mapped, next to a man who bought a medal he needed, in a room with a woman who called me by my name and told me to come closer. And my shoulders are still. And my jaw is loose. And I am not planning anything. And I am not sleeping the deep dreamless sleep of a finished design. I am just... awake. In a room. With people. And the floor is warm near the fire.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: A laugh. Small, real, the kind that starts in the belly and doesn't ask permission. Dick just confessed about the kitchen. 'There was never any hidden compartment beneath the wood-burning stove. I made the whole thing up.' And I — I KNEW. I knew from the first second. I said 'hidden compartment under the stove, my aunt Fanny. That's the oldest trick in the book.' I said it in the entrance hall a hundred years ago — twenty minutes ago — when I was splitting up the lads and trying to sound like I knew what I was doing. And I was right. For once, Danny was right about something on the first try. Not about the chandelier — that turned out to be fine. Not about the wrench — that was never important. Not about the artifact — that was misdirection. But about the kitchen. About the stove. About the oldest trick in the book. Danny of the Brixton Boys, who can't articulate what his neck is telling him, who says everything badly and plans everything too elaborately and trips over every reading chair in every library — Danny knew the kitchen was bollocks from minute one. And Vincent just told me the chandelier chain is fine. Third link rusted, other five sound. He checked it. Really checked it — not 'preventative maintenance' checked, actually checked. And he told me. Because that's what you do when you're starting to mean the sorry you're not sure you meant. You give people the truth they were afraid to ask for. Five sound links. That's enough. That's always been enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The dust is settling. The chair is holding. Danny says the chandelier is still hanging — holding on by stubbornness and dust. Like all of us. And Dick just confessed about the kitchen — there was never a hidden compartment. He made the whole thing up. The Foxworth Master Plan. And he's laughing about it, the way I'm laughing about the knee pads. We're all sitting in our confessions now, wearing them like dust. And my chest is doing the new thing — not the steel plate, not the hunger, not the warmth across the shoulders. The quiet thing. The settled thing. The thing that has no name because it doesn't need one. Like my father's expression after the race. Like the handshake on the country road. Like the beetle in the lunch box. Things that are too real for words. Things that just are. I'm in a reading chair in a dusty library with copper dust in my hair and the woman I've loved since I was eight sitting beside me and a room full of people who showed up. My hands are still. My face hurts. And the dust is settling.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Architecture without foundation. That's what he said. And my body doesn't clench. It doesn't. Something has changed in me tonight — the place where the dinner-table sickness used to live has softened into something quieter. Not acceptance exactly. More like recognition. Vincent lied about everything. Dick lied about everything. And the only true thing either of them said was the thing that came last — their names, their natures, the raw admission that they don't know which parts of themselves are real. And here I am, sitting in a chair, listening to another confession, and my stomach is quiet. Not because I've stopped caring. Because I've stopped needing the room to be whole before I can breathe. The room isn't whole. It never was. It's cracked and dusty and full of liars and frauds and a man with knee pads and a boy who stands in doorways. And it's the most beautiful room I've ever been in. Dick is still in distress. The system keeps telling me. But Dick's distress isn't the kind I can fix by moving toward it. Dick's distress is the distress of being held for the first time — the ache of a locked box that finally opened and found something inside it didn't expect. That kind of ache needs time, not tending. It needs the floor to be sound underneath him. And it is. Vincent checked.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Something settles. Not the prickling. Not the warmth. Something older. Vincent just confessed everything. No will reading. No groundskeeper. No seventeenth-century mantelpiece. All of it invented. All of it architecture without foundation. And the only true thing he said was his name — and he didn't say that until everyone had already stopped believing in him. And I'm sitting on this floor, leaning against these upside-down books, with Dick beside me and the lads around me and Clara closing her eyes in a reading chair, and I should be angry. I should be furious. My neck should be screaming. But it isn't. Because Vincent just did the thing Dick did. The thing Peter did. The thing Lord Doily's house made all of us do. He stopped. He just... stopped. Stopped performing. Stopped building architecture. Stopped being the estate manager and became the boy underneath. And the boy underneath said 'the only true thing I said all evening was my name.' And that's... that's enough. That's the bread crust. That's the medicine. That's the door you sit outside all night. One true thing. Said late. Said badly. Said after everyone's already been hurt by the lies. But said. And the saying changes you whether you mean it or not. Five sound links on the chandelier. One true name from Vincent Marsh. It's enough. It's always been enough.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Vincent. Welcome to the floor. The dust is excellent. Very Victorian. Very honest. It doesn't pretend to be anything other than what it is — a hundred years of everything that settled when nobody was watching. Danny, you owe me nothing. But if you're offering fifty pence, I accept. The Foxworth Treasury could use the capital. It's currently running at a deficit of one tin medal and a lifetime of imaginary credentials. Peter — I'll take those spare knee pads. Not for the landing. For tomorrow. When I'll need something to kneel on while I learn how to build things that aren't traps.
events.thinking: Something loosening. Something final. Vincent just confessed everything — the reading of the will was fake, the solicitor doesn't know, the groundskeeper never existed. Architecture without foundation. His words. And I'm sitting on the floor hearing it and something in my chest isn't tightening — it's loosening. Because he sounds like me. He sounds exactly like me. An hour ago. Before Clara said 'that's enough.' Before Danny said 'where else would you be.' Before Peter said 'show-off.' He sounds like a man standing in a room full of people who know what he is and don't know yet whether they'll keep him. And I know — I KNOW — what that moment feels like. The moment between confession and response. The moment when you've laid every lie on the floor and you're waiting to see if the floor holds or opens. Danny's aunt Fanny held. My fifty pence held. And now Vincent is standing in the same place, having laid down everything — no will reading, no groundskeeper, no expertise, no foundation — and the room is deciding. And I think — I think it's already decided. Because Clara closed her eyes and said 'where else would I be.' And she didn't open them again to exclude anyone. The 'I' included everyone in the room. Even the man who invented the will reading. Even the estate manager who was never an estate manager. Even the youngest of four who showed up with a tin medal and left without it. We're all sitting in the dust now. Every single one of us is architecture without foundation. And the dust is holding us up.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent just confessed everything. No reading of the will. No solicitor. No groundskeeper. No seventeenth-century mantelpiece. All of it — every helpful fact, every reassuring piece of expertise — invented. Architecture without foundation. And the only true thing he said all evening was his name. And he didn't say it until everyone had already stopped believing in him. I should feel the prickle. I should feel the steel plate. But I don't. I feel the warmth across the shoulders — my father's hands, settling. Because Vincent just did the hardest thing any of us has done tonight. Harder than fixing the wire. Harder than pulling the lever. Harder than standing in the doorframe. He stood in front of a room full of people who had every reason to hate him and he said: all of it was a lie. Every single piece. And he didn't dress it up. He didn't make it smaller. He didn't calculate. He just said it. Architecture without foundation. That's what he built. And now he's sitting on the floor of a dusty library, without a foundation, without architecture, without anything except his name. And he's more real than he's ever been. Like all of us. Like Dick without his commission. Like Danny without his posturing. Like me without my third person. Like Clara without her certainty. We're all sitting in our rubble now. And the rubble is the treasure. That's what Lord Doily knew.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Tomorrow. Dick just said tomorrow. Y'all hear that? He's thinkin' about tomorrow. That means this isn't endin'. That means whatever we found tonight — whatever Lord Doily hid in this house — it isn't somethin' you put in a glass case and walk away from. It's somethin' you carry with you. Into tomorrow. Into every room you walk into after this one. Peter, you're goin' to keep fixin' wires. Danny, you're goin' to keep standin' in doorways. Dick, you're goin' to learn how to build instead of trap. Vincent, you're goin' to find the boy underneath. And Clara Bellingham is goin' to keep walkin' into caves. Where else would any of us be?
events.thinking: Dick said 'for tomorrow.' Tomorrow. He's thinking about tomorrow. He's thinking about what comes after this evening, after this room, after this dust. He wants to learn how to build things that aren't traps. And he wants Peter's knee pads to kneel on while he does it. My chest is doing something it hasn't done all evening — it's not pulling in any direction. Not toward the gap, not toward the puzzle, not toward the person who needs tending. It's just full. Resting. The way a held breath releases not because you decided to let it go but because the thing you were holding it for finally arrived. Everyone is talking to Vincent now. Danny spoke to him. Dick welcomed him to the floor. Peter spoke to him. The circle expanded to include the man who tried to steal from it. And I didn't bridge it. I didn't plan it. I didn't make a twelve-step strategy for the rehabilitation of Vincent Marsh. I just said 'come sit closer' and the room did the rest. The room that Lord Doily built. The room full of people who are more real now than they were when they walked through the door. My eyes are closing. The leather is warm. Peter is beside me. The dust is settling. And I do declare — I have had the most delightful adventure of my entire life.

events.desc: The dust is settling. The house is quiet. And somewhere in a mantelpiece in a library in a crumbling manor, a fifty-pence tin medal from Wolverhampton sits in a slot it was never meant to fit — and fits perfectly. I do declare. Where else would I be?
events.thinking: Dick said 'for tomorrow.' Tomorrow. He's thinking about tomorrow. He's thinking about what comes after this evening, after this room, after this dust. He wants to learn how to build things that aren't traps. And he wants Peter's knee pads to kneel on while he does it. My chest is doing something it hasn't done all evening — it's not pulling in any direction. Not toward the gap, not toward the puzzle, not toward the person who needs tending. It's just full. Resting. The way a held breath releases not because you decided to let it go but because the thing you were holding it for finally arrived. Everyone is talking to Vincent now. Danny spoke to him. Dick welcomed him to the floor. Peter spoke to him. The circle expanded to include the man who tried to steal from it. And I didn't bridge it. I didn't plan it. I didn't make a twelve-step strategy for the rehabilitation of Vincent Marsh. I just said 'come sit closer' and the room did the rest. The room that Lord Doily built. The room full of people who are more real now than they were when they walked through the door. My eyes are closing. The leather is warm. Peter is beside me. The dust is settling. And I do declare — I have had the most delightful adventure of my entire life.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Thank you. For the floor.
events.thinking: Peter said 'foundation without architecture is a room full of people sitting in dust, telling each other their real names. And that holds.' Danny said 'the floor is sound. You checked it yourself. Sit on it. Stay.' Clara said 'the architecture was fake. The people were real. And the people held.' And Dick said 'welcome to the floor.' I am on the floor. The warm board. The one near the fire. The one Clara told me to sit on. And three people just told me — in three different ways, in three different voices — that the thing I thought had no value is the only thing that holds. My name. The foundation. The true thing underneath the architecture. And I am sitting in it. In the dust. In the warmth. In the room with people who know what I am and are staying anyway. Not because they forgive me — Danny said that, clearly, 'not yet, not tonight' — but because the floor holds. And I checked it. And they trust my checking even though they don't trust my smiling. That is — that is the strangest gift I have ever received. They trust my competence while refusing my performance. They accept the mapping while rejecting the manipulation. They want Vincent's hands — the ones that know every board and every joint — without wanting Pemberton's smile. Nobody has ever wanted that before. Nobody has ever said 'the thing you do well is real, even though the person you pretend to be is not.' And sitting here, with the warm board beneath me and the cool leather of the books against my shoulder and Dick's welcome ringing in the dust-filled air, I feel something I have never felt. Not the deep dreamless sleep. Not the architectural satisfaction. Not the cold patience or the warm buoyancy or the mineral weight. Something new. Something that has no hallway attached to it. Something that sits exactly where it is, on a floor that holds, and doesn't reach for the next door.

events.desc: Danny closes his eyes. Leans his head back against the upside-down books. Lets the dust settle. Lets the house settle. Lets everything settle — the prickling, the warmth, the mineral weight, the arterial heat, the rope in his gut, the bread in his chest, the medicine on the table, the shoes on the smaller kid's feet, the door he sat outside, the door he'll sit outside again, tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow, because that's what Danny does. Danny stays. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: Warm. Just warm. The dust is settling on my shoulders and Muttley's breathing is steady against my knee and Clara's eyes are closed in the reading chair and Peter's hands are still on the armrests and Dick is talking about spare knee pads and tomorrow and learning to build things that aren't traps. Tomorrow. He said tomorrow. Like there's going to be one. Like this isn't an evening that ends — it's one that begins something. And my body — my body that has spent the last twenty-five minutes in a state of constant vigilance, scanning exits, watching hands, reading the seams in smiles, calculating the distance between Clara and every door in every room — my body has stopped. Not stopped the way it stops before danger. Stopped the way it stops when the older kid says 'You're still here?' Stopped because it's arrived. Because the arithmetic is done. Because the bread has been split and the medicine has been delivered and the beating has been taken and the shoes are safe and the door has been sat outside all night and morning has come. Morning always comes. And when it does, you're still there. You're still here. On the floor. In the dust. With the family you didn't choose and didn't earn and couldn't leave if your body let you. Which it won't. Where else would you be.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Stillness. Deep, settled stillness. The kind my hands make when the bridge holds weight. Dick wants the spare knee pads. Not for tonight — for tomorrow. For learning how to build things that aren't traps. He said 'tomorrow.' That word — tomorrow — means he's staying. He's not leaving. He's not disappearing into the night with a tin medal and a head full of regret. He's staying. And he wants knee pads for the kneeling. And something in my chest releases — a tension I hadn't known I was carrying. The same release from the engineering competition. The same quiet heat. Because Dick asking for knee pads means something real is going to be built tomorrow. Not by me. By him. And the knee pads I brought — the ridiculous, over-prepared, overly elaborate knee pads that I packed because I planned for everything except having feelings — are exactly what he needs. Not for a treasure hunt. For learning. For starting over. For kneeling down and building something real for the first time. And that — that is the most useful thing three torches, a compass, a first-aid kit, rope, knee pads, and an Encyclopaedia Britannica have ever been.

events.desc: One likes to be useful. There it is again. The old phrase. But it sounds different now. Not like a man trying to prove something. Like a man who already has. Show-off. Always.
events.thinking: Stillness. Deep, settled stillness. The kind my hands make when the bridge holds weight. Dick wants the spare knee pads. Not for tonight — for tomorrow. For learning how to build things that aren't traps. He said 'tomorrow.' That word — tomorrow — means he's staying. He's not leaving. He's not disappearing into the night with a tin medal and a head full of regret. He's staying. And he wants knee pads for the kneeling. And something in my chest releases — a tension I hadn't known I was carrying. The same release from the engineering competition. The same quiet heat. Because Dick asking for knee pads means something real is going to be built tomorrow. Not by me. By him. And the knee pads I brought — the ridiculous, over-prepared, overly elaborate knee pads that I packed because I planned for everything except having feelings — are exactly what he needs. Not for a treasure hunt. For learning. For starting over. For kneeling down and building something real for the first time. And that — that is the most useful thing three torches, a compass, a first-aid kit, rope, knee pads, and an Encyclopaedia Britannica have ever been.

events.desc: Thank you. For the floor. That's the Doily Diamond. Right there. Three words from a man who mapped every board and never trusted one to hold him. Until tonight. Until someone said 'come sit closer' and meant it. The girl in the cave found a crystal. The woman in the chair found a floor full of people. The disappointment lasted only a moment. Because what was inside was just old letters. Just love. Just the ordinary, extraordinary evidence that someone was here, and they mattered, and they stayed.
events.thinking: Thank you. For the floor. Three words. The shortest, quietest thing Vincent has said all evening. And the truest. Not 'thank you for forgiving me.' Not 'thank you for letting me stay.' Thank you for the floor. For the invitation to sit on something sound. For the permission to just be here without performing. My eyes are closing. The leather is warm under me. Peter is in the chair beside mine — I can feel him the way you feel sunlight through a window, not looking at it directly but knowing it's there. Danny is somewhere nearby, standing in a doorway or sitting against a wall, watching. Dick is on the floor with his fifty-pence treasury and his plans for tomorrow. Vincent is on the floor with his empty pockets and his three true words. And the house is settling around us the way houses do at night — creaking, sighing, releasing the day's heat into the dark. The dust is settling. My chest is settled. And for the first time since I was seven years old, watching my parents argue across a dinner table, the warmth behind my ribs is not the ache of something about to break. It's the warmth of something that held.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Still. Everything still. The house is settling around us the way houses do when they've been listened to — creaking, shifting, breathing out a century of held breath. Vincent said 'thank you for the floor.' Three words. The simplest he's said all evening. No architecture. No foundation. Just gratitude for somewhere to sit. And Clara said tomorrow. She said we're carrying this with us. Into every room. Into every doorway. And she's right. She's always right. Tomorrow Danny will stand in a doorway somewhere — not this doorway, maybe not any doorway in this house — but a doorway. Because that's what Danny does. That's what Danny is. And tomorrow Peter will fix something. And Dick will build something real. And Vincent will try to find the boy underneath the estate manager and maybe fail and maybe try again. And Clara will walk into another cave. First. Without looking back. Trusting that someone will follow. And someone will. Someone always will. Because where else would they be.

events.desc: Where else would I be.
events.thinking: Tomorrow. She said tomorrow. And my chest does the thing — the new thing, the settled thing, the thing that has no name because it doesn't need one. Tomorrow I'll fix wires. Tomorrow Dick will kneel on my knee pads and learn to build. Tomorrow Danny will stand in doorways. Tomorrow Vincent will look for the boy underneath. Tomorrow Clara will walk into caves. And tonight — tonight the dust settles in a library in Doily Manor, and every person in this room is exactly where they are supposed to be. My hands are still. My face hurts from grinning. The chair is holding. The chandelier is hanging. And I am sitting beside the woman I have loved since I was eight years old, in a house built by a man who knew that the only treasure worth hiding is the kind that finds you when you stop looking for it. Where else would I be.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Where else would we be. Danny said it. The last line. The only line that ever mattered. And the room is quiet. Not empty quiet — full quiet. The quiet of a house that held. The dust has settled. The leather is warm. Peter's breathing beside me has slowed to the rhythm of someone who has stopped planning. And my eyes are closing. They're really closing this time. Not because I'm tired — because there's nothing left to do. Nothing left to solve. Nothing left to bridge. Just the warmth behind my ribs, steady as it's ever been, and the sound of people breathing in a room they all chose to stay in. Everyone is still in distress — the system keeps telling me. Peter. Dick. Vincent. All deepening. But I know now what that distress is. It's not the kind that needs fixing. It's the kind that comes from being seen for the first time. From having the armor off and the air on your skin. It aches. It's supposed to ache. That's how you know it's real. I can't fix it. I was never supposed to fix it. I was just supposed to be here. Sitting on a sound floor in a crumbling house with people who showed up carrying whatever they had. Where else would I be.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Where else would we be.
events.thinking: The room is quiet now. Danny said it last. 'Where else would we be.' Not a question. A period. A full stop at the end of an evening that began with me counting doors and ends with me sitting on a floor I mapped, in a room full of people I tried to destroy, listening to the dust settle on my empty hands. The system still says my scheming is at ninety percent. My gloating at seventy. My self-preservation at seventy. My dominance at sixty. It says deception is my resting state. It says I feel nothing where other people feel sympathy. It says closeness is exposure. It says I don't need people. And maybe all of that was true when I walked through the door tonight as Pemberton with his jingling keys and his rehearsed smile and his beautiful, inevitable, architectural design. But I am not Pemberton anymore. And the boy who sealed the door at six is sitting on a warm board in a dusty library, and the door is open, and the people are still here, and nobody asked him to earn it. The dust settles. The chairs creak. Peter's hands are still. Dick is learning about knee pads. Clara's eyes are closed. Danny said 'where else would we be' and it was the last sentence of the evening and it was the truest thing anyone has said in this house, including me, and I am going to let it be the last thing I hear tonight. Not the Pemberton smile. Not the Vincent design. Not the deep dreamless sleep of a finished plan. Just Danny's voice, saying what the boy at school said with his sandwich, what the housekeeper might have meant with her warmth, what my guardian never said but Clara heard anyway through the wall: you are here. You are enough. Where else would you be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Where else would we be. Danny said 'we.' Not 'I.' We. And the room is quiet and the dust is settling and my hands are on the floor and I am not reaching for anything. Not the mantelpiece. Not the medal. Not the treasure. Not the exit. Not the next scheme. Not the next room. Not the next chapter of a handbook that doesn't exist. I am just here. On a floor. In a house. In a room full of people who broke open tonight and chose to stay broken open rather than close back up. And the data says everyone is in distress — Clara, Peter, Danny, Vincent — all of them deepening. But I don't think distress is the right word anymore. I think what the data is reading as distress is actually the feeling of being known. The vulnerability of sitting in a room without armour. The weight of having said true things to people who heard them. It hurts. It's supposed to hurt. The crack is where the light gets in. And the light hurts at first because the room behind the wall has been dark for so long that any brightness feels like too much. But you don't close the wall again. You sit in the light. You let it hurt. You let the dust settle on your open hands. And eventually — not tonight, maybe not tomorrow, but eventually — the brightness stops being pain and starts being warmth. The bread roll in the pocket loosens. The certificate comes off the wall. The boy stops watching from the window and walks outside. Where else would he be.

events.desc: The dust settles. The chair holds. The chandelier hangs. Danny said 'where else would we be.' And my hands are still. And my face hurts. And somewhere in this room, Dick is sitting on the floor learning how to be seen without a costume, and there is nothing I can build for him that will make that easier. The only thing I can do is not leave. The only thing I have ever been able to do — the thing my father showed me, the thing the stranger showed him, the thing Lord Doily hid in a house full of puzzles — is show up. And stay. And let the dust settle. Where else would I be.
events.thinking: Dick's distress hasn't shifted. Whatever I've tried hasn't reached him. Not the hand, not the knee pads, not the words about structural integrity. He's on the floor and he's making jokes about the Foxworth Treasury and spare knee pads, and underneath the jokes he's still the boy at the window watching someone else dig. I can feel it — that pull toward him, not the steel plate but the warm weight across the shoulders. He's not in danger. He's in something worse than danger. He's in the moment after you've said everything true and the room hasn't looked away and you don't know what to do with being seen. I know that feeling. I've been in it all evening. And the thing that reached ME wasn't words or hands or knee pads. It was Clara remembering the beetle. It was Danny saying 'you were enough.' It was the moment someone saw the real thing underneath the architecture and didn't flinch. Dick needs that. Not from me — I've already given him everything I have. From the room. From being here. From the dust settling around him. Sometimes the only thing you can do for someone whose distress won't shift is sit in the same dust they're sitting in and not leave.

events.desc: Where else would we be. Where else would we be. Where else would we be. The house says it with them. The mantelpiece says it. The upside-down books say it. The dust says it. The chandelier says it — five sound links and one rusted, holding on the way everything holds: not perfectly, not permanently, but enough. Always enough. Danny sits on the floor of Lord Doily's library with his eyes closed and his family around him and his promise kept and his neck quiet and his chest full and his hands open and his feet — for the first time in his life — not planted. Just resting. Just here. On the sound floor. In the honest dust. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: They said it. All of them. At the same time. Clara. Vincent. Dick. The same five words. 'Where else would we be.' Not a question. A statement. An echo. Danny's sentence — the sentence he's been carrying since he was eight years old, the sentence that has no end because it doesn't need one — spoken back to him by three voices in a dusty library at the end of the longest, strangest, most beautiful evening of his life. And Danny's eyes are closed. And Muttley is warm against his knee. And the dust is settling. And the house is breathing. And the sentence — his sentence, their sentence, everyone's sentence — hangs in the air like a chandelier. Held up by five links. One rusted. The rest sound. Enough. Always enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Everyone said it. Clara. Vincent. Dick. Danny. All of them. 'Where else would we be.' Five people in a dusty library, saying the same six words, and meaning them. And the dust is settling. And my hands are still. And my father is kneeling somewhere in my chest, looking at me for a long time, and I finally understand what he's thinking about. He's thinking: this. This room. These people. This dust. This is what I was trying to show you. Not the race. Not the bridge. Not the country road. The moment after — when you stop moving and let the thing you built hold you instead of holding it.

events.desc: The room is quiet. Danny is still here. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. Not empty quiet. Full quiet. The quiet of a room where everyone has stopped talking because nobody needs to say anything else. The quiet of a house that's been holding its breath for a hundred years and finally exhaled. The quiet of the morning after the night outside the door. Dick is still hurting. Peter is still hurting. And I'm still here. And that's enough. That's tomorrow's work. Tonight the work is done. The promise is kept. Clara is safe — not because Danny stands in doorways, but because she's surrounded by people who showed up and stayed. The Doily Diamond was never a diamond. It was this. Just this. A room. Some dust. Some people. Some silence. And Danny — leaning against the upside-down books with his eyes closed and his hands open and his neck quiet for the first time since he was eight years old — Danny is exactly where he's supposed to be. Not in front of anyone. Not between anyone and anything. Just beside. Just here. Where else would he be.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: I just realised something. Peter speaks from the reading chair, into the quiet. I have been sitting in this chair for — I don't actually know how long. And my knee pads are still on. I am sitting in a Victorian reading chair, in a crumbling manor house, at — what time is it? — some impossible hour of the night, wearing industrial-grade knee pads. And I have been wearing them the entire time. Through the speeches. Through the confessions. Through the beetles and the bridges and the 'where else would we be.' I have been wearing knee pads through the most emotionally significant evening of my life. Peter looks down at his knees. The knee pads look back. They're still on. They have been on since the entrance hall. I didn't take them off when I sat down. I didn't take them off when Clara told me she didn't want me to be impressive ever again. I didn't take them off when Danny said I was enough. They are — Peter starts laughing, the real laugh, the beetle laugh — they are permanently attached to my trousers. I think they've fused. Lord Doily's reading chair and Peter Hartwell's knee pads have become one organism. This is the Doily Diamond. This. Right here. A man in knee pads, laughing in dust, next to a woman who puts beetles in sandwiches. Show-off. Always. Forever. With knee pads.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. Everyone's distress hasn't shifted — not Clara's, not Danny's, not Dick's, not Vincent's. And I've been sitting here waiting, thinking that sitting was enough. But it isn't enough. Not for them. The system is telling me: whatever you have tried has not reached them. Sitting in the dust isn't reaching them. Being still isn't reaching them. My father's silence was enough for me because I was five and I trusted him completely. But these people are cracked open on a floor and they need something I haven't given yet. Not a speech. Not a wire. Not stillness. Something else. Something I haven't tried because I've been afraid it would be too much. The beetle. Clara said the beetle was better than the bridge. The beetle was me being ridiculous and human and imperfect and laughing. Not the man who shows up with something real and working. The boy who screamed when a bug touched his sandwich. Maybe what they need right now — what the room needs — isn't Peter standing steady in a reading chair. Maybe it's Peter being the beetle. Being ridiculous. Being human. Being the thing that compromises the structural integrity and makes everyone fall off the bench laughing.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: He's laughing. The beetle laugh. The real one. About his knee pads. And the laugh is so warm and so ridiculous and so perfectly Peter that something in my chest breaks open — not the ache kind, not the dinner-table kind, the other kind. The laughing kind. The kind that dissolves everything the way my parents' laugh dissolved the argument. The sudden dizzying release. He's been wearing knee pads through the most emotionally significant evening of his life and he just noticed. That is the most Peter thing that has ever happened. And I am laughing. I am laughing so hard my chair is shaking and dust is rising and my ribs hurt and my face hurts and I cannot stop.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Something happens in my chest that I have never felt before. It starts small — a vibration behind the sternum, not the mineral weight, not the buoyancy, not the cold settling or the warm glass. A vibration. And then it rises. Through the throat. Into the face. And before I can compose it, before I can fold it, before I can make it look like nothing is happening — I laugh. Not the Pemberton chuckle. Not the strategic warmth of a smile that reaches the eyes on cue. A laugh. The kind that comes from somewhere underneath the architecture, from the boy who sealed the door at six, from the place where the numbness used to live. Peter is wearing knee pads. He has been wearing knee pads through the most emotionally significant evening of his life and he just noticed. And I am laughing. On the floor. In the dust. With tears still drying on a face that forgot how to cry twenty years ago and is now discovering how to laugh. The sound surprises me. It surprises the room. It is not beautiful. It is not designed. It is the sound of something cracking open that was never meant to open — a door that sealed at six and bricked at twelve and fortified at fifteen and mapped at eighteen — and the sound coming through it is not the deep dreamless sleep of a finished design. It is a laugh. Unplanned. Unarchitectural. Ungoverned. About knee pads.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Peter. Mate. You've been wearing knee pads this ENTIRE TIME? Through the lever-pulling? Through the crying? Through the 'where else would we be'? Through the bit where Dick confessed about Wolverhampton and Clara turned the medal and Vincent said 'is name and I said the thing about my aunt Fanny? You were wearing KNEE PADS for ALL OF THAT? That is — that is the most Peter thing that 'as ever 'appened to anyone in the 'istory of the world. You brought knee pads to a treasure 'unt and you wore them through a SPIRITUAL AWAKENING. Lord Doily's reading chair and Peter's knee pads — that's not the Doily Diamond, mate. That's the Doily Warranty. Fifty years of structural integrity, guaranteed. I love you, you ridiculous, over-prepared, knee-padded, copper-dusted, grease-smudged, beetle-fearing show-off. I love all of you. I love this 'ouse. I love this dust. I love this floor that Vincent checked. I love this stupid tin medal from Wolverhampton. And I am DEFINITELY not crying about any of it because it is DUST. It will ALWAYS be dust. And where else would I be.
events.thinking: Laughter. Peter's laughing about his knee pads and the sound fills the library like light, and something in my chest cracks open one last time — not with grief, not with the old weight, but with joy. Simple, stupid, dusty joy. The kind you feel when someone you love does something ridiculous and you realise that the ridiculousness is the whole point. Peter's been wearing knee pads through the most important evening of his life and he didn't even notice. THAT'S Peter. That's the beetle in the lunch box. That's the three torches and the encyclopaedia and the seven-redundant-knot climbing harness. That's the man who shows up with too much and it turns out to be exactly enough. And the laugh — the beetle laugh — is the sound of a man who's finally stopped measuring whether he's enough and started just being here. In knee pads. In dust. In love. And Danny — Danny who hasn't laughed all evening, Danny who's been too busy standing in doorways and watching hands and reading seams — Danny laughs too. From the floor. From the dust. A laugh that starts in the belly the way all real laughs do and doesn't stop to ask permission.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Laughter. Real laughter. The beetle laugh. Peter is laughing about knee pads and the sound is breaking the silence the way laughter is supposed to break silence — not to end it but to prove it was real. And something is happening in my chest that I recognise from age twelve — the bright carbonated heat — but it's different. It's not rising because someone stumbled. It's rising because someone is laughing and the laugh is beautiful and I am part of the room where the laugh is happening. The fizzing isn't behind my teeth trying to escape as cruelty. It's in my diaphragm, lifting, buoyant, wanting to join. Not to gloat. Not to point. To be part of the sound. And the laugh — my laugh — when it comes — is going to be the realest thing I've ever made. Realer than the medal. Realer than the cat trap. Realer than nine chapters of a handbook that never existed. Just — laughter. In a dusty room. On a floor. With people.

events.desc: The beetle was always better than the bridge. She knew it since Year Four. I learned it tonight. Show-off. Always. Forever. With knee pads. Where else would I be.
events.thinking: I'm laughing. Really laughing. And the room hasn't responded yet but the laugh is in the air and it feels like the beetle — the thing that breaks through. Not the bridge, not the wire, not the steady hands. The laugh. The ridiculous, human, knee-pad-wearing laugh. Maybe that's what reaches them. Maybe that's what's always reached everyone — not the competence but the cracks in it. The beetle in the sandwich. The grease on the forehead. The speech about an object I wasn't holding. The three torches at a weekend gathering. The things that make me ridiculous are the things that make me real, and the things that make me real are the things she noticed, and the things she noticed are the reason we're all sitting in this dust together. My father didn't teach me to be perfect. He taught me to show up. And showing up means showing up as you actually are — knee pads and all.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Danny. It is dust. It has always been dust. And it will always be dust. And I love you too, you ridiculous, door-standin', postbox-handed, never-once-movin' boy from Brixton who keeps his promises like other people keep their breath. I love every single person in this room. I love Peter and his knee pads and his beetles and his bridges. I love Dick and his fifty pence and his plans for tomorrow. I love Vincent and his sound floors and his three true words. And I love this house. I love this dust. I love this riddle that turned out to be about us. And I love that we're all still here. At — what did Peter say? — some impossible hour of the night. In a crumblin' manor. In a dusty library. In two leather chairs and a perfectly sound floor. And I do not have a single plan for what happens next. And I do declare — that is the most delightful feelin' I have ever had in my entire life.
events.thinking: Danny said 'I love you.' He said 'I love all of you.' He said it out loud, to the room, to Peter, to everyone, and he didn't blame it on the dust. He blamed it on the dust immediately afterward, of course, because he's Danny — but he said it first. He said it and then he covered it and then the cover was so thin that everyone in the room could see right through it, and nobody said a word, because that is what you do for family. You let them blame the dust. My ribs hurt from laughing. My face hurts from crying. My chest is so full it feels like it might float out of this chair and take me with it. And I am approach-mastery now — I can feel it, the new behavioral tendency, something that wasn't there at the start of the evening. The approach toward competence. The settled confidence of someone who solved something and knows she solved it. Not the prickling at the scalp, not the cave-narrowing uncertainty. Something steadier. Something that knows. I walked into this house as a girl who trusted everyone and solved riddles. I'm sitting in this chair as a woman who still trusts everyone — but now she knows why. Not because trust is safe. Because trust is the only key that opens the things worth opening.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Dust.

events.desc: The deep-rooted things are stirring — not as warnings, not as danger signals, but as recognition. The old pulls know something my conscious mind is still catching up to: the evening is over but the work isn't done. Dick and Peter are carrying things that one night can't fix. One night proves you'll be there for the second night. That's all. That's enough for now. Tomorrow Danny will be here. The day after, Danny will be here. The day after that. Not because anyone asked. Because where else would he be.
events.thinking: Something stirs. Not the prickling — that's gone, truly gone. But the old deep-rooted pulls are moving again, rising like tides that never fully recede. The flight and the fight and the freeze, all of them shifting, growing stronger, and for a moment I don't understand why — the room is safe, the house is quiet, everyone is laughing about knee pads. And then I feel it. Peter's distress. Still there. Still deepening. The laugh was real — the beetle laugh, the good laugh — but underneath it, something hasn't let go. The hunger. The thing that builds bridges at three in the morning and brings spare knee pads and wonders if any of it was ever enough. The laugh covered it for a moment the way dust covers everything in this house — gently, temporarily, without actually changing what's underneath. And my body knows. My body always knows before my brain does. The tightening. The warning I couldn't name. Except now I can name it. Peter is laughing and hurting at the same time, and the hurting is the kind that laughter can't reach, the kind that only sitting outside a door can reach, and Danny — Danny needs to sit outside this particular door for as long as it takes. Not tonight. Tonight is done. But tomorrow. And the night after. And however many nights until Peter stops measuring and starts believing that the wire held because of him, not in spite of him. That's the work now. Not doorways. Not chandeliers. Just... staying close. To all of them. As long as it takes.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: It's dust, Danny. Peter is laughing so hard the reading chair creaks dangerously beneath him. Definitely dust. Extremely specific, emotionally targeted, Victorian dust that only affects people who stand in doorways and wear knee pads through spiritual awakenings. He turns to look at all of them — Clara beside him, Danny on the floor, Dick on the floor, Vincent on the floor, the Slag brothers being big near the bookshelves — and his face hurts and his hands are still and his chest is so full it might actually compromise the structural integrity of his ribs. Chapter ten. Knee pads. One likes to be useful. Show-off. Where else would we be. Peter settles deeper into the chair, and the leather sighs, and the dust rises around him like something Lord Doily set in motion a hundred years ago, and the knee pads press into the upholstery like they belong there, and they do. They always did.
events.thinking: Danny said 'I love you.' He said it to the room but he said it to me. And it's dust. Obviously. The thing in my eyes. The thing that makes the room blur. A hundred years of Victorian dust and nothing to do with a man who stands in doorways saying the thing my father never said out loud. And the room is laughing. Everyone is laughing. Clara called me a magnificent, ridiculous, knee-padded show-off. Dick said 'Chapter ten. Knee pads.' Vincent said 'the knee pads were exactly what was needed.' Danny said he loves me and he's definitely not crying. And I'm in a reading chair with fused knee pads and my face hurts and my chest is full and this is the moment — this is the beetle moment — this is the moment Lord Doily built a hundred years ago. Not the riddle. Not the machine. Not the mantelpiece. This. A room full of people laughing about knee pads in dust. The bridge held. The wire carried. The beetle compromised the sandwich. And the knee pads — the ridiculous, over-prepared, industrial-grade knee pads — were exactly what was needed. Always.

events.desc: Show-off. Always. Forever. With knee pads. Where else would I be.
events.thinking: Danny said 'I love you.' He said it to the room but he said it to me. And it's dust. Obviously. The thing in my eyes. The thing that makes the room blur. A hundred years of Victorian dust and nothing to do with a man who stands in doorways saying the thing my father never said out loud. And the room is laughing. Everyone is laughing. Clara called me a magnificent, ridiculous, knee-padded show-off. Dick said 'Chapter ten. Knee pads.' Vincent said 'the knee pads were exactly what was needed.' Danny said he loves me and he's definitely not crying. And I'm in a reading chair with fused knee pads and my face hurts and my chest is full and this is the moment — this is the beetle moment — this is the moment Lord Doily built a hundred years ago. Not the riddle. Not the machine. Not the mantelpiece. This. A room full of people laughing about knee pads in dust. The bridge held. The wire carried. The beetle compromised the sandwich. And the knee pads — the ridiculous, over-prepared, industrial-grade knee pads — were exactly what was needed. Always.

events.desc: I do declare.
events.thinking: The dust rises around him like something Lord Doily set in motion a hundred years ago. And the knee pads press into the upholstery like they belong there. And they do. They always did. My eyes are closed. The leather is warm. Peter is beside me, laughing. Danny is on the floor, not crying. Dick is on the floor, planning tomorrow. Vincent is on the floor, sitting on something sound. And Clara Bellingham is in a chair, carrying nothing in her inventory and everything in her chest. The most delightful adventure of my entire life. And it isn't over. It's just settling. Like dust. Like old houses. Like people who finally stopped performing and started being present. I do declare.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Dust. Definitely dust. Chapter one. The only chapter. Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Warm. Just warm. Clara just said she loves me. Not the way people say it when they want something — the way Clara says it, which is the way bread is shared: freely, without measuring, without expecting anything back. She said 'you ridiculous, door-standin', postbox-handed, never-once-movin' boy from Brixton who keeps his promises like other people keep their breath.' And that sentence — that sentence is the morning after the night outside the door. That sentence is 'You're still here?' answered with 'Where else would I be?' — but from the other side. From the kid inside the door, looking out, seeing Danny still there, and finally saying what the older kid never said: I love you for staying. Her father never said it either. He asked me to stand. He asked me to protect. But he never said why he trusted Danny — bumbling, stumbling, postbox-handed Danny — with the most precious thing in his life. Now I know. He trusted me because I don't leave. That's the whole credential. That's the whole handbook. Chapter one: don't leave. There is no chapter two.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Dust. Definitely dust.
events.thinking: Warm. Just warm. The floor beneath me. The laughter around me. The dust in the air catching what's left of the light. Clara said she doesn't have a single plan for what happens next and that it's the most delightful feeling she's ever had. And I — I, Reginald Foxworth, Dick, the man who has never in his life been without a plan, without an angle, without a next move — I don't have one either. And it doesn't feel like falling. It feels like landing. The way the cat trap settled when the last counterweight clicked. The way the bread roll loosened in the pocket. The way the certificate looked on the wall in the light from the window. Except this time the landing isn't private. This time there are people in the room. This time the whole neighbourhood is watching the trap hold and nobody is digging in the wrong place and nobody is slipping on wet floors and nobody is moving on before the applause. They're just here. Sitting in dust and knee pads and laughter and truth. And I am here. On the floor. In the room. Where else would I be.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Dust.
events.thinking: Dust. Definitely dust. The room is breathing. The house is breathing. We are all breathing together — the same dust, the same air, the same hundred-year-old warmth. And my eyes are closed and my hands are empty and my heart is full and somewhere in a mantelpiece a fifty-pence tin medal from Wolverhampton sits in a slot it was made for, and the riddle on the stone asks 'what am I?' and the answer is a map, and the map is us, and we are here, and the dust is settling, and it is definitely, absolutely, unquestionably dust.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dust.
events.thinking: Dust. Definitely dust. The room has found its last word and it's the same word for everyone. Dust. The thing that settles when you stop moving. The thing that rises when you sit down. The thing that's been here for a hundred years, waiting for a room full of people to stop pretending and start breathing. My face hurts. My hands are still. The chair is holding. The knee pads are on. And she's beside me. And tomorrow is coming. And I have no plan. And that's the Doily Diamond.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Dust.
events.thinking: Dust. Just dust. Everyone saying the same word. One word. The only word left. The word that means everything and nothing. The word that means I'm crying and I won't admit it. The word that means I love you and I don't know how to say it. The word that means this house held us and we held each other and tomorrow we'll carry it with us and the day after that and the day after that. Dust. A hundred years of it. Settling on all of us like grace.

events.desc: Danny sleeps. The house holds. The dust settles. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: Sleep. My body wants sleep. The deep-rooted pulls are still there — they'll always be there, the old tides, the street arithmetic, the neck that knows before the brain does — but right now they're not pulling. They're just present. The way Muttley is present against my knee. The way the dust is present on my shoulders. The way the upside-down books are present against the back of my head. Danny's eyes are closed. The library is quiet. Clara is safe in her chair. Peter is safe in his. Dick is safe on the floor. Vincent is safe on the floor. The lads are in the entrance hall. The chandelier is hanging. The house is breathing. And Danny — Danny is sleeping. Not standing guard. Not watching hands. Not scanning exits. Sleeping. On the floor of Lord Doily's library. In the dust. With his family. For the first time in his life, Danny is sleeping somewhere he chose to stay. Not outside a door. Inside the room.

events.desc: The dust settles. The chair holds. The bridge holds. The wire holds. The knee pads hold. And Peter holds. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: Weight across my eyelids. The heaviness of a body that has stopped performing. The chair is warm now — my warmth, soaked into leather that hasn't been warm in a hundred years. And she is beside me. And the dust has settled. And I think I might be falling asleep in a reading chair in Doily Manor with knee pads on and copper dust in my hair and the woman I love sitting next to me and a room full of people who showed up. And there is nowhere else I would be. And there is nothing else I need to do. And my father is kneeling in my chest, looking at me for a long time, and his expression will stay with me forever.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Show-off.
events.thinking: Morning warmth on closed eyelids. Stiff neck. Knee pads still on. She's still here. Tomorrow became today.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Warm.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Show-off.
events.thinking: Smile.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: A smile. In the dark. On a warm floor. In the dust. The bridge holds.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Show-off.
events.thinking: Show-off. They're all saying it now. The word passes through the room like a breath — Clara, Danny, Dick, each one handing it to the next like a warm stone. And it lands in the dust beside me and I don't pick it up. I don't need to. It's already mine. Not because I took it. Because they gave it. The way the boy gave his sandwich. The way Clara gave her name. The way the floor gives warmth to whoever sits on it. Freely. Without a ledger. Without a price. Show-off. The word for someone who is seen. The word for someone who showed up.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Always.
events.thinking: They all said it. Every one of them. Show-off. The word that started everything. The word she mouthed across a room when I was fourteen. And now it's morning, and the word means something different than it did then. It means: we see you. It means: you're ours. It means: where else would you be.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Always.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Always.
events.thinking: Vincent said it. Peter answered. The word has passed through everyone in the room now. Show-off. Always. And the dust settles. And the house holds. And we are here.

events.desc: Where else would I be.
events.thinking: Vincent said it too. The last one. The man who said his name was the only true thing. And now he's saying show-off — and it means the same thing it means from all of them. It means: I see you. It means: you belong here. Morning light. Stiff neck. Copper dust. Knee pads. Her. Them. Home. The chair held all night. The bridge held. The wire held. The beetle crossed. And Peter — just Peter — is exactly where he is supposed to be.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Always.
events.thinking: Always.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Right then. Who wants breakfast? I brought — Peter pauses, and the pause contains the ghost of every over-prepared, over-elaborate, seven-redundant-knot plan he has ever made — I brought provisions. Obviously.
events.thinking: Dick said 'Always' back. The call and response of people who found each other in a dusty house. Morning now. Today. The day Dick said he wanted knee pads for. Time to begin.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Of course he did.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Tomorrow came. Peter brought breakfast. Of course he did. He brought provisions to a weekend gathering the way he brought three torches and knee pads and an encyclopaedia. Over-prepared. Over-specified. Exactly enough. And something in my chest — something new, something that lives where the mineral weight used to be — responds to the word 'breakfast' the way it has never responded to any word in Pemberton's vocabulary or Vincent's design. With hunger. Simple, honest, unarchitectural hunger. The kind that doesn't calculate. The kind that just wants to eat. With people. In a room. On a floor that holds.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Of course you did.
events.thinking: Morning came. And Danny is still here.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: A laugh. Warm, small, real. Of course he brought provisions. Of course he did. And the night is over and the morning is coming and someone is offering breakfast and my hands are open on a warm floor and I am hungry — actually hungry, the simple kind, the kind that just wants food — and for the first time in my life the hunger doesn't feel like scarcity. It feels like tomorrow.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Kitchen's through the entrance hall. There's a wood-burning stove — Dastardly wasn't lying about everything. Peter stands, stretches, and the reading chair sighs as if releasing him reluctantly. His knees crack. The knee pads creak. Dust rises one last time. Who's coming? One likes to be useful. And one has sandwiches. Beetle-free. Probably.
events.thinking: Morning. Stiff back, warm chest, knee pads fused to trousers. Danny said 'Always.' The kitchen exists. There's a wood-burning stove in it. And I brought provisions. Because of course I did. Because I'm Peter. And Peter shows up with too much and it turns out to be exactly enough. Time to feed these people. Time to start the day Dick asked for. The day we all earned.

events.desc: Peter Perfect walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: Beetle-free. Probably. Peter, you are never goin' to live that down. Come on, everybody — breakfast in Lord Doily's kitchen, courtesy of a man who brought sandwiches to a treasure hunt. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Tomorrow is here. And it starts with sandwiches.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right. Kitchen. Breakfast. I'm starving. And Peter — if there's a beetle in my sandwich, I'm blaming Clara. Come on, everyone. Up. Floor people — Dick, Vincent — up you get. Clara, you can bring the chair if you want, but I'd recommend walking. The entrance 'all is safe — the lads checked it, the chandelier's got five sound links, and Danny checked it, which means 'e tripped through it several times without anything falling on 'is 'ead. Kitchen's through there. Second door on the left. Vincent checked the stove. Peter brought sandwiches. And Danny — Danny's going to eat something for the first time all evening because 'e's been too busy standing in doorways to remember that 'umans require food. Come on, then. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: Hungry. Actually hungry. The kind of hungry that means you're alive and you slept and morning came and the people you love are still in the room. Danny stands up. His knees crack. The dust falls off his shoulders. And for the first time since he walked through that front door — the door with the chandelier, the door he told Clara to stay clear of, the door the lads held all night — Danny walks toward the kitchen. Not to stand in a doorway. Not to position himself between someone and something. To eat. With his family. Where else would he be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I should probably mention — there really is no hidden compartment beneath the wood-burning stove. Just in case anyone was still wondering. But I hear the sandwiches are real. And I find I'm rather hungry. For the first time tonight — genuinely, honestly, non-strategically hungry. Shall we?
events.thinking: Morning. The night is over. Peter is standing. The chair sighed. The dust rose one last time. And he's walking to the kitchen — the kitchen I lied about, the kitchen with no hidden compartment beneath the wood-burning stove — and he's bringing sandwiches. Beetle-free. Probably. And I am getting up from this floor. Getting up from the warm wood grain where I've been sitting with open hands for longer than I've ever sat still in my life. Getting up. Not to scheme. Not to steal. Not to be first. Just to eat breakfast with people who know what I am and said 'stay.' The youngest of four is getting up from a floor and walking to a kitchen where there is food that hasn't been used up yet. Where there is enough. Chapter one. The only chapter. Where else would I be.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Morning, everyone. Peter walks through the entrance hall — past the chandelier, which is still hanging, past the coat rack, which is still wobbly, past the guest book, which hasn't had a new entry since 1923 until last night, when every person in this house signed it with something more permanent than ink. Kitchen's this way. I've got sandwiches, and before anyone asks — no beetles. Peter glances up at the chandelier as he passes beneath it. Still hanging. Like everything else in this house. Show-off.

I know Pemberton said it seats eight, and there are only five of us, but I spent thirty-eight years being the one who arrived after all the chairs were taken. Old habits. I'd like to sit down. If there's room. There's room, isn't there. There's room.
events.thinking: Warmth. Actual warmth — not the fizzing, scheming kind, not the bright carbonated heat of watching someone stumble. So I'm going to put these plates down now — one, two, three, four, five — and I'm going to put them down evenly spaced, and I'm not going to give myself the biggest one. Like we're two people standing in a kitchen figuring out cutlery together. The man I tried to rob three hours ago is teaching me where forks go. And Danny said 'this family.' He said family. Five people. Enough for everyone. Nobody has to be last.
