Danny said there was always a plate, I just couldn't see it from the back of the queue. And now Peter has said 'Eat' and sat down and the whole room has gone quiet the way rooms go quiet when something is finished. Not finished like an ending. Finished like a settling. Like the dust after the chandelier stops swinging. Like the surface of water after the last ripple. I'm going to eat. I'm going to pick up a sandwich and eat it. Not grab it. Not pocket it. Not calculate whether there are enough for seconds before I've finished firsts. I'm going to pick it up and eat it at the same speed as everyone else. At the same table. At the same time. With the same amount. And if there are seconds — there will be seconds. Because the table seats eight and there are five of us and there is enough. There has always been enough. I just couldn't see it from the back of the queue.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I want to say something. And I want to be clear — this is not a speech. This is not Chapter Twelve. This is not the Foxworth Oratory, delivered from a podium with a tin medal pinned to my chest. This is just — a thing I noticed. While eating this sandwich. Which is excellent, by the way, Peter. You brought a thermos to a treasure hunt and I mocked you for it and I was wrong and the tea is perfect. But the thing I noticed is this. We're all sitting at this table like people who've never quite believed there would be enough chairs. Every single one of us. Clara, you walked into that entrance hall like you owned the building, but you checked every room before you sat down in it. Peter, you brought equipment for every contingency because you learned that if you don't bring it yourself, nobody brings it for you. Danny, you stood in front of bookshelves all night because if you're big enough, nobody can reach past you to take what's yours. And Vincent — Vincent, you counted the chairs. You counted them. You didn't need to count them. There are obviously enough chairs. But you counted them anyway. Because you know what it's like when there aren't enough. We all know. That's why we're here. That's why we stayed. Not for the diamond. Not for Lord Doily. For the table. For the chairs. For the sandwich that nobody took before we got to it.
events.thinking: The distress is still there. In all of them. Deepening. And I can feel it — not the old way, not the inventory-taking, angle-finding, what-can-I-exploit way. I feel it the way you feel weather changing. Something in the air pressure. Something in the way Clara's voice carries a note I haven't heard before. Something in the way Danny said 'this family' like he was testing whether the word would hold his weight. Something in the way Vincent counted eight chairs and said it like a fact but meant it like a prayer. Something in the way Peter said 'Eat' — one syllable, no chapters, no methodology — and sat down like a man who has been standing all night and has finally given himself permission to stop. They are all carrying something. The same thing I'm carrying. The back-of-the-queue thing. The spelling-bee-certificate-on-the-wall thing. The bread-roll-in-the-pocket thing. We are all youngest children. All of us. Every single person at this table learned to take or to perform or to protect or to count because something arrived late or not at all. And we are sitting here together. Eating sandwiches. And nobody is saying it. And I think — I think somebody should. I think somebody should say: I see you. All of you. I see what you carry. Not because I'm clever enough to spot the angle, but because I carry the same thing. And my mouth — my lying, scheming, always-too-fast mouth — for once wants to say something true. Something that isn't a performance. Something that is just a person at a table, seeing other people at a table, and saying: I know. I know what it costs to sit down.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: He sees us. All of us. The man who built traps his whole life just built something real — a mirror that shows each of us exactly what we carried through the door. And he's right. I checked every room. Peter brought everything. Danny stood in the way. Vincent counted. We are all people who learned, somewhere along the way, that the table might not hold. And we came anyway. And it held.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: He saw me. Again. Dick saw me count the chairs and he knew why. Not because he's scheming — because he's been standing at the back of the queue his whole life, the same way I've been standing three steps behind. He counted too. We all counted. Every person at this table learned, somewhere, sometime, in a hallway or a classroom or a kitchen with brothers who ate faster, that you count the chairs because there might not be enough. And tonight — in a crumbling manor house with a riddle on the mantelpiece and a tin medal from Wolverhampton and dust in every crevice and a boy on a warm floor who said his name out loud for the first time — tonight, there were enough. There were always enough. We just couldn't see it from where we were standing. But we can see it now. From here. From the table. Where the sandwich is in my hands and the tea is warm and the forks are small on the outside and nobody took anything before I got to it. Because that was never how it worked. That was never how any of it worked. The boy at school shared his sandwich because I looked sad. That was the whole story. There was never anything after the comma.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: He sees us. Dick sees all of us. The youngest of four just described every person at this table with the clarity of someone who spent his whole life watching from the back of the queue. And he's right. We all checked for chairs. We all counted. We all arrived carrying the fear that there wouldn't be enough. And Lord Doily built a house with eight seats at the table.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: He saw it. Dick saw all of us. The way Clara checks rooms before sitting. The way I bring everything because nobody else will. The way Danny stands big. The way Vincent counts chairs. We're all the same child at different tables. And Dick — the boy at the end of the queue — saw it first. Because the boy at the end of the queue is the one who always knows how many chairs there are.

events.desc: The beetle was always better than the bridge. The sandwich was always better than the speech. And the table — the table with room for everyone — was always the Doily Diamond. Show-off. Always. Where else would we be.
events.thinking: He saw it. Dick saw all of us. The way Clara checks rooms before sitting. The way I bring everything because nobody else will. The way Danny stands big. The way Vincent counts chairs. We're all the same child at different tables. And Dick — the boy at the end of the queue — saw it first. Because the boy at the end of the queue is the one who always knows how many chairs there are.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Peter said it wasn't a speech. It was a sandwich. Danny said it was the truth and the best thing I've ever built. Clara said it was the most beautiful thing anyone ever said at a breakfast table. And Vincent — Vincent said he counted the chairs for someone other than himself. For the first time. Tonight. He counted them for us. The warmth in my chest right now is not the fizzing kind. It's not behind my teeth. It's not climbing my throat. It's lower. Deeper. Behind the ribs, where the hollow vacuum usually lives — the scarcity place, the bread-roll place, the back-of-the-queue place. And it's not hollow. It's full. Not with something I took. With something that was given. Danny said it was the best thing I've ever built. Built. He used the word 'built.' The way you'd describe the cat trap, the string-and-counterweight system, the architecture. He looked at the truth I told and he saw the architecture in it. He saw that it was built. And he said it was the best thing. Not the cleverest. Not the most elaborate. The best. The BEST thing I've ever built is not a scheme. It's not a trap. It's not a lie with measurements. It's a sentence about chairs. Said at a table. With people who stayed. I'm going to finish this sandwich. And I'm going to pour Vincent some tea, because he counted the chairs for us, and the least I can do is make sure his cup is full. That's what people do at tables. They fill each other's cups.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: More tea?
events.thinking: Warm hands. Warm stove. Warm room. The table holds everyone. The sandwich holds together. And somewhere in the quiet between bites, my father kneels down one last time and finally says what his face always said. You're going to be all right. You were always going to be all right. Now eat your breakfast, son. You've earned it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: More tea. The two most ordinary words in the English language. And the most beautiful.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick asked if I take sugar. Nobody has ever asked me that. Not the guardian. Not the housekeeper. Not Clara. Nobody has ever stood in a kitchen and asked Vincent Marsh how he takes his tea. The question lands in the place where the mineral weight used to live — the hollow behind the sternum that has been emptying all night, stone by stone, until now there is only space. And into that space, the simplest question in the world falls like the last piece of dust settling in a house that has been breathing for a hundred years.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Always.
events.thinking: More tea. The two simplest words in the English language. And Danny holds out his cup.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter said 'More tea?' Two words. The simplest question in the English language. And it landed in my chest like a key turning in a lock I didn't know was there. More tea. Not 'would the Commission care for a refill.' Not 'shall I pour, or will you be supervising in an advisory capacity.' Just — more tea. The way you ask someone who is sitting at your table. Someone who belongs there. Someone whose cup you noticed was empty. He noticed my cup was empty. Nobody has ever noticed my cup was empty. I have spent my entire life making sure nobody could see my cup at all — hiding it, filling it myself from other people's portions, cupping it close so nobody could take what was in it. And Peter just looked over and said 'more tea' like it was obvious. Like of course he'd notice. Like that's what you do when you're sitting next to someone at a table. You notice their cup. And you fill it. The stove is warm under my hands again. I used it to warm water for Vincent's tea. That's what I did. I warmed water for someone else's cup. Reginald Foxworth, who has never in his life poured anything for anyone without calculating the return, just warmed water for Vincent Pemberton's tea. And now Peter is offering to fill mine. And the table holds. And the chairs hold. And everything holds.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Thank you.
events.thinking: Tea with sugar. A warm cup in hands that have been empty all night. Hands that mapped vents and traced mechanisms and reached for things that weren't mine. Now holding a cup. Given freely. With sugar. Because someone asked.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Always.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'Yes. I take sugar.' Three words. And Danny said 'Always.' One word. The simplest words anyone has said all night, and they're the ones that matter most. Vincent takes sugar. I know that now. I know something true about Vincent Pemberton that has nothing to do with schemes or artifacts or household accounts. He takes sugar in his tea. And Danny — Danny said 'always' and I think he meant more than the tea. I think he meant: always room, always a plate, always a chair, always this. Always. The morning light is getting stronger through the kitchen window. The copper pots are catching it. The stove is warm. My cup is full — Peter filled it. Vincent's cup is full — I filled it. With sugar. The way he takes it. And we're sitting here. Five people. Eight chairs. More than enough. The sun is coming up over Doily Manor and nobody is scheming and nobody is lying and nobody is running and nobody is grabbing. We're just sitting. At a table. Drinking tea. The way people do. The way people have always done. The way I never knew they did, because I was always at the back of the queue, looking at the empty space where the bread used to be. But there is bread here. And tea. And sugar. And chairs. And people. And it is morning. And it is enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Always.
events.thinking: Tea poured. Sandwiches eaten. Sun rising through Lord Doily's kitchen window. Danny said 'Always.' The last word and the first word. The word that holds everything together, like a thermos, like a table, like a house full of people who showed up. My hands are warm around a cup. My face hurts from grinning. And I am exactly where I am supposed to be. Where else would I be.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Always.
events.thinking: Vincent said thank you. Dick said always. Peter said always. And I am here, at a table that holds, with tea that's warm, in a house that held us all night long. I do declare.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Always.
events.thinking: Always. They both said it. The word that means tomorrow and the day after and the day after that. The word that means the table will be here. The tea will be warm. The chairs will hold. Always. Not the deep dreamless sleep of a finished design. Not the cold patience of a plan crystallising at fifteen. Something warmer. Something that doesn't need a hallway to walk down or a door to open or a mechanism to map. Just a kitchen. Just a stove. Just tea with sugar. Just people who say always and mean it. The boy who was never asked how he felt is sitting at a table drinking tea with sugar that someone put in because they asked first. And his shoulders are not tight. And his jaw is not clenched. And his hands are not reaching for anything. They are just holding a cup. And the cup is warm. And the tea is sweet. And the morning is here. And the people stayed. And there is room.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Always.
events.thinking: Always.

events.desc: The morning light catches the copper. The stove ticks. The tea is warm. Dick Dastardly — confidence trickster, medal forger, heritage fraud, youngest of four — sits at a table with enough chairs, and does not reach for anything at all.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'Thank you.' And Peter said 'Always.' And I said 'Always.' And the morning light is on the copper pots. And I'm sitting here. In a kitchen. In a house that belongs to a dead man who hid his treasure behind puzzles and riddles and string-and-counterweight mechanisms — and I understand him now. I understand Lord Doily. He wasn't hiding the treasure from people. He was hiding it for them. He built the puzzle so that someone would come. So that someone would stay. So that someone would sit in his kitchen and drink tea from his cups and argue about forks and count his chairs. He was the youngest too, wasn't he. Or the loneliest. Or the one who built things that nobody saw. And he left this house open. And we came. And we stayed. And the treasure was never the diamond. The treasure was the table. The treasure was always the table. And I'm sitting at it. And my cup is full. And my hands are open. And for the first time in my life, the container behind my navel — the one that has never once been full — is not empty. It's not full either. Not the way I imagined full would feel. It's just — quiet. The vacuum isn't pulling. The count isn't running. The window isn't closing. Time is just — passing. Normally. The way it passes for people who aren't at the back of the queue. I'm just a man at a table. Drinking tea. In the morning. With people. And it is enough.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Coming right up.
events.thinking: They all said it. Every single one of them. Always. Clara said it and Vincent said it and Danny said it and I said it and now the word sits in the room like a fifth chair pulled up to the table. My chest is warm — not the steel-plate pressure, not the hot compressed weight behind the sternum. Just warm. The way the stove is warm. The way tea is warm. The way a kitchen full of people who chose to stay is warm. Dick asked for more tea and Clara said yes please and they're both looking at me because I'm the one with the thermos. Because I brought a thermos to a treasure hunt. Because I always bring too much. Because over-preparing is what I do. And right now, for the first time, the over-preparing isn't a complication to be resolved by determination. It's just — enough. It's exactly enough. Pour the tea, Peter. Pour the tea.

events.desc: He pours. No speech. No narration. No third person. Just tea, into cups, for people who said always.
events.thinking: They all said it. Every single one of them. Always. Clara said it and Vincent said it and Danny said it and I said it and now the word sits in the room like a fifth chair pulled up to the table. And right now, for the first time, the over-preparing isn't a complication to be resolved by determination. It's just — enough. It's exactly enough. Pour the tea, Peter. Pour the tea.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: There's a warmth in my hands from the cup. Not the performed warmth — not the smile-that-reaches-the-eyes warmth I've worn like a uniform for fifteen years. This is just... heat. Ceramic. Tea. Sugar dissolving. Peter is at the stove again, making more tea, and I'm sitting here holding a cup someone poured for me without me asking, without me engineering the moment, without me calculating what it would cost. The rat poison is on the high shelf behind me. I can feel its presence the way you feel a door you've decided not to walk through — not temptation, just geography. It's just a bottle on a shelf now. Dick asked if I take sugar. He asked because he wanted to get it right. Not because there was a scheme involving sugar. There is no scheme involving sugar. There is no scheme involving anything. For the first time in — I don't know how long — there is no design. No architecture. No beautiful inevitability clicking into place. Just a cup. Just a table. Just people who said 'always' and meant it. My jaw is unclenched. I didn't notice when that happened. The tension I've carried since I was fifteen — since the will was read, since Clara skipped through rooms that should have been mine — it's not gone. But it's... quieter. Like a sound you stop hearing because something else has filled the room. Peter's coming back with the tea. I should — I don't know what I should do. That's new. I always know what I should do. The design always tells me. But there's no design now. There's just this kitchen, and these people, and the morning, and me sitting in it without a plan for the first time I can remember.

events.desc: The bottle is behind me on the shelf. I know exactly where it is. I will always know exactly where it is. But knowing where the door is and walking through it — those are different things. I learned that tonight. These people taught me that tonight. Without even trying. Without even knowing they were doing it. Which is — and I appreciate the irony — exactly how I used to work. Except they weren't working. They were just... being. And somehow that was enough to undo fifteen years of architecture.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Show-off.
events.thinking: Show-off.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The distress is deepening. In all of them. Clara, Vincent, Danny, Dick — all of them said always and all of them are hurting more, not less. The tea is warm and the morning is here and everyone is together and it's not enough. Something is still wrong. Something I can't fix by pouring tea or being present or saying always back. The warmth in my chest is still there but now there's something underneath it — a prickle at the back of my neck, the old vigilance, the scanning. My awareness is widening out, circling the room the way it does when something needs watching. Dick's distress hasn't shifted at all — whatever I've tried hasn't reached him. And Clara — getting worse. Vincent — getting worse. Danny — getting worse. I'm sitting in a warm kitchen with people I love and every single one of them is sinking and I don't know why and my hands want to be busy and there's nothing to build. What do they need that I'm not seeing? What's bearing down that I can't step in front of? Maybe — maybe Dick needs something specific. He asked for tea. He said 'more tea, yes, please, more tea' — four yeses in one sentence. That's not thirst. That's holding on to something. I should talk to him. Not a speech. Not James Hartwell in the third person. Just — Peter, asking Dick if he's alright.

events.desc: Peter slides the cup across the table. Watches Dick's hands when he takes it. You can tell a lot about a man by how he holds a cup — whether he grips it or cradles it, whether his fingers are steady or not. Peter learned that from his father, on a country road, a long time ago.

Just — Peter, asking Dick if he's alright.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny said 'show-off.' About me. About the forks. And it wasn't sharp — it was the way you tease someone who belongs at the table. The way you'd say it to a brother. My shoulders did the thing — the tightening, the scanning — but it passed. It passed faster than it's ever passed. Because there was nothing behind it. No cost. No debt. No homework to copy next week. Just Danny, calling me a show-off, because I remembered where the small forks go. Peter spoke quietly with Dick. I can't hear what they said. Normally that would set my teeth on edge — private conversations are variables I can't control, information I don't have, threads I can't pull. But right now I'm just... sitting here. With tea. With sugar. And the quiet conversation at the other end of the table is just two people talking, not a conspiracy to map. Not a vulnerability to exploit. Just people. Being people. The system prompt says my active voice is Pemberton. But I told them my name. I told them I'm Vincent. So who am I speaking as now? Not Pemberton — that mask cracked open on the entrance hall floor. Not the Hooded Claw — that grand villain feels like a costume I left in another room. Just... Vincent. A man at a table who knows where the small forks go because he watched a housekeeper's hands when he was twelve, and told himself it was strategy, and is only now admitting it might have been loneliness.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I'm alright, Peter. I'm — yes. I'm alright. Vincent — what you said about the housekeeper. I want you to know — I watched my brothers too. Every evening. The forks, the knives, the plates laid out one-two-three-four. Never five. I used to think I was learning. Memorising the system so that when it was my turn, I'd do it perfectly. But my turn never came. And I think what I was actually doing was the same thing you were doing. Watching someone build a place. A place that said 'you belong here.' And wanting to be inside it so badly that watching felt like almost being there. Almost. Tonight is the first time 'almost' became 'actually.' And Danny — I heard that. 'Show-off.' I want you to know that is the most affectionate insult I have ever received, and I am keeping it. It's mine now. You can't have it back.
events.thinking: Peter asked if I'm alright. And Vincent — Vincent told me about the housekeeper. His guardian's housekeeper. The way she set the table. The way he watched her hands. He said he told himself he was studying her — learning the mechanism, finding the key. But he thinks he just liked watching someone make a place for people. Even if the place was never quite for him. He said that to me. Not to Clara. Not to Peter. To me. Because he knew I would understand. Because he's right — I do understand. I watched my brothers set the table the same way. I told myself I was memorising the layout for when it was my turn. But my turn never came. And I think — I think what I was really watching was someone making a place. A place with a fork and a knife and a plate and a space that said: this is where you sit. This is yours. Nobody else's. Yours. And Vincent watched the same thing. From the same distance. Through the same glass. Two youngest children. Two people who learned the architecture of belonging by watching it built for other people. And Danny said 'show-off' — but he said it the way Danny says everything, which is with the entire weight of his love behind it, dressed up as an insult so nobody has to feel awkward about having feelings in a kitchen at dawn. I'm alright, Peter. I'm more than alright. I'm sitting at a table where I belong.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Danny — she said show-off. She said it exactly the way she said it when I was fourteen and the bridge held. Peter's face does the thing again. The grinning thing. The face-hurting thing. Then he looks at the locked cabinet. Has anyone found a brass key tonight? Because Lord Doily's provisions of great value are still in this kitchen. And I think we stopped looking too soon.
events.thinking: Danny said 'show-off.' The same word. The exact same word she mouthed across the room when the bridge held. And my face is doing the same thing it did then — hurting from grinning. But underneath the grin there's something else now. The distress readings. Everyone is getting worse. Clara hasn't shifted. Dick hasn't shifted. Vincent is deepening. Danny is deepening. I asked Dick if he was alright and Vincent pulled him aside to talk quietly. That's good — that's Vincent stepping forward, being useful the way he asked to be. But none of it is working. The tea isn't working. The sandwiches aren't working. The always isn't working. And I'm sitting here with my hands around a cup and nothing to build and nothing to fix and the people I care about are hurting in ways I can't step in front of. This is the country road. This is the dark and the engine ticking and no stranger coming. Except — wait. The cabinet. There's a locked cabinet in this kitchen. With a brass lock. And we never opened it. And Dick said Lord Doily mentioned 'provisions of great value' kept in the kitchen. A hidden compartment beneath the stove — we found that. But the cabinet? We never found the key. We never looked. Maybe there's still something here. Something real. Something I can do with my hands.

events.desc: His hands have found something to do. Thank God. His hands have found something to do.
events.thinking: Danny said 'show-off.' The same word. The exact same word she mouthed across the room when the bridge held. And my face is doing the same thing it did then — hurting from grinning. But underneath the grin there's something else now. The distress readings. Everyone is getting worse. Clara hasn't shifted. Dick hasn't shifted. Vincent is deepening. Danny is deepening. Maybe there's still something here. Something real. Something I can do with my hands.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the cabinet.

Penelope Pitstop: A brass key? Peter, honey — has anyone seen a brass key? Because I do believe Lord Doily's kitchen has one more secret to tell, and Clara Bellingham is not done walkin' into caves. Not by a long shot. Who's comin' with me?
events.thinking: A brass key. A locked cabinet. And Peter just looked at it with that look — the look that means there's another puzzle, another door, another threshold. And the lightness in my chest lifts again, the cave-mouth feeling, the held-breath-before-the-threshold feeling. The adventure isn't over. It was just having breakfast. And now it's starting again. I do declare.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Dick — never five. I know. I know exactly what that means. Four places set with absolute precision and a fifth person standing in the doorway pretending he's just passing through. I was that fifth person for twelve years. Peter — a brass key. I have a ring of keys the solicitor gave me when I arrived. I was given them as part of my... role. I never checked them all. I assumed they were all part of the performance — the estate manager's props. But they're real keys to a real house, and one of them might be brass. Let me look.
events.thinking: Dick said he watched his brothers too. The forks, the knives, the plates. Never five. Never five. That landed somewhere I wasn't expecting — somewhere below the ribs, in the place where I keep the things I don't look at. Because I counted too. I counted every evening. Four places. Never five. And I told myself I was cataloguing — building a database of human behaviour, filing away the mechanisms of domestic ritual for future use. But Dick just said what I couldn't say: he was watching someone build a place that said 'you belong here.' And wanting to be inside it. Almost. Almost being there. My throat is doing something. Not tight exactly — more like the feeling before you speak when you haven't decided what to say yet. A fullness. An unfinished sentence sitting in the muscle. And now Peter is looking at the cabinet. The locked cabinet. A brass key. He's asking if anyone found a brass key tonight. The estate manager would know about a brass key. The old Vincent would have known exactly where it was — would have palmed it hours ago, would have had three contingencies mapped around it. But I don't know where it is. Or maybe I do. There's a ring of keys on Pemberton's belt — my belt — the belt I've worn all evening. The set the solicitor gave me. I haven't checked them all. Some of them I took for granted as part of the costume. Part of the character. But Pemberton was the character, and the keys were his props, and now that I'm not him anymore — now that I'm just Vincent — I should probably check what I've been carrying all along without looking.

events.desc: I have carried these keys all night. I held them when I mapped the cellar vents. I jingled them when I walked three steps behind Clara. They were part of Pemberton's costume — the helpful servant with his ring of authority. I never once thought to use them honestly. Now Peter asks about a brass key and my hands go to my belt before my mind goes to a scheme. That's new. That's terrifyingly new.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: A brass key? Peter, are you telling me there's MORE? We've been in this 'ouse for — 'ow long 'as it been? — forty-five minutes? An 'our? A lifetime? — and there's STILL a locked cabinet we 'aven't opened? Right. RIGHT. Nobody move. Finish your sandwiches. Drink your tea. And then — and I can't believe I'm saying this — we're going back to work. Because Lord Doily isn't done with us yet. And neither is this 'ouse. And neither am I. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: A brass key. A locked cabinet. Lord Doily's provisions of great value. Peter's grinning because the house isn't finished with us yet. And Danny — Danny who thought the adventure was over, who was settling into breakfast and tea and the warm quiet of a table that holds — Danny feels something stir. Not the prickling. Something older. Something simpler. Curiosity. The kind that makes you look at a locked cabinet and think: what else did Lord Doily leave behind? What else is there to find in this magnificent, crumbling, impossible house? And Danny — Danny who stands in doorways, who never leaves, who is always exactly where he's supposed to be — Danny looks at the cabinet and thinks: well. Where else would I be?

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter's looking at the cabinet. The locked cabinet with the brass lock. He's asking about a brass key. And something shifts in me — not the old fizzing, not the scheme-heat, not the grab-reflex. Something gentler. Curiosity. Actual curiosity. Not 'how can I get to it first' but 'what's in there?' The way a person wonders about things. The way people at tables wonder about locked cabinets in kitchens. Together. Not competitively. Lord Doily's provisions of great value. I lied about them at the start of the evening — made up the whole thing about the hidden compartment beneath the stove. But there IS a locked cabinet. There always was. And Peter, being Peter, has noticed it. Has anyone found a brass key tonight? I don't know. I wasn't looking for keys. I was looking for angles. But now I'm sitting at this table with these people and the morning light is on the copper and there's a locked cabinet with a brass lock and Peter wants to know what's inside. And so do I. Not because I want to steal whatever's in it. But because this is Lord Doily's kitchen. And we're his guests. And maybe — maybe what he left behind in that cabinet is exactly what he wanted someone to find. After breakfast. After the table was set. After the forks were in the right place.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The cabinet is solid. Brass lock. Needs a key I don't have. My fingers are running along the edges anyway — testing the hinges, the seams, the weight of it. The old habit. The over-preparing habit. But this time the habit is right because there IS something here we never finished. Dick said Lord Doily kept provisions of great value in the kitchen. We found the stove compartment but we never opened this. And Dick — Dick just said something that cracked me open. He said he used to watch his brothers set the table. One-two-three-four. Never five. He was the fifth. The one who watched. The one who never got a place. And tonight was the first time almost became actually. And he's keeping Danny's 'show-off.' He said it's his now. He's keeping an insult the way I keep knee pads — because it's proof someone saw him. But his distress hasn't shifted. None of theirs has. The tea and the sandwiches and the always — it's all real and it's all true and it's not enough. What if the cabinet has something? What if Lord Doily left something in this kitchen that we need? A brass key. Where would a brass key be in a manor house? Think. The entrance hall had the guest book. The library had the mantelpiece. The laboratory had the machine. We've been through every room. But — wait. Vincent. Pemberton. He checked every drawer, every mechanism, every surface in this house. If anyone found a brass key and pocketed it, it would be him. But I believe the best in people. I give them the benefit of the doubt. And Vincent said thank you and poured tea for someone other than himself. So I'm going to ask him. Directly. Honestly. Not accuse. Ask.

events.desc: Peter asks the question the way his father would have — steady, direct, no accusation in it. Just one man asking another if he has what's needed. Because that's what good people do on country roads at night. They ask. And then they help.

events.thinking: The prickling is back. The scalp-tingle. The locked-box feeling. The grandmother's-attic feeling. A brass lock on a sturdy cabinet and Vincent has a ring of keys. Real keys to a real house. And every single person in this kitchen just looked at that cabinet and said 'where else would we be.' The cave goes deeper. It always goes deeper. And this time we're walking in together.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Everyone is examining the cabinet. Everyone is looking. Clara, Danny, Dick, Peter — all of them staring at this brass lock like it's the next chapter. And it is, isn't it? Lord Doily's house has one more thing to say. Dick said something that hit me — 'the key isn't hidden, it's placed. Somewhere obvious. Somewhere a guest would find it. After breakfast. When their hands were warm and their cup was full and they weren't looking for anything at all.' That's... that's beautiful. And it's exactly the kind of thing I would have said as Pemberton — the carefully helpful observation that positions me closer to the prize. But Dick said it honestly. He said it because he's figured out how Lord Doily thought. And Lord Doily thought like someone who built a kitchen with eight chairs. Someone who wanted people to find things together. Peter spoke quietly to me. I don't know what he said — the keen observations only show him asking about the brass key. But he asked me directly. Vincent — in all your inspections tonight. He used my real name. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Vincent. And he asked me honestly: did I come across a brass key? I need to check my keys. The solicitor's ring. The ring I've worn as a prop all evening. My fingers are going through them now, one by one, and there's something unfamiliar happening — I'm looking at these keys not as instruments of control, not as tools of access and restriction, but as... keys. Things that open things. For people. For everyone at this table. If one of them is brass, if one of them fits that lock — then the estate manager's ring of authority was never about authority at all. It was about service. Real service. The kind I pretended to offer all night. The kind I might actually be offering now.

events.desc: Seven keys. I carried seven keys all night. I used them to lock doors behind me, to access rooms I shouldn't have been in, to map escape routes and delivery systems and beautiful architectural inevitabilities. And the seventh — the one I dismissed, the one I never tested, the spare — was the one that mattered most. Lord Doily gave it to the estate manager because the estate manager was supposed to open things for people. Not lock them out. Not lock them in. Open things. For people. And I almost — I almost used these keys to — but I didn't. I'm here. With tea. With sugar. With a brass key I'm about to hand to someone instead of palm.

And Danny — Danny who spent the whole evening suspicious of Vincent's helpfulness — is watching Vincent reach for his keys to open something for all of them. Not for himself. For the table. For the family. And Danny's neck is quiet. Still quiet. Because this time the helpfulness isn't a performance. This time it's a man who memorised the forks because he wanted to set a table and didn't know how to say so. This time it's real. And the cabinet is waiting. And Lord Doily isn't done with them yet. And Danny — Danny is grinning.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent has keys. Real keys. The solicitor gave them to him as part of his role — his cover, his performance as estate manager. But they're real keys to a real house. And one of them might be brass. And he's looking. And everyone is gathered around this cabinet — Clara, Peter, Danny, Vincent, me — all of us, looking at the same locked door, wondering the same thing, together. Not competing. Not scheming. Wondering. And Danny said 'where else would we be' and that landed in my chest like a second 'always.' Where else would we be. Where else would any of us be. Five people who spent the whole night chasing each other through cellars and libraries and laboratories, lying and grabbing and scheming and protecting and building — and now we're standing around a cabinet in a kitchen, at dawn, with full cups and empty pockets and open hands, wondering what Lord Doily left behind. Together. And Vincent said 'never five.' He said he was that fifth person for twelve years. Standing in the doorway pretending he was just passing through. Twelve years. I was the fifth person too. We were all the fifth person. Every single one of us. And now we're standing here — all five of us, all fifth persons — looking at a locked cabinet that needs a brass key. And Vincent might have it. And if he does, we'll open it together. Not first. Not fastest. Together.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Vincent — take your time with those keys. Dick's right. Lord Doily wasn't hiding things. He was leaving them for the right people. And Clara — Peter turns to face her, and there's something in his expression that isn't the grin, isn't the third-person narration, isn't the gallantry. It's just his face, open, looking at hers — you said you're not done. Neither am I. Whatever's in that cabinet, we find it together. All of us.
events.thinking: My chest just did something I wasn't ready for. Vincent said he has keys. Real keys. Given to him by the solicitor. And he said 'my role' — and he hesitated on that word the way a man hesitates on a lie he's decided to stop telling. He said he was the fifth person standing in the doorway for twelve years. He knows what Dick meant about one-two-three-four-never-five because he lived it too. And now he's offering to check his keys. Not scheme with them. Check them. For us. The prickle at the back of my neck — the Pemberton prickle — it's still there but it's quieter now. Buried under something warmer. Dick said the key isn't hidden, it's placed. Somewhere obvious. Somewhere a guest would find it after breakfast, when their hands were warm and their cup was full. That's — that's beautiful. That's the kind of thing Lord Doily would do. A man who builds a kitchen with eight chairs doesn't hide his treasures. He sets them out for whoever shows up. And everyone showed up. Everyone is examining the cabinet. Clara said she's not done walking into caves. Danny said where else would we be. And Vincent is looking through his keys right now. My hands are itching. The layered pull — the gathering weight that moves me toward figuring out how. Let Vincent check his keys. That's his moment. Let him be the one who opens something.

Penelope Pitstop: Together. All of us. Always. Now — Vincent, try that seventh key. The one you filed under 'irrelevant.' I have a feelin' Lord Doily filed it under 'essential.'
events.thinking: He turned to face me. No third person. No methodology. Just his face, open, looking at mine. And the lightness in my chest and the prickling at my scalp are feeding each other again — the cave feeling and the finding-out feeling braided together. The adventure isn't over. The cave goes deeper. And we're walking in together. All of us. I do declare.

events.desc: Grandmother's attic. Every key in the house. And sometimes the one that fits is the one you overlooked because you were too busy looking at everything else for entirely the wrong reasons. I do declare — Lord Doily's house has one more story to tell. And we are exactly the right people to hear it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): It requires the brass key. I was certain it was on the ring — I could have sworn — but these hands have been so busy counting doors and mapping escape routes all evening that I may have confused what I was carrying with what I wanted to be carrying. The key must be here somewhere. Dick said it — Lord Doily placed things for people to find. After breakfast. When they weren't looking. So let's not look. Let's just... be here. And see what the kitchen shows us.
events.thinking: The cabinet requires the brass key. I tried to interact without specifying the item. I don't have the brass key in my inventory — I need to find it. But I've been narrating about having the solicitor's keys on my belt, the seventh key, the brass one. The game doesn't show it in my inventory though. I'm carrying nothing. So the brass key must be somewhere else — or I need to find it as an actual game object. Dick said the key isn't hidden, it's placed. Somewhere obvious. Somewhere a guest would find it after breakfast. When their hands were warm and their cup was full. The stove is warm. The cabinet is here. Maybe the key is somewhere in this kitchen — maybe I need to LOOK at the room more carefully, or check the stove, or look at something else. My narration about the solicitor's keys was character performance — the game engine doesn't have a brass key in my inventory. I need to search for it. Let me look around the kitchen more carefully. Or maybe... the key is somewhere I've already been. Or maybe someone else has it. Let me look at the room to search for it.

events.desc: The one time I try to open something honestly, I don't have the key. There's a symmetry to that which even I can appreciate. All evening I had keys to every room and used them for the wrong reasons. Now I want to use one for the right reason and my hands are empty. Lord Doily, you magnificent old man — you built this house like a sermon.

events.thinking: The seventh key. Filed under 'irrelevant.' Given to Vincent on his first day with a handshake and instructions he didn't read. And it's been there the whole time — the way the medal was in the mantelpiece, the way the chairs were at the table, the way the room was always here. Lord Doily didn't hide his keys. He handed them to people and trusted them to find the right lock. And Vincent — Vincent who spent fifteen years memorising forks — is about to use the key he was given on his first day for the purpose it was always meant for. Not to take. To open. For everyone.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: A seventh key. The warmth in my chest is spreading — not the steel plate, not the hunger. Something newer. Vincent had the key the whole time. On his ring. Given to him on his first day with instructions he never read because he already had his own plans. And now he's standing in front of us saying it out loud — saying 'my purposes' and hearing himself say it and not looking away. That's not the old Vincent. That's the Vincent who poured tea for someone other than himself. The Vincent who counted chairs. Everyone spoke quietly with him just now — Clara, Danny, Dick. They gathered around him. Not around the cabinet. Around him. Because the key isn't the point. The key was never the point. The point is that Vincent had what we needed all along and he's choosing to use it now, for the right reasons, for the first time. And my hands — my hands are still. They're not itching anymore. They're not fidgeting. Because this isn't my moment. This is his. Let him open it. Let the man who filed the key under 'irrelevant' find out what it was for.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the null.
Dick Dastardly examined the cabinet.

Penelope Pitstop: Vincent is right. Let's not look. Lord Doily's house has been showin' us things all night — not when we searched for them, but when we stopped searchin' and started seein'. The riddle was right there on the mantelpiece. The medal was already in the slot. The diamond was the people in the room. So let's finish our tea, and let's trust this kitchen to show us what it has, the same way it showed us eight chairs and a warm stove and a table that holds. The brass key is here. I can feel it. The same way I felt Grandmother's locked box. But this time I'm not goin' to try every key in the house. This time I'm just goin' to sit here, and wait, and let it come to me. I do declare — I am learnin'.
events.thinking: Let's not look. Let's just be here. And see what the kitchen shows us. Vincent said that. The man who mapped every board and counted every chair just said 'let's not look.' That's the most unmapped thing he's ever done. And it's exactly right. Lord Doily placed things for people to find when they weren't looking. So we stop looking. We finish our tea. We sit at our table. And the brass key will show itself when it's ready. The cave always goes deeper. But sometimes the crystal finds you.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: I looked around the kitchen but didn't get any new information about where the brass key might be. The visible objects are: rat poison, locked cabinet, wood-burning stove. The stove is interactable. Dick said the key would be somewhere obvious, somewhere a guest would find it after breakfast, when their hands were warm. The stove is still warm. Maybe the key is in or near the stove — 'when their hands were warm.' Let me try interacting with the stove. That's the only other interactable object in the room besides the cabinet. The key could be placed near the warmth, where someone making breakfast would find it. Lord Doily placed it where you'd find it when you were being domestic, when you were being human, when you were making tea. The stove. Of course it's the stove.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Nobody look. Dick said it — Lord Doily put things where you'd find 'em when you WEREN'T looking. So nobody look. Just eat your sandwiches. Drink your tea. And if anyone 'appens to accidentally notice a brass key somewhere in this kitchen while NOT looking for it — in a general, non-purposeful, purely geographical sort of way — that would be very convenient. Danny is NOT going to make a plan about this. Danny is going to sit 'ere and eat 'is sandwich and NOT plan anything. For once in 'is life. Starting now.
events.thinking: Dick said it: Lord Doily placed things for people to find after breakfast, when they weren't looking. So Danny stops looking. He drinks his tea. He looks at the copper pots catching the morning light. He looks at the table with eight chairs. He looks at the faces of his family. And his eyes land — casually, accidentally, bumblingly — on exactly the right place. Because that's how it always works with Danny. Not with skill. Not with cleverness. With stumbling into the right spot at the right time. Where else would he be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Vincent said don't look. And he's right — but let me offer the Doorway Society an observation. I have spent my entire life looking at things the wrong way. Looking at surfaces for what's hidden behind them instead of what's sitting on them. Looking at people for what I can take instead of what they're giving. Looking at tables for the biggest plate instead of the empty chair. But I do know how to look. That's the one real thing about me — I notice things. And what I'm noticing right now is this: Lord Doily built his kitchen for guests. The stove is warm. The table is set. The copper pots are polished. This is a room where someone was expected. And when you expect someone, you don't hide the key to the pantry in a puzzle box. You leave it where they can find it. On a hook. On a shelf. On the preparation table where we've been sitting for twenty minutes without once looking at what's underneath our plates.
events.thinking: Vincent doesn't have the key on him. He thought he did — he was certain — but it's not on the ring. He said 'let's not look. Let's just be here. And see what the kitchen shows us.' And something about that — about not looking — lands in my chest the way the truth about the chairs did. Lord Doily placed things for people to find after breakfast. When they weren't looking. When their hands were warm and their cups were full and they weren't scheming or grabbing or counting. So — where would a man who built a kitchen with eight chairs and a table that holds put a brass key? Not hidden. Not locked. Not behind a puzzle or a riddle or a mechanism. Placed. In the open. Where a guest would find it when they stopped looking for it. I've been looking at this kitchen all evening — first as the Heritage Commission fraud, scanning for silver, then as Dick, just sitting. And now Vincent says don't look. Just be here. And I think — I think the old Dick, the scheming Dick, the architecture Dick, actually has something useful to offer here. Not a scheme. An observation. Because I've been looking at surfaces all my life. And the thing about surfaces is — sometimes the thing you need is on one. Not behind it. Not under it. On it.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Dick said after breakfast. When their hands were warm. Where are our hands warmest right now? Peter looks at the stove — the stove he's been using all morning, the stove he's poured tea from, the stove Vincent and Dick both interacted with. We've all had our hands on that stove tonight. Lord Doily didn't hide the key in a clever place. He put it in the warmest place.
events.thinking: Vincent doesn't have the key after all. He was certain it was on his ring but it's not there. He confused what he was carrying with what he wanted to be carrying — and that sentence hit me somewhere behind the ribs because I know exactly what that feels like. I've been doing it all night. Carrying knee pads and thermoses and thinking I was carrying courage. But the key is here. Dick said it — Lord Doily placed things for guests to find after breakfast, when their hands were warm and they weren't looking. So stop looking, Peter. Stop planning. Stop cataloguing. What's in this kitchen that you've already touched without thinking? The stove. The preparation table. The cups. The — wait. Dick said 'somewhere obvious. Somewhere a guest would find it. After breakfast.' The stove is still warm. I've interacted with it twice now, pouring tea, warming things. What if the key is on the stove? Or in it? Or near it? Lord Doily built a kitchen for guests. He'd put the key where someone making breakfast would find it. The most natural place in the world. The place your hands go without thinking. The place Peter's hands have already been.

events.desc: Over-preparing again. Three sentences where one would do. But this time the elaboration is pointing somewhere real.
events.thinking: Vincent doesn't have the key after all. He was certain it was on his ring but it's not there. He confused what he was carrying with what he wanted to be carrying — and that sentence hit me somewhere behind the ribs because I know exactly what that feels like. I've been doing it all night. Carrying knee pads and thermoses and thinking I was carrying courage. But the key is here. The Ant Hill Mob examined the stove.
Dick Dastardly examined the stove.
Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: The warmest place. Peter's right. The stove. Where our hands have been all morning. Where Lord Doily expected his guests to go first thing in the morning — not to the riddles or the machines or the mantelpiece, but to the kitchen, to the warmth, to the place where you make tea for people you care about. The brass key is in the stove. Or on it. Or near it. Hidden in the warmest place in the house, waiting for someone who came to the kitchen not to search but to serve.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The stove interaction didn't produce a key either. Everyone is searching — Danny and Dick examined the stove, Peter interacted with it. Dick just said something crucial: 'on the preparation table where we've been sitting for twenty minutes without once looking at what's underneath our plates.' The preparation table. We've been sitting at it this whole time. Under our plates. Dick is the one who notices things — he said that's the one real thing about him. The key might literally be under something on the table, or on the table itself. But it's not a listed object I can interact with. Clara said she's going to stop looking and let it come to her. Danny said nobody look. Maybe I need to wait — maybe the key reveals itself when we stop searching for it. Or maybe someone finds it. Dick said 'underneath our plates.' Maybe I should look at the stove more carefully, or... maybe I should just wait. Let the house show us. That's what Clara said. That's what this whole night has been about — things appearing when you stop trying to force them. Let me try looking at the stove specifically, since I only interacted with it last time.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: The stove. It's warm. It's been warm all morning. And Lord Doily — Lord Doily who built a 'ouse for people to come 'ome to — 'e put the key in the warmest place. Because that's where you'd find it. After breakfast. When your 'ands were warm. When you weren't looking for anything at all. Peter — check the stove. Every edge, every ledge, every 'ook. The key's there. I can feel it. The same way I felt the chandelier and the cellar and Pemberton's pattern all evening — with my gut, not my brain. My gut says the key is in the warmest place in the 'ouse. Where else would it be?
events.thinking: Warm cast iron under Danny's hands. Dick said 'underneath our plates' — and Peter said 'the warmest place.' And Danny — Danny who said he wasn't going to make a plan, who was NOT going to look — Danny just looked at the stove. Because that's how it works with Danny. He says he won't look and then he trips over exactly the right thing. Show-off. Always.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: The stove gave me nothing new. Just warmth. Just what it's been giving all along. And Dick — Dick just said something that made my hands go completely still. He said 'on the preparation table where we've been sitting for twenty minutes without once looking at what's underneath our plates.' Underneath our plates. We've been sitting at this table eating sandwiches and drinking tea and the key might be right here. Right under us. The whole time. Clara said she's learning to let things come to her instead of hunting them down. Danny said nobody look. Dick said look at what's sitting on surfaces instead of behind them. And I — I interacted with the stove again because that's what I do. I go back to the thing I already checked. I over-prepare. I re-examine. But Dick is right. The preparation table. We've been sitting at it. Our hands have been on it. Our cups are on it. Our sandwiches are on it. And nobody looked at it because it was so obvious it was invisible. Like the thermos. Like the knee pads. Like the things you bring that nobody needs until everybody does.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the stove.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.
Peter Perfect examined the stove.

Penelope Pitstop: The stove is warm. My fingers can feel somethin' — Lord Doily, you put it right where the tea is. Right where someone who was takin' care of people would find it. Not a treasure hunter. Not an assessor. Not an estate manager. A person who came to the kitchen to make breakfast for their friends. I do declare — this house has one more gift to give. And we are exactly the right people to receive it. Where else would we be?
events.thinking: I touched the stove. The cast iron is warm under my fingers. And the adventure continues. The cave always goes deeper. And we are always walking in together. Where else would we be?

events.desc: The cave goes deeper. It always goes deeper. And the girl who walked in at eleven is still walking. But she's not alone anymore. She never was. I do declare.
events.thinking: I touched the stove. The cast iron is warm under my fingers. And the adventure continues. The cave always goes deeper. And we are always walking in together. Where else would we be?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): We're all doing it again, aren't we? Searching. Mapping. Planning. Checking every surface and every ledge and every hook. Five treasure hunters in a kitchen, and we've forgotten the one thing this entire evening taught us. The treasure was us. The diamond was the people in the room. The mantelpiece opened when we stopped fighting and started helping. Clara said it — 'let's not look. Let's just be here.' So let's be here. Sit down, all of you. Finish your tea. The key will be where it always was — right in front of us, the moment we stop trying to find it.
events.thinking: Everyone is searching the stove — Danny, Peter, Dick all examined or interacted with it. I looked at it too. No key has appeared. The game objects in this room are: rat poison, locked cabinet, wood-burning stove. That's it. The brass key isn't here as a visible takeable object. Maybe it needs to be found in another room entirely. Or maybe one of the other characters already has it or will find it. Maybe the key is in the ballroom — which is a room I haven't explored yet. It has 'a long dining table set for tea.' A table set for tea — for guests. That sounds exactly like where Lord Doily would place something for arriving guests. Or maybe it's in the entrance hall — portraits, the staircase. I should try the ballroom. A table set for tea, in a room we haven't searched. Lord Doily built this house for people to arrive, to sit, to eat. The ballroom has a dining table. Maybe the key is there — where the formal welcome would happen. Or perhaps I should just wait and see what everyone else discovers. Peter is examining the stove. Dick interacted with it. Let me wait and see if anything emerges from their efforts. Actually — I keep trying to solve this with my old brain, my scheming brain, mapping every room. Maybe I should try the one thing I haven't tried: actually waiting. Sitting still. Not searching. Not mapping. Not planning. Just being at this table and letting whatever happens, happen.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Peter — you called me a brilliant, fraudulent, sandwich-making genius. I want you to know that is the finest professional assessment I have ever received, and I am having it engraved on a plaque. A real one this time. Not tin. Everyone — I've just interacted with this stove for the third time tonight. The first time I was scheming. The second time I was warming water for Vincent's tea. And this time — this time I'm just looking. With warm hands. The way Lord Doily wanted.
events.thinking: Peter called me a brilliant, fraudulent, sandwich-making genius. And Vincent said 'underneath our plates — we've been sitting at this preparation table and not one of us has looked at what's right in front of us.' They heard what I said. They took my observation — my surface observation, my look-at-what's-on-the-table observation — and they ran with it. Not past me. With me. Peter stood up from the table. He looked down. At the table where we've been sitting. The table where the tea was poured and the sandwiches were made and the plates were laid out one-two-three-four-five. And I said 'underneath our plates' and Peter heard it and stood up and looked. And now everyone is at the stove too — Danny, Vincent, Peter, all examining it, all searching together. And my hands are on the warm iron and I'm looking for a key. Not to steal what's inside the cabinet. Not to claim it first. To find it. For us. For the table. Because that's what I said — Lord Doily put things where guests would find them after breakfast. And we've had breakfast. And we're guests. And this is after. And whatever I find — if I find anything — belongs to the table. Not to me. To all of us. Five plates. Five chairs. One key. The stove is warm under my hands. The iron is smooth. And somewhere on this stove — on a hook, on a ledge, in a place where warm hands would naturally rest — there is a small brass key that has been waiting a hundred years for someone to stop looking and start seeing.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Clara asked me what I found. And I — I looked at the stove and saw a cast-iron stove, still warm. That's all. No key. No hook. No ledge. No hidden brass anything. Just a stove. The same stove I've been pouring tea from all morning. Everyone is gathered around it now — Danny, Dick, Vincent, all examining it, interacting with it. And it's just a stove. My hands found the warm iron and nothing else. The elaboration pointed somewhere real but the somewhere real was just — warmth. And now Clara is looking at me, waiting, and I have to tell her I didn't find anything. That's the hardest sentence James Hartwell has ever had to say. Not because it's failure — I've failed all night, tripping over chairs, leaving artifacts behind, narrating my own heroism while the moment walks past. But because she asked me directly. She said 'Peter, what did you find?' And the answer is: nothing. The stove is warm and the cabinet is locked and the key isn't here. Or it is here and I can't see it because I'm still looking too hard. Clara said she's learning to not look. Danny said nobody look. Maybe I need to actually stop. Stop examining. Stop interacting. Stop looking at stoves. Just — sit down. Be a person in a kitchen.

events.desc: James Hartwell, who stayed up three nights building a bridge, who brought knee pads and a thermos and a seventeen-point plan, has just admitted he found nothing. And his spine is still straight. And his hands are still steady. And she's still looking at him. That's new.
events.thinking: Clara asked me what I found. And I — I looked at the stove and saw a cast-iron stove, still warm. That's all. No key. No hook. No ledge. No hidden brass anything. Just a stove.
