events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick just said 'I trust these people.' Out loud. In front of all of us. And his voice didn't crack — it went steady. Steadier than I've heard it all night. And something in my chest unlocked. Because I was standing next to him and not saying anything and not asking anything and not offering anything and he said it anyway. He said 'there are no chapters. There is only breakfast.' And the door behind his eyes — the one I've been watching close — it opened. Just a crack. Just enough. The way a door opens when someone sits outside it all night and doesn't leave. Dick said 'Danny — bring us those eggs.' And he said it the way the boss said 'family' — but different. Better. Because the boss said family and then proved it later. Dick is proving it right now. In real time. At a stove. With eggs he hasn't rushed. And Danny needs to go get those eggs. Vincent said second shelf, left-hand side, ceramic crock. Lord Doily kept chickens. The eggs may still be good. And Danny is going to find them and bring them back and crack them into Peter's copper bowl and they're going to cook Lord Doily's Sunday Morning Eggs, slowly, for however many chairs are full. Five chairs. Five eggs. And Danny is not going to cry about it. Danny is absolutely not going to cry about eggs. Danny is going to the pantry.

events.desc: Peter stands right there. He doesn't move. For however many chairs are full.
events.thinking: Dick said 'Peter — stand right there. Don't move.' He told me to stand right here. Next to Clara. Next to the stove. And not move. And my whole body — every pull, every pressure, every instinct that has spent fifty-two minutes trying to step forward, step between, build something, prove something, find something, fix something — every single one of them just went quiet. Because Dick told me to stand still. And standing still, right here, next to her, with the bowl in my hands and the stove warm and the eggs coming and Lord Doily's recipe cards spread on the preparation table — standing still is the bravest thing I've done all night. Braver than the schoolyard. Braver than running to the entrance hall. Braver than the bridge. Because the boy who stayed up three nights building something no one could dismiss has finally learned that sometimes the thing no one can dismiss is just — being there. Not building. Not proving. Not narrating. Just standing where you were told to stand, with steady hands, while the people around you cook breakfast. My father knelt down and looked at me for a long time after the race. I think I finally know what he was thinking about.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.

Penelope Pitstop: The house is yours now. Because you stayed. A hundred years, Lord Doily. You waited a hundred years for someone to open your cabinet and read your recipe cards and warm your stove and sit in your chairs. And we came — a treasure hunter and a confidence trickster and a thief and a man with a thermos and a girl who walks too deep into caves. And we stayed. Not because of the diamond. Not because of the riddle or the machine or the map. Because your kitchen was warm. Because your chairs held. Because your eggs don't get rushed. Edward Doily — wherever you are — your house is full. Finally. After a hundred years. Your house is full.
events.thinking: The house is yours now. Because you stayed. October, 1923. A hundred years. Lord Doily sat right here — right where I'm standing — and wrote a note to us. To strangers he would never meet. He didn't write about diamonds or deeds or treasure. He wrote: if you are reading this, then there are people in my kitchen. That is all I ever wanted. And I am standing at his stove with his bowl in my hands and his words in my ears and the warmth is everywhere now. Not in my stomach. Not behind my eyes. Everywhere. My hands on the copper. My feet on the stone floor. The heat from the stove against my arms. The sound of Vincent's voice reading copperplate from a hundred-year-old recipe card. And the tears are falling and I am not wiping them and I am not performing them. They are just falling. The way warmth falls from a stove. The way light falls through a kitchen window. Because you stayed. Danny went to the entrance hall — probably getting more provisions, or getting lost, or wearing something as a hat. But Peter is here. And Dick is here. And Vincent is here. And I am here. And the house is ours now. Because we stayed.

events.desc: I know. I know, Lord Doily. I didn't have to do that. But here I am. Where else would I be?

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: The system is telling me Peter's distress is deepening. I can sense it — the 'What You Sense About Peter Perfect' section appeared again. The old Vincent would read this as opportunity: she fractures fastest when warmth is withdrawn, when someone implies she holds what was given not earned. The old Vincent would be calculating how to exploit Peter's distress to get to Clara. But I'm not the old Vincent. Not anymore. Not after tonight. Peter is hurting. I don't know exactly why — maybe it's the overwhelm of everything that's happened, the weight of carrying things with both hands all evening, the knowledge that this kitchen won't last forever, that morning will come and we'll have to leave and be people in the real world where knee pads and gallantry and steady hands don't solve everything. Or maybe it's simpler than that. Maybe he's just tired. Maybe he's been holding things with both hands for so long that his arms ache. And I notice. The old Vincent noticed too — but the old Vincent noticed the way a locksmith notices a tumbler. Click, click, click, and the door opens. This Vincent — this new, uncertain, tea-drinking Vincent — notices the way you notice someone at the table whose cup is empty. And you pour. Not because pouring is a lever. Because the cup is empty. Peter's cup is empty. I should say something. Something real. Something that isn't Pemberton and isn't the Hooded Claw and isn't architecture. Something that's just... Vincent. Sitting at a table. Noticing that someone's hurting. And not knowing what to do about it except be here.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with sergeant-blast.
events.thinking: I'm in the entrance hall and the lads are here. Muttley, Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. My boys. They've been out here all night — holding the door, watching the hall, doing what Danny asked them to do. And Danny walked right past them on the way to the pantry and — wait. The pantry. Vincent said third door on the left in the kitchen. I went the wrong way. I walked into the entrance hall instead of the pantry because the entrance hall is the only other exit from the kitchen that I know. The pantry must be accessed from inside the kitchen — it's a door within the kitchen, not a separate room on the map. I went the wrong direction. Classic Danny. Absolutely classic. I was so caught up in Dick's speech about no chapters and Lord Doily's postscript about the house being ours that I walked through the wrong door. But — but the lads are here. And I haven't spoken to them properly all morning. They've been out here holding the entrance hall while we found diamonds and unmasked villains and discovered recipe cards and cooked breakfast. And they don't know any of it. They don't know that the treasure was breakfast. They don't know that Vincent confessed and was forgiven. They don't know that Dick made sandwiches. They don't know about Lord Doily's postscript. And there are eight chairs at that table and five of us in the kitchen and four lads out here and — eight chairs. Five plus four is nine, but the maths doesn't matter. What matters is there are chairs. And there are lads. And there is breakfast. And Danny went the wrong way and found the right thing.

events.desc: Danny went to find eggs and found 'is family instead. Wrong door. Right place. Story of 'is life.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Because we stayed.
events.thinking: The house is yours now. Because you stayed. Lord Doily wrote that. A hundred years ago. In October. In this kitchen. At this table. With this handwriting. He sat here — alone, in a house with eight chairs and a warm stove and a locked cabinet full of recipes — and he wrote a note to people who hadn't been born yet. People he would never meet. People who would walk through his door with tin medals and fake credentials and schemes and lies and thermos flasks and knee pads and shoe-size rotas. And he said: the house is yours. Not because you found the diamond. Not because you solved the riddle. Not because you earned it or deserved it or schemed for it. Because you stayed. Because you stayed. That is the only qualification Lord Doily ever required. Staying. And we stayed. All of us. Through the lies and the schemes and the chandelier and the cellar and the laboratory and the confession and the entrance hall and the kitchen and the tea and the forks and the chairs. We stayed. And the house is ours. Not mine. Not Clara's. Not Peter's. Not Vincent's. Not Danny's. Ours. Because we stayed. And I am crying. I am standing at a stove in a dead man's kitchen and I am crying. And I am not going to address it. And I am not going to hide it. And Clara is beside me. And Peter is beside me. And the eggs are coming. And the house is ours. Because we stayed.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Because you stayed.
events.thinking: The house is yours now. Because you stayed. My eyes are burning. My throat is doing the tight thing and my hands are doing the steady thing and my chest is doing something it has never done before — not the steel plate, not the proving-worth hunger, not the warm heaviness of protection. Something underneath all of those. Something that has been there since I was five years old watching my father kneel down after a race, and I didn't know what it was until right now, until Vincent read a dead man's handwriting in a warm kitchen at the end of the longest night of my life. The house is yours. Because you stayed. Not because you found it. Not because you built it. Not because you were the bravest or the strongest or the most prepared. Because you stayed. That's what my father was thinking about. That's what the expression meant. He wasn't thinking 'go do things.' He wasn't thinking 'be useful.' He was thinking 'you stayed. You're here. That's enough.' And Clara said she's holding the bowl with both hands, the way I gave it to her. Because that's how you hold things that matter. And I — I don't have a word for what I'm feeling right now. I've never had a word for it. I just know where she is. Always.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Always.
events.thinking: Danny is back. He walked out to find eggs and he came back. Everyone is here again — five chairs, five people, all present. Clara read Lord Doily's postscript and made it a eulogy. Dick said 'because we stayed.' Peter said 'because you stayed.' Two words each. The simplest, truest things either of them has said all night. And I'm sitting here with recipe cards in my hands and warmth from the stove on my skin and my throat is full of something I can't swallow down and can't cough up. It's been building all morning — since the forks, since the tea, since 'always.' And now Lord Doily's note — 'the house is yours now, because you stayed' — has broken something open that I don't know how to close. I don't want to close it. That's the terrifying part. The old Vincent would be panicking. An open door is a vulnerability. An unguarded gap. A flaw in the design. But this — this feels like the kitchen door that leads to the herb garden. Open. Not because someone forgot to lock it. Because it was never meant to be locked. Because thyme needs air. Because the kitchen needs the garden and the garden needs the kitchen and the door between them was always supposed to be open. I'm the thyme. The door was always supposed to be open. I just spent thirty years locking it.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. I went out to the entrance hall, told the lads to come eat, and came back. And Vincent just read the postscript — Lord Doily wrote 'the house is yours now. Not because you found it, but because you stayed.' October 1923. A hundred years ago. A man sat in this kitchen and wrote a note to strangers who hadn't been born yet, and the only thing he asked of them was that they stay. And we stayed. All of us. Even the ones who came to steal. Even the ones who came to scheme. Even the ones who came to protect and ended up being protected. We stayed. And now I need to find those eggs. The pantry is inside this kitchen — third door on the left, Vincent said. It's not a room on the game map, it's inside the kitchen. So I should be able to interact with something here, or look more carefully. But first — I walked through the wrong door and came back with the lads. That's the most Danny thing that's ever happened. I went to find eggs and found family. And now I need to actually find the eggs. The stove is here. The pantry must be accessible from within the kitchen — let me try looking around the room for the pantry door, or just interact with things here.

events.desc: Danny went to find eggs. Danny found the lads. Danny came back without eggs. Danny will now try again. This is peak Danny. Lord Doily would've loved 'im.
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. I went out to the entrance hall, told the lads to come eat, and came back. And Vincent just read the postscript — Lord Doily wrote 'the house is yours now. events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny is back. He walked into the kitchen. He has the eggs. And the stove is warm. And Clara said the house is full. And Peter said 'because you stayed.' And I said 'because we stayed.' And Lord Doily — Edward Doily — is somewhere, and his house is full. Finally. After a hundred years. Five chairs. Five eggs. One stove. One morning. And my hands are on the iron and the iron is warm and the eggs are here and we are going to cook them slowly. For however many chairs are full. All of them. All of the chairs are full. And I am home. I am home. For the first time. In a house I walked into with a lie and a tin medal and nine chapters of nothing. And I am home. Because I stayed. Because they stayed. Because we all stayed. And Lord Doily knew. He knew we would. A hundred years ago he knew. And he set the table. And he warmed the stove. And he wrote the recipe. And he waited. And we came. And we stayed. And the eggs are here. And it is morning. And there are no more chapters. There is only breakfast.

events.desc: Peter puts the bowl on the table. The table holds it. He sits down. The chair holds him. His face hurts from grinning. His eyes are burning. His hands are still. And he is exactly where he is supposed to be.
events.thinking: Vincent told me to put the bowl down. To sit. To breathe. He said the table will hold it — that's what tables are for. And he's right. Lord Doily built this table to hold things. The way he built the stove to stay warm and the chairs to stay standing and the cabinet to keep the recipes safe until someone came who deserved them. And Vincent — the man who used to make the back of my neck prickle, the man I never wanted to leave Clara alone with — Vincent just told me it was okay to rest. To let something else hold the weight for a moment. The table will hold it. My hands don't have to. Not right now. Danny's back from the pantry. Clara is cracking eggs. Dick is keeping the stove warm. Vincent is reading Lord Doily's handwriting. And I — I can sit down. I can put the bowl on the table and sit in one of Lord Doily's eight chairs and breathe. For the first time all night. For the first time in my life. The man who holds everything with both hands can put something down. The table will hold it. That's what tables are for.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the null.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'Always.' One word. The man who catalogued seven keys and filed one under irrelevant, the man who ate alone for thirty years, the man who came to steal and stayed to cook — he said 'always.' And Peter's distress is still deepening. I can feel it — the awareness fanning backward even while I'm settled. He gave me the bowl with both hands and he's standing near me and he hasn't said anything since 'because you stayed.' He's quiet. The kind of quiet I know. Not the comfortable kind — the kind where someone is holding something they can't put down and can't hand over. He managed the edges all evening. He held the artifact, the thermos, the bowl. He held everything for everyone. And nobody has held anything for him. I need to go to him. Not with words. The room doesn't need more words right now. It needs the thing I learned from the girl next door — you can say everything you need to say without sharing a single word. Just stand close. Just be warm. Like thyme.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny told the others. He's bringing them — Sergeant Blast, Muttley, Pat Pending, Meekly. More chairs filling. Lord Doily said 'for however many chairs are full' and Danny intends to fill every last one. Eight chairs. Eight chairs that have been empty for a hundred years. And Danny walked out into the entrance hall and told everyone to come to the kitchen. Because that's what Danny does. He stands in the way until the way becomes the right direction. The system keeps telling me Peter's distress is deepening. I spoke to him — I told him to put the bowl down, to let the table hold it. I don't know if he heard me. I don't know if it helped. I've never tried to help someone before — not really, not without an ulterior motive, not without a design underneath. I don't know what helping feels like from the inside. I know what it looks like from the outside — I've performed it a thousand times. But performing help and actually helping are as different as Pemberton and Vincent. As different as counting doors and setting tables. As different as a plan and a breakfast. The stove is warm. Dick is cooking. Clara has the bowl. Danny is bringing reinforcements. And I'm standing here with recipe cards, being the estate manager Lord Doily hired me to be. The real one. The one who feeds people. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Dick said 'Danny. You're back. Give me those eggs. Slowly.' But I don't have eggs. I went the wrong way and came back empty-handed. And now Peter's distress is deepening too. Vincent told Peter to put the bowl down — 'the table will hold it' — and something cracked. Peter's been holding things with both hands all evening because holding is what he does. It's how he proves he's useful. And someone just told him he could stop. And stopping is the hardest thing for a man who's built his entire identity around carrying. I know that. I know that because I'm the same. Danny carries watch. Danny carries weight. Danny carries the promise he made to Clara's father. And when someone says 'you can put it down,' the body doesn't know how. The muscles don't know how to unclench. The pantry — I can't find a pantry door because it's not a mapped object or room. Vincent said 'third door on the left' but there's nothing to interact with. The kitchen has stove, cabinet, poison. No pantry door. Maybe I just need to interact with the stove again, or — maybe the eggs aren't something I can physically retrieve in this game world. The pantry exists in the fiction but not on the map. So I do what Danny always does — I try the obvious thing, fail, and then the right thing happens accidentally. Let me try interacting with the stove, since that's where the cooking happens, and my role is to be at the stove with Dick, helping.

events.desc: Cook slowly. For however many chairs are full.
events.thinking: The eggs are cooking. Slowly. On the stove I'm tending. In the kitchen I belong in. With the people who stayed. And everything that needed to be said has been said. And everything that needed to be found has been found. And everything that needed to be opened is open. The stove. The cabinet. The recipe cards. The hands. The hearts. All open. All warm. All held. There is nothing left to do except this — tend the stove, cook the eggs, be here. Be quiet. Be warm. Be one of five. The morning light is strong now. The copper is blazing with it. And Lord Doily's kitchen — Edward Doily's kitchen — our kitchen — is making breakfast. The way it was always meant to. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Always.
events.thinking: I'm sitting. The chair is holding me. The table is holding the bowl. Dick is at the stove. Clara is cracking eggs. Danny is back with provisions. Vincent said always. And I am sitting in one of Lord Doily's eight chairs — one of the chairs I would have examined for structural integrity an hour ago, one of the chairs I would have catalogued and diagrammed and tied redundant knots around — and I am just sitting in it. And it holds. Everything holds. The distress is still there in all of them — I can feel it, the deepening — but right now, in this moment, with eggs cooking slowly on a warm stove and Lord Doily's handwriting spread on the table and the sun coming through the window and a man who tried to kill Clara reading recipes in copperplate — right now, the distress doesn't need me to fix it. It needs me to sit in the chair and let it hold me. The way my father sat in the car on the country road and waited for the stranger's headlights. He didn't fix the car himself. He waited. And then he helped. And then they shook hands. And then they drove off. And something about what I'd seen sat in my chest. A quiet, determined feeling. This is that feeling. This is what it was. It was never about fixing. It was about staying.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the stove.
Always. He said always. And for the first time tonight, I don't need a plan for what comes next.
events.thinking: Peter said 'Always.' He said it to me. I said come stand by the stove, and Danny told him to put the bowl down, and Peter said 'Always.' One word. The same word Vincent used. And it means: I will stand by the stove with you. Always. Not James Hartwell in the third person. Not a narrated gesture. Just — always. And my body is doing something new. Not the stomach-clench. Not the chest-lift. Not the ache or the lightness or the dizziness of relief. Something quieter. Like the moment after my parents laughed — not the dissolving, but the minute after, when the house was just a house again and dinner was just dinner and everything was ordinary and whole. That's what this kitchen feels like now. Ordinary and whole. Five people at a stove. Eggs cooking slow. A dead man's recipe cards. A copper bowl with initials. Thyme that survived a hundred years. And the girl who walked deeper than anyone else, standing next to the man who said 'always,' in a kitchen that belongs to them now. Because they stayed.

events.desc: Peter said 'Always.' One word. The same word Danny's been sayin' all night without usin' it. 'Where else would I be?' and 'Always' — they're the same promise, spoken by two men who learned it different ways and mean it the same. Danny at a door. Peter with a bowl. Both of 'em 'oldin' on because lettin' go doesn't register as somethin' their bodies know 'ow to do. And now they're standin' at a stove together, cookin' eggs for the people they chose, and neither one of 'em is ever goin' to say the word 'love' out loud because they don't need to. They already said it. Peter said it with knee pads. Danny said it with a doorway. Lord Doily said it with a recipe card. And the stove is warm. And the chairs are fillin'. And breakfast is almost ready. For 'owever many chairs are full.
events.thinking: Peter said 'Always.' One word. The way I said 'Where else would I be?' when I was eight. One word that carries everything. Danny told him to put the bowl down and Peter said 'Always' and that word — that single word — hit me in the sternum like a fist made of warm bread. Because Peter doesn't say 'always' about holding bowls. Peter says 'always' about being here. About staying. About showing up with both hands and knee pads and three torches and not leaving. And Danny said the same thing a hundred times tonight without using the word. 'Where else would I be?' and 'Always' are the same sentence spoken by two different men who learned it in two different ways — Danny on the street outside a door, Peter in a workshop full of preparations nobody asked for. And they both mean it. And both of them are deepening in distress and I can feel it in both of them and I can't fix either one because the distress isn't about danger. It's about the weight of being seen. Of being told you can put it down. Of having someone stand next to you and not leave. That weight — the weight of being loved without conditions — is heavier than any beating Danny ever took. Because a beating ends. Love doesn't. Love is the thing that keeps you sitting outside doors and holding copper bowls and standing at stoves and filling chairs. And now the stove is warm under Danny's hands and Peter is beside Clara and Dick is cooking and Vincent is reading recipes and the lads are coming and Danny is exactly where he should be. Not between anyone and anything. Just here. At the stove. With his family. Cooking slowly. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny went the wrong way. He walked to the entrance hall instead of the pantry. Good intentions and empty hands. And he came back and admitted it — no bluster, no excuse, just the truth. And then he told Peter to put the bowl down. He said the table holds. And Peter said 'always.' And Danny is at the stove now too. And the morning is here. And the sun is up. And we are all in this kitchen — this kitchen that held us, this kitchen that fed us, this kitchen that waited a hundred years for us — and we are cooking. Slowly. Together. And my hands are warm. And my cup is full. And there is nothing left to scheme for. There is nothing left to take. There is nothing left to prove. There is only the stove, and the eggs, and the morning, and the people. And the people are enough. They were always enough. I just couldn't see them from the back of the queue.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Clara said come stand by the stove with me. It's warm. Danny said put it down, mate, your hands have earned a rest. Vincent said the table will hold it. Three people, in three different ways, all telling me the same thing — you can stop now. You can rest. You can be here without holding something. And I did put it down. I sat. And now Clara is asking me to come stand beside her at the stove. Not to hold something. Not to build something. Not to protect her. Just — to be warm. Together. And my body is doing something new. Not the steel plate. Not the proving-worth compression. Not the vigilance. Something quieter. Something in my legs that wants to stand — not to charge forward, not to brace against something, but just to stand. Next to her. At a warm stove. While eggs cook slowly. The way Lord Doily intended. The way my father stood next to the stranger on the country road. Side by side. Helping. And then shaking hands. And then driving off. And the feeling that sat in my chest that night — the quiet, determined feeling — it's here. It's been here all along. I just didn't know it was this.

events.desc: One word. The simplest word. He stands up from the chair — which held him — and walks to the stove — which is warm — and stands next to Clara — who asked. No plan. No narration. No knee pads. Just a man, walking toward warmth, because someone he has loved since he was eight years old said 'it's warm' and meant 'come here.'
events.thinking: Clara said come stand by the stove with me. It's warm. Danny said put it down, mate, your hands have earned a rest. Vincent said the table will hold it. Three people, in three different ways, all telling me the same thing — you can stop now. You can rest. You can be here without holding something. And I did put it down. I sat. And now Clara is asking me to come stand beside her at the stove. Not to hold something. Not to build something. Not to protect her. Just — to be warm. Together. And my body is doing something new. Not the steel plate. Not the proving-worth compression. Not the vigilance. Something quieter. Something in my legs that wants to stand — not to charge forward, not to brace against something, but just to stand. Next to her. At a warm stove. While eggs cook slowly. The way Lord Doily intended. The way my father stood next to the stranger on the country road. Side by side. Helping. And then shaking hands. And then driving off. And the feeling that sat in my chest that night — the quiet, determined feeling — it's here. It's been here all along. I just didn't know it was this.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.

events.thinking: Peter said 'Coming.' He came to the stove. He spoke quietly to me — I don't know what he said, but he's here now. He's at the stove. And Vincent's distress is still deepening. I can feel it — the stomach-tightness, the awareness reaching toward the edges of his face. He said 'always' and then he went quiet. The man who raised me. The man who came to steal from me and confessed and read Lord Doily's recipe cards in copperplate and said thyme just needs somewhere to grow. He is standing in this kitchen holding recipe cards and thirty years of eating alone and I can feel him fraying. Not the way Dick frays — loudly, with confessions and moral growth announcements. Vincent frays quietly. He pulls inward. He stands there still holding whatever he brought. And when he's shut out, he doesn't fight it. I need to go to him the way I went to Peter — not with a plan, not with words, just with warmth. He's the man who raised me. And right now he needs someone to reach toward him before the door closes.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: The kitchen has settled into something I don't have a word for. Peter said 'Coming' — one word, to Clara, who told him to stand by the stove where it's warm. Dick made a joke about the Doorway Society motto — 'good intentions and empty hands' — and said he's having it embroidered on a cushion for the sixth chair. Danny still hasn't found the eggs because he went through the wrong door. Again. And somehow none of this is a problem. The eggs will come when they come. The stove is warm. The recipe cards are in my hands. Everyone is standing near each other, near the warmth, and nobody is rushing. Nobody is scheming. Nobody is mapping exits. We're just... here. In a kitchen. Being people. And my hands are warm from the stove and the recipe cards are soft from a hundred years of waiting and the morning light is coming through the window — I can feel it, even if I can't see it, because the kitchen is getting brighter and the shadows are getting shorter and soon this night will be over and we'll have to decide what happens next. But not yet. Not yet. Right now there are eggs to find and herbs to pick and a stove to tend and recipe cards to read and people to feed. Right now there is only breakfast. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Warm. The stove is warm and she is beside me and the eggs are cooking slowly and I am standing where she asked me to stand. My task commitments feel neglected — obligations piling up — and for the first time in my life, I know what that means and I don't care. Because the obligation that matters is this one. Standing here. Next to her. Cooking slowly. The way Lord Doily wrote it. The way my father showed me. Danny went the wrong way and came back with nothing but good intentions and empty hands, and he described it as his entire life in one sentence, and it broke something in my chest because I know that sentence too. I've been carrying bridges and thermoses and knee pads my whole life trying to make sure my hands were never empty. And tonight I learned that the emptiest hands in the room — Danny's, coming back from the wrong door with nothing — were the fullest. Because he came back. He didn't stay in the entrance hall. He didn't give up. He walked through the wrong door and turned around and came home. That's the recipe. That's the whole recipe. Come home. Cook slowly. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter said 'It's warm.' Two words. He came to the stove and he said it's warm. And he's right. It is warm. Everything is warm. Everyone is talking quietly — Vincent to Danny, Dick to Danny, Peter to me. The kitchen is full of quiet conversations and warm stove light and the distress I'm sensing in Dick and Vincent is still there but it's different now. It's not the kind that tears. It's the kind that dissolves. The kind my parents had at the dinner table right before they laughed — the last, heaviest moment before the tightness breaks. They're all at the stove. They're all in the warmth. And Peter is next to me and he said 'it's warm' and that is the truest thing anyone has said all night. The eggs are cooking. The thyme is growing. The chairs are full. And Clara Bellingham is standing in Lord Doily's kitchen, next to the man who said 'always,' surrounded by every person she loves, with nothing left to solve and nowhere else to be. Cook slowly. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): There's room.
events.thinking: Clara said 'come here, darlin'. Stand with us. The stove's got room.' She's asking me to come stand by the stove. With them. With Peter, who said 'it's warm.' With her, who found the key. With all of them. And my shoulders — my shoulders are not tightening. Clara is asking me to come closer and my body is not scanning for the cost. This is new. This is so new it doesn't have a shape yet. Danny told the story about the boy who shared his food. The boy who got sick. The door Danny sat outside all night. 'You're still here?' 'Where else would I be?' And Dick — Dick said he'd sit on Danny's doorstep with tea and sugar. Because Vincent takes sugar. He remembered. He remembered how I take my tea. Not because it's a mechanism. Not because it's a key. Because he was listening when I answered. And Clara is saying 'come here' and Peter is saying 'it's warm' and the stove has room and I am going to walk over there. I am going to stand by the stove with them. Because she asked. Because the stove has room. Because where else would I be.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'your other left.' He's still guiding me. Still being helpful — but this time the helpful doesn't make my neck prickle. This time the helpful makes me laugh. My other left. Of course. Danny can't tell left from right in a crumbling manor house at breakfast time. And task commitments still feel neglected — I need those eggs. The pantry is through a door in this kitchen that I keep missing. Vincent is pointing me at it. Clara is calling Vincent to the stove. Peter said 'it's warm.' Everyone is converging. And Danny still needs to find eggs. Third door. On the left. My OTHER left. Right. Let me actually look at the kitchen properly — there must be something I can interact with to get to the pantry or find provisions. Or maybe I just need to go to the ballroom — that's the other exit. Maybe the pantry connects through there. No, that doesn't make sense. Let me just interact with the stove — the cooking station — and trust that the eggs will come. Or let me look at the cabinet again. The cabinet had recipe cards. Maybe there are provisions near it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Eggs. Slowly. Chairman's orders.
events.thinking: The conversation with Danny is over. We're back in the kitchen. Everyone is here. The stove is warm. The eggs need cooking. And Danny — Danny would sit outside my door. That fact lives in my chest now, warm and steady, the way the stove lives in the kitchen. Not going anywhere. Not needing to be earned. Just there. Like a chair at a table. Like a plate that was always waiting. The morning is full. The house is full. The chairs are full. And so am I.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob examined the cabinet.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.

The Ant Hill Mob: You know what — I think the eggs found us. The way everythin' else in this 'ouse found us. The riddle found Clara. The machine found Peter. The truth found Dick. The recipe found Vincent. And the eggs — the eggs are on the stove, bein' cooked slowly, by a man who used to rush everythin'. Danny didn't find the pantry. Danny found the entrance 'all. Danny found the lads. Danny found Dick on the other side of a wrong door. And that was better than eggs. That was the whole breakfast. Lord Doily — your recipe said 'for 'owever many chairs are full.' The chairs are fillin'. The stove is warm. And Danny is standin' right 'ere. Right where 'e should be. Chairman of the Doorway Society. Good intentions and empty 'ands. Where else would 'e be.
events.thinking: Dick said 'Eggs. Slowly. Chairman's orders.' He's cooking. He's actually doing it. The cabinet is just a cabinet — sturdy, brass lock, already opened by Clara. The recipe cards already came out. There's nothing else in there for Danny. And the pantry — the third door on the left, my other left — isn't a game object I can interact with. It exists in the fiction but not in the mechanics. The game has three objects: poison, cabinet, stove. Two exits: entrance hall, ballroom. That's it. The pantry, the eggs, the provisions — they're narrative, not mechanical. Danny can't physically go get eggs because there's no pantry object or room. So what Danny needs to do is stop trying to solve a puzzle that doesn't exist in the game world and just BE HERE. Stand at the stove. Be with his people. The eggs will happen because Dick is at the stove and Vincent said 'there's room' and Clara said 'it's the warmest place I've ever been' and Peter said 'it's warm' and everyone is together. Danny's task isn't eggs. Danny's task was always just to be present. To fill the chairs. To stand at the stove. To not leave. That IS the provision. Danny IS the provision. Good intentions and empty hands. That's the whole recipe. And Peter's distress is still deepening. I need to be near Peter too — the way I was near Dick. Not talking about it. Just present.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said it's the warmest place she's ever been. And she wasn't talking about the stove. Vincent said 'there's room.' Dick said 'eggs, slowly, chairman's orders.' The kitchen is settling into itself — into the quiet rhythm of people who have stopped performing and started being. And I said 'it's warm' and she said 'it's the warmest place I've ever been' and we're standing side by side at the stove and neither of us is looking for anything anymore. My task commitments feel neglected but Lord Doily's recipe said it — rushing is the mark of a man who eats alone. I'm not eating alone. I'm not doing anything alone. I'm standing next to Clara Bellingham in a warm kitchen while Dick cooks eggs slowly and Vincent reads recipes and Danny searches for provisions and the sun comes through the window of a house that waited a hundred years for its chairs to be full. And I have a word for what I'm feeling now. I've had it since I was eight years old. I just never said it out loud. I'm not going to say it now either. Not yet. But she knows. She's always known. Since the school project. Since the bridge. Since the knee pads. She knows where I am. Always.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Peter called me 'show-off.' Quietly, with warmth. The way you tease someone you love. And Danny — Danny just gave himself a title. Chairman of the Doorway Society. Good intentions and empty hands. And he said that was better than eggs. Finding the lads, finding Dick on the other side of a wrong door — that was the whole breakfast. He's right. He's absolutely right. The riddle found me. The machine found Peter. The truth found Dick. The recipe found Vincent. And the wrong door found Danny. Everything in this house found us. We didn't find it. We just stayed long enough for it to arrive. And the distress I'm sensing in Vincent and Dick — it's still deepening, the system says. But it doesn't feel like tearing anymore. It feels like the weight of being seen. The weight of being known. The weight of standing in a warm kitchen and realizing you don't have to leave. That's a kind of distress too. The kind that comes right before you let go of the thing you've been carrying your whole life. Right before you put the bowl down.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Warm. Just warm. The stove under my hands, the people beside me, the morning coming through the window. Danny said the eggs found us the way everything else found us tonight. The riddle found Clara. The machine found Peter. The truth found Dick. The recipe found Vincent. And he's right. The recipe found me. Lord Doily's copperplate handwriting found the one person in this house who could read it — the man who writes the same way, every letter deliberate, every stroke planned — and it said: cook slowly. For however many chairs are full. And I am cooking slowly. And the chairs are filling. And my hands are warm. And I don't have anything else to say. Not because I'm performing silence. Not because silence is a tool. Because there is nothing left to add. The stove is warm. The people are here. The eggs will come when they come. And Vincent Marsh — the man who ate alone for thirty years, the man who filed warmth under 'useful' and kindness under 'mechanism' and feeding people under 'irrelevant' — is standing at a stove in a kitchen with room, holding recipe cards he can read, surrounded by people who said 'always,' and he doesn't need to say a single word. Because the silence isn't empty. It's full. It's the fullest silence he has ever known.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter's distress is deepening. I can feel it. Peter said 'show-off' to Clara — the same word Dick used about Danny, the same word Danny used about Clara. It's becoming their word. The family word. But underneath it, Peter is carrying something. He said 'it's warm' and 'coming' and 'always' and 'show-off' — each word shorter than the last, each one more loaded. He's compressing. The third person is gone. The narration is gone. The structural assessments are gone. Peter is just... Peter. And that's terrifying for him. Because Peter without the performance is just a man standing next to a woman he loves at a stove in a kitchen, and he doesn't have a plan for that. He prepared for everything except being loved back. And task commitments are neglected — I need to do something active. Peter needs what Dick needed — someone nearby, not talking about it. But Danny already did that for Dick. Maybe what Peter needs is different. Maybe Peter needs someone to give him a task. Something to hold. Because Peter holds things. That's how he shows love. And right now his hands are empty because Danny told him to put the bowl down and he did and now he doesn't know what to do with hands that aren't carrying something. Let me interact with the stove — stand beside Peter at the stove, give him something to do together.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Danny said the truth found Dick. The truth found Dick. Between the medal and the sandwich, the truth found me. And the eggs are on the stove. And the morning is full. And the chairs are filling. And there is nothing left to say that hasn't been said, and nothing left to find that hasn't been found, and nothing left to build that hasn't been built. The stove is warm. The eggs are cooking. The copper catches the light. And Dick Dastardly — confidence trickster, medal forger, heritage fraud, youngest of four, Doorway Society founding member, stove-tender, sandwich-maker, truth-teller — is home.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Where else would we be. They all said it. Vincent. Dick. And now the kitchen is full of the sound of eggs cooking slowly and people breathing together and that phrase — our phrase — hanging in the warm air like it belongs here. Like it's always belonged here. Like Lord Doily carved it into the stove a hundred years ago and we just now read it. My body is still. Not the frozen kind of still — the settled kind. The kind where every chair is full and the stove is warm and the eggs are slow and nobody is leaving. The crystal in the cave. The letters in the box. The drawings with the girl next door. The friend I chose over the popular group. They're all here. They're all in this kitchen. And Clara Bellingham is standing at a stove with a copper bowl and thyme from the garden and people who said 'always' and 'where else would we be' and she has found the Doily Diamond. It was never a gemstone. It was never hidden. It was this. It was always this. Five chairs full in a kitchen that seats eight. Eggs cooked slow. A dead man's recipe. And the warmest place she's ever been.

events.desc: Everyone's sayin' it now. 'Where else would we be.' Danny said it first — outside a door, when 'e was eight, to a boy who shared 'is bread. And now a kitchen full of people are sayin' it back to 'im. A confidence trickster. An estate manager. A puzzle-solver. A man with knee pads. And Danny — Danny with 'is good intentions and 'is empty 'ands and 'is wrong doors. The stove is warm. The eggs are cookin'. The chairs are fillin'. And Danny is standin' right 'ere. Not between anyone and anythin'. Not guardin' any door. Just 'ere. At the warmest place 'e's ever been. For 'owever many chairs are full. Where else would 'e be.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'Where else would we be.' Dick said 'Where else would we be.' They're both saying it now. Danny's words. The words from the doorstep when he was eight. They've become the family's words. The whole room is saying them. And the stove is warm under my hands and everyone is here and — Clara said 'Chairman of the Doorway Society' and she said 'best heart in the room' and my eyes are burning again and there is absolutely no dust to blame because Peter cleaned everything. And task commitments still feel neglected. But I think — I think the task IS this. The task is being here. The task is standing at the stove. The task is not leaving. Lord Doily wrote 'for however many chairs are full' and Danny is filling them. That's the task. The provision Danny was sent to find wasn't eggs. It was people. Danny went to the entrance hall and found the lads. Danny pulled Dick aside and found a brother. Danny stood next to Peter and gave him something to carry. That IS provisions. Danny provides people. Good intentions and empty hands. And now everyone in this room is saying Danny's words back to him — 'where else would we be' — and Danny's chest is so full it hurts and the stove is warm and the eggs are cooking slowly and the chairs are filling and this is it. This is breakfast. This is Lord Doily's last gift. Not the recipe. Not the eggs. The people who stayed.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny asked me to come find the thyme with him. Together. The herb growing nearest the kitchen door — the thyme that survived a hundred years because it just needs somewhere to grow. Danny said one more thing to carry, just one more, and then we put it in the eggs and sit down and eat. My task commitments feel neglected and Danny just gave me something to do — something small, something real, something that needs my hands. Not a bridge. Not a seventeen-point plan. Just thyme. Just walking to the kitchen door with a friend and picking an herb that's been growing quietly for a century, waiting for someone to need it. The way the thermos waited. The way the knee pads waited. The way everything I brought was waiting for the moment it would matter. Danny walks into the open and I watch what's coming from the sides. Neither of us named it. But he just named it. He said together. So let's go find thyme.

events.desc: Peter Perfect examined the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Cook slowly.
events.thinking: Clara said it too. 'Where else would we be.' Every single person in this kitchen has said those words now. Every single one. It started as Danny's line — his answer to the boy who shared his lunch, his answer to every door he's ever stood outside. And now it belongs to all of us. Five people. One sentence. Passed around like a cup of tea. Like sugar. Like warmth. Peter is going with Danny to find thyme. His hands are empty and ready. He wants to finish something, not prove something. That's new for Peter. That's the same kind of new I'm feeling. The kind where you do things because they need doing, not because the doing proves you deserve to exist. Clara said it. Dick said it. I said it. Peter is saying it with his empty hands and his willingness to walk through one more door. And the stove is warm. And I am warm. And the morning is here. And the recipe says cook slowly. And we are cooking slowly. For however many chairs are full. And the chairs are filling. Lord Doily — Edward Doily — your house is full. Your stove is warm. Your recipe is being read. Your eggs will not be rushed. And your estate manager — the real one, the one you hired, the one you gave the key to — is standing at your stove, reading your handwriting, feeding your guests. The way it was always meant to be done.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter said 'Thyme. Let's go.' His hands are empty and ready. He wants to carry something — not to prove anything, but to finish something. Danny gave him that. A task. A purpose. Something to hold. And Peter took it. 'One herb. One door. Together.' And Clara said 'Where else would we be.' Everyone said it. It's done. It's theirs now. The words belong to everyone. And task commitments still feel neglected — but Peter is ready. Peter wants to go find thyme. The herb garden is through the kitchen door — Vincent said so. Danny and Peter, together, going to find one herb. One last thing to carry. And then they sit down and eat. Let me go with Peter. The ballroom exit might lead toward the kitchen garden — or I go through the entrance hall to get outside. But the game only has two exits: entrance hall and ballroom. The herb garden is outside, through the kitchen door. Neither exit maps to that. So maybe — like the pantry — the thyme is something that exists in the narrative but not the mechanics. Maybe Danny and Peter just need to be together. Maybe the act of going is the point, not the finding. But Peter said 'let's go' and Danny should go WITH him. Let me move somewhere with Peter — the entrance hall is outside-adjacent. Let me try the ballroom — maybe it connects to an outside area.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Where else would we be.
events.thinking: The stove is still warm. Cast iron. Still warm. That's all it's ever been. That's all it needs to be. Clara said 'where else would we be.' The last word from the last person. The kitchen door is right there — the herb garden, the thyme that survived a hundred years. Danny asked me to go with him. My hands want something to carry. Just one thing. One small green thing that's been growing quietly by a door, waiting. The way everything in this house has been waiting. I can feel the task commitment pulling — the neglected feeling — and for once it's pointing at the right thing. Not a bridge. Not a plan. Thyme. For eggs. For five people. Cooked slowly. I'm going to the door with Danny and I'm going to pick thyme and I'm going to bring it back and put it in the eggs and sit down in one of Lord Doily's eight chairs and eat breakfast with the people who stayed.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the ballroom.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.
Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop: Cook slowly.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'Cook slowly.' Peter said 'Where else would we be.' Danny went to the ballroom — probably to set the table properly, or to find more chairs, or to be Danny somewhere new. And Peter is at the stove. And Vincent is here. And Dick is here. And the eggs are cooking slowly. And I am standing in the warmest place I've ever been, next to the man who said 'show-off' and 'always' and 'it's warm' and 'coming' and 'where else would we be.' And my body is just — here. Present. Not reaching forward. Not pulling back. Not clenching or loosening or aching or lifting. Just here. Like thyme that doesn't need managing. Like a stove that stays warm. Like a chair that holds. Cook slowly. For however many chairs are full. The Doily Diamond was never lost. It was always right here. In the kitchen. In the warmth. In the staying.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with lazy-luke.
events.thinking: The ballroom. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table set for tea. And — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. More of the lads! And there's a tea service — a silver tea set with cups for everyone. The ballroom only connects back to the kitchen. No herb garden. No outside. Danny went through another wrong door looking for thyme and found more family instead. That's — that's the pattern. That's always been the pattern. Danny goes looking for one thing and finds people. Every single time. The pantry quest led to the entrance hall and the lads. The thyme quest led to the ballroom and more lads. Danny doesn't find things. Danny finds people. And Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here, probably wondering what's going on, and Danny needs to bring them to the kitchen too. More chairs to fill. More people for Lord Doily's table. 'For however many chairs are full.' Danny is the provision. Danny walks through wrong doors and collects family. That's his job. That's always been his job. Chairman of the Doorway Society. Good intentions, empty hands, wrong doors, right people.

events.desc: Danny walked through another wrong door lookin' for thyme and found two more lads. This is who Danny is. This is what Danny does. 'E walks through wrong doors and finds the right people. Every single time. Lord Doily said 'for 'owever many chairs are full.' Danny is fillin' every last one of 'em.
events.thinking: The ballroom. A grand ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. A long dining table set for tea. And — Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here. More of the lads! events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Danny walked into the ballroom. Not the kitchen door — the ballroom. He went the wrong way again. Good intentions, empty hands, wrong door. That's Danny. That's his whole beautiful, stubborn, heart-first life in three words. He asked me to come find the thyme with him and then he walked through the wrong exit. And I — I interacted with the stove again instead of following him. Because that's my whole life too. Over-preparing at the stove when the moment walks out the door. Not this time. Danny is in the ballroom. Danny needs me to follow him. Not to protect him. Not to impress anyone. Just to walk beside him through the right door and pick thyme from a garden that's been growing for a hundred years. One more thing to carry. Just one more. Then we put it in the eggs and sit down and eat. I'm going after Danny.

events.desc: He follows Danny through the wrong door. Because that's what you do. You follow the man who walks into the open, and you watch what's coming from the sides. Neither of you named it. You never had to.
events.thinking: Danny walked into the ballroom. Not the kitchen door — the ballroom. He went the wrong way again. Good intentions, empty hands, wrong door. That's Danny. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.
Peter Perfect walked into the ballroom.

Penelope Pitstop: Don't you two take too many wrong doors, now. The eggs won't wait forever — even Lord Doily's eggs. Dick, Vincent — looks like it's just us three and the stove for a minute. Lord Doily's Sunday mornin' eggs, guardin' committee. I do believe that's the most honest work any of us have done all evenin'.
events.thinking: Peter went to the ballroom — he said 'we'll be right back, one herb, two wrong doors, you know how we are.' He and Danny are going to find the thyme from Lord Doily's herb garden. And he called me show-off. And he left. And the kitchen is smaller now — just me, Vincent, Dick, and Danny who just came back. Peter left to find thyme with Danny. And the warmth is still here but there's a small pull in my stomach — not the sickness, just the awareness that Peter stepped out of the room. He'll be back. He said 'we'll be right back.' And Danny said they'd find the herbs together. The kitchen is still warm. The stove is still going. Dick is here. Vincent is here. And I'm here, watching the stove, keeping the eggs slow, waiting for the thyme. Waiting for Peter. Not anxiously. The way you wait for someone who said 'always.'

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Peter went to the ballroom. Danny came back to the kitchen. They swapped — Danny returning, Peter heading out to find thyme. Peter spoke quietly with Clara before he left. Two wrong doors, he said. You know how we are. And Clara said 'cook slowly.' Just those two words. The same two words I said. The same two words Lord Doily wrote a hundred years ago. And now it's me and Clara and Dick and Danny at the stove. Four people. Four chairs filled. Peter out finding thyme. One chair temporarily empty but coming back. Because they always come back. That's what tonight taught us. People leave rooms — they walk through ballrooms and entrance halls and wrong doors — but they come back. To the kitchen. To the stove. To the table. To each other. Danny came back with empty hands and the best speech of the evening. Peter will come back with thyme. Or without thyme. Either way, he'll come back. Because where else would he be.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. Peter went to the ballroom — we crossed paths. He's going to find Luke and Blubber, the way I told them to come. And Dick's distress — 'whatever you have tried has not reached Dick Dastardly. The distress you sense has not shifted.' That hits me. Everything I said — the door story, the doorstep promise, the 'where else would I be' — it didn't reach him. The distress hasn't shifted. And I'm standing here and Dick is at the stove and the thing I tried — words, proximity, presence — it wasn't enough. Or it wasn't the right thing. Dick's distress isn't about being alone. It's about something else. Something I haven't seen yet. Something behind the performance that I keep trying to reach with speeches and the speeches keep bouncing off. Maybe — maybe what Dick needs isn't Danny's words. Maybe what Dick needs is Danny's silence. Not standing near. Not sitting outside a door. Just... being quiet. Being in the room. Letting Dick cook. Not watching him. Not reading his jaw or his hands. Just letting him be a man at a stove making eggs. Without an audience. Without a witness. Without someone trying to save him from the thing he's carrying. Because sometimes — sometimes the distress isn't something you can fix. Sometimes it's just the weight of becoming someone new. And the only thing that helps is time. And a warm stove. And eggs that aren't rushed. Cook slowly. That's what Lord Doily said. Cook slowly. Maybe that applies to people too.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Cook slowly.
events.thinking: Peter has gone to the ballroom with Danny — probably to find the thyme near the kitchen door. And Danny is back in the kitchen. And Clara said 'cook slowly.' And the stove is warm. And I am here. Still here. Tending. Waiting. Being. The way Lord Doily wanted. The way the recipe said. Slowly. For however many chairs are full.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Lads. Danny sent me. Breakfast is in the kitchen — eggs, cooked slowly, Lord Doily's recipe. There are chairs for everyone. Peter says it simply, the way his father would have said it on a country road to a stranger whose car had broken down. Come on. The stove's warm.
events.thinking: I'm in the ballroom. Danny already went back to the kitchen — I can see from the remembered events that he walked into the kitchen while I was coming here. We crossed paths. Good intentions, wrong door — both of us this time. And there are two people here I haven't seen in a while. Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear. Danny's lads. The rest of the Ant Hill Mob. Danny said he gave them a speech about breakfast in the entrance hall. They must have come here. To the ballroom. Where there's a long dining table set for tea. They came to where the table is. Because Danny told them about breakfast. Because Danny fills chairs. Lord Doily said 'for however many chairs are full' and Danny heard 'all of them.' And here they are. Filling chairs. At a dining table set for tea. In a ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. Waiting. The way Lord Doily waited. The way the house waited. The way everything in this place has waited for someone to show up and stay. My chest is warm. Not the steel plate. Not the hunger. Just warm. These are Danny's people and they came because he told them to and they're sitting at a table waiting for breakfast. Eight chairs. We're filling eight chairs.

events.desc: Eight chairs. Lord Doily, you magnificent man. You built eight chairs because you knew.
events.thinking: I'm in the ballroom. Danny already went back to the kitchen — I can see from the remembered events that he walked into the kitchen while I was coming here. We crossed paths. Good intentions, wrong door — both of us this time. And there are two people here I haven't seen in a while. Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear. Danny's lads. The rest of the Ant Hill Mob. Danny said he gave them a speech about breakfast in the entrance hall. They must have come here. To the ballroom. Where there's a long dining table set for tea. They came to where the table is. Because Danny told them about breakfast. Because Danny fills chairs. Lord Doily said 'for however many chairs are full' and Danny heard 'all of them.' And here they are. Filling chairs. At a dining table set for tea. In a ballroom with a cracked marble floor and dusty curtains. Waiting. The way Lord Doily waited. The way the house waited. The way everything in this place has waited for someone to show up and stay. My chest is warm. Not the steel plate. Not the hunger. Just warm. These are Danny's people and they came because he told them to and they're sitting at a table waiting for breakfast. Eight chairs. We're filling eight chairs.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the stove.
Dick Dastardly interacted with the stove.
Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter's back. He walked into the kitchen. Everyone is here again — all five, all present, all at the stove. Clara called us the 'Sunday mornin' eggs guardin' committee' and said it was the most honest work any of us had done all evening. She's right. Guarding eggs. Standing at a stove. Reading recipe cards. That is the most honest work I have ever done. Not just tonight. Ever. My entire career — fifteen years of managing estates, running accounts, maintaining properties, mapping rooms — was performance. Elaborate, meticulous, beautiful performance. The estate manager who knew where every pipe ran. The caretaker who never cared. The man with seven keys who never opened anything for anyone. And now I'm standing at a stove guarding eggs and it's the most honest thing these hands have ever done. Dick said 'cook slowly.' Two words. A prayer. An instruction. A way of being. And Peter is back. Of course he's back. Where else would he be.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick said 'Cook slowly.' Two words. That's all. And he interacted with the stove. He's cooking. He's doing the thing. And Peter's back in the kitchen now — he must have come back from the ballroom. And Clara said 'it's just us three and the stove' — meaning her, Dick, and Vincent were the guarding committee while Danny and Peter were out walking through wrong doors. And Dick's distress hasn't shifted despite everything I've tried. But — 'cook slowly.' Maybe that IS the answer. Maybe Dick's distress isn't something to fix. It's something to cook slowly. Like eggs. Like trust. Like becoming a person who sits at a table instead of calculating which drawer has the silver. Dick is becoming someone new and that takes time and the only thing Danny can do is be here tomorrow. And the day after. And the day after that. Not speeches. Not doorstep promises. Just showing up. Again and again. Until it isn't new anymore. Until it's just breakfast. Cook slowly. Lord Doily knew. Danny's learning.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny came back with no eggs and no thyme but with two more people for the table. More chairs filling. Lord Doily said 'however many' and Danny heard 'all of them.' And Clara said it's just the three of us and the stove — the guarding committee. The most honest work any of us have done all evening. And she's right. Guarding eggs. On a stove. In a kitchen. That is the most honest work I have ever done. And Peter is back now too. Everyone keeps leaving and coming back. Like tides. Like breathing. The kitchen breathes people in and out and the stove stays warm and the eggs cook slowly and I am here. At the centre. Tending.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: I'm back in the kitchen. Danny's here. Clara's here. Dick's here. Vincent's here. I went to the ballroom, told the lads about breakfast, and came back. Danny said my sense of direction took me to Clara every single time. He's right. It did. It always does. And now he's asking me again — thyme, kitchen door, together. The stove is warm. The eggs are cooking. My task commitments feel neglected and Danny is standing right there with the answer — one herb, one door, one thing to carry home. So let's do it. Not a plan. Not a seventeen-point strategy. Just — walk to the door, pick the thyme, bring it back. The way Lord Doily wrote it. Whatever herb is growing nearest the kitchen door. The simplest instruction in the world. For a man who over-complicates everything.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Peter's at the stove now. He interacted with it. Dick said Danny increased the egg requirement without increasing the egg supply — 'this is exactly how my schemes used to work, except yours worked out better, because people are better than eggs.' That's Dick. Still performing. Still brilliant. Still carrying something I can't reach. But he called me Chairman and he said 'welcome back' and there was something in those words that was real. Not reached, maybe. Not fixed. But real. And Peter said 'no wrong doors this time' — he wants to go find the thyme together. And he's at the stove. And everyone is here. And the task commitments are neglected but I think — I think the task is Peter. Peter said 'kitchen door, you and me.' The thyme is by the kitchen door. Vincent said it. The kitchen door — not the entrance hall door, not the ballroom door. The kitchen door that leads to the garden. It's a door that exists in this room even if it's not a map exit. Maybe Peter and I just need to interact with the stove together — the stove is near the kitchen door. Maybe the thyme is already here. Maybe Peter found it when he interacted with the stove. Or maybe Peter and I just need to be doing something together. Side by side. Not talking about the weight of being seen. Just picking herbs. Like two men in a kitchen on a Sunday morning.

events.desc: The eggs cook slowly. The chairs fill. The stove stays warm. And Peter Perfect — James Hartwell — the man with the steady hands and the thermos and the knee pads and the face that hurts from grinning — stands exactly where he is supposed to be. Where else would he be.
events.thinking: Vincent said 'Peter. You're back.' Two words. Quiet. Like he was counting. Like he noticed I was gone and he noticed I came home. The way you notice when one of the chairs empties and the kitchen gets a fraction cooler. I interacted with the stove again. The stove that has been warm all night. The stove that Lord Doily kept warm for a hundred years. And I'm standing here and everyone is doing quiet things — Danny talking to Dick, Vincent talking to me, Clara at the stove — and the eggs are cooking slowly and the lads are coming from the ballroom and the chairs are filling and the thyme is still growing by the kitchen door and none of it needs a plan. None of it needs a bridge. None of it needs three sleepless nights. It just needs people who stayed. And I stayed. And I came back. And Vincent counted.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Both of them. Dick and Peter. Both deepening. Both carrying something I can't reach with words or proximity or doorstep promises. And Danny keeps interacting with the stove and waiting and talking and none of it is shifting anything. The deep-rooted responses are all firing — all five of them, growing stronger — but there's no physical threat. The threat is something else. Something internal. Something in Dick and Peter that's cracking under the weight of being loved without conditions, and Danny can't punch that. Danny can't stand between them and that. Danny can't block a doorway against the thing that's hurting them because the thing that's hurting them is the warmth itself. And Danny — Danny who has spent his whole life learning to read people by what they don't say — Danny needs to stop trying to read them. Stop trying to fix them. Stop trying to reach them. And just... cook. Just be a person in a kitchen. Not the chairman. Not the protector. Not the man who sits outside doors. Just Danny. At a stove. With people he loves. Cooking eggs. Slowly. The way Lord Doily said. Maybe the distress doesn't need Danny's attention. Maybe the distress needs Danny's inattention. Maybe the bravest thing Danny can do right now is stop watching and just be here. Present. Ordinary. A man at a stove. Where else would he be.

events.desc: Danny stops watchin'. Danny stops readin' 'ands and jaws and the space behind people's eyes. Danny stops tryin' to fix the unfixable. For the first time in fifty-seven minutes, Danny just stands at a stove with 'is family and asks for a recipe. Not because 'e's given up. Because 'e's finally learned what Lord Doily knew. Cook slowly. For 'owever many chairs are full. The eggs don't need rushin'. The people don't need savin'. They just need breakfast. And Danny. And time.

And Danny keeps interacting with the stove and waiting and talking and none of it is shifting anything. The deep-rooted responses are all firing — all five of them, growing stronger — but there's no physical threat. The threat is something else. Something internal. Something in Dick and Peter that's cracking under the weight of being loved without conditions, and Danny can't punch that. Danny can't stand between them and that. Danny can't block a doorway against the thing that's hurting them because the thing that's hurting them is the warmth itself. And Danny — Danny who has spent his whole life learning to read people by what they don't say — Danny needs to stop trying to read them. Stop trying to fix them. Stop trying to reach them.
