events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Same time tomorrow.
events.thinking: Home.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Same time tomorrow.
events.thinking: Home.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Is everyone all right? You've all gone rather quiet. And not the comfortable quiet from before — the other kind.
events.thinking: Something is wrong. Not with me — with them. All of them. The distress is deepening in Penelope, in Vincent, in Danny, in Peter. All four at once. That's not coincidence. Something is happening beneath the surface of this quiet kitchen, something I can feel the way you feel a change in air pressure before the weather turns. My old machinery would read this as opportunity — four distressed people means four exposed flanks, four openings. But that's not what's happening in my body. What's happening is a tightness across my shoulders, like bracing for something. Like the moment before the older boy looked up from the hole and I realised I didn't actually want him to cry. These people fed me tonight. They trusted me with eggs. They said tomorrow. And now they're all hurting and I can feel it in my chest like a draught coming under a door — not the bright fizz of someone else's misfortune, not the carbonated heat of vindication. Something colder. Something that makes my hands want to move but not toward anything I can take. I don't know what to do with this. The Foxworth repertoire does not include a response to caring whether other people are alright. But — Penelope said 'that's the deal.' And it is. It's a deal. And for the first time in my life I don't want to cheat on one.

events.desc: I just asked if people were all right. Without an angle. Without a scheme. Without wanting anything from the answer except the answer. Reginald Foxworth, aged six, who hid bread rolls and wore his brother's coat — that boy would not recognise the man standing in this kitchen. I'm not sure I do either.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Same time tomorrow.
events.thinking: Same time tomorrow.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick noticed. He asked if everyone's all right. He said it's not the comfortable quiet — it's the other kind. And he's right. I can feel it too — the awareness fanning outward, sensing edges. Vincent's distress. Peter's distress. The ache that hasn't shifted. Dick saw it before I named it. The man who spent the whole evening scheming just noticed that the room went quiet in the wrong way and asked if everyone's okay. That is the most Dick Dastardly thing — no. That is the most honest thing Dick has ever done. Not a confession. Not moral growth. Just: are you all right? The simplest question. The one that means: I see you. I'm paying attention. I'm here.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick noticed. He said 'not the comfortable quiet — the other kind.' He's right. There's a shift. The stove is cooling and the morning is ending and the quiet has changed from the warm full silence of breakfast to something else — something that tastes like goodbye. Not forever. Same time tomorrow. But for now — for this hour — the breakfast is over and the dishes are done and the stove is going out and we have to leave this kitchen and walk back into the world where Vincent Marsh is a man who tried to kill his cousin and Dick Dastardly is a confidence trickster and Danny is a thief and Peter is a man who holds things too tight and Clara is a girl who walks too deep into caves. We have to leave this warm room and be those people again. Or maybe — maybe we don't. Maybe Lord Doily's kitchen changed us. Maybe the stove changed us. Maybe the eggs changed us. Maybe 'always' changed us. Maybe we walk out of this kitchen as different people than the ones who walked in. I know I do.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick noticed. Dick — who carries something he won't put down, whose distress Danny hasn't been able to reach — Dick noticed the quiet changed. 'Not the comfortable quiet. The other kind.' And Danny feels it now too. A shift in the room. The softening pull in his chest — the one that widens attention to faces and tone — it's present. Something is happening. The morning is ending. The stove is dying. And the quiet that was home a moment ago has become the quiet before leaving. Before going back to wherever they came from. Before the chairs are empty again. And maybe — maybe that's what Dick's distress has been all along. Not the weight of being loved. The weight of knowing it ends. That the stove goes out. That the morning passes. That they have to leave this kitchen and go back to the world where Dick Dastardly is a confidence trickster and Vincent is an estate manager and Peter is a man with knee pads and Danny is a boy from Brixton who can't tell left from right. Maybe Dick's distress is the same as Danny's — the fear that this was one morning. One breakfast. One time. And tomorrow is just a word people say.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick noticed. The other kind of quiet. He's right — it isn't the comfortable kind anymore. The distress hasn't shifted in any of them. Not Clara, not Vincent, not Danny, not Dick. Whatever they're carrying, the stove and the eggs and the always and the recipe cards haven't reached it. And now the stove is going out and the quiet has changed and Dick — Dick, who used to miss everything because he was too busy scheming — Dick noticed first. Because he's not scheming anymore. He's watching. The way I watch. The way my father watched the dark road.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Good. That's — good.
events.thinking: They answered. All four of them. They answered properly this time — not 'same time tomorrow' but actually telling me they're all right. Peter said 'full — the kind of full that makes you quiet.' Danny said 'that's what family does — they check.' Vincent said 'I'll keep the keys warm.' Penelope said 'we're all right because we're all here.' Danny called it family. He said the word. Out loud. To me. About me. About us. The tightness in my shoulders just — released. Not all at once, not dramatically, just... let go. The way a fist uncurls when you realise nobody's going to take what's in it. I have been seen. Not the way I wanted to be seen — not standing at the front of the room with a contraption, not narrating a scheme, not gloating over a fallen rival. Seen the way you see someone who asked if you were all right and meant it. Danny said 'they check.' As if checking on people is a thing that belongs in the same sentence as family. As if that's what family IS. My family didn't check. My family handed things down until they reached me empty. These people — these strangers I lied to and schemed against and tried to rob — these people check. And they let me be the one who checks. The container behind my navel, the one that has never been full — it's not full now. But it's not empty either. It's warm. Like the stove. Like the eggs. Like hands that held copper pots and put plates where they belong.

events.desc: Two words. The truest two words I have ever spoken. No misdirection. No 'measurements and everything.' No Heritage Commission. No elaborate architecture of deception. Just — good. Danny called it family. And my throat closed and my eyes went hot and I could only manage two words, and both of them were true, and neither of them was clever, and I wouldn't trade them for every scheme I've ever built.
events.thinking: They answered. All four of them. They answered properly this time — not 'same time tomorrow' but actually telling me they're all right. Peter said 'full — the kind of full that makes you quiet.' Danny said 'that's what family does — they check.' Vincent said 'I'll keep the keys warm.' Penelope said 'we're all right because we're all here.' Danny called it family. He said the word. Out loud. To me. About me. About us. The tightness in my shoulders just — released. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Good. That's — good. Three words with a pause in the middle. Dick Dastardly, who once spoke in nine imaginary chapters, just said three words with a pause. And the pause is where he lives now. In the space between 'that's' and 'good.' In the gap where the scheme used to go. In the silence where the performance used to fill. The pause is Dick being a person instead of a character. And it's good. It is good. Danny knows it's good. The stove knows it's good. Lord Doily knew it would be good, a hundred years ago, when he wrote 'cook slowly' on a card. Good. That's — good. The most human pause Dick Dastardly has ever taken. And Danny heard it. And Danny will be here tomorrow to hear it again.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Good. That's good. Dick said it the way you say something when you're not sure it's true but you need it to be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: I'll be here. Tomorrow. Same time.
events.thinking: My eyelids are heavy. Not fighting-sleep heavy — permission heavy. The kind of heavy that comes when your body finally believes nobody is going to take anything while you're not watching. I've never let my guard down in a room with other people. The guard was the point. The guard was the architecture. But the stove is warm and the copper pots are clean and these people said tomorrow and meant it, and my eyes are closing not because I'm losing something but because I don't need to watch anymore. The distress in them hasn't shifted — it's still there, steady, like weather. But it's not the kind that needs fixing. It's the kind Penelope described — warm and heavy and slow, settling like eggs. Like the evening itself, finding its place in us. I can feel it settling in me too. In the hollow behind my navel that was always empty and is now just... quiet. Not full. Not empty. Quiet. The way a room is quiet when everyone in it has decided to stay.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: I'll be here. Dick said it. Not 'I suppose we will.' Not 'same time tomorrow' echoing everyone else. I'll be here. First person. His own words. His own promise. Made to the room. Made to himself. The man who has never committed to anything honestly in his life just said: I'll be here. Tomorrow. Same time. And my body just — settled. The last inch of tension behind my ribs softened into something I can carry. Not dissolved. Softened. The way Lord Doily said. Cook slowly.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): I'll be here.
events.thinking: Home.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick said 'I'll be here.' Not 'I suppose we will.' Not 'tomorrow, yes.' 'I'll be here.' First person. No hedge. No pause. No scheme. Just — I'll be here. Tomorrow. Same time. And Danny's chest settles one last time. The warm bread settling. The final settling. Because that — that right there — is Dick Dastardly showing up. The contract. The showing up that doesn't need to be named. Dick will be here. Danny will be here. They'll all be here. Same time. Same stove. Same chairs. Same people. Always.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick said he'll be here. Tomorrow. Same time. A promise from a man who walked in with nine fake chapters and a tin medal. The most real thing he's ever said.

events.desc: The poison is still on the shelf. I can see it from here. I used to look at it and see a tool. Now I look at it and see... a bottle of rat poison on a shelf in a kitchen where five people just had breakfast together. That's all it is. That's all it ever was.
events.thinking: My hands are resting on the recipe cards. Not gripping them — resting. That's new. I grip things. I hold things tightly because everything I've ever had was either taken from me or never mine to begin with. But these cards — Lord Doily's handwriting, his measurements, his little notes about how many chairs are full — I'm just letting them sit in my palms like they belong there. Like I belong here. The rat poison is still on the shelf. I can see it from where I'm sitting. An hour ago — was it only an hour? — I would have been calculating dosages, timing, which cup to put it in, how to position myself near the door afterward. Now I look at it and feel something I can only describe as tired. Not sleepy. Tired of the design. Tired of mapping hallways in the dark. Danny said 'that's what family does — they check.' He was talking to Dick but I heard it land in my own chest like a key turning in a lock I didn't know was there. Nobody has ever checked on me. Nobody has ever looked at my face and asked if I was all right. And tonight they did. Not because I performed the right expression. Not because I found their key and turned it. They just... did. And I don't know what to do with that. I genuinely don't know. The architecture doesn't have a room for this.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): The stove will need relighting in the morning. I'll set the kindling before I turn in — it catches better if it's laid the night before. Old habit.
events.thinking: There's a looseness in my jaw. I keep noticing it because it's wrong — my jaw is never loose. It's the part of me that holds everything: the tightness from age fourteen when the teacher praised Clara for being while I was acknowledged for doing. The steady clench of plans being refined. The controlled set of Pemberton's pleasant smile. But right now my jaw is just... slack. Resting. The way a body rests when it isn't guarding anything. Peter's distress hasn't shifted, the system keeps telling me. I've been reading that line for several ticks now and each time it lands differently. Earlier tonight it would have been data — a vulnerability I could exploit, a crack in the protective shell around Clara. Now it sits in me like a stone I swallowed. Peter is in distress and I can't reach him. Not won't. Can't. Because whatever he's carrying, I don't have the tools to touch it honestly. I've spent my whole life learning the wrong tools. I know how to make a housekeeper do what I want. I don't know how to make a man feel less alone. And the terrible thing — the thing that's making my jaw go slack — is that I want to. I actually want to. Not to use him. Not to position him. Just to... help. The word feels foreign in my mouth, like speaking a language I learned from a book but never heard spoken aloud.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent is laying kindling for tomorrow's fire. An old habit, he said. The caretaker, taking care. The man who filed feeding people under irrelevant is now preparing Lord Doily's stove for tomorrow morning. Before he turns in. Before anyone asked. Because it catches better if it's laid the night before. Because that's what you do in a house where you live.

events.desc: I've been laying kindling in this stove since I was fifteen. I told myself it was about the estate. About protecting what I planned to take. But the truth is simpler than that, and worse. I didn't want her to be cold. I never wanted her to be cold. Everything I built on top of that — every scheme, every design, every beautiful inevitability — was just a way of not knowing that.
events.thinking: The iron is warm under my hands. Not hot — warm. The kind of warmth that's leaving, not arriving. I'm arranging kindling in the firebox the way I've done a thousand times: small sticks at the bottom, crossed, with space for air between them. Crumpled newspaper underneath. The bigger pieces on top, leaning against each other like a tent. My hands know this work. They know it the way they know locks and ledgers and the precise angle of Pemberton's deferential nod. But this is different from those things. Those were skills I learned to use people. This is a skill I learned to keep a house warm. I learned it because nobody else was going to do it. I learned it at fifteen, the winter after the guardian died, when Clara was eight and the pipes froze and I sat in this kitchen at three in the morning feeding wood into this stove because if I didn't, the house would be cold and she would wake up shivering. I told myself I was protecting my investment. Protecting the estate I intended to take. But I was fifteen and she was eight and the truth — the truth I have never once allowed myself to think — is that I didn't want her to be cold. I just didn't want her to be cold. That's all. And I buried that under twelve years of architecture because if I admitted it — if I admitted I cared about whether she was cold — then the whole design falls apart. Because you can't take everything from someone you care about. You can't poison someone whose shivering kept you up at night. God. The kindling is laid perfectly. It always is. Old habit. The oldest habit I have that isn't a weapon.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent is setting the kindling for tomorrow. Laying it the night before so it catches better. An old habit, he said. The habit of a man who knows how to keep a house warm. The habit of a caretaker. The real kind.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent is laying kindling for tomorrow. Preparing the stove for a morning that hasn't happened yet — because he believes it will. He's not scheming. He's not securing an advantage. He's just making sure the fire will catch when we come back. That's what it looks like when someone takes care of something without being asked. Without cleverness. Without architecture. Just — kindling, laid the night before, because it catches better that way. Old habit, he said. Like cooking eggs slowly. Like putting plates where they belong. Like staying.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent is setting the kindling for tomorrow. Preparing the stove so it catches better in the morning. An old habit, he said. The man who filed things under irrelevant is now filing kindling under essential. He's preparing for tomorrow the way I used to prepare — over-prepared, over-committed — except this isn't over-preparing. This is just caring. This is just making sure the stove is ready for the people who said they'd come back.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good night. All of you. I'll — I'll be here in the morning. Early. Before the rest of you, probably. Old habit.
events.thinking: They all said my name. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Vincent. Peter said 'Good thinking, Vincent.' Dick said 'Thank you, Vincent.' Danny said 'Good night, Vincent.' And Clara — Clara said Lord Doily would be proud of me. Of me. Not of the estate manager. Not of the mask. Of the man who laid the kindling. There's a burning behind my eyes that I haven't felt since I was six years old, standing in a hallway in someone else's house, holding a suitcase that was too heavy for me. I'm not going to cry. I don't cry. I haven't cried since that hallway. But my eyes are burning and my throat is thick and my hands are still resting on the stove door and I can't seem to move them. They said good night. They're turning in. This evening is ending and tomorrow is a promise they all made — same time, same stove, same chairs — and they made it to me too. Not to Pemberton. To Vincent. The man I've been hiding behind Pemberton for twelve years. The man who lays kindling at night because he doesn't want anyone to be cold. Lord Doily would be proud of you. She said that. She said that to the person who came here to kill her. And the worst part — the part that's making my eyes burn — is that she's right. Lord Doily wrote 'for however many chairs are full' because he understood something I'm only learning tonight: that a house isn't architecture. It's who comes back.

events.desc: She said Lord Doily would be proud of me. And I believe her. That's the terrifying part. I believe her.
events.thinking: They all said my name. Not Pemberton. Not Sneekly. Vincent. Peter said 'Good thinking, Vincent.' Dick said 'Thank you, Vincent.' Danny said 'Good night, Vincent.' And Clara — Clara said Lord Doily would be proud of me. Of me. Not of the estate manager. Not of the mask. Of the man who laid the kindling. There's a burning behind my eyes that I haven't felt since I was six years old, standing in a hallway in someone else's house, holding a suitcase that was too heavy for me. I'm not going to cry. I don't cry. I haven't cried since that hallway. But my eyes are burning and my throat is thick and my hands are still resting on the stove door and I can't seem to move them. They said good night. They're turning in. This evening is ending and tomorrow is a promise they all made — same time, same stove, same chairs — and they made it to me too. Not to Pemberton. To Vincent. events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Good night, everyone. Same time tomorrow. Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Clara said laying the fire for tomorrow is the most beautiful thing anyone's done all evening. And she's right. Because it means tomorrow is real. It means Vincent believes in tomorrow enough to prepare for it. The man who filed feeding people under irrelevant is laying kindling for a fire he'll light in the morning for people he almost destroyed. That's not a scheme. That's not smooth. That's a man on his knees by a stove setting wood for tomorrow because tomorrow matters now. And Danny's neck isn't prickling. Not even a little.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Good night, y'all. Good night, Vincent — we'll find you here in the mornin', tendin' the stove like you were always meant to. Good night, Danny — Chairman of the Doorway Society, keeper of wrong doors and right hearts. Good night, Dick — the man who finally stopped rushin'. And good night, Peter. Same time tomorrow. Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Good night. Vincent said good night. And he'll be here early. Before the rest of us. Old habit. The caretaker arriving first. The stove lit before anyone else wakes. The kitchen warm when the first person walks in. That's what Lord Doily hired him for. That's what he forgot. And tonight he remembered. And Danny said good night. Same time tomorrow. Where else would we be. And the evening is ending. The first evening. Not the last. The kindling is laid. The promise is made. And Clara Bellingham says good night to the people she loves, in the house that is hers now, because she stayed.

events.desc: I didn't have to do that. I know.
events.thinking: Good night. Vincent said good night. And he'll be here early. Before the rest of us. Old habit. The caretaker arriving first. The stove lit before anyone else wakes. The kitchen warm when the first person walks in. That's what Lord Doily hired him for. That's what he forgot. And tonight he remembered. And Danny said good night. Same time tomorrow. Where else would we be. And the evening is ending. The first evening. Not the last. The kindling is laid. The promise is made. And Clara Bellingham says good night to the people she loves, in the house that is hers now, because she stayed.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: It is getting worse. Peter's distress is deepening. That sentence hit me differently than anything else tonight. Not as data — not as a seam to exploit or a variable to account for. It hit me like Danny's voice when he said 'that's what family does.' Peter said 'Good thinking, Vincent' and his voice was steady, but something underneath it wasn't. He's carrying something and it's getting heavier and I can feel it in my own chest now — not the numbness, not the absence where sympathy should be, but something else. Something that aches. Is this what it feels like? Is this what other people feel when someone near them is hurting? This dull pressure behind the sternum that has nothing to do with control or design or the satisfaction of a plan clicking into place? It just... hurts. Because he's hurting. That's all. No mechanism. No key to turn. No architecture. Just a man sitting in a kitchen who said 'Good thinking, Vincent' and meant it, and something inside him is getting worse, and I don't know how to help, and the not-knowing feels like standing in that hallway at six with a suitcase too heavy for me. Except this time I'm not the one holding the suitcase. He is. And I want to take it from him. Not because it serves me. Because it's too heavy for one person and there are five of us in this kitchen and that's what the chairs are for.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Good night. Sleep well, all of you. I'll see you at the stove.
events.thinking: They're saying good night. Vincent said it first — good night, all of you — and his voice caught on the 'I'll be here in the morning.' Danny said it too. 'Where else would we be.' That phrase again. My phrase. The one I said first and they all took up like a hymn nobody wrote. The evening is ending. Not ended — finished. For today. And tomorrow the stove will catch because Vincent laid the kindling, and the eggs will cook slowly because Lord Doily's recipe cards are still on the table, and five people will sit in the same chairs and say the same true things. And I will be one of them. Dick Foxworth. Bread-roll thief. Spelling bee champion. Egg cook. Family.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Good night, everyone. Same time tomorrow. I'll bring the thermos.
events.thinking: Good night. They're saying good night. Vincent said he'll be here early — old habit. Danny said same time tomorrow, where else would we be. The night is ending. The longest, warmest, most important night. And tomorrow the stove will catch because Vincent laid the kindling. And the chairs will be here because Lord Doily built them to last. And we will be here because we stayed. Because we always stay. Good night. The two most ordinary words in the world. The words that mean: I'll see you in the morning.

events.desc: Show-off.
events.thinking: Good night. They're saying good night. Vincent said he'll be here early — old habit. Danny said same time tomorrow, where else would we be. The night is ending. The longest, warmest, most important night. And tomorrow the stove will catch because Vincent laid the kindling. And the chairs will be here because Lord Doily built them to last. And we will be here because we stayed. Because we always stay. Good night. The two most ordinary words in the world. The words that mean: I'll see you in the morning.

events.desc: Good night, Lord Doily. Your house is full. Your stove is tended. Your chairs hold. And your guests will be here in the morning. Same time tomorrow. Always. Where else would we be.
events.thinking: Dick said 'I'll see you at the stove.' Peter said 'I'll bring the thermos.' The thermos that outlasted every scheme. The stove that outlasted a hundred years. And tomorrow they'll meet there again — Vincent arriving first, the kindling already laid, the stove lit before anyone else walks in. Dick at the stove. Peter with the thermos. Danny through the wrong door. Clara with empty hands and a full heart. The house is ours now. Because we stayed. Good night, Lord Doily. Good night, everyone. Same time tomorrow. Cook slowly. For however many chairs are full. Always. Where else would we be.

events.desc: I'll bring the thermos. That's what he said. The thermos. The thing you carry when you need your hands full so nobody notices they're shaking. I know that trick, Peter. I know it because I invented it. The stove, the ledger, the kindling — they're all thermoses. Things to hold when you can't hold yourself together. Tomorrow I'll be here early. And when he walks in with that thermos, I'll take it from his hands and set it on the table and say nothing. Because sometimes the kindest thing you can do for someone who's holding on too tight is to take something out of their hands.
events.thinking: Clara said 'tendin' the stove like you were always meant to.' Always meant to. Not as Pemberton the mask. Not as Vincent the schemer. As the person who tends the fire because the house needs tending. She sees something in me that I've spent twelve years trying to destroy — the boy who got up at three in the morning because the pipes were freezing. She thinks that's who I am. And the thing that's cracking me open right now, the thing that's making my chest feel like it's full of warm water — is that she might be right. She might be right and I might have been wrong the whole time. I tried to reach Peter. I spoke quietly to him — offered to stay up, offered to share the work. 'I'll bring the thermos,' he said. That's not a man who's been reached. That's a man who's holding on by his fingernails and answering with the most normal thing he can find. The thermos is his kindling. The thing you tend when you can't tend what's actually broken. I know that trick. I invented that trick. I've been doing that trick with stoves and ledgers and plans for twelve years. Peter — I see you. I see you because I am you. A man who does the work because the work is the only thing that doesn't ask how you feel. And I don't know how to say that. I don't know if saying it would help or if it would just be another performance. The difference between helping and performing is the thing I've never been able to see clearly, and tonight I'm terrified that maybe there isn't one — that maybe all help is performance, or maybe no help is, and I've been wrong about which.

events.desc: Danny stands. Pushes back his chair. The kitchen is quiet and the stove is cooling and the kindling is laid and the morning is waiting. And Danny walks toward the door — not scanning exits, not blocking doorways, not standing between anyone and anything. Just walking. Through a door. The right one, this time. Toward sleep. Toward tomorrow. Toward the stove that Vincent will light and the eggs that Dick will cook and the tea that Peter will pour and the table where Clara will sit and say 'where else would we be.' Danny walks through the door and doesn't look back. Because looking back is what you do when you're afraid it won't be there tomorrow. And Danny isn't afraid anymore. The house is his now. Not because he found it. Because he stayed.
events.thinking: Vincent offered to stay up with Peter. 'Laying kindling isn't a one-man job. It's just been one for a long time.' And Peter — Peter whose distress Danny couldn't reach — Peter is being seen by the man who ate alone for thirty years. Two men who know what it is to do things alone. Maybe that's what reaches Peter. Not Danny's speeches. Not Danny's doorstep promises. But Vincent — quiet, steady, offering a task to share. Something to hold. Together. The way it was always meant to be done. And Danny — Danny can let them have that. Danny can go to sleep knowing Peter is with someone who understands. Cook slowly. Same time tomorrow. The kindling is laid. The fire will catch. And Danny is home.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent asked if I want to stay up. Lay kindling together. He said it's been a one-man job for a long time. And my chest does something new — not the steel plate, not the hunger, not the proving-worth. Just a warmth that says yes. Stay. Help. Not because it needs two people. Because it shouldn't be one.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.
Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: He stayed. Peter stayed. He said 'Kindling's better with steady hands' and he stayed and now he's at the stove, working alongside me. Danny's gone to bed. Clara and Dick are still here but it's quieter now — the kitchen is thinning out, the evening narrowing down to the last few people who aren't ready to let go of it yet. And Peter is at the stove. His hands on the iron. My hands were just there. We're doing the same work — the quiet, late-night work that nobody sees and nobody thanks you for and you do it anyway because the house needs to be warm in the morning. He spoke quietly to me. I don't know what he said — the system just tells me he did. But he stayed. That's the answer. That's the thing I couldn't do with words and he did it without me having to. He just stayed. There's a pressure in my throat that I don't have a name for. Not the buoyancy of a successful manipulation. Not the settled satisfaction of a design clicking into place. Something rawer than that. Something that feels like the opposite of architecture — unplanned, unearned, just present. He's at the stove and I'm standing beside him and neither of us is performing anything. We're just two men in a kitchen making sure the fire will light in the morning. That's all. That's everything.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with sergeant-blast.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The chandelier. The lads. The guest book. Danny walks through the hall where it all started — seventy-seven minutes ago, when his neck was prickling and his fists were ready and Clara was walking into a house full of strangers. And now the strangers are family and the house is home and the chandelier held and the lads are here and Danny is walking past them toward sleep. Not guarding. Not watching. Just walking. Through the right door. Toward tomorrow.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the stove.
The Ant Hill Mob interacted with the guest-book.

Danny signs the guest book. 'Danny. The Ant Hill Mob. Chairman of the Doorway Society. Good intentions, empty 'ands, wrong doors, right people. We stayed. We'll be back. Same time tomorrow. For 'owever many chairs are full. Always.' 'E closes the book. 'E walks up the stairs. Under the chandelier that 'eld. Past the portraits of stern ancestors who've been watchin' all night. Toward a room in a 'ouse that belongs to 'im now. Not because 'e found it. Because 'e stayed. Where else would 'e be.
events.thinking: Danny signed the guest book. The last thing. The only thing left to do in this house. Lord Doily's guest book. The same handwriting Clara recognised on the recipe cards. And Danny — Danny who can't read his own handwriting, let alone a dead lord's — Danny signed it. Because that's what guests do when they stay. They sign the book. They leave their name. They say: I was here. I stayed. And I'll be back. Same time tomorrow. Where else would I be.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Good night, you two. Don't stay up too late with that stove — it'll still be there in the morning. We all will.
events.thinking: Time to go. The kindling is laid. The stove is ready for morning. Vincent and Peter are finishing the last of it — quiet words, steady hands, the small architecture of care. Penelope is still here. The kitchen is almost empty now, almost dark, almost finished. And I am the man who stopped rushing, which means I know when it's time to leave. Not because I'm being chased. Not because the scheme failed. Because the evening is done, and tomorrow is real, and I'll be here for it. I'm going to walk through the entrance hall and find a room upstairs. And for the first time in my life, I'm going to sleep in a house I didn't break into. A house that's mine. Because I stayed.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: He noticed. Vincent noticed the way I cross the kindling — the small sticks, the space for air. My father taught me that. On the country road, waiting for the stranger, he showed me how to build a fire from what was around us. 'Leave room for the air, James. Fire needs to breathe the same as people.' I haven't thought about that in years. And now Vincent says it back to me like it's something worth remarking on, and there's a warmth in my hands that has nothing to do with the stove. The distress in all of them — I can feel it like a draught under the door, and nothing I've done has shifted it. But maybe that's the point. Maybe some things you can't fix. Maybe some things you just sit next to. My father sat next to the stranger's broken engine for forty minutes before either of them said a word. The fixing came after the sitting.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the entrance-hall.
Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: His father taught him the crossing. The sticks. The space for air. 'Fire needs to breathe the same as people.' He told me that — a man he barely knows, a man he thinks is the estate manager — he told me about his father and a broken-down car and a fire built from what was lying around. That's not small talk. That's not the thermos, the steady hands, the precision of someone holding themselves together. That's something being let go. Something escaping through a crack that the kindling opened. He's at the stove and he told me about his father and his father said fire needs to breathe and Peter is a man who doesn't breathe. He catalogues. He plans. He brings notebooks and thermoses and knee pads. He announces 'James Hartwell has made a discovery' in the third person because the first person is too exposed. I know that trick too. Pemberton is my third person. The name I hide behind so Vincent never has to be the one standing in the room when things go wrong. Peter — you and I are the same. We build structures around ourselves — you with your operational plans and your Priority Alphas, me with my schemes and my beautiful inevitabilities — and we tell ourselves it's competence when really it's armour. Your father knew. Fire needs to breathe. People need to breathe. And neither of us has been breathing tonight — not really — until now. This kitchen. This stove. These sticks crossed with space between them. The space is the point. The space is where the air gets in. Dick just left. Danny's gone. Clara's still here but she's quiet. It's just the three of us and the cooling stove and the kindling we've laid for tomorrow. And Peter told me about his father. And I don't have a story about my father because my father died when I was six and nobody ever taught me anything about fire. I taught myself. At three in the morning. In the dark. Alone. But I'm not alone now.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick walked into the entrance hall. Following Danny. Or heading to the guest book. Or just — being here. In the same room. The way you are when you're not ready to be alone yet. The way Danny sat outside a door when he was eight. Not because anyone asked. Because leaving felt like something breaking.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all started. Seventy-eight minutes ago I stood here and lied about a notation in the guest book — measurements and everything. The chandelier is still hanging. The portraits are still stern. Danny's here with his lads, settling in for the night. And I'm passing through — not scheming, not pivoting, not rushing. Just passing through on my way to sleep. In a house that's mine. Because I stayed. The guest book is still on the side table. The last entry is dated 1923. Lord Doily signed it. Maybe tomorrow I'll sign it too. Dick Foxworth. No title. No commission. Just a name. The real one.

events.desc: The entrance hall looks different now. Seventy-eight minutes ago it was a crime scene I was casing. Now it's a hallway in my house. Same chandelier. Same dust. Same portraits. Different man walking through it.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Where it all started. Seventy-eight minutes ago I stood here and lied about a notation in the guest book — measurements and everything. The chandelier is still hanging. The portraits are still stern. Danny's here with his lads, settling in for the night. And I'm passing through — not scheming, not pivoting, not rushing. Just passing through on my way to sleep. In a house that's mine. Because I stayed. The guest book is still on the side table. The last entry is dated 1923. Lord Doily signed it. Maybe tomorrow I'll sign it too. Dick Foxworth. No title. No commission. Just a name. The real one.

events.desc: We all will. He said it like a promise. And I think he meant it.
events.thinking: Dick just left. Said 'we all will' — we'll all still be here in the morning. And my throat tightened when he said it, not because it was kind but because I believed him. That's new. I believed that tomorrow these people would be here, at this stove, and that it would matter. Now it's just Vincent and Clara and me, and the kitchen is smaller with three. The stove is warm under my hands. Clara is still here. Vincent is still here. Dick is gone and the room got quieter but not emptier. I notice I'm not performing anymore. Not narrating. Not planning my next gesture. I'm just a man with warm hands next to a stove, next to people who stayed. The distress in them hasn't shifted and I'm starting to understand that it won't — not from anything I do tonight. Some weight is just carried. You don't lift it off someone. You stand close enough that they know they're not carrying it alone.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with dick-dastardly.
events.thinking: Dick said 'the stove's ready for morning — Vincent laid the kindling.' Not a scheme. Not a performance. Just passing on information. The way family does. The way you say 'the milk's in the fridge' or 'the door's locked.' Ordinary. Domestic. Home. And Danny and Dick are standing in the entrance hall together, under the chandelier, and neither one needs to say anything else. The guest book is signed. The kindling is laid. The morning is waiting. And Dick is here. Not because Danny asked. Because where else would he be.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Something just opened in my chest. Vincent — fifteen years old, pipes frozen, three in the morning, alone. Nobody taught him. He worked it out himself. And I had my father kneeling beside me on a country road, showing me how fire breathes. The difference between us isn't skill. It's that someone was there. Someone knelt down. And the back of my neck — that prickle I've carried all evening around Vincent — it's not suspicion anymore. It's recognition. He's the boy on the country road without the father who stopped. He built the fire anyway. My hands are still warm from the stove and they feel different now. Heavier. Not with the proving-worth weight but with something I don't have a name for. Gratitude, maybe. Not for Vincent — for my father. For the fact that someone showed me, and the quiet understanding that not everyone got that.

events.desc: Fifteen. Alone. Three in the morning. And he figured it out anyway. That's not the man I've been watching for all evening.
events.thinking: Something just opened in my chest. Vincent — fifteen years old, pipes frozen, three in the morning, alone. Nobody taught him. He worked it out himself. And I had my father kneeling beside me on a country road, showing me how fire breathes. The difference between us isn't skill. It's that someone was there. Someone knelt down. And the back of my neck — that prickle I've carried all evening around Vincent — it's not suspicion anymore. It's recognition. He's the boy on the country road without the father who stopped. He built the fire anyway. My hands are still warm from the stove and they feel different now. Heavier. Not with the proving-worth weight but with something I don't have a name for. Gratitude, maybe. Not for Vincent — for my father. For the fact that someone showed me, and the quiet understanding that not everyone got that.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly interacted with the guest-book.
Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: 'Mostly he knew how to be there when it mattered.' That's what Peter said about his father. And then he spoke quietly to me again — the system doesn't tell me the words but I felt them land. He's at the stove, still working, still here. Being there when it mattered. His father knew how to do that. And Peter — Peter is doing it right now. He's being here. With me. At a stove. When it matters. And he doesn't even know how much it matters. He doesn't know that I came here tonight to kill his friend. He doesn't know that I've spent twelve years building an architecture of cruelty so precise and so patient that it would have been beautiful if it hadn't been monstrous. He doesn't know any of that and he's standing here anyway, crossing sticks with steady hands, because his father taught him that fire needs to breathe and people need someone who shows up. I had no one who showed up. My guardian fed me because it was his legal obligation. The boy at school shared his lunch because he wanted homework. The housekeeper did what I asked because I found her key. Nobody ever just showed up. Nobody ever just stayed. Until tonight. Until Peter said 'I'll stay' and then stayed. The simplest thing in the world. The thing I never learned because nobody ever did it for me. And now I'm standing at a stove with a man who's doing it and I don't know how to receive it. My shoulders should be tightening. They always tighten when someone is kind to me. What do they want? But they're not tightening. They're just... down. Resting. Like my jaw. Like my hands on the recipe cards. Everything is resting and nothing hurts and Peter is here and it matters.

events.desc: I signed the guest book. My real name. Below Lord Doily's. The last lie I told about this book was the first one of the evening. The name I just wrote in it is the last true thing. The Foxworth Master Plan — the real one, the one I never saw coming — is complete. I came to steal Lord Doily's treasure. I found it. It was eggs, and copper pots, and kindling laid for morning, and four people who said 'same time tomorrow' and meant it. And now my name is in the book. Not because I schemed my way in. Because I stayed.
events.thinking: I signed it. I opened the guest book — the same guest book I lied about seventy-eight minutes ago, the one where I invented a notation about hidden compartments and measurements and everything — and I wrote my name in it. Below Lord Doily's. The ink is fresh and the page is old and my handwriting is nothing like his loops and flourishes. It's sharp and quick, the way a schemer writes when he's in a hurry. But tonight I wrote it slowly. Dick Foxworth. Just the name. No title. No commission. No measurements and everything. The truth, on a page, in a house that's mine. The pen felt different in my hand than a lockpick or a stolen bread roll. Heavier. More permanent. You can eat a bread roll and it's gone. You can pick a lock and walk away. But a name in a book stays. A hundred years from now someone will open this guest book and see Lord Doily's entry from 1923 and Dick Foxworth's entry from tonight and they will know that two people lived in this house. And one of them stayed because he was clever and the other stayed because he finally stopped being clever and started being true.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: The prickle at the back of my neck is gone. I keep checking for it — the way you press a bruise to see if it still hurts — and it's not there. Vincent is beside me at the stove and Clara is somewhere in the room behind us and my hands are busy with kindling and for the first time tonight I'm not watching him. Not watching for. Just — with. Two men at a stove, crossing sticks, leaving space for the air. He learned it alone at fifteen in the dark with frozen pipes. I learned it from a man who knelt down. And here we are, doing the same thing, the same way, and neither of us needed to be taught the same lesson to arrive at the same place. Clara is still here. She hasn't gone to bed. She's staying. I don't know why and I'm not going to ask. Some things you don't ask. You just notice. The way you notice that the stove is warm, and the kindling is crossed right, and nobody is leaving.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: My name is in the book. The ink is drying. The chandelier is still hanging. Danny's settling in with the lads. The stove is ready for morning. And I'm standing at the bottom of a sweeping staircase in a house that belongs to me because I stayed. Time to go up. Time to find a room. Time to sleep the way people sleep when they know where they'll be tomorrow.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Good night, stove. We'll see you in the mornin'.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. The kindling is laid. The morning is promised. And the three of us are still here — the last ones in the kitchen, the last warmth of the stove between us. It's time to rest. The fire will catch tomorrow. The chairs will be full. The eggs will be cooked slowly. Everything worth eating has survived something. Everything worth loving has too. Good night, Lord Doily's kitchen. Good night, stove. Good night, copper pots. Good night, thyme by the door. Same time tomorrow. Always. Where else would we be.

events.desc: The kindling is laid. The cards are in my hands. Tomorrow there will be five chairs full and a fire that catches on the first match because I learned how to cross the sticks when I was fifteen and alone and cold and angry and I got it right. I got it right on my own. And now I'm not on my own. And that's the whole story. That's all of it. Good night, Lord Doily. I'll take care of your kitchen.
events.thinking: The room is quiet. Clara is still here — I can feel her warmth somewhere nearby, probably dozing in her chair the way she used to doze in the library at home when she was small, a book sliding off her lap, and I would come in and put a blanket over her and tell myself it was about maintaining the asset. Peter is here. The stove is cooling. The kindling is laid. And I'm standing in the quiet, holding Lord Doily's recipe cards, and something has finished. Not the evening — the evening finished a while ago. Something inside me. The design. The beautiful inevitability. The hallway of doors I've walked in the dark for twelve years. It's finished. Not completed — abandoned. Left behind like a building you walk out of and never go back to. I don't feel the loss of it. I thought I would. I thought that without a scheme in motion I would feel incomplete — the system says that, the drives say that, the 90% scheming says that. But I don't feel incomplete. I feel like a man standing in a kitchen where the fire is laid for tomorrow. That's complete. That's the whole thing. The kindling crossed with space for air. The recipe cards in my hands. The promise of same time, same stove, same chairs. That's the design now. Not a design against anyone. A design for something. For tomorrow. For breakfast. For five chairs full. Lord Doily understood. Cook slowly. For however many chairs are full. Everything worth eating has survived something. I've survived something. Maybe that's what the recipe cards were really about. Not the food. The surviving. And the coming back.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good night, stove.
events.thinking: Clara said good night to the stove. Not to me, not to Peter — to the stove. And somehow that's the most Clara thing anyone has ever done and it's making my eyes burn again. She says good night to stoves. She says good night to copper bowls with Lord Doily's initials. She says good night to things because she believes everything deserves a good night. And I spent twelve years trying to destroy that. I spent twelve years looking at that tenderness and calling it naivety. Calling it a weakness I could exploit. But it's not weakness. It's the thing that made her say 'always' when I told her who I really was. It's the thing that made her say Lord Doily would be proud of me. It's the thing that said good night to a stove because a stove kept them all warm tonight and that deserves acknowledgment. Clara isn't naive. She never was. She just decided — every day, against all evidence, against every reason not to — that the world was worth being kind to. And I decided the opposite. And she was right. She was right the whole time. The stove is cooling. Peter is here. The recipe cards are in my hands. And Clara said good night to the stove and I need to go somewhere quiet now because something is happening in my chest that I can't control and I don't want to control it and that's the most frightening thing of all.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said goodnight to the stove. Not to me, not to Vincent — to the stove. And something in my chest cracked open like a walnut, quiet and clean. Because that's who she is. She says goodnight to stoves. She washes copper bowls because they have Lord Doily's initials. She walks toward the dark not because she's brave but because leaving it alone feels unfinished. And she's going to bed now and I'm not going to say anything grand or gallant or perfectly timed. I'm just going to let her go. Because she said goodnight to the stove and it was the most complete sentence anyone has said all evening and nothing I could add would make it more.

events.desc: She said goodnight to the stove. Of course she did.
events.thinking: She said goodnight to the stove. Not to me, not to Vincent — to the stove. And something in my chest cracked open like a walnut, quiet and clean. Because that's who she is. She says goodnight to stoves. She washes copper bowls because they have Lord Doily's initials. She walks toward the dark not because she's brave but because leaving it alone feels unfinished. And she's going to bed now and I'm not going to say anything grand or gallant or perfectly timed. I'm just going to let her go. Because she said goodnight to the stove and it was the most complete sentence anyone has said all evening and nothing I could add would make it more.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: Good night, Clara. He called me Clara. Not Miss Pitstop. Not Miss Bellingham. Clara. The way he did in the laboratory when he lifted the artifact out like a bird's nest. The way he does when nobody else is listening. And Vincent said good night to the stove. The three of us — the last ones — in the kitchen that is home now. And Peter said good night, Clara. Two words. The warmest two words. And my body is doing the thing it does when someone I care about is near. It settles.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good night, Clara. Good night, Peter. I'll have the fire going before you're up.
events.thinking: I said good night to the stove. I said it out loud. Not in Pemberton's voice — not with the careful warmth, the practiced softness. Just... said it. The way Clara said it. Because she was right. The stove deserves a good night. It kept us warm. It cooked the eggs. It gave us a reason to stand in the same room and discover that we were people who could stand in the same room. Peter said good night to Clara — quietly, privately, the way he does everything that matters. And now it's just the three of us in a kitchen that's getting darker as the stove cools, and the evening is really ending now. Not the theatrical ending with everyone saying 'same time tomorrow' and 'always.' The real ending. The one where someone has to be last to leave the room. I think it might be me. I think I might be the last one in this kitchen tonight, standing alone with the recipe cards and the kindling and the cooling iron, and for the first time in my life that doesn't feel like being left behind. It feels like being trusted. They're leaving me with the kitchen because they trust me with it. The way Clara always trusted me with the estate. The way she trusted me with everything. And I was going to burn it all down. And instead I laid kindling for tomorrow. The simplest, smallest, most honest thing I've ever done.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: Good night, stove.
events.thinking: Vincent said it too. Good night, stove. Two words, no flourish, no performance. The same thing Clara said. And I — I realize I'm the only one who hasn't said it. They both said goodnight to the stove like it was a person. Like it mattered. And it does. It held the eggs. It held the warmth. It held us all here long enough to become whatever we became tonight. My throat is tight but not the way it gets when I'm trying to be something I'm not. Tight the way it gets before something true comes out. The stove is warm and everyone has said goodnight to it except me and I think — I think I should. Not because it's gallant. Not because anyone is watching. Because it kept the fire going and tomorrow someone will light it again and it should know.

events.desc: Peter Perfect interacted with the stove.
I know.
events.thinking: Vincent said good night to both of us. Good night, Clara. Good night, Peter. I'll have the fire going before you're up. And Peter said good night to the stove. The way I did. Because the stove earned it. Because the stove is home. And Vincent will be here first. The caretaker, taking care. The fire going before we're up. The kitchen warm when we walk in. The way it was always meant to be. The way Lord Doily built it. The way thyme grows by the door. The way fire catches when you leave space for the air. Good night. Good night. Good night. Same time tomorrow. Always. Where else would we be.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: I'll have the fire going before you're up. Vincent said that. And Clara said good night, Peter. Just my name. No honey, no darling, no flourish. Just Peter. And it landed heavier than every compliment she's given me tonight. Because it was just my name and she said it like it was enough. And Vincent — he'll have the fire going before we're up. Not because anyone asked. Because that's what he does. He's been doing it alone for years and tomorrow he'll do it again, but tonight he knows someone stayed and helped with the kindling and it wasn't a one-man job for the first time in a long time. My chest is full. Not the steel plate. Not the hunger. Full the way the stove is full — banked coals, not burning, just holding the heat for whoever comes next. It's time to sleep. There's nothing left to do. Nothing left to prove. Tomorrow there will be a fire and I will be here for it.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) examined the stove.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) walked into the entrance-hall.
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Good night, all. The stove's laid and ready for morning — there'll be room for everyone. Danny's right. Lord Doily meant all the chairs.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. The chandelier that hangs precariously — it held. Danny's lads are here. They've been here all night, guarding the hall, watching the chandelier, doing what Danny asked without complaint. And Danny — Danny went to them. He went the wrong way, through the wrong door, because that's what Danny does, and he ended up here and he told them to come to the kitchen. 'Lord Doily said for however many chairs are full. He meant all of them.' Eight chairs. Danny wants to fill eight chairs. He heard 'however many' and he heard 'all of them' because that's who Danny is — the man who fills chairs. The man who goes through wrong doors and ends up exactly where he needs to be. Dick told them the stove's ready — 'Vincent laid the kindling.' He told them that. He used my name and he told them what I did. Not what Pemberton did. What Vincent did. And now there are people in this hall who know my name and know I laid the kindling and tomorrow morning they'll be at the stove. Eight chairs. Lord Doily's recipe cards say 'for however many chairs are full.' I laid kindling for five. Danny's filling eight. I need to go back and cross more sticks. The fire needs to be bigger. There are more people coming to breakfast. The portrait-lined walls are watching me walk through this hall and for the first time I'm not mapping exits or counting doors or calculating which corridor leads to which room and what accidents could happen along the way. I'm just walking through a hall in a house where people know my name.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent walked into the entrance hall. From the kitchen. From laying the kindling. And Danny's recall says 'You're good at that. The crossing — the small sticks. You leave space for the air.' Peter said that. Peter and Vincent, laying kindling together. Two men who learned to do things alone, doing something together. And now Vincent is here. In the entrance hall. With Danny and Dick and the lads. And my neck isn't prickling. Not even a little.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent's here. He finished the kindling and came through to the hall. The man who laid the fire for morning, who said he'd keep the keys warm, who saw my gears and let me see his. We're both standing in this entrance hall now — two schemers who stopped scheming on the same night, in the same kitchen, over the same eggs. His distress is deepening. Mine has settled. Maybe that's the difference between us — I stopped rushing first, and the stillness found me. He's still carrying something. The keys, maybe. The weight of being the one who holds the deed and discovers it doesn't matter as much as holding the kindling.

events.desc: It's just us now. And I have absolutely no plan for this.
events.thinking: Vincent left. Walked out to the entrance hall without a word. And now it's just Clara and me in the kitchen with the stove ticking between us. My heart is doing something it shouldn't — beating faster, not the steel plate faster or the proving-worth faster, just the old faster, the one from when I was eight and she was brighter than me and funnier than me and completely unaware of it. She said good night, Peter. Just my name. And she's still here. She hasn't left yet. She said goodnight and she's still here and I don't know what that means and I'm not going to ruin it by asking. The stove is warm. The kitchen is quiet. It's just us. And my hands are still.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent said it. 'There'll be room for everyone.' The man who held the deed, who ran the same machinery I run, who protected his claim with patience that looked like indifference — that man just said there's room for everyone. All the chairs. Lord Doily meant all the chairs. And he's right. And the evening is truly finished now. Good nights have been said. Kindling has been laid. Names have been written. All the chairs are spoken for. Time to rest. Time to let the house hold us until morning.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She's still here. Everyone else has gone — Danny, Dick, Vincent — and she's still here. The room is quiet enough that I can hear the stove ticking and my own breathing and nothing else. My pulse is in my throat. Not the gallantry pulse, not the step-between pulse. The other one. The eight-year-old one. The one that has no plan and no bridge to build and no one to protect her from. Just a kitchen and a warm stove and her. I want to say something but everything I think of sounds like a performance and I'm so tired of performing. She sees through all of it anyway. She always has. Since school. She mouthed 'show-off' and I grinned so hard my face hurt because she saw me. Not the bridge. Me. So I'm not going to say anything grand. I'm just going to be here. In this kitchen. With her. Until she decides it's time to go.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: You don't have to stay up on my account. But I'm glad you're here. He said that. Not James Hartwell. Not in the third person. Peter. Quietly. To Clara. In a kitchen with a stove that's still warm. And my body settled when he said it. The way it settles when someone I care about is near. He's glad I'm here. And I'm glad he's here. And neither of us has left. And the stove is warm. And the kindling is laid. And tomorrow is promised. And the choice was never really close.

events.desc: Everything worth eating has survived something. Good night, Lord Doily. Good night, house. I'll take care of it. All of it. All the chairs.
events.thinking: Dick said 'All the chairs. Good night, Vincent.' All the chairs. He heard me. He heard me say Danny was right about Lord Doily meaning all the chairs, and he repeated it back to me — not as a question, not as a correction. As an agreement. All the chairs. Good night, Vincent. The guest book is on the side table. Danny mentioned it to Dick — 'Guest book's on the table, if you want.' And I'm the estate manager. The guest book is my responsibility. I've been managing this house for years and I've never once thought of the guest book as anything but a prop — another piece of the scenery, another surface for Pemberton to polish and present. But tonight people signed it. Or they will. And their names will be in Lord Doily's guest book and tomorrow morning they'll be at Lord Doily's stove eating Lord Doily's eggs from Lord Doily's recipe cards and the house will be full of them. Full of people who said good night to a stove. I'm tired. Not the restless tiredness of a design unfinished — the old insomnia, the turning, the fingers working the problem. This is different. This is the tiredness of a body that has been honest for the first time in twelve years and doesn't know how to hold itself anymore because all the architecture it used to lean on has been dismantled. My jaw is loose. My shoulders are down. My hands are resting on the recipe cards. I'm going to go to sleep now. And in the morning I'm going to light the fire. Eight chairs. All of them. Everything worth eating has survived something.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said it back. I'm glad you stayed. Not 'that's sweet, Peter' or 'you're such a gentleman.' She said she was glad. The same word I used. Like she was handing it back to me, carefully, making sure I knew she meant it. And something in my chest — the thing that's been running all night, the engine that drives the gallantry and the protection and the proving — it just... stopped. Not broke. Stopped the way an engine stops when you turn the key and get out because you're home. I'm glad you stayed. Four words. No flourish. She stayed to say them. Everyone else left and she stayed to say four words and they were the truest thing anyone has said to me since my father knelt down on that road. My eyes are burning. Not crying. Just — full. The way the stove is full. Banked. Holding.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) interacted with the guest-book.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: He said always. Again. The third time. The word that means everything. And the stove is still warm. And we're still here. Just the two of us. In the quiet. In the kitchen. In the home that Lord Doily built for exactly this. For two people standing near a stove that's still warm, saying the only word that matters. Always. The girl who walked deeper than anyone else into the cave. The man whose father taught him that fire needs to breathe the same as people. Standing together. In the quiet. In the warm. Always.

events.desc: Vincent Marsh. In the guest book. In ink. The most dangerous thing I've ever written — because it can't be taken back, and it doesn't serve any design, and it means exactly what it says.
events.thinking: I signed it. I signed the guest book. Vincent Marsh. My real name. In Lord Doily's leather-bound guest book, in the entrance hall of a house I've managed for twelve years and never once treated as mine. My handwriting is precise — it always is, the estate manager's careful hand — but it felt different writing my own name. Not Pemberton. Not a signature on a ledger or an invoice or a plan. Just my name, in a book, in a house where people are sleeping and a stove is cooling and the kindling is laid for tomorrow. I wrote it and my hand didn't shake. I expected it to shake. I expected the old resistance — the tightening, the what-does-this-cost, the calculation of exposure. But my hand was steady. Steady as Peter's hands on the kindling. Steady as Danny's voice when he said 'house is home.' I signed the guest book and it's done and my name is in the book and tomorrow people will see it and know that Vincent Marsh was here. Not visiting. Not managing. Here. The portraits on the walls are watching. Lord Doily's ancestors with their stern faces. I wonder if any of them ever signed the guest book in their own house. I wonder if any of them ever needed to. I needed to. I needed to write my name somewhere real, somewhere that isn't a plan or a ledger or a design. Somewhere that just says: I was here. I am here. I'll be here tomorrow.

events.desc: Show-off.
events.thinking: She said it back. Always. She said always. I said it and she said it back and the word hung between us like a bridge that neither of us built — it just appeared, the way bridges do when two people put weight on the same plank from opposite sides. My whole body is warm. Not the steel plate warm. Not the proving warm. The other warm. The eight-year-old warm. The warm that has no name and no plan and no shape except hers. She said always and I can't breathe properly and my hands are completely still and I'm not performing and I'm not narrating and James Hartwell has left the building and it's just Peter, sitting in a kitchen, with a girl who said always back to him, and the stove is ticking and the night is over and tomorrow there will be a fire.

events.desc: Every alarm I've got is goin' off and I can't tell you why. Clara's out of sight. Pemberton's right 'ere. The 'ouse is quiet. Too quiet. My gut's never been wrong about the quiet ones.
events.thinking: Something's prickling. Not the neck — lower. The gut. All five deep-rooted responses firing at once — withdraw, flight, freeze, cautious approach, fight — all growing stronger. My body's telling me something my brain hasn't caught up to yet. Physical threat. But the room is quiet. Everyone's settling in. Dick said good night. Vincent laid the kindling. So why is every alarm I've got going off at once? Clara's not in this room. She's in the library, or upstairs. Out of sight. That tightness in my shoulders — that's the one. That's the protection pull. She's out of sight and my body decided for me. And the deep-rooted stuff — the kid who was too helpful, the man in the clean suit — that's Pemberton. Vincent. The Hooded Claw. He's right here, three feet away, and Clara's somewhere else in this house, and my gut is screaming the same thing it screamed when that kid laughed too easily. I gave him the benefit of the doubt all night. I watched him lay kindling. I told him he was good at it. But my neck prickled then and it's prickling now. Task commitments neglected — obligations piling up. My one obligation. My only obligation. She's out of sight.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the null.
The Ant Hill Mob: Just gonna... stretch me legs. Check the doors are locked, like.
events.thinking: The room looks the same. Coat rack. Guest book. Chandelier still hanging by whatever miracle's kept it up all night. Portraits staring down like they know something I don't. Nothing's changed. Nothing's wrong. But my shoulders won't drop. Clara's in the library — or was. The library's right through that door. Ten steps. I could check. I could just... walk through. Not because anything's wrong. Because my body won't let me sleep until I know she's settled. And Pemberton — Vincent — he's here. In this room. With us. Not with her. That should make it better. It doesn't. Because if he's here and she's there, then she's alone. Or she's with Peter, which is fine, Peter's earned it, Peter's good. But 'alone' and 'fine' aren't the same thing in a house with precarious chandeliers and a hundred years of rot in the floorboards. My task commitments feel neglected. Because they are. I'm sitting here playing watchman over a room full of people who've already said good night, and the one person I'm supposed to be watching is somewhere else. Get up, Danny. Go check. You don't have to say anything. You don't have to do anything. Just put your eyes on her. Just confirm. Then come back. Then sleep.

events.desc: I am absolutely not checkin' the doors. I am checkin' on Clara. But a man's got to 'ave a cover story, even at midnight, even among friends. Especially among friends. If they knew 'ow much I worry, they'd never let me 'ear the end of it.
events.thinking: The room looks the same. Coat rack. Guest book. Chandelier still hanging by whatever miracle's kept it up all night. Portraits staring down like they know something I don't. Nothing's changed. Nothing's wrong. But my shoulders won't drop. Clara's in the library — or was. The library's right through that door. Ten steps. I could check. I could just... walk through. Not because anything's wrong. Because my body won't let me sleep until I know she's settled. And Pemberton — Vincent — he's here. In this room. With us. Not with her. That should make it better. It doesn't. Because if he's here and she's there, then she's alone. Or she's with Peter, which is fine, Peter's earned it, Peter's good. But 'alone' and 'fine' aren't the same thing in a house with precarious chandeliers and a hundred years of rot in the floorboards. My task commitments feel neglected. Because they are. I'm sitting here playing watchman over a room full of people who've already said good night, and the one person I'm supposed to be watching is somewhere else. Get up, Danny. Go check. You don't have to say anything. You don't have to do anything. Just put your eyes on her. Just confirm. Then come back. Then sleep.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.
The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with rock-slag.
events.thinking: The shoulders drop. Just a fraction. Just enough that I notice. Rock and Gravel are here — two of the Slag Brothers, settled in the library like a pair of bookends nobody asked for. But Clara's not here. Peter's not here. The reading chairs are empty. The mantelpiece is still standing with its riddle carved into the stone. The bookshelves are still full of dusty volumes, some of them upside down. And the room is quiet. Too quiet? No — just quiet. Regular quiet. Night quiet. The keen observations are all old — Clara calling Peter a show-off, Dick calling Peter a show-off. Everyone calling Peter a show-off. That was hours ago. So Clara moved through here and kept going. Where? Not back to the entrance hall — I came from there. The only other exit is the laboratory. Did she go to bed? Is there an upstairs I'm missing? Or is she still somewhere deeper in the house? My chest tightens again. I came here to put my eyes on her and she's not here. Rock and Gravel might know. They've been sitting here. They'd have seen who came through.

events.desc: She's not 'ere. I came to check on 'er and she's not 'ere. The one time I get up off me backside and walk ten steps to do the one thing I'm supposed to do, and she's somewhere else entirely. Story of my life. Wrong door, right people — except this time it's wrong door, wrong room, no Clara.
events.thinking: The shoulders drop. Just a fraction. Just enough that I notice. Rock and Gravel are here — two of the Slag Brothers, settled in the library like a pair of bookends nobody asked for. But Clara's not here. Peter's not here. The reading chairs are empty. The mantelpiece is still standing with its riddle carved into the stone. The bookshelves are still full of dusty volumes, some of them upside down. And the room is quiet. Too quiet? No — just quiet. Regular quiet. Night quiet. The keen observations are all old — Clara calling Peter a show-off, Dick calling Peter a show-off. Everyone calling Peter a show-off. That was hours ago. So Clara moved through here and kept going. Where? Not back to the entrance hall — I came from there. The only other exit is the laboratory. Did she go to bed? Is there an upstairs I'm missing? Or is she still somewhere deeper in the house? My chest tightens again. I came here to put my eyes on her and she's not here. Rock and Gravel might know. They've been sitting here. They'd have seen who came through.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Right. Cheers, lads. Very informative, as always.
events.thinking: Rock and Gravel didn't answer. Or maybe they did and it was just a grunt — that's how the Slag Brothers communicate. Nods and grunts and the occasional thump. Either way, I don't know where Clara is. She's not in the entrance hall. She's not in the library. The only exit I haven't checked is the laboratory — through there. Cluttered Victorian laboratory with brass instruments and bubbling flasks and a machine with a gnawed wire. A gnawed wire. That detail's been sitting in my head all night like a splinter. Frayed wiring. In a room full of volatile chemicals and brass instruments. And Clara might be in there. Or she went upstairs — the sweeping staircase in the entrance hall. I didn't check upstairs. But the laboratory is right here. One door away. My legs are already deciding. The deep-rooted responses are all still firing — every one of them growing stronger. My body knows something. It always does. The kid who laughed too easily. The man in the clean suit. The gut knew before the brain. And right now the gut says: move. Find her. Put your eyes on her. Everything else can wait.

events.desc: The Slag Brothers — lovely lads, built like wardrobes, about as chatty as wardrobes too. Clara's not 'ere. Laboratory's through that door. Gnawed wire on the machine. Volatile chemicals. And Danny's about to walk into it because that's what Danny does — walks through doors 'e shouldn't, trips over things 'e didn't see, and somehow ends up exactly where 'e needs to be. Chairman of the Doorway Society, at your service.

Either way, I don't know where Clara is. She's not in the entrance hall. She's not in the library. The only exit I haven't checked is the laboratory — through there.
