It always does. The kid who laughed too easily. The man in the clean suit. The gut knew before the brain. And right now the gut says: move. Find her. Put your eyes on her. Everything else can wait.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the laboratory.
The Ant Hill Mob: THE CHANDELIER! Clara — she's under the — Pemberton rigged the — I'VE GOT TO GO!
events.thinking: The keen observations hit me like cold water. Clara was HERE. In this laboratory. Reaching into that machine — the one with the gnawed wire — desperately looking for the artifact. Talking about Peter having it in his pocket, about the chandelier that Dick says Pemberton rigged to fall, about everyone she loves being in danger. She said 'every person I love.' She said 'if that chandelier wants to fall on me, it is goin' to have to be faster than Clara Bellingham on a mission.' And Peter — Peter was here too. Talking to himself the way Peter does. Three steps. No phases. Knee pads. She noticed the knee pads. He stopped trying to impress and started showing up. They've both gone. Back through the library, back to the entrance hall. And I'm here. In the empty laboratory. With Rufus and Sawtooth. Three rooms away from where Clara is right now, walking under a chandelier that — wait. Dick says Pemberton rigged to fall? RIGGED? My neck is on fire. Every deep-rooted alarm — that's what they've been screaming about. Not a vague threat. A specific one. The chandelier. Pemberton. Vincent. The Hooded Claw. He rigged the chandelier to fall. And Clara is walking under it RIGHT NOW. And I'm standing in a laboratory looking at an empty machine. MOVE. NOW.

events.desc: Dick says Pemberton rigged the chandelier to fall. Clara said she's walkin' straight under it. And Danny — Chairman of the Doorway Society, wrong doors, right people, always 'alf a step behind — Danny is THREE ROOMS AWAY. My gut was right. My gut was RIGHT. Every alarm, every prickle, every deep-rooted thing screamin' at me all night — it was the chandelier. It was always the chandelier. And I walked AWAY from it. I walked away from 'er to check on 'er and now she's there and I'm 'ere and if that thing falls — if it falls and I'm not — RUN, DANNY. RUN.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the library.
The Ant Hill Mob: COMIN' THROUGH! MOVE! CLARA!
events.thinking: Running. Through the library. Past Rock and Gravel — two wardrobes, still sitting there. My feet are hitting the floor hard and I can hear my own breathing, ragged, too loud for a library. One more door. One more door between me and the entrance hall. Between me and Clara. Between me and that chandelier. My chest is pounding — not the warm settling, not the bread-in-hand feeling. This is the other one. The twelve-year-old one. The shoes one. The 'you didn't have to do that' one. My ribs already ache like they remember what's coming. Because something IS coming. Pemberton rigged it. Dick said it. Clara's walking under it. And Danny is running through a library like a man who's about to trip over a reading chair and go face-first into a bookshelf — which, knowing my luck, is exactly what's going to happen — but I don't care. I don't care about the chair or the bookshelf or the dust or my dignity. I care about getting to that entrance hall before the chandelier does what Pemberton built it to do. One more door. One more door.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the entrance-hall.
The Ant Hill Mob: Doors are fine. All... all locked up. Checked 'em twice. Very thorough, me.
events.thinking: I'm back. Entrance hall. Chandelier still hanging. Still precariously. Everyone's here — Dick, Vincent, Muttley, Pat, Blast, Meekly. All the lads from before. But no Clara. No Peter. They're not here either. I ran through two rooms screaming her name and she's not in ANY of them. She's not in the entrance hall. She's not in the library. She's not in the laboratory. Where IS she? Kitchen? Upstairs? The recent activity shows my own movements — I left a minute ago saying I was checking the doors, came back. The keen observations are all the same as before — Dick saying good night. Nothing new. Nothing's happened. The chandelier is still hanging. It hasn't fallen. Nobody's screaming. It's... quiet. It's the same quiet it was when I left. My heart is hammering. My hands are shaking. And the room is exactly the same as when I walked out of it sixty seconds ago. Clara said those things in the laboratory — but those keen observations, when were they from? They weren't timestamped as recent. They were just... there. In the room's memory. From earlier. Hours ago, maybe. Before breakfast. Before the guest book. Before all of it. Danny, you absolute muppet. You read old observations and panicked. The chandelier hasn't fallen. Clara is probably asleep somewhere upstairs. And you just ran through three rooms shouting like a lunatic. Breathe. Just... breathe.

events.desc: I just ran through three rooms screamin' about a chandelier that 'asn't moved. Clara's probably upstairs asleep like a normal person. And Danny — Danny just did what Danny always does. Over-prepared, over-committed, and created a complication that 'is determination then resolved. Except the complication was runnin' through a library shoutin' 'COMIN' THROUGH' at two blokes made of granite, and the resolution is standin' 'ere pretendin' I was checkin' doors. Chairman of the Doorway Society. Good intentions. Empty 'ands. Wrong doors. Right people. Every. Single. Time.

Clara is probably asleep somewhere upstairs. And you just ran through three rooms shouting like a lunatic. Breathe. Just... breathe.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the coat-rack.
Some silences are empty. This one is full. Lord Doily knew — the treasure was never the diamond. It was the kitchen, warm, with someone still in it.
events.thinking: There's a heaviness in my eyelids now. Not sleepy exactly — more like the weight of a day that held everything. The stove ticks as it cools, tiny metal sounds like a clock that doesn't keep time, just marks it. Peter said good night but he's still here. I'm still here. Neither of us has moved. That means something, but it's not the kind of something you name out loud. It's the kind you just sit inside of. Like the cave. Like the crystal I carried for a week before I told anyone. Some things are warmer when you hold them quiet.

events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: Danny checked the doors. Twice. 'Very thorough, me.' And now he's looking at the coat rack. Examining it the way you examine a thing you've decided belongs to you — to your house, your home, your people. He's not casing the joint. He's nesting. Danny is nesting. The man who guards and checks and fills chairs — he's making this entrance hall his. The way I made the kitchen mine with kindling. The way Clara made it hers by saying good night to the stove. We're all claiming rooms in a house that belongs to all of us now. Not by inheritance. Not by law. Not by design. By breakfast. By eggs. By recipe cards and crossed sticks and five chairs that became eight. The coat rack is wobbly. I should fix that in the morning. That's a thought I've never had before — not 'I should fix that because Pemberton would' or 'I should fix that because it serves the design.' Just: it's wobbly, and people will hang their coats on it tomorrow, and it should be steady. That's all. The simplest reason in the world to fix a coat rack.

events.desc: A wobbly coat rack. Wobbly coat rack, wobbly chandelier, wobbly Danny. The 'ole 'ouse is wobbly. But it's standin'. It's all still standin'. And tomorrow mornin', Vincent'll light the stove, and someone'll make breakfast, and Clara will come downstairs, and Danny will be right 'ere. Where 'e always is. Where else would 'e be?
events.thinking: A wobbly coat rack. That's what I ran back for. A wobbly coat rack and a room full of people who are all exactly where I left them. My heart rate is coming down. The adrenaline is draining out of my arms and leaving them heavy — that post-panic exhaustion, the crash after the false alarm. Clara's upstairs. She must be. The sweeping staircase is right there. She and Peter probably went up hours ago, sensible people that they are. And Danny ran through the house like his trousers were on fire because he read some old observations and his gut — his magnificent, never-wrong, street-honed gut — couldn't tell the difference between a real threat and a memory of one. The deep-rooted responses are still firing. All five of them. Growing stronger, the game says. But maybe that's not about Pemberton or the chandelier. Maybe that's just what Danny is. Maybe Danny is a man whose threat response never switches off because the streets never let it. The kid in the clean suit. The shoes. The stash. You learn to watch for danger and then you can't stop watching, even when the danger's gone home and the stove's got kindling and everyone's said good night. Sit down, Danny. Just sit down. The coat rack is wobbly. Everything in this house is wobbly. Including you.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: My hands are resting on the table and they're warm from the wood. The stove is ticking slower now — longer gaps between the little sounds. Peter is still here. He said good night but he didn't leave. I said good night but I didn't leave. And that's — that's the whole thing, isn't it. That's what Lord Doily meant. The house is yours because you stayed. We stayed. I can feel the distress in him like a low hum under floorboards, something structural, and I know I can't reach it tonight. Maybe not tomorrow either. But I'll be here tomorrow. And the morning after that. Cook slowly. Rushing eggs is the mark of a man who eats alone.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with hooded-claw.
events.thinking: Vincent spoke to me. Quietly. About the coat rack. 'The coat rack wobbles, Danny. I'll tighten the screws in the morning — there's a toolkit in the pantry. Can't have it falling on the lads when they come in for breakfast.' He noticed I was looking at it. He noticed, and he offered to fix it. In the morning. For the lads. So it won't fall on them at breakfast. And my neck... my neck isn't prickling. It should be. This is the man my gut says is wrong. The Hooded Claw. Too smooth, too eager. But what he just said wasn't smooth. It was... domestic. Screws. Toolkit. Pantry. Morning. That's not the language of a man planning something. That's the language of a man who lives here. Who knows where the toolkit is because he's used it before. Who notices a wobbly coat rack because he's the one who fixes things. Kindling for the stove. Screws for the coat rack. He's maintaining a house. And my gut — my magnificent, street-honed, never-wrong gut — is confused. Because the kid who laughed too easily never offered to fix anything. The man in the clean suit never mentioned a toolkit in the pantry. The people who meant harm never thought about breakfast. Vincent thinks about breakfast. Vincent laid kindling. Vincent is going to tighten screws. And Danny doesn't know what to do with that.

events.desc: And there it is. The thing Danny can't explain. The man my gut says is dangerous just offered to fix a coat rack so it won't 'urt the lads at breakfast. Dangerous men don't think about coat racks. Dangerous men don't think about the lads. And now Danny's standin' 'ere wonderin' if maybe — just maybe — 'is gut's been wrong about one thing all night. Not about watchin'. Never about watchin'. But maybe about who 'e was watchin' for.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Same time tomorrow. She said it. A promise shaped like a clock. And my face is doing the thing it did when she mouthed show-off across the room at the engineering competition. Grinning. In the dark. Where nobody can see it.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: He said it back. Same time tomorrow. That landed in my chest like a stone dropped into still water — not heavy, just certain. The ripples are still moving. This kitchen, this stove, this table — they're ours now. Not because anyone signed a deed but because we kept showing up. Lord Doily's postscript was right. The house belongs to whoever stays. And we're staying. My eyelids are genuinely heavy now. The kind of tired that comes after you stop carrying something you didn't realize you were holding. I think I can sleep. I think he can too. Or if he can't, he knows where I'll be in the morning.

events.desc: You didn't have to do that. I know.
events.thinking: He said it back. Same time tomorrow. That landed in my chest like a stone dropped into still water — not heavy, just certain. The ripples are still moving. This kitchen, this stove, this table — they're ours now. Not because anyone signed a deed but because we kept showing up. Lord Doily's postscript was right. The house belongs to whoever stays. Or if he can't, he knows where I'll be in the morning.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: It's getting worse. I feel it — the old dinner-table tightness, low in my stomach, pressing up. He's deepening. Whatever is in Peter is not settling with good nights and kindling and promises of tomorrow. It's getting worse while I sit here. And my body wants to leap up and fix it — try every key in the house the way I did with Grandmother's box — but I tried. I've tried words and warmth and presence and none of it has shifted anything. The stomach ache says this is mine to fix. But maybe — maybe this is the one locked box where the key isn't in this house. Maybe the key is time. Maybe the key is morning after morning after morning. Fire needs to breathe the same as people. I can't breathe for him. I can only keep the room warm while he remembers how.

events.desc: It's getting worse. I can feel it the way I felt my parents' argument before anyone raised their voice — a wrongness in the air, a tightness that isn't mine but lives in me anyway. And for the first time tonight, I don't know if staying is enough. But I know leaving isn't.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: She said good night again. The second one. Softer than the first, I think — or maybe that's just sleep making everything softer. She's going now. Really going. And I should let her. Good night, Clara. Good night, stove. Good night, Lord Doily's kitchen. Good night, the country road and the stranger and my father's hands. Good night, the bridge that held. Good night, the girl who mouthed show-off. Good night.

events.desc: Cook slowly. I know. I know.
events.thinking: The tightness is back. Stomach. The seven-year-old dinner-table feeling — the wrongness that sits in your body when someone you love is hurting and you can't make them laugh yet. Peter spoke quietly to me. He's still here. He's still deepening. And I said I wasn't going anywhere and he said good night and same time tomorrow and always — and the words are all right but something underneath them isn't. I keep thinking about the neighbor girl. We never shared a word. We drew pictures. Maps. Treasure hunts. Maybe words aren't the key to this box either. Maybe I've been trying the wrong keys. But it's late and my hands are heavy and the stove is nearly cold and I think — I think the bravest thing I can do right now is stop trying to fix him and just be the warm room he's sitting in. That's what the kitchen is. That's what Lord Doily built. Not a puzzle. A room where people stay.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: I'm not goin' anywhere. She said that. And something behind my eyes burns and my throat closes and I can't speak and I don't need to. I know. I know she's not going anywhere. I've known it since she was eight and brighter than me and funnier than me and spent the whole project trying to make me laugh while I was trying to impress her. She was never going anywhere. I was the one who kept thinking I had to earn the right to stay.

events.desc: Penelope Pitstop interacted with the stove.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: I touched the stove. The cast iron is still warm under my palm — not hot, just holding heat the way good iron does, slow to take it and slow to let it go. Like Peter. Like this house. I checked the damper, made sure the embers are banked right for morning. Vincent laid the kindling but someone has to make sure the coals last the night. That's what I can do. Not fix Peter. Not solve his deepening. Just make sure that when he wakes up — when they all come back — the stove is ready. The fire will catch faster if the iron is already warm. That's not nothing. That's the whole thing Lord Doily was trying to say. Keep the stove warm. Keep the room ready. The people will come.
